## 1. Foundations of Computer Networking

This chapter builds the vocabulary and mental models that every later chapter depends on: what a network actually is, how networks are classified by scale and shape, the two fundamentally different ways data can be moved across a shared infrastructure, and the numbers used to measure whether a network is doing its job well. Everything that follows — layering, addressing, routing, congestion control — is an elaboration of the ideas introduced here. Get these foundations right and the rest of networking becomes engineering detail rather than memorisation.

<a id="11-what-is-a-network"></a>
### 1.1 What Is a Network

This subchapter defines the basic objects of study — the machines, the wires between them, the roles they play, and the historical accidents that made today's Internet look the way it does.

#### Definition and Purpose of Networks

**Theory**

Before networks, a computer was an island. Data moved between machines by physically carrying tapes or disks — the "sneakernet". This is slow, error-prone, and impossible to automate. The moment two organisations or two people need to cooperate in real time, physical transport of media stops being viable.

A **computer network** is a collection of autonomous computing devices interconnected by a communication system that allows them to exchange data. Two words in that definition carry weight:

- **Autonomous** — no device controls another's execution. A CPU and its RAM are connected, but RAM is not autonomous, so that is not a network. Two laptops exchanging files are.
- **Exchange data** — the purpose is moving information, not sharing a clock or a power supply.

Why build one? Four enduring motivations:

| Motivation | What it means | Everyday example |
|---|---|---|
| Resource sharing | Expensive or scarce resources serve many users | One office printer, one GPU cluster |
| Communication | People and programs exchange messages | Email, chat, video calls |
| Remote access | Use a machine you are not sitting at | SSH into a server, cloud computing |
| Reliability | Replicate data and paths so failure is survivable | RAID across hosts, multiple ISP links |

A useful analogy is the road system. Individual buildings (computers) are useless in isolation for commerce; roads (links) plus junctions (routers) plus traffic rules (protocols) turn a set of buildings into an economy. Notice that the road network does not care what is in the truck — it only cares about getting the truck from A to B. Networks are the same: they move bits and are deliberately ignorant of their meaning.

**Examples**

```text
Without a network: three isolated islands
  [PC A]        [PC B]        [PC C]
   (files)       (files)       (printer)
   -> to print from A, walk a USB stick to C

With a network: one shared system
  [PC A]---+
           |
  [PC B]---+---[ switch ]---[ printer ]
           |
  [PC C]---+
   -> any host uses any resource, programmatically
```

```bash
# The simplest possible demonstration that a network exists:
# send a probe to another host and see whether it answers.
ping -c 3 example.com
# 64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=1 ttl=56 time=11.3 ms
#        ^ the other machine exists, is reachable, and answered in 11.3 ms
```

**Key takeaways**

- A network is autonomous devices plus a communication system used to exchange data.
- The four classic drivers are resource sharing, communication, remote access, and reliability.
- Networks are content-agnostic: they move bits, not meaning.
- The value of a network grows superlinearly with the number of connected parties, which is why interconnection (the Internet) beat isolated private networks.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. List five networked interactions you personally performed in the last hour, and classify each under one of the four motivations in the table above.
> 2. Argue whether a USB flash drive carried between two buildings counts as a network. Define precisely which part of the definition it satisfies or violates. (Hint: consider latency and bandwidth — a station wagon full of tapes has enormous bandwidth.)
> 3. Interview-style: *Your company has 50 employees who each need occasional access to a very expensive rendering machine. Describe two designs — one networked, one not — and state the dominant cost in each.* (Hint: think about idle time of the expensive resource, not just purchase price.)

#### Hosts, Links, and Nodes

**Theory**

To reason about networks precisely, we abstract them as a **graph**. The vertices are devices; the edges are communication channels.

- A **host** (also *end system*) is a device that originates or ultimately consumes data: a laptop, a phone, a web server, a sensor. Hosts run the applications people care about.
- A **link** is a communication channel connecting two or more devices. It may be a copper cable, a fibre strand, or a slice of radio spectrum. Links are characterised by their capacity (bits per second) and their propagation delay.
- A **node** is any device attached to the network. Every host is a node, but so is every *intermediate* device — switches, routers, access points — whose job is to relay data it did not create and will not consume.

The critical distinction is between end systems and intermediate systems. Hosts sit at the edges and care about *what* is being sent. Intermediate nodes sit in the middle and care only about *where* it must go next. This separation is the reason the Internet scales: a router in Frankfurt forwarding your video stream neither knows nor cares that it is video.

Links come in two connectivity flavours:

- **Point-to-point** — exactly two endpoints share the link (a fibre between two routers). No contention.
- **Broadcast / multi-access** — many devices share one medium (classic Ethernet coax, Wi-Fi). Simultaneous transmissions interfere, so an access-control rule is needed (covered in Chapter 4).

**Examples**

```text
Graph abstraction of a small network

   [Host A]                         [Host D]
       \                               /
        \                             /
     [Switch S1]---[Router R1]---[Switch S2]
        /                             \
       /                               \
   [Host B]                         [Host E]

 Hosts:  A, B, D, E          (create and consume data)
 Nodes:  A, B, D, E, S1, S2, R1   (everything attached)
 Links:  A-S1, B-S1, S1-R1, R1-S2, S2-D, S2-E   (7 edges)
```

```bash
# traceroute reveals the intermediate nodes between you and a host.
traceroute -n example.com
#  1  192.168.1.1      1.2 ms    <- your home router (intermediate node)
#  2  10.20.0.1        9.8 ms    <- ISP access router
#  3  62.115.120.1    11.4 ms    <- ISP backbone router
#  4  93.184.216.34   11.9 ms    <- the destination host (end system)
# Each line is one node; each hop between lines traverses one or more links.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Model a network as a graph: nodes are devices, links are edges.
- Hosts are end systems that produce or consume data; intermediate nodes only relay it.
- The host/intermediate split lets the core stay application-agnostic, which is what makes the Internet scalable.
- Links are either point-to-point (no contention) or broadcast (contention, needs a MAC protocol).

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Draw the graph of your home network, labelling every node as host or intermediate and every link as point-to-point or broadcast.
> 2. Run `traceroute` (or `tracert` on Windows) to three websites in different countries. How many intermediate nodes does each path contain, and where do the paths diverge?
> 3. A network has 6 hosts all connected to a single switch. How many links exist? Now replace the switch with a shared Wi-Fi access point — how many *physical* links exist, and how does contention change?

#### Clients, Servers, and Peers

**Theory**

"Client" and "server" describe **roles in a conversation**, not categories of hardware. The role is defined by who initiates:

- A **client** initiates a request and waits for a response. It typically has an intermittent connection, a dynamic address, and does not need to be reachable from outside.
- A **server** waits passively for incoming requests and responds. It must be always-on and reachable at a stable, well-known address, because clients must be able to find it.

A single machine is routinely both. Your laptop is a client to a web server, and a server to the phone streaming from it. A web server is a server to browsers and a client to its database.

The **peer-to-peer (P2P)** model removes the asymmetry: every participant both requests and serves. Its defining property is *self-scaling* — each new peer adds demand but also adds capacity. In a pure client-server system, every new user adds load with no added capacity, so the server must be scaled by its operator.

| Property | Client-Server | Peer-to-Peer |
|---|---|---|
| Who initiates | Client only | Any peer |
| Capacity as users grow | Fixed (operator must scale) | Grows with the user base |
| Address stability needed | On the server | Ideally on all peers (hard behind NAT) |
| Failure of one node | Server failure kills service | Degrades gracefully |
| Management, billing, control | Centralised and simple | Distributed and hard |
| Typical examples | HTTP, SMTP, SQL databases | BitTorrent, blockchain gossip, WebRTC |

Most real systems are **hybrid**: a central server handles discovery, identity, and coordination, while bulk data flows peer-to-peer. A video-call service uses servers for signalling ("who is in this room?") and direct peer connections for the media itself.

**Examples**

```python
# The role difference expressed in code — same library, opposite posture.

# SERVER: binds a well-known address and waits.
import socket
srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
srv.bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))   # claim a stable, known address:port
srv.listen(5)                  # become passive: wait for others
conn, addr = srv.accept()      # blocks until a client initiates
conn.sendall(b"hello\n")

# CLIENT: knows where the server is and initiates.
import socket
cli = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
cli.connect(("example.com", 8080))  # the active, initiating side
print(cli.recv(1024))
```

```text
Scaling behaviour with N downloaders of one 1 GB file

Client-server:            Peer-to-peer:
  server upload = 100 Mb/s  each peer uploads what it has
  N=10  -> 10 Mb/s each     N=10  -> peers feed each other
  N=100 -> 1 Mb/s each      N=100 -> aggregate capacity also x10
  capacity is CONSTANT      capacity GROWS with N
```

**Key takeaways**

- Client and server are roles per conversation, not machine types; one host can be both simultaneously.
- The client initiates; the server waits at a stable, well-known address.
- P2P self-scales because every new participant contributes capacity as well as demand.
- Hybrid designs dominate in practice: centralised coordination, decentralised data transfer.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. For each of these, name the client and the server: loading a web page, sending an email, a DNS lookup, a printer receiving a job. Identify any case where one machine plays both roles.
> 2. Modify the Python server above to echo back whatever the client sends, then connect to it with `telnet localhost 8080` or `nc localhost 8080`.
> 3. Interview-style: *Why is pure peer-to-peer file distribution rare for commercial video streaming despite its scaling advantage?* (Hint: think about upload bandwidth asymmetry in consumer connections, NAT, and who is accountable for content.)

#### Network Edge vs Network Core

**Theory**

It is useful to split the Internet into two regions with completely different jobs.

The **network edge** is where hosts attach: your devices, plus the **access network** that connects them to their provider — DSL, cable, fibre-to-the-home, Wi-Fi, 4G/5G. The edge is where applications live, where policy about users is enforced, and where bandwidth is usually scarcest and most variable.

The **network core** is the mesh of high-capacity routers and long-haul links that interconnect access networks. The core has one job: forward packets toward their destination as fast as possible. It deliberately holds no per-application state.

This split reflects a deep design decision known as the **end-to-end principle**: put functionality (reliability, encryption, ordering) at the edges in the end systems, and keep the core simple and dumb. A simple core is fast, cheap, and easy to scale; a smart core would need to be upgraded for every new application. That the Internet could accommodate the Web, video streaming, and video calling without core routers being redesigned each time is the payoff of this choice.

Access networks vary along a few axes worth remembering:

| Access type | Typical downstream | Shared or dedicated | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| DSL | 10–100 Mb/s | Dedicated to the exchange | Rate falls with distance |
| Cable (HFC) | 100 Mb/s–1 Gb/s | Shared among neighbours | Peak-hour contention |
| Fibre (FTTH) | 1–10 Gb/s | Often shared (PON) | Lowest latency and jitter |
| 4G/5G cellular | 10 Mb/s–1 Gb/s | Shared per cell | Mobility, variable quality |
| Enterprise Ethernet | 1–100 Gb/s | Dedicated per port | Switched, full-duplex |

**Examples**

```text
                     NETWORK CORE
        (high-capacity routers, no per-app state)

              [R]========[R]========[R]
             //  \\      //         \\
          [R]     [R]==[R]           [R]
           |                          |
      -----+--------------------------+-----
           |         NETWORK EDGE     |
      [ISP access net]          [Data centre]
       /     |     \                  |
  [phone] [laptop] [TV]          [web servers]
```

**Key takeaways**

- The edge holds hosts and access networks; the core holds routers whose only job is forwarding.
- The end-to-end principle puts intelligence at the edge and keeps the core simple, which is why the Internet absorbed new applications without redesign.
- Access networks differ in capacity, in whether the medium is shared, and in latency stability.
- Performance problems are far more often at the edge (the "last mile") than in the core.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Identify your own access network type and find its advertised downstream and upstream rates. Is the medium shared with neighbours?
> 2. Run a speed test at 3 a.m. and at 9 p.m. Explain any difference using the shared/dedicated distinction.
> 3. Interview-style: *Give one concrete function that the end-to-end principle says belongs in the hosts rather than in routers, and one exception where putting it in the network is justified anyway.* (Hint: reliable delivery versus congestion signalling.)

#### Brief History of the Internet

**Theory**

The Internet's design is not the product of a single clean specification; it is the accumulated result of specific problems solved in a specific order. Knowing the sequence explains many otherwise puzzling details.

**1961–1968 — Packet switching is invented.** Leonard Kleinrock analyses queueing for store-and-forward networks; Paul Baran (RAND) and Donald Davies (NPL) independently propose chopping messages into blocks to survive link failure. The telephone network's dedicated-circuit model is rejected as too fragile and too wasteful for bursty computer traffic.

**1969 — ARPANET.** Four nodes (UCLA, SRI, UCSB, Utah) are connected using Interface Message Processors — the first routers. The first message crashes the receiving host after two characters.

**1973–1974 — TCP/IP is designed.** Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn address *internetworking*: joining heterogeneous networks that each have their own technology. Their answer is a universal packet format and a gateway that translates nothing but forwards everything. The original single TCP is later split into TCP (reliability, end systems) and IP (addressing and forwarding, everywhere).

**1983 — Flag day.** ARPANET switches from NCP to TCP/IP on 1 January. This is the birth of the Internet as we know it, and the last time a coordinated protocol switch of that kind was possible.

**1983–1985 — DNS.** Hosts had been found via a manually distributed `HOSTS.TXT` file, which stopped scaling. Paul Mockapetris designs a hierarchical, delegated, cached naming system.

**1986–1995 — NSFNET and commercialisation.** The US National Science Foundation builds a backbone connecting supercomputing centres, and the acceptable-use policy barring commercial traffic is lifted in the early 1990s. NSFNET is decommissioned in 1995; the backbone becomes a market of competing commercial providers.

**1989–1993 — The Web.** Tim Berners-Lee at CERN specifies URLs, HTTP, and HTML. The Mosaic browser (1993) makes it visual, and traffic explodes.

**1998 onward — Scaling pains and repairs.** IPv6 is specified in response to address exhaustion; CIDR and NAT buy time; CDNs move content closer to users; TLS becomes default; QUIC (2021) rebuilds transport on UDP because middleboxes had ossified TCP.

| Year | Event | Why it still matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1969 | ARPANET's first four nodes | Proof that packet switching works |
| 1974 | TCP/IP design published | The "internetworking" idea: one format over many networks |
| 1983 | NCP to TCP/IP cutover | IP becomes the narrow waist |
| 1984 | DNS deployed | Names decouple from addresses |
| 1991 | World Wide Web released | Drives mass adoption |
| 1993 | Mosaic browser | Makes the Web usable by non-specialists |
| 1995 | NSFNET retired | Internet becomes commercial and multi-provider |
| 1998 | IPv6 standardised (RFC 2460) | Response to IPv4 exhaustion |
| 2021 | HTTP/3 and QUIC standardised | Transport innovation routed around ossification |

**Key takeaways**

- Packet switching was chosen over circuit switching for resilience and for efficiency with bursty traffic.
- "Internetworking" means connecting heterogeneous networks with a common packet format — that is the actual invention behind TCP/IP.
- The 1983 flag day was the last coordinated upgrade; ever since, changes must be incrementally deployable, which explains the slowness of IPv6.
- Commercialisation in 1995 turned a single backbone into a competitive market of interconnected providers, making routing policy an economic question.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Build a timeline of ten events from 1960 to today, and for each write one sentence on what present-day design detail it explains.
> 2. Explain why a coordinated "flag day" upgrade to IPv6 is impossible now but was possible for TCP/IP in 1983. Quantify your reasoning with rough host counts.
> 3. Interview-style: *What problem was NAT introduced to solve, and what property of the original Internet architecture did it break?* (Hint: think about address exhaustion and about which host can initiate a connection.)

<a id="12-network-types-and-scale"></a>
### 1.2 Network Types and Scale

Networks are classified first by geographic reach, because scale dictates the technology, the ownership model, and the economics.

#### PAN, LAN, MAN, and WAN

**Theory**

The physics of distance drives everything. A signal over one metre of copper and a signal over 5,000 km of fibre face completely different problems: the long link cannot avoid propagation delay (about 5 microseconds per kilometre in fibre), costs orders of magnitude more per metre, and usually crosses property boundaries it does not own. So networks are built in distinct classes.

- **PAN (Personal Area Network)** — a few metres, around one person. Bluetooth earbuds, a smartwatch, a wireless keyboard. Optimised for very low power, not speed.
- **LAN (Local Area Network)** — a room, floor, or building, typically under a few hundred metres. Ethernet and Wi-Fi. Owned entirely by one organisation, so it can be fast and cheap: high bandwidth, microsecond latency, no leasing fees.
- **MAN (Metropolitan Area Network)** — a city or campus cluster, tens of kilometres. Often provider-operated metro Ethernet or fibre rings connecting an organisation's several sites.
- **WAN (Wide Area Network)** — countries and continents. Almost always built on circuits leased from carriers, because laying your own transoceanic fibre is a different business. High latency is unavoidable, and cost per bit is highest.

The key inversion to remember: **as distance grows, bandwidth gets more expensive and latency becomes irreducible**. A LAN can afford to be wasteful; a WAN cannot. This is why techniques like caching, compression, and chattiness-reduction matter enormously over a WAN and barely at all over a LAN.

| Class | Typical span | Typical technology | Typical rate | Latency | Ownership |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PAN | 1–10 m | Bluetooth, BLE, NFC, Zigbee | 1–50 Mb/s | ms | Personal |
| LAN | 10 m – 1 km | Ethernet, Wi-Fi | 1–100 Gb/s | < 1 ms | Single organisation |
| MAN | 1–50 km | Metro Ethernet, fibre ring, DOCSIS | 1–100 Gb/s | 1–5 ms | Provider or city |
| WAN | 50 km+ | MPLS, leased lines, SD-WAN, submarine fibre | 1 Mb/s – 400 Gb/s | 10–300 ms | Carrier, leased |

Two boundary cases are worth noting. A **SAN** (Storage Area Network) is a LAN-scale network specialised for block storage traffic, and a **WLAN** is simply a LAN whose medium is radio — the "W" changes the medium, not the scale.

**Examples**

```text
Scale ladder, with a representative round-trip time

 PAN   [watch]~[phone]                          RTT ~ 10 ms   (2 m)
 LAN   [laptop]--[switch]--[NAS]                RTT ~ 0.3 ms  (30 m)
 MAN   [office A]==[metro ring]==[office B]     RTT ~ 2 ms    (20 km)
 WAN   [London]=====[submarine fibre]=====[NY]  RTT ~ 70 ms   (5,600 km)

 Note: the PAN has the SHORTEST distance but NOT the lowest RTT.
 Radio protocol overhead, not distance, dominates at small scale.
```

```bash
# Measure the ladder yourself: each should land in a different order of magnitude.
ping -c 4 192.168.1.10        # LAN host      -> ~0.3 ms
ping -c 4 your-isp-gateway    # access/MAN    -> ~5-15 ms
ping -c 4 www.example.com     # WAN           -> ~80-250 ms
```

**Key takeaways**

- Classification is by geographic span, and span determines cost, achievable latency, and ownership model.
- LANs are owned outright, so bandwidth is cheap; WANs are leased, so bandwidth is expensive and latency is bounded by physics.
- Propagation in fibre is roughly 200,000 km/s — about 5 µs per km — and no protocol can beat it.
- Application design that ignores the LAN/WAN distinction (chatty request-response over a WAN) produces the classic "works in dev, crawls in production" failure.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Classify each of these: Bluetooth headphones, an office Wi-Fi network, a university connecting three city campuses, a bank linking London and Singapore.
> 2. Compute the minimum possible round-trip time between London and Sydney (about 17,000 km of fibre) at 200,000 km/s. Compare it with a real `ping` result and explain the gap.
> 3. Interview-style: *An application makes 200 sequential database queries per page load. It is fast in the same data centre and unusable when the database is moved to another continent. Explain why, in numbers.* (Hint: multiply the query count by the RTT.)

#### Enterprise, Campus, and Data Center Networks

**Theory**

Beyond raw distance, networks are also classified by *what they are for*, because purpose determines traffic pattern, and traffic pattern determines topology.

An **enterprise network** is the whole of an organisation's networking: offices, remote workers, branch sites, WAN links, and the security perimeter. Its defining characteristic is heterogeneity and policy — who may reach what matters more than raw throughput.

A **campus network** covers several buildings in one geographic area under one owner (a university, a hospital, a corporate headquarters). Classically built in three tiers:

- **Access layer** — switches that end-user devices plug into. High port count, low cost.
- **Distribution layer** — aggregates access switches, enforces policy, does inter-VLAN routing.
- **Core layer** — high-speed backbone that moves traffic between distribution blocks and does as little as possible.

A **data centre network** connects servers to each other and to the outside. Its traffic profile is radically different from a campus. In a campus, most traffic is **north-south**: from a user, up through the tiers, and out to the Internet. In a data centre, most traffic is **east-west**: server to server, as one user request fans out across microservices, caches, and databases. Three-tier trees handle north-south well but create bottlenecks and unused links for east-west traffic, so data centres moved to **leaf-spine** designs where every leaf connects to every spine, giving equal-cost paths and uniform any-to-any bandwidth.

| Aspect | Campus | Data centre |
|---|---|---|
| Dominant traffic | North-south (user to Internet) | East-west (server to server) |
| Typical topology | Three-tier tree | Leaf-spine (Clos) |
| Endpoints | Laptops, phones, printers | Servers, VMs, containers |
| Endpoint mobility | High (people move) | Low physically, high virtually |
| Key metric | Coverage, policy, cost per port | Bisection bandwidth, latency, oversubscription |
| Typical port speed | 1 Gb/s | 25–400 Gb/s |

**Examples**

```text
CAMPUS: three-tier                DATA CENTRE: leaf-spine
                                  every leaf reaches every spine
        [ Core ]                     [Spine1]   [Spine2]
        /      \                      |  \       /  |
   [Dist A]   [Dist B]                |   \     /   |
    /    \     /    \                 |    \   /    |
[Acc][Acc] [Acc][Acc]              [Leaf1] X X  [Leaf2]
  |    |     |    |                   |           |
users users users users           servers      servers

Tree: one path up, blocked links   Clos: many equal-cost paths,
under spanning tree.               all links carry traffic (ECMP).
```

**Key takeaways**

- Purpose determines traffic direction, and traffic direction determines topology.
- Campus networks are three-tier (access, distribution, core) and optimised for north-south traffic.
- Data centres are east-west dominated and use leaf-spine so any server can reach any other at predictable bandwidth.
- Enterprise networking is mostly about policy and heterogeneity; data centre networking is mostly about uniform bandwidth and low latency.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Draw a three-tier campus for a school with four buildings of 200 users each, and label which layer enforces VLAN policy.
> 2. In a leaf-spine fabric with 4 spines and 16 leaves, how many spine-facing links does each leaf need, and how many total leaf-to-spine links exist?
> 3. Explain why a microservices architecture increases east-west traffic. Estimate the internal request count for one user page load that touches 8 services, each calling 2 others.

#### Internet, Intranet, and Extranet

**Theory**

These three terms are distinguished by **who is allowed in**, not by technology. All three use the same protocols — IP, TCP, HTTP, DNS. The difference is the access boundary.

- The **Internet** (capital I) is the single global network of interconnected autonomous networks, publicly reachable, using the public IP address space and the global DNS root. There is exactly one.
- An **intranet** is a private network using Internet technologies, reachable only by an organisation's own members. Company wikis, HR portals, internal APIs. It typically uses private address space (RFC 1918) and an internal DNS view.
- An **extranet** is an intranet with controlled access extended to specific outside parties — suppliers, partners, key customers. It is the intersection: private, but deliberately porous at named points, usually via VPN, federated identity, or a mutually authenticated API.

Think of it as a building. The Internet is the public street. The intranet is the interior of your offices, badge-controlled. The extranet is the meeting room a courier is escorted into: inside the building, but only that room, and only for named visitors.

| | Internet | Intranet | Extranet |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who can access | Anyone | Employees only | Employees plus named partners |
| Address space | Public IP | Usually private (RFC 1918) | Private, reached via VPN or gateway |
| DNS | Global root | Internal zones, split-horizon | Internal zones exposed selectively |
| Trust model | Zero | Historically high (now questioned) | Explicit, per-partner |
| Example | `example.com` | `wiki.internal` | Supplier ordering portal |

A modern caveat: the assumption that "inside the intranet means trusted" is now considered a design flaw. **Zero trust** networking treats every request as untrusted regardless of where it originates, authenticating and authorising each one. The perimeter still exists, but it is no longer the security model.

**Examples**

```text
                    [ THE INTERNET ]
                           |
                    [ firewall / VPN gateway ]
                     /                    \
            [ INTRANET ]              [ EXTRANET zone ]
      wiki, HR, internal APIs      partner order portal,
      employees only               supplier file exchange
                                   named partners only
```

```bash
# Split-horizon DNS: the same name resolves differently
# depending on which side of the boundary you ask from.
dig +short portal.example.com @8.8.8.8          # public resolver
# 203.0.113.50      <- the extranet gateway, publicly reachable

dig +short portal.example.com @10.0.0.53        # internal resolver
# 10.4.2.17         <- the real internal server, private address
```

**Key takeaways**

- Internet, intranet, and extranet differ by access policy, not by protocol — all three run TCP/IP.
- There is exactly one Internet; there are countless intranets.
- An extranet is a deliberately controlled opening in an intranet for named external parties.
- "Inside equals trusted" is obsolete; zero trust authenticates every request regardless of origin.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. For your own organisation or school, name one service on each of the three: Internet-facing, intranet-only, extranet.
> 2. Explain how split-horizon DNS works and one concrete problem it solves. What breaks if a laptop caches the internal answer and then goes home?
> 3. Interview-style: *An attacker phishes one employee laptop and gains a foothold on the intranet. Explain why a perimeter-only security model fails here and what zero trust would change.* (Hint: consider lateral movement.)

#### Internet Service Providers and Tiers

**Theory**

No single organisation owns the Internet. It is roughly 75,000 independently operated networks that agree to carry each other's traffic. Providers are informally ranked by how much of the Internet they can reach without paying anyone.

- **Tier 1** — can reach the entire Internet purely through **settlement-free peering** with other Tier 1 networks. They buy transit from nobody. There are only a handful (examples: Lumen, Arelion, GTT, NTT, Tata, Telia-class carriers). Membership is defined by this property, not by size alone.
- **Tier 2** — has substantial peering but must buy **transit** from at least one upstream provider to reach the whole Internet. Most large national and regional carriers are Tier 2.
- **Tier 3** — buys transit only; a local access provider selling connectivity to homes and businesses.

Two commercial relationships explain nearly all Internet routing policy:

- **Transit** — a customer pays a provider to carry its traffic to and from *everywhere*. Money flows one way; the provider advertises the customer's routes to the whole Internet.
- **Peering** — two networks exchange traffic between *their own customers only*, usually without payment, because both benefit by avoiding transit fees. Crucially, a peer will not carry your traffic onward to its other peers or providers. That restriction is what keeps the hierarchy from collapsing.

The consequence: a route's selection is often about money, not distance. A path with fewer hops may be rejected because it would cost transit fees, while a longer peering path is free. This is why Internet paths are frequently not the geometrically shortest ones.

**Examples**

```text
The money flows downward; traffic flows both ways.

        [Tier 1 A]<--- settlement-free peering --->[Tier 1 B]
             |                                         |
        $ transit                                 $ transit
             |                                         |
        [Tier 2 C]<--- peering (own customers) --->[Tier 2 D]
             |                                         |
        $ transit                                 $ transit
             |                                         |
        [Tier 3 E]                                [Tier 3 F]
             |                                         |
          homes                                     homes

Rule: C will carry E's traffic to A (E is a paying customer).
      C will NOT carry D's traffic to A (D is a free peer, not a customer).
```

```bash
# Inspect which networks a path crosses and who operates them.
traceroute -A example.com
#  3  10.x.x.x       [AS64500]   <- your Tier 3 ISP
#  5  62.x.x.x       [AS1299]    <- a Tier 1 transit provider
#  8  93.184.216.34  [AS15133]   <- the destination's network
# The [ASnnnn] tags name the independently operated networks crossed.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Tier 1 is defined by needing no transit — reaching everything via settlement-free peering.
- Transit is a paid, full-reachability service; peering is usually free and covers only each party's own customers.
- Peering does not transit: a peer will not carry your traffic to its own upstream.
- Internet routes follow commercial policy at least as much as geography, so paths are often not the shortest ones.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Look up your own ISP's AS number (for example with `whois` or a public BGP looking glass) and find out whether it buys transit.
> 2. Using the diagram above, explain why traffic from E to F might traverse a Tier 1 even though C and D peer directly.
> 3. Interview-style: *Two large networks of similar size refuse to peer, forcing their mutual customers onto slower paths. What is each side's incentive, and what leverage ends such disputes?* (Hint: consider traffic ratios and who feels customer complaints first.)

#### Autonomous Systems and Peering

**Theory**

An **Autonomous System (AS)** is the unit of independent routing policy: a collection of IP prefixes under a single administrative domain that presents one coherent routing policy to the outside world. Each AS gets a globally unique **ASN** (Autonomous System Number), 16-bit originally (0–65535) and now 32-bit, assigned by IANA through the Regional Internet Registries.

Why does this abstraction exist? Because global routing cannot scale to individual routers. If every router had to know the path to every other router, the routing table would be unmanageably large and unstable. Instead the problem is split in two:

- **Intra-AS routing** (interior gateway protocols: OSPF, IS-IS) — inside one AS, where the operator controls everything and can optimise for shortest path or lowest delay.
- **Inter-AS routing** (BGP) — between ASes, where the goal is not the shortest path but the policy-compliant path. BGP exchanges reachability as AS paths, not as internal details, so each AS keeps its interior private.

**Peering** is where ASes physically and logically connect. Two forms:

- **Private peering** — a dedicated link (often a cross-connect in a colocation facility) between exactly two networks. Predictable capacity, used for large traffic volumes.
- **Public peering at an IXP** — an **Internet Exchange Point** operates a shared switching fabric; each member connects once and can then peer with many others over that single port. Far cheaper per peer. Major IXPs (AMS-IX, DE-CIX, LINX) carry multiple terabits per second.

Peering policies are usually published as one of: **open** (will peer with anyone), **selective** (criteria such as traffic ratio, geographic presence, minimum volume), or **restrictive** (effectively closed — typical of Tier 1 networks protecting transit revenue).

**Examples**

```text
Public peering at an IXP: one port, many peers

    AS 64500 ---+
                |
    AS 64501 ---+---[ IXP switching fabric ]---+--- AS 64510
                |                              |
    AS 64502 ---+                              +--- AS 64511

 Without the IXP: each pair needs its own cross-connect (N*(N-1)/2 links).
 With the IXP:    each member needs exactly 1 link (N links).
 For 6 members: 15 links becomes 6 links.
```

```text
How BGP describes a route — an AS path, not a hop list

 Prefix 93.184.216.0/24  reachable via  AS_PATH: 64500 1299 15133
                                                  |     |     |
                                                  |     |     +-- origin AS
                                                  |     +-------- a transit provider
                                                  +-------------- your ISP

 Shorter AS_PATH is usually preferred, but LOCAL_PREF (policy)
 outranks path length in BGP's decision process.
```

**Key takeaways**

- An AS is one administrative domain with one routing policy, identified by a globally unique ASN.
- Routing is split into interior (optimise cost inside your own network) and exterior (obey policy between networks).
- IXPs reduce the cost of interconnection from O(N²) private links to O(N) ports.
- BGP advertises AS-level paths, hiding interior structure and keeping the global routing table AS-granular rather than router-granular.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Find the ASN of three organisations you use daily. Which of them operate their own AS rather than relying on a provider's?
> 2. Calculate the number of cross-connects needed for 40 networks to fully interconnect privately, versus the number of IXP ports for the same result.
> 3. Interview-style: *Why does BGP prefer policy over shortest path, and what would break if it simply always picked the shortest AS path?* (Hint: consider a network being forced to carry free traffic between two of its paying competitors.)

<a id="13-network-topologies"></a>
### 1.3 Network Topologies

A topology is the shape of a network — which nodes connect to which. Shape determines cost, fault tolerance, and how traffic contends, so it is a design decision with permanent consequences.

#### Bus and Ring Topologies

**Theory**

A **bus** topology attaches every node to one shared cable. Any transmission propagates along the whole cable and reaches everyone; each node inspects the destination address and ignores what is not addressed to it. This was original Ethernet (10BASE5, 10BASE2), where a thick coaxial cable ran through the building and machines tapped into it.

The bus is maximally cheap in cable: N nodes need one cable. But it has three fatal properties. First, only one node can transmit at a time — the medium is shared, so total capacity is divided among all users and collisions must be detected and resolved (CSMA/CD). Second, a single break in the cable splits the network in two and typically kills it entirely. Third, troubleshooting is miserable: a fault anywhere affects everyone, with no way to isolate a segment.

A **ring** topology connects each node to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop. Data travels in one direction, node to node, each regenerating the signal as it passes. Access is usually mediated by a **token**: a special frame circulates, and only the holder may transmit. This eliminates collisions entirely and makes worst-case delay deterministic — important for industrial and real-time systems. Token Ring (IEEE 802.5) and FDDI used this.

The ring's weaknesses mirror the bus. A single node or link failure breaks the loop. Latency grows with node count because every hop adds a regeneration delay. **Dual-ring** designs (FDDI) add a second counter-rotating ring so the network can "wrap" around a break — the ancestor of today's resilient metro fibre rings.

| | Bus | Ring |
|---|---|---|
| Cable cost | Lowest | Low (N links) |
| Media access | Contention (CSMA/CD) | Token, collision-free |
| Delay determinism | Poor, probabilistic | Good, bounded |
| Single failure | Kills the network | Kills the ring (unless dual) |
| Scalability | Poor, degrades with load | Degrades with node count |
| Modern use | Obsolete in LANs; survives in CAN bus, I2C | Metro fibre rings, SONET/SDH, industrial |

**Examples**

```text
BUS                                  RING
                                          .--[B]--.
[A]--+--[B]--+--[C]--+--[D]              /         \
     |       |       |                 [A]         [C]
  ===========================           \         /
  one shared coaxial cable               '--[D]--'
                                      token circulates clockwise;
  A transmits -> B, C, D all hear it   only the holder may transmit
  B transmits at the same time
       -> COLLISION, both back off
```

```text
Why a dual ring survives a cut

  Normal:            After a cut between B and C:
   A -> B -> C -> D    A -> B  ][  C -> D
   ^              |    ^    |      ^    |
   '--------------'    '----+------+----'
                       traffic "wraps" onto the
                       counter-rotating secondary ring
```

**Key takeaways**

- A bus shares one medium: cheap in cable, but capacity is divided, collisions occur, and one cable fault kills everything.
- A ring passes data node to node, usually with a token, giving collision-free access and bounded worst-case delay.
- Both have a single point of failure; dual counter-rotating rings fix this by wrapping around a break.
- Neither survives in modern LANs, but ring resilience lives on in metro and carrier fibre.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. In a 10 Mb/s bus with 20 equally active nodes, what is the average throughput per node ignoring collision overhead? How does the real figure compare, and why?
> 2. A token ring has 12 nodes, each adding 1 bit-time of latency, on a 4 Mb/s link. Roughly how long does the token take to circulate once if the ring's total propagation delay is 20 µs?
> 3. Interview-style: *Modern Ethernet is logically descended from a bus but no longer suffers collisions. What changed?* (Hint: think about what a switch does to the collision domain, and about full-duplex.)

#### Star and Extended Star

**Theory**

In a **star**, every node connects by its own dedicated link to a central device. Nothing connects directly to anything else. This is how essentially every modern wired LAN is built: hosts plug into a switch.

The star fixes the bus's problems by construction:

- **Fault isolation** — a cut cable affects exactly one node. The rest of the network does not notice.
- **Dedicated bandwidth** — with a switch (rather than a hub) at the centre, each link is its own collision domain running full-duplex. A 1 Gb/s port gives that host 1 Gb/s in each direction simultaneously, not a share of a common pool.
- **Simple diagnosis** — every link terminates in one place, so link status per port is directly observable.
- **Easy growth** — adding a node is plugging in a cable, with no disruption.

The cost is more cable (N links for N nodes, all radiating from one point) and a **single point of failure at the centre**. If the switch dies, everything attached dies with it. This is mitigated with redundant switches, stacking, or dual-homed hosts.

An **extended star** (hierarchical star, star-of-stars) scales the idea: central devices connect to a higher-level central device. This is exactly the campus three-tier design — access switches form stars for users, and those switches are themselves points in a star centred on a distribution switch. It keeps the star's fault isolation while avoiding the impossible cable runs a single flat star would need across a building.

**Examples**

```text
STAR                              EXTENDED STAR

   [A]   [B]                               [Core switch]
     \   /                                  /         \
      \ /                          [Dist switch]   [Dist switch]
   [switch]                          /      \          /     \
      / \                        [Acc]    [Acc]    [Acc]   [Acc]
     /   \                        /|\      /|\      /|\     /|\
   [C]   [D]                    users    users    users   users

 Each link is private:          Fault isolation at every level;
 A's cable break affects        one access switch failing affects
 only A.                        only its own users.
```

```bash
# On a switch, per-port state makes fault isolation observable.
# (Cisco-style CLI)
show interfaces status
# Port    Name    Status       Vlan   Duplex  Speed
# Gi1/0/1 alice   connected    10     a-full  a-1000
# Gi1/0/2 bob     notconnect   10       auto    auto   <- only bob's cable is down
# Gi1/0/3 carol   connected    20     a-full  a-1000
```

**Key takeaways**

- A star gives every node a dedicated link to a central device — the dominant modern LAN topology.
- Fault isolation, per-port full-duplex bandwidth, and trivial diagnosis are the reasons it won.
- The centre is a single point of failure; redundancy must be added deliberately.
- Extended (hierarchical) stars scale the pattern across buildings while preserving isolation at each level.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Compare total cable length for 24 users in a bus versus a star, assuming users are spread along a 100 m corridor and the switch sits at the midpoint.
> 2. Design an extended star for three floors of 48 users each. How many access switches, how many uplinks, and where would you add redundancy?
> 3. Interview-style: *A star's centre is a single point of failure. Name two concrete mitigations and the trade-off each introduces.* (Hint: consider redundant uplinks and what protocol must then prevent loops.)

#### Mesh and Partial Mesh

**Theory**

In a **full mesh**, every node has a direct link to every other node. It is the maximally redundant topology: any node can reach any other in one hop, and it takes N−1 simultaneous link failures to isolate a node.

The cost is combinatorial. The number of links is:

```text
L = N * (N - 1) / 2
```

and each node needs N−1 interfaces. For 5 nodes that is 10 links; for 50 nodes it is 1,225 links and 49 ports per device. This is why full mesh is essentially never used physically beyond a handful of nodes.

A **partial mesh** connects only the pairs that matter — typically every node has two or three links, chosen so that at least two disjoint paths exist between any pair. This buys most of the resilience for a small fraction of the cost, and is how the Internet core and most WAN backbones are actually built.

The distinction between *physical* and *logical* mesh matters here. VPN overlays and MPLS often create a full logical mesh (every site can reach every site directly at the tunnel level) on top of a sparse physical partial mesh. The classic scaling problem this creates — N² tunnels to configure — is what hub-and-spoke and dynamic multipoint VPN designs exist to solve.

| Nodes (N) | Full mesh links | Ports per node |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 6 | 3 |
| 5 | 10 | 4 |
| 10 | 45 | 9 |
| 20 | 190 | 19 |
| 50 | 1,225 | 49 |

**Examples**

```text
FULL MESH (N=5, 10 links)        PARTIAL MESH (N=5, 6 links)

      [A]-------[B]                   [A]-------[B]
       |\       /|                     |         |
       | \     / |                     |         |
       |  \   /  |                     |         |
       |   [E]   |                    [E]       [C]
       |  /   \  |                      \       /
       | /     \ |                       \     /
      [D]-------[C]                       '-[D]-'
   any pair: 1 hop               A to C: 2 disjoint paths exist
   fails only if isolated        (A-B-C and A-E-D-C)
```

```python
def mesh_links(n: int) -> int:
    """Links required for a full mesh of n nodes."""
    return n * (n - 1) // 2

def redundancy_cost(n: int, partial_degree: int = 3) -> None:
    full = mesh_links(n)
    # Partial mesh: each node holds `partial_degree` links,
    # each link shared by 2 nodes -> divide by 2.
    partial = n * partial_degree // 2
    print(f"N={n}: full={full} links, partial(deg {partial_degree})={partial} links")
    print(f"       saving: {100 * (1 - partial / full):.1f}%")

redundancy_cost(50)
# N=50: full=1225 links, partial(deg 3)=75 links
#        saving: 93.9%
```

**Key takeaways**

- Full mesh gives one-hop reachability and maximum redundancy at a cost of N(N−1)/2 links.
- Link count grows quadratically, so full physical mesh is impractical past a handful of nodes.
- Partial mesh with two or three links per node delivers path redundancy at near-linear cost — the real-world choice for WAN cores.
- A logical full mesh (tunnels, MPLS) over a sparse physical partial mesh is common, but reintroduces the N² problem in configuration.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Compute the link count for a full mesh of 8, 16, and 64 nodes. At what point does the cost become obviously prohibitive?
> 2. Design a partial mesh for 6 branch offices such that any single link failure leaves everything reachable. What is the minimum number of links?
> 3. Interview-style: *A company has 30 sites and wants any-to-any VPN connectivity. Compare full-mesh VPN with hub-and-spoke, in tunnel count and in latency.* (Hint: hub-and-spoke has N−1 tunnels but doubles the path for spoke-to-spoke traffic.)

#### Tree and Hybrid Topologies

**Theory**

A **tree** (hierarchical) topology arranges nodes in parent-child levels with exactly one path between any two nodes. It is the natural shape for aggregation: many cheap low-speed ports at the leaves, fewer expensive high-speed links as you move up.

Its defining property is that it has **no loops**. Exactly one path exists between any pair. This is a virtue for Ethernet, where frames have no TTL and a loop would let broadcast traffic circulate forever, amplifying until the network collapses — a *broadcast storm*. Spanning Tree Protocol exists precisely to reduce any physical Ethernet topology to a logical tree.

But it is also the tree's weakness: no alternative path means no redundancy, and all traffic between subtrees must cross the root, making upper links a bottleneck. Real designs therefore add redundant physical links (making the physical topology a partial mesh) and let STP, or better, link aggregation and routed designs, manage them.

A **hybrid** topology combines forms deliberately — which is what every real network is. A campus is a tree of stars. A data centre is a Clos fabric (a structured partial mesh) whose leaves are stars of servers. A carrier network is a ring of partial meshes. Purity is an exam concept; hybrids are practice.

**Oversubscription** is the key tree metric: the ratio of aggregate downstream capacity to upstream capacity. An access switch with 48 × 1 Gb/s ports and one 10 Gb/s uplink is 48:10, or 4.8:1 oversubscribed. That is fine for office users who are idle most of the time, and disastrous for backup traffic that saturates every port at once.

**Examples**

```text
TREE with oversubscription annotated

                 [Core]
              2 x 40 Gb/s up = 80 Gb/s
                /        \
        [Dist A]          [Dist B]
   4 x 10 Gb/s down        ...
   = 40 Gb/s               |
      /   |   \
 [Acc] [Acc] [Acc]
  48 x 1 Gb/s each = 144 Gb/s of edge ports
  into 40 Gb/s of uplink  ->  3.6 : 1 oversubscribed

HYBRID: a tree of stars, with a redundant ring at the core
   [Core1]===[Core2]
      |  \   /  |        <- redundant core (mesh)
      |   \ /   |
   [Dist]  X  [Dist]     <- dual-homed distribution
      |         |
   [Acc]     [Acc]       <- stars of users
```

**Key takeaways**

- A tree has exactly one path between any two nodes: no loops, natural aggregation, but no redundancy.
- Ethernet needs loop-freedom because frames have no TTL; STP enforces a logical tree over a looped physical topology.
- Oversubscription ratio quantifies the bottleneck at each tier and must match the real traffic profile.
- Every production network is a hybrid; the named topologies are building blocks, not choices.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Calculate the oversubscription ratio for an access switch with 24 × 1 Gb/s ports and two 10 Gb/s uplinks in a LAG. Is that acceptable for office users? For a backup network?
> 2. Explain why an Ethernet loop causes a broadcast storm but an IP routing loop does not cause an equivalent meltdown. Name the specific header field responsible.
> 3. Sketch a hybrid topology for a hospital with an emergency department that cannot tolerate any single failure. Mark every redundant element.

#### Physical vs Logical Topology

**Theory**

The **physical topology** is how the cables actually run. The **logical topology** is how data actually flows. They are frequently different, and confusing them is a classic source of misdiagnosis.

The canonical example is 10BASE-T Ethernet with a hub. Physically it is a star: every machine has its own cable to a central box. Logically it is a bus: the hub repeats every incoming signal out of every other port, so all machines share one collision domain and contend exactly as they would on a coax cable. Replace the hub with a switch and the physical topology is unchanged, but the logical topology becomes a set of independent point-to-point links — collisions vanish.

Other important mismatches:

- **Token Ring** was physically a star (all cables to a central MAU) but logically a ring — the MAU wired the ports into a loop internally.
- **VLANs** create several logical LANs on one physical switch. Two machines in the same rack, in the same switch, on different VLANs cannot reach each other without a router. Physically adjacent, logically distant.
- **Wireless** is physically a star (all clients to an access point) but logically a shared bus — everyone contends for the same radio channel.
- **VPNs and overlays** (VXLAN, GRE, WireGuard) build a logical topology of tunnels across an arbitrary physical Internet path. Two hosts one logical hop apart may be 15 physical hops apart.

| Technology | Physical topology | Logical topology |
|---|---|---|
| 10BASE-T with hub | Star | Bus (one collision domain) |
| 10BASE-T with switch | Star | Point-to-point per port |
| Token Ring with MAU | Star | Ring |
| Wi-Fi | Star (to the AP) | Bus (shared channel) |
| VLANs on one switch | Star | Multiple isolated broadcast domains |
| VXLAN overlay | Whatever the underlay is | Flat L2 across data centres |

The practical rule: **cable faults are physical; reachability faults are logical.** When a link light is on but traffic does not flow, stop looking at cables and start looking at VLANs, routing, and firewall policy.

**Examples**

```text
IDENTICAL physical star, OPPOSITE logical behaviour

  With a HUB (logical bus):        With a SWITCH (logical p2p):
     [A]  [B]                         [A]  [B]
       \  /                             \  /
      [HUB]                          [SWITCH]
       /  \                             /  \
     [C]  [D]                         [C]  [D]

  A sends to B:                    A sends to B:
   -> signal repeated to B,C,D      -> frame forwarded ONLY to B
   -> C and D must ignore it        -> C and D see nothing
   -> C transmitting = collision    -> C and D can transmit
   -> 1 collision domain               simultaneously
   -> 100 Mb/s shared by all        -> 4 collision domains
                                    -> 100 Mb/s per port, full-duplex
```

```bash
# Physically adjacent, logically separated: same switch, different VLANs.
show vlan brief
# VLAN Name      Status  Ports
# 10   staff     active  Gi1/0/1, Gi1/0/2
# 20   guest     active  Gi1/0/3, Gi1/0/4
# Gi1/0/1 and Gi1/0/3 are 2 cm apart in the same chassis,
# but a packet between them must leave the switch and be routed.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Physical topology is cabling; logical topology is data flow. They routinely differ.
- A hub makes a physical star behave as a logical bus; a switch makes it behave as point-to-point links.
- VLANs, wireless, and overlays are all cases where logical distance has nothing to do with physical distance.
- Diagnose accordingly: link lights and cable testers address physical faults; VLAN, routing, and ACL inspection address logical ones.

> 2. Two servers in the same rack cannot ping each other, but both reach the Internet. List three logical causes and the command you would run to check each.
