#### IS-IS Overview

**Theory**

**IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System)** is the other major link-state IGP. Algorithmically it is OSPF's twin — flood link state, build an identical database, run Dijkstra — but it comes from a different lineage, and that lineage gives it properties that made it the preferred protocol among large service providers.

IS-IS was designed by **ISO for the OSI protocol suite**, not for IP. "Intermediate System" is OSI's word for a router. It was later extended to carry IP routing information (**Integrated IS-IS**, RFC 1195), and the key architectural consequence is that **IS-IS does not run over IP**. It runs **directly over layer 2**, as its own protocol with its own frames.

That single fact produces several practical advantages:

**Protocol independence.** Since IS-IS does not depend on IP, carrying IPv6 required only a new **TLV** — no new protocol version. Compare OSPF, where IPv6 support required **OSPFv3**, effectively a separate protocol with a separate process and separate adjacencies. An IS-IS network can be dual-stacked with one protocol instance and one set of adjacencies.

**Immunity to IP-level attacks.** You cannot reach the IS-IS control plane by sending IP packets to a router, because IS-IS does not listen on IP at all. For a service provider backbone, this is a meaningful security property.

**Extensibility via TLVs.** IS-IS encodes everything as **Type-Length-Value** structures, so new capabilities are new TLVs that older routers ignore. This is why IS-IS absorbed **traffic engineering**, **segment routing**, and **multi-topology** extensions smoothly, while OSPF needed opaque LSAs and, in places, new protocol versions.

IS-IS addressing uses **NSAP/NET** rather than IP. A NET looks like `49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00`, decomposing into an **area ID** (`49.0001`), a **system ID** (six bytes, usually derived from an IP address for readability), and an **NSEL** of `00`. Each router has **one** NET, so — unlike OSPF — **a router belongs to exactly one area**.

That difference reshapes the hierarchy:

| | OSPF | IS-IS |
|---|---|---|
| Hierarchy | Area 0 plus other areas | **Level 2** (backbone) and **Level 1** (area) |
| Area boundary | On the **router** (ABRs have interfaces in two areas) | On the **link** between routers |
| Router membership | Can be in multiple areas | **Exactly one area** |
| Levels | — | L1 (intra-area), L2 (inter-area), **L1/L2** (both) |
| Runs over | IP (protocol 89) | **Layer 2 directly** |
| IPv6 | Requires **OSPFv3** | A **new TLV** in the same protocol |
| Units flooded | LSAs (several types) | **LSPs** (one type, TLV-structured) |
| Terminology | Router, network | **IS**, **ES**, **NET**, **PDU** |

Because the boundary is on the *link*, the backbone is not a designated area but a **contiguous chain of L2-capable routers**. Providers find this more flexible than OSPF's rule that every area must touch area 0.

Two smaller differences matter operationally. IS-IS elects a **DIS (Designated Intermediate System)** on broadcast segments, analogous to OSPF's DR, but with two differences: there is **no backup** (the DIS is re-elected quickly if it fails), and the election **is preemptive**. And IS-IS metrics were originally 6 bits (max 63), which the **wide metrics** extension raised to 32 bits — essential for modern networks and standard practice today.

The practical summary: **both are excellent, and the choice is usually organisational**. Enterprises pick OSPF (more familiar, better documented, more vendor-neutral tooling). Large providers pick IS-IS (cleaner IPv6 story, TLV extensibility, layer-2 isolation, and demonstrated scaling to thousands of routers in a single level).

**Examples**

```text
Area boundaries: on the ROUTER (OSPF) vs on the LINK (IS-IS)

  OSPF — the ABR sits IN both areas:

      area 1            area 0
      [R1]---[R2]---[ABR]---[R3]---[R4]
                     ^^^^^ this router has interfaces in BOTH areas

  IS-IS — the boundary is the LINK; each router is in exactly one area:

      area 49.0001          area 49.0002
      [R1]---[R2]==========[R3]---[R4]
        L1     L1/L2   ^     L1/L2   L1
                       |
                the L2 adjacency IS the boundary.
                R2 is in area 0001. R3 is in area 0002. Neither is in both.

  The L2 backbone = the contiguous chain of L2-capable routers,
  not a numbered area that everything must touch.


A NET address, decomposed

     49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00
     \_/ \__/ \________________/ \/
      |    |          |          |
      |    |          |          NSEL (always 00 for a router)
      |    |          system ID (6 bytes; here 192.168.1.1 written
      |    |                     as 1921.6800.1001 for readability)
      |    area ID
      AFI (49 = private/local, like RFC 1918 for OSI)


IPv6 support: one TLV vs a whole new protocol

   OSPF:   OSPFv2 process (IPv4)  +  OSPFv3 process (IPv6)
           two processes, two LSDBs, two sets of adjacencies,
           two configurations that can silently diverge

   IS-IS:  ONE process, ONE set of adjacencies
           TLV 128/130 -> IPv4 reachability
           TLV 236     -> IPv6 reachability
           Dual-stack for the cost of one more TLV.
```

```python
def parse_net(net):
    """Decompose an IS-IS NET address."""
    parts = net.split(".")
    afi, area = parts[0], ".".join(parts[1:-4])
    system_id = ".".join(parts[-4:-1])
    nsel = parts[-1]
    # System IDs are conventionally an IP address padded to 12 hex digits.
    raw = system_id.replace(".", "")
    ip_like = ".".join(str(int(raw[i:i+3])) for i in range(0, 12, 3))
    return {"AFI": afi, "area_id": f"{afi}.{area}", "system_id": system_id,
            "looks_like_ip": ip_like, "NSEL": nsel}

for net in ["49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00", "49.0002.1921.6800.2002.00"]:
    d = parse_net(net)
    print(f"{net}")
    for k, v in d.items():
        print(f"    {k:<14} {v}")
# 49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00
#     AFI            49
#     area_id        49.0001
#     system_id      1921.6800.1001
#     looks_like_ip  192.168.1.1
#     NSEL           00

# Level roles determine what a router floods and what it knows.
LEVELS = {
    "L1":    ("intra-area only", "area topology + a default toward the nearest L1/L2"),
    "L2":    ("backbone only",   "inter-area routes; the L2 chain IS the backbone"),
    "L1/L2": ("both",            "full area topology AND backbone — like an OSPF ABR"),
}
print()
for lvl, (scope, knows) in LEVELS.items():
    print(f"{lvl:<6} {scope:<18} knows: {knows}")
# L1     intra-area only    knows: area topology + a default toward the nearest L1/L2
# L2     backbone only      knows: inter-area routes; the L2 chain IS the backbone
# L1/L2  both               knows: full area topology AND backbone — like an OSPF ABR

# Metric ranges: why wide metrics are mandatory on modern networks.
def max_path_cost(metric_bits, hops):
    return (2 ** metric_bits - 1) * hops

print()
for bits, name in [(6, "narrow (original)"), (32, "wide (RFC 5305)")]:
    per_link = 2 ** bits - 1
    print(f"{name:<20} max per-link metric {per_link:>12,}  "
          f"10-hop path max {max_path_cost(bits, 10):>14,}")
# narrow (original)    max per-link metric           63  10-hop path max            630
# wide (RFC 5305)      max per-link metric 4,294,967,295  10-hop path max 42,949,672,950
#   With only 63 values, a 10 Gb/s and a 100 Gb/s link cannot be distinguished
#   meaningfully — the same problem as OSPF's reference bandwidth.

# The dual-stack configuration burden, compared.
def dual_stack_cost(protocol):
    if protocol == "OSPF":
        return {"processes": 2, "adjacency_sets": 2, "databases": 2,
                "note": "OSPFv2 + OSPFv3 are separate protocols"}
    return {"processes": 1, "adjacency_sets": 1, "databases": 1,
            "note": "one protocol; IPv6 reachability is TLV 236"}

print()
for p in ("OSPF", "IS-IS"):
    c = dual_stack_cost(p)
    print(f"{p:<7} processes={c['processes']} adjacencies={c['adjacency_sets']} "
          f"databases={c['databases']}  ({c['note']})")
# OSPF    processes=2 adjacencies=2 databases=2  (OSPFv2 + OSPFv3 are separate protocols)
# IS-IS   processes=1 adjacencies=1 databases=1  (one protocol; IPv6 reachability is TLV 236)

# DIS vs DR — similar idea, different behaviour.
print()
comparison = [("backup elected?", "OSPF: yes (BDR)", "IS-IS: no backup"),
              ("preemptive?",     "OSPF: NO",        "IS-IS: YES"),
              ("tie-break",       "OSPF: highest router ID", "IS-IS: highest MAC")]
for aspect, ospf, isis in comparison:
    print(f"{aspect:<18}{ospf:<26}{isis}")
# backup elected?   OSPF: yes (BDR)           IS-IS: no backup
# preemptive?       OSPF: NO                  IS-IS: YES
# tie-break         OSPF: highest router ID   IS-IS: highest MAC
```

```bash
# IS-IS runs over layer 2 — there is no IP socket to attack or filter.
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -e isis -c 1
# 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e > 01:80:c2:00:00:14, 802.3, length 1497: OSI, IS-IS,
#                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the AllL1ISs multicast MAC
#   length 1476, L1 LSP, hlen 27, v1, pdu-v1, sys-id 1921.6800.1001.00-00
#   NOTE: no IP header anywhere in this frame.
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 "ip proto 89" -c 1      # OSPF's protocol number
# (nothing — IS-IS does not appear here, because it is not carried in IP)

# Basic configuration:
# router isis CORE
#   net 49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00
#   is-type level-2-only                 <- backbone router
#   metric-style wide                    <- ESSENTIAL on modern networks
#   address-family ipv6 unicast          <- same process, just another TLV
# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
#   ip router isis CORE
#   ipv6 router isis CORE                <- ONE adjacency carries both

$ vtysh -c "show isis neighbor"
# Area CORE:
#   System Id    Interface  L  State   Holdtime SNPA
#   1921.6800.2002 eth0     2  Up      27       2020.2020.2020
#                           ^ level 2 adjacency

$ vtysh -c "show isis database"
# Area CORE:
# IS-IS Level-2 link-state database:
# LSP ID              PduLen SeqNumber  Chksum Holdtime ATT/P/OL
# 1921.6800.1001.00-00   578 0x00000012 0x8a21     1140  0/0/0
#                                                        ^^^ attached/partition/overload

# One protocol, both address families — inspect the TLVs:
$ vtysh -c "show isis database detail" | grep -E "IPv4|IPv6"
#   IPv4 Reachability: 10.1.0.0/24 (Metric: 10)
#   IPv6 Reachability: 2001:db8:1::/64 (Metric: 10)
#   ^ same LSP, same adjacency, both families. No second process.

# The overload bit — gracefully remove a router from transit paths,
# something OSPF emulates only with max-metric:
# router isis CORE
#   set-overload-bit on-startup 300
#   ! do not use me for transit for 5 minutes after boot, until BGP converges
```

**Key takeaways**

- **IS-IS** is link-state like OSPF, but descends from **OSI** and runs **directly over layer 2**, not over IP.
- Running below IP gives **protocol independence**, **immunity to IP-based control-plane attacks**, and clean extensibility.
- Everything is encoded as **TLVs**, so **IPv6 needed only a new TLV** — while OSPF required a separate protocol, **OSPFv3**.
- Dual-stack IS-IS uses **one process, one adjacency set, one database**; dual-stack OSPF needs two of each.
- Addressing uses **NET/NSAP** (`49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00` = AFI + area + system ID + NSEL); **a router belongs to exactly one area**.
- Hierarchy is **Level 1** (intra-area) and **Level 2** (backbone), with **L1/L2** routers bridging; the **area boundary is on the link**, not on the router.
- The **L2 backbone is a contiguous chain** of L2 routers rather than a numbered area everything must touch.
- The **DIS** parallels OSPF's DR but has **no backup** and **is preemptive**.
- **Wide metrics (32-bit)** are mandatory on modern networks; the original 6-bit metric allowed only 63 values.
- Choice is organisational: enterprises favour **OSPF**, large providers favour **IS-IS**.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Decompose the NET `49.0005.1921.6800.3003.00` into AFI, area ID, system ID, and NSEL.
> 2. Explain why adding IPv6 to IS-IS required no new protocol version while OSPF needed OSPFv3.
> 3. Contrast OSPF's area boundary with IS-IS's, and state how many areas a router can belong to in each.
> 4. Interview-style: *Why do large service providers tend to choose IS-IS over OSPF for backbone networks?* (Hint: consider the operational cost of running two parallel protocols for dual-stack, and what it means that the control plane is unreachable by IP.)

#### EIGRP and DUAL

**Theory**

**EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol)** occupies a category of its own. It is distance-vector at heart — routers exchange distances, not topologies — but it eliminates distance-vector's fatal weakness through a genuinely different mechanism. It is therefore usually called an **advanced distance-vector** or **hybrid** protocol. Originally Cisco-proprietary, it was opened as an informational RFC (7868) in 2016.

The core is **DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm)**, and its central insight is a way to identify backup paths that are **provably loop-free without knowing the topology**.

Recall the count-to-infinity problem (6.2): a router cannot tell whether a neighbour's advertised path passes back through itself. DUAL answers this with the **feasibility condition**:

> A neighbour is a **feasible successor** if its **reported distance** (its own cost to the destination) is **strictly less than** my current **feasible distance** (my best known cost to that destination).

The reasoning is elegant. If a neighbour's cost to the destination is already lower than my best cost, then its path **cannot** run through me — because if it did, its cost would have to include the cost of reaching me *plus* my cost onward, which would necessarily be greater than my cost. A strictly lower reported distance is therefore proof of loop-freedom, obtained with no topology knowledge whatsoever.

This yields EIGRP's defining terminology:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Successor** | The current best next hop (installed in the routing table) |
| **Feasible distance (FD)** | My best-known total cost to the destination |
| **Reported distance (RD)** | A neighbour's own cost to the destination, as advertised |
| **Feasible successor (FS)** | A backup whose `RD < FD` — guaranteed loop-free |
| **Topology table** | All known paths, including all feasible successors |

The operational payoff is dramatic. When a successor fails:

- **If a feasible successor exists**, EIGRP switches to it **immediately** — typically in **tens of milliseconds** — with no computation and no queries, because loop-freedom was already proven.
- **If none exists**, the route goes **Active** and EIGRP sends **queries** to its neighbours asking whether they have a path. Convergence now waits for replies.

That second case has a failure mode worth knowing: **Stuck-In-Active (SIA)**. If a query goes unanswered — a slow, overloaded, or unreachable neighbour — the route stays Active until a timer (default 3 minutes) expires, and the neighbour relationship may be torn down. The query scope is therefore what limits EIGRP's scale, and the defences are **summarisation** and **stub routers**, both of which stop queries from propagating.

EIGRP's **composite metric** uses bandwidth and delay by default, scaled by **K-values**. The classic formula:

```text
metric = 256 * ( K1*bandwidth + (K2*bandwidth)/(256-load) + K3*delay ) * ( K5/(reliability+K4) )
```

with defaults `K1=K3=1` and `K2=K4=K5=0`, which simplifies to `256 * (bandwidth + delay)`. Bandwidth here is `10^7 / minimum_bandwidth_kbps` along the path, and delay is the **sum** of interface delays in tens of microseconds. K-values **must match** between neighbours or the adjacency will not form. Including load and reliability (K2, K4, K5) is strongly discouraged, because metrics then change with traffic and the network oscillates.

EIGRP also supports **unequal-cost load balancing** via `variance` (6.1) — the only common IGP that does.

Its remaining drawback is deployment reality: despite RFC 7868, **multi-vendor support is thin**, so EIGRP is effectively a Cisco-environment protocol. In mixed environments, OSPF or IS-IS is the safer choice.

**Examples**

```text
The feasibility condition, and why it proves loop-freedom

   Destination Z. Router A's best cost (FD) = 10.

   Neighbour B reports RD = 6.
     Is 6 < 10?  YES -> B is a FEASIBLE SUCCESSOR.
     WHY IT IS SAFE: if B's path ran through A, B's cost would be
     (B->A cost) + (A's cost to Z) = something + 10 > 10.
     It reported 6. Therefore B's path CANNOT pass through A. Proven.

   Neighbour C reports RD = 12.
     Is 12 < 10?  NO -> C is NOT a feasible successor.
     C's path MIGHT loop back through A. Cannot use it without asking.
     (It might still be a perfectly good path — DUAL is conservative.)


Failover with and without a feasible successor

   WITH FS:
     successor fails at t=0
     t=0.00  DUAL promotes the feasible successor — already proven safe
     t=0.02  done.  ~20 ms, NO queries, NO computation.

   WITHOUT FS:
     successor fails at t=0
     t=0.00  route goes ACTIVE
     t=0.00  QUERY sent to all neighbours: "do you have a path to Z?"
     t=0.05  replies arrive -> recompute -> install
     t=0.05  done.  Slower, and it consumed neighbours' CPU.

     If ANY neighbour does not reply:
     t=180   STUCK-IN-ACTIVE timer fires -> neighbour relationship torn down
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the failure mode that limits EIGRP's scale


Containing queries — the real scaling control

   WITHOUT summarisation:   a query floods outward through the whole network
       [A]--[B]--[C]--[D]--[E]--[F]  ... every router must answer

   WITH summarisation at B:
       [A]--[B]| summary boundary |--[C]--[D]...
                ^ B answers the query itself from its summary.
                  The query STOPS HERE. Scale is preserved.
```

```python
class EIGRPTopologyEntry:
    def __init__(self, dest):
        self.dest = dest
        self.paths = {}        # neighbor -> (reported_distance, link_cost)
        self.fd = float("inf") # feasible distance: my best known total cost
        self.successor = None

    def add_path(self, neighbor, reported_distance, link_cost):
        self.paths[neighbor] = (reported_distance, link_cost)
        total = reported_distance + link_cost
        if total < self.fd:
            self.fd = total
            self.successor = neighbor

    def feasible_successors(self):
        """FEASIBILITY CONDITION: reported distance strictly less than FD."""
        return {nb: (rd, rd + lc) for nb, (rd, lc) in self.paths.items()
                if nb != self.successor and rd < self.fd}

    def successor_fails(self):
        fs = self.feasible_successors()
        if fs:
            best = min(fs.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1][1])
            self.successor, self.fd = best[0], best[1][1]
            return f"INSTANT failover to {best[0]} (total {best[1][1]}) — no queries"
        return "no feasible successor -> route goes ACTIVE, queries sent"

e = EIGRPTopologyEntry("10.9.0.0/16")
e.add_path("B", reported_distance=6,  link_cost=4)    # total 10 -> successor
e.add_path("C", reported_distance=12, link_cost=3)    # total 15
e.add_path("D", reported_distance=8,  link_cost=9)    # total 17

print(f"successor: {e.successor}, feasible distance (FD) = {e.fd}")
print(f"{'neighbor':<10}{'RD':>5}{'total':>8}   feasible successor?")
for nb, (rd, lc) in e.paths.items():
    if nb == e.successor:
        print(f"{nb:<10}{rd:>5}{rd+lc:>8}   (this IS the successor)")
    else:
        ok = "YES — RD < FD, loop-free by proof" if rd < e.fd else \
             f"no  — RD {rd} >= FD {e.fd}, might loop back through me"
        print(f"{nb:<10}{rd:>5}{rd+lc:>8}   {ok}")
# successor: B, feasible distance (FD) = 10
# neighbor     RD   total   feasible successor?
# B             6      10   (this IS the successor)
# C            12      15   no  — RD 12 >= FD 10, might loop back through me
# D             8      17   YES — RD < FD, loop-free by proof
#   NOTE: D's TOTAL cost (17) is worse than C's (15), yet D is usable
#   immediately and C is not. Feasibility is about SAFETY, not cost.

print()
print(e.successor_fails())
# INSTANT failover to D (total 17) — no queries

# The case with no feasible successor.
e2 = EIGRPTopologyEntry("10.8.0.0/16")
e2.add_path("B", reported_distance=5,  link_cost=5)   # total 10, FD = 10
e2.add_path("C", reported_distance=11, link_cost=2)   # RD 11 >= 10: not feasible
print(e2.successor_fails())
# no feasible successor -> route goes ACTIVE, queries sent

# The composite metric.
def eigrp_metric(min_bandwidth_kbps, total_delay_tens_us, K1=1, K3=1):
    bw = (10 ** 7) // min_bandwidth_kbps       # scaled minimum bandwidth
    return 256 * (K1 * bw + K3 * total_delay_tens_us)

print()
print(f"{'link':<22}{'min bw (kbps)':>14}{'delay':>8}{'metric':>12}")
for name, bw, delay in [("GigabitEthernet", 1_000_000, 10),
                        ("FastEthernet",      100_000, 100),
                        ("T1 serial",           1_544, 2000),
                        ("64k serial",             64, 2000)]:
    print(f"{name:<22}{bw:>14,}{delay:>8}{eigrp_metric(bw, delay):>12,}")
# link                   min bw (kbps)   delay      metric
# GigabitEthernet            1,000,000      10       5,120
# FastEthernet                 100,000     100      51,200
# T1 serial                      1,544    2000   2,169,856
# 64k serial                        64    2000  40,512,000
#   Unlike RIP's hop count, the metric reflects real link capacity.

# Why K-values beyond the defaults are discouraged.
print()
for use_load in (False, True):
    label = "K2 (load) enabled" if use_load else "defaults (K1=K3=1)"
    if use_load:
        note = "metric changes as traffic changes -> routes flap -> OSCILLATION"
    else:
        note = "metric is stable: bandwidth and delay do not vary with load"
    print(f"{label:<22} {note}")
# defaults (K1=K3=1)     metric is stable: bandwidth and delay do not vary with load
# K2 (load) enabled      metric changes as traffic changes -> routes flap -> OSCILLATION
```

```bash
# The topology table — this is where feasible successors live.
$ show ip eigrp topology
# P 10.9.0.0/16, 1 successors, FD is 2560
#   ^ Passive = stable. "A" here would mean ACTIVE = querying.
#         via 10.0.0.2 (2560/1280), GigabitEthernet0/1
#                       ^^^^ ^^^^ (my total / neighbour's reported distance)
#                                 RD 1280 < FD 2560 -> feasible
#         via 10.0.0.6 (3072/1536), GigabitEthernet0/2
#                                   RD 1536 < FD 2560 -> FEASIBLE SUCCESSOR
#         via 10.0.0.9 (5120/3584), GigabitEthernet0/3
#                                   RD 3584 >= FD 2560 -> NOT feasible

# Only successors appear in the routing table; feasible successors wait:
$ show ip route eigrp | grep 10.9
# D    10.9.0.0/16 [90/2560] via 10.0.0.2, GigabitEthernet0/1
#      ^ AD 90              ^ the successor only

# A route that is stuck active — the failure mode to recognise:
$ show ip eigrp topology active
# A 10.8.0.0/16, 0 successors, FD is Inf, Q
#   ^ ACTIVE, querying    1 replies, active 00:02:41, query-origin: Local origin
#         Remaining replies:
#           via 10.0.0.9, r, GigabitEthernet0/3
#                         ^ 'r' = reply still outstanding. If this persists,
#                           SIA fires at 3 minutes and the adjacency drops.

# The two defences that bound query scope:
# router eigrp 1
#   eigrp stub connected summary     <- stub routers are never queried
# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
#   ip summary-address eigrp 1 10.1.0.0 255.255.0.0
#                              ^^^^^^^^ a query for 10.1.x.x STOPS here

# K-values must match, or no adjacency forms:
$ show ip protocols | grep -i "K1"
#   EIGRP metric weight K1=1, K2=0, K3=1, K4=0, K5=0
#                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ identical on both ends,
#                                                   or the neighbour never comes up

# Unequal-cost load balancing — unique among common IGPs:
# router eigrp 1
#   variance 2          <- also use paths up to 2x the best metric,
#                          proportionally to their cost
$ show ip route 10.9.0.0
#   Routing Descriptor Blocks:
#   * 10.0.0.2, from 10.0.0.2       traffic share count 3
#     10.0.0.6, from 10.0.0.6       traffic share count 1
#                                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ 3:1 split by metric
```

**Key takeaways**

- **EIGRP** is **advanced distance-vector**: it exchanges distances, not topology, but avoids count-to-infinity through **DUAL**.
- The **feasibility condition** — a neighbour's **reported distance < my feasible distance** — **proves** its path cannot loop back through me, with no topology knowledge.
- Terms: **successor** (installed best path), **feasible distance (FD)**, **reported distance (RD)**, **feasible successor (FS)**, **topology table**.
- With a **feasible successor**, failover is **immediate** (tens of milliseconds) — no queries, no computation.
- Without one, the route goes **Active** and EIGRP **queries** neighbours; an unanswered query leads to **Stuck-In-Active** and a torn-down adjacency.
- **Query scope limits EIGRP's scale**; **summarisation** and **stub routers** are the defences that stop query propagation.
- A feasible successor may have a **worse total cost** than a non-feasible path — feasibility is about **provable safety**, not optimality.
- The **composite metric** uses bandwidth and delay by default (`K1=K3=1`); **K-values must match** between neighbours, and enabling load/reliability causes **oscillation**.
- EIGRP is the only common IGP offering **unequal-cost load balancing** (`variance`).
- Despite **RFC 7868**, multi-vendor support is limited, so it is effectively a Cisco-environment protocol.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. A router's FD to a prefix is 25. Neighbours report RD values of 12, 25, and 30. Identify the feasible successors and explain each verdict.
> 2. Explain, in terms of costs, why `RD < FD` guarantees a neighbour's path does not pass back through the local router.
> 3. Describe what happens when a successor fails with no feasible successor available, and name the failure mode if a neighbour never replies.
> 4. Interview-style: *EIGRP is distance-vector, yet it converges faster than OSPF in many topologies. How?* (Hint: OSPF must recompute after a failure — ask what EIGRP has already done and verified before the failure occurs.)

#### Route Redistribution and Summarization

**Theory**

Real networks rarely run a single routing protocol. Mergers, acquisitions, legacy equipment, partner connections, and migrations all produce boundaries where one protocol must hand routes to another. **Redistribution** is that handoff — and it is the single most common source of serious routing incidents, because it removes the protections each protocol builds for itself.

The fundamental problem: **metrics are not comparable across protocols.** RIP has hop counts (1–15), OSPF has bandwidth-derived costs, EIGRP has a composite in the millions, and BGP has path attributes rather than a metric at all. When redistributing, the router **must invent** a metric for the receiving protocol, because no meaningful translation exists. That invented value is called the **seed metric**, and forgetting to set it is a classic failure — some protocols default to **infinity**, so the routes are advertised as unreachable and silently discarded.

| Into | Default seed metric | Result if unset |
|---|---|---|
| RIP | **Infinity** | Routes are not advertised at all |
| OSPF | 20 (E2) | Works, but every route has the same cost |
| EIGRP | **Infinity** | Routes are not advertised at all |
| BGP | Uses IGP metric as MED | Usually acceptable |

The deeper danger is **routing loops from mutual redistribution**. With two or more boundary routers between the same pair of protocols, a route can leave protocol A, enter protocol B, travel around, and re-enter protocol A — now appearing to originate from the wrong direction. Since the receiving protocol's own loop prevention (split horizon, SPF, AS-PATH) operates only *within* that protocol, it cannot detect a loop that passed through a foreign protocol. Administrative distance interacts badly here: a re-injected route may have a *better* AD than the original, so the router prefers the looped path.

The defences, in order of reliability:

**Route tagging** is the primary control. Mark routes as they are redistributed, and filter on that tag at every other boundary. A route tagged "came from OSPF" is never allowed back into OSPF. This works regardless of topology and is the mechanism to reach for first.

**Filtering** with prefix lists or distribute lists explicitly controls which routes cross.

**One-way redistribution** wherever possible: redistribute into the core and use a default route outward. If routes only flow one way, no loop can form.

**AD manipulation** can help but is fragile and should not be the primary defence.

**Summarisation** is the complementary technique and is mostly beneficial. Advertising `10.1.0.0/16` instead of 256 individual /24s:

- **Shrinks routing tables** — less memory, faster lookups.
- **Hides instability**, which is the most valuable property: a flapping /24 inside the summary causes **no** advertisement outside it, so remote routers never recompute.
- **Bounds query scope** in EIGRP and LSA flooding in OSPF.

Its costs are real but usually acceptable: **suboptimal routing** is possible, since remote routers cannot distinguish members of the summary and may send traffic to the wrong exit when the block is split across locations. And a summary is advertised as long as **at least one** component exists, so traffic for missing components is attracted and dropped — the standard mitigation is a **discard route** (a route to Null0 for the summary) so those packets are dropped locally rather than looping.

The practical rule: **summarise wherever addressing is hierarchical, and redistribute as little as possible.** Where you must redistribute, tag and filter at every boundary without exception.

**Examples**

```text
Mutual redistribution — how the loop forms

      OSPF domain          R1, R2 both redistribute      RIP domain
   +---------------+                                +---------------+
   |  10.1.0.0/16  |------[R1]--------------------- |               |
   |   (origin)    |                                |               |
   |               |------[R2]--------------------- |               |
   +---------------+                                +---------------+

   1. 10.1.0.0/16 originates in OSPF.
   2. R1 redistributes it into RIP.        RIP: "10.1.0.0/16, 1 hop"
   3. It propagates through RIP to R2.
   4. R2 redistributes it BACK into OSPF   as an EXTERNAL route.
   5. Routers near R2 now see 10.1.0.0/16 as external via R2,
      possibly preferring it over the real internal route.
   6. Traffic goes to R2 -> into RIP -> to R1 -> back into OSPF -> LOOP.

   OSPF's SPF cannot detect this: the route left OSPF's world entirely
   and came back wearing a disguise.

   THE FIX — tag at every boundary:
     R1: redistribute ospf into rip, set tag 100
     R2: deny any route with tag 100 from entering ospf
     (and symmetrically for the other direction)


Summarisation hides instability — the property that matters most

   WITHOUT summary:  10.1.5.0/24 flaps
                     -> LSA/update floods the entire network
                     -> every router recomputes, repeatedly

   WITH summary at the ABR (10.1.0.0/16):
                     10.1.5.0/24 flaps inside the area
                     -> the SUMMARY does not change (other /24s still exist)
                     -> NOTHING is advertised outward
                     -> zero remote recomputation

   The summary is a firewall against churn.


The summary black hole, and the discard route

   ABR advertises 10.1.0.0/16 (covering .0 to .255)
   But only 10.1.1.0/24 and 10.1.2.0/24 actually exist.

   Packet for 10.1.9.9 -> attracted by the summary -> arrives at the ABR
                       -> ABR has no specific route -> may follow its OWN
                          default route back out -> LOOP

   FIX: ip route 10.1.0.0 255.255.0.0 Null0
        A discard route: the packet is dropped locally, at the ABR.
```

```python
SEED_METRIC_DEFAULTS = {
    "rip":   (None, "INFINITY — routes silently NOT advertised"),
    "ospf":  (20,   "E2 type, cost 20 — all routes get the SAME cost"),
    "eigrp": (None, "INFINITY — routes silently NOT advertised"),
    "bgp":   ("igp","IGP metric used as MED — usually fine"),
}
print(f"{'redistribute into':<20}{'default seed':<10}consequence")
for proto, (seed, note) in SEED_METRIC_DEFAULTS.items():
    print(f"{proto:<20}{str(seed):<10}{note}")
# redistribute into   default seed  consequence
# rip                 None      INFINITY — routes silently NOT advertised
# ospf                20        E2 type, cost 20 — all routes get the SAME cost
# eigrp               None      INFINITY — routes silently NOT advertised
# bgp                 igp       IGP metric used as MED — usually fine

# Redistribution with tag-based loop prevention.
class Boundary:
    def __init__(self, name, from_proto, into_proto, tag, deny_tags=()):
        self.name, self.from_proto, self.into_proto = name, from_proto, into_proto
        self.tag, self.deny_tags = tag, set(deny_tags)

    def redistribute(self, route):
        if route.get("tag") in self.deny_tags:
            return None, (f"{self.name}: BLOCKED — tag {route['tag']} came from "
                          f"{self.into_proto}; refusing to send it back")
        if route["proto"] != self.from_proto:
            return None, f"{self.name}: not a {self.from_proto} route, ignored"
        out = dict(route, proto=self.into_proto, tag=self.tag, external=True)
        return out, f"{self.name}: redistributed with tag {self.tag}"

# Two boundary routers, each tagging outbound and denying the other's tag.
R1 = Boundary("R1", "ospf", "rip",  tag=100, deny_tags={200})
R2 = Boundary("R2", "rip",  "ospf", tag=200, deny_tags={100})

route = {"prefix": "10.1.0.0/16", "proto": "ospf", "tag": None}
print(f"\norigin: {route['prefix']} in OSPF")

in_rip, msg = R1.redistribute(route)
print(f"  {msg}")
back_to_ospf, msg = R2.redistribute(in_rip)
print(f"  {msg}")
print(f"  result: {'LOOP PREVENTED' if back_to_ospf is None else 'LOOP CREATED'}")
# origin: 10.1.0.0/16 in OSPF
#   R1: redistributed with tag 100
#   R2: BLOCKED — tag 100 came from ospf; refusing to send it back
#   result: LOOP PREVENTED

# Without tags, the same sequence creates the loop.
R1_untagged = Boundary("R1", "ospf", "rip",  tag=None)
R2_untagged = Boundary("R2", "rip",  "ospf", tag=None)
in_rip, _ = R1_untagged.redistribute(route)
back, _ = R2_untagged.redistribute(in_rip)
print(f"\nwithout tags: route returns to OSPF as external = "
      f"{back is not None} -> LOOP RISK")
# without tags: route returns to OSPF as external = True -> LOOP RISK

# Summarisation: table reduction and, more importantly, churn suppression.
import ipaddress

def summarise(prefixes):
    return list(ipaddress.collapse_addresses(
        [ipaddress.ip_network(p) for p in prefixes]))

subnets = [f"10.1.{i}.0/24" for i in range(256)]
summary = summarise(subnets)
print(f"\n{len(subnets)} prefixes -> {len(summary)}: {[str(s) for s in summary]}")
print(f"table reduction: {100*(1-len(summary)/len(subnets)):.1f}%")
# 256 prefixes -> 1: ['10.1.0.0/16']
# table reduction: 99.6%

def churn(flaps_per_hour, summarised):
    """Advertisements leaving the area per hour."""
    return 0 if summarised else flaps_per_hour

print()
for summarised in (False, True):
    adverts = churn(120, summarised)
    label = "summarised" if summarised else "not summarised"
    print(f"{label:<16} one /24 flapping 120x/hour -> {adverts:>3} external "
          f"advertisements/hour")
# not summarised   one /24 flapping 120x/hour -> 120 external advertisements/hour
# summarised       one /24 flapping 120x/hour ->   0 external advertisements/hour
#   THIS is summarisation's most valuable property, not the memory saving.

# The black hole a summary can create.
def summary_blackhole(summary, existing, dst):
    s = ipaddress.ip_network(summary)
    d = ipaddress.ip_address(dst)
    if d not in s:
        return "not covered by the summary — routed normally elsewhere"
    if any(d in ipaddress.ip_network(e) for e in existing):
        return "delivered to a real subnet"
    return ("ATTRACTED by the summary but no specific route exists -> "
            "needs a Null0 discard route, or it may loop")

print()
for dst in ["10.1.1.5", "10.1.9.9", "10.2.0.1"]:
    print(f"{dst:<12} {summary_blackhole('10.1.0.0/16', ['10.1.1.0/24','10.1.2.0/24'], dst)}")
# 10.1.1.5     delivered to a real subnet
# 10.1.9.9     ATTRACTED by the summary but no specific route exists -> needs a Null0 discard route, or it may loop
# 10.2.0.1     not covered by the summary — routed normally elsewhere
```

```bash
# Redistribution done properly: seed metric, tag, and filter — all three.
# route-map OSPF_TO_RIP permit 10
#   match ip address prefix-list ALLOWED
#   set metric 5                      <- SEED METRIC: without it, infinity
#   set tag 100                       <- mark the origin
# route-map RIP_TO_OSPF deny 10
#   match tag 100                     <- never let our own routes back in
# route-map RIP_TO_OSPF permit 20
#   set metric 50
#   set metric-type type-1
#   set tag 200
#
# router rip
#   redistribute ospf 1 route-map OSPF_TO_RIP
# router ospf 1
#   redistribute rip route-map RIP_TO_OSPF subnets
#                                            ^^^^^^^ without 'subnets', OSPF
#                                            redistributes ONLY classful routes

# Finding redistributed routes and their tags:
$ vtysh -c "show ip route ospf" | head -3
# O E2 10.5.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.0.2, eth0
#   ^^^^ E2 = external type 2: cost does NOT increase with distance
#        E1 would add internal cost to the external cost
$ show ip ospf database external | grep -A4 10.5.0.0
#   Link State ID: 10.5.0.0 (External Network Number)
#   Metric Type: 2 (Larger than any link state path)
#   Metric: 20
#   External Route Tag: 100          <- the tag, visible and filterable

# Summarisation, per protocol:
# OSPF at an ABR:       area 1 range 10.1.0.0 255.255.0.0
# OSPF at an ASBR:      summary-address 10.5.0.0 255.255.0.0
# EIGRP per interface:  ip summary-address eigrp 1 10.1.0.0 255.255.0.0
# BGP:                  aggregate-address 10.1.0.0 255.255.0.0 summary-only

# The discard route is created automatically by some platforms — verify it:
$ show ip route 10.1.0.0 255.255.0.0
# O    10.1.0.0/16 is a summary, 00:12:41, Null0
#                                          ^^^^^ discard route: packets for
#                                          non-existent components die HERE
#                                          instead of following a default route

# Detecting a redistribution loop — look for routes that should be internal
# appearing as external:
$ vtysh -c "show ip route 10.1.0.0/16"
# Routing entry for 10.1.0.0/16
#   Known via "ospf", distance 110, metric 20, type extern 2
#                                              ^^^^^^^^^^^^ EXTERNAL, but this
#   prefix ORIGINATES inside our OSPF domain. It went out and came back.
#   -> mutual redistribution without tag filtering. Fix the boundaries.
```

**Key takeaways**

- **Redistribution** moves routes between protocols and is the most common source of serious routing incidents.
- **Metrics are not comparable across protocols**, so a **seed metric** must be invented; **RIP and EIGRP default to infinity**, silently dropping the routes.
- **Mutual redistribution** at two or more boundaries can loop: a route leaves protocol A, traverses B, and re-enters A disguised as external, where A's own loop prevention cannot see it.
- **Route tagging** is the primary defence — mark on the way out, filter that tag on the way back in, at **every** boundary.
- Supporting defences: **prefix filtering**, **one-way redistribution with a default route**, and (fragile) AD manipulation.
- OSPF requires the **`subnets`** keyword, or only classful routes are redistributed.
- **Summarisation** shrinks tables, but its most valuable property is **hiding instability** — a flapping component inside a summary causes **zero** external advertisements.
- Summarisation costs: possible **suboptimal routing**, and a **black hole** for non-existent components — mitigated with a **Null0 discard route**.
- Practical rule: **summarise wherever addressing is hierarchical; redistribute as little as possible, and always with tags and filters.**

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Explain why redistributing into RIP or EIGRP without a seed metric results in no routes being advertised.
> 2. Trace how a route loops through mutual redistribution between OSPF and RIP at two boundary routers, and show where tags break the cycle.
> 3. Summarise `172.20.0.0/24` through `172.20.15.0/24` into one prefix and state the number of external advertisements caused by one component flapping.
> 4. Interview-style: *After a merger you must connect an OSPF network to an EIGRP network at two points. What is your primary loop-prevention mechanism and why not administrative distance?* (Hint: AD is a local preference value — ask whether it travels with the route to the *other* boundary router.)

<a id="64-exterior-gateway-routing"></a>
### 6.4 Exterior Gateway Routing

This subchapter covers BGP, the protocol that joins tens of thousands of independently operated networks into one internet — where the objective is not the shortest path but the path that policy permits.

#### Autonomous Systems and AS Numbers

**Theory**

The IGPs covered so far all assume a single administration: one organisation, one set of goals, and routers that trust each other completely. That assumption fails at the scale of the internet, where competing companies must exchange traffic without trusting each other and without revealing their internal topology.

An **Autonomous System (AS)** is the unit of that division: a network, or set of networks, under **one administrative authority** with a **single, coherent routing policy**. "Autonomous" is the operative word — an AS decides for itself which routes to accept, which to advertise, and to whom, and no external party can override those decisions.

This produces a two-level routing architecture that mirrors the trust structure:

| | Interior (IGP) | Exterior (EGP) |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Within one AS | Between autonomous systems |
| Goal | **Find the shortest path** | **Enforce policy** |
| Trust | Full | None |
| Topology visible | Yes | **Deliberately hidden** |
| Protocols | OSPF, IS-IS, EIGRP, RIP | **BGP** |
| Scale | Thousands of routers | ~75,000 ASes, ~1M prefixes |

The shift from "shortest" to "policy" is the conceptual heart of this subchapter. Inside an AS, a shorter path is simply better. Between ASes, the best path is frequently *not* the shortest — because a longer path may be cheaper, contractually required, or the only one permitted. BGP is built to express those constraints, which is why it carries **attributes** rather than a metric.

**AS numbers (ASNs)** identify each AS. Originally 16-bit (1–65535), the space was exhausted, and **32-bit ASNs (RFC 6793)** extended it to about 4.3 billion. Private ranges exist for internal use, analogous to RFC 1918:

| Range | Type |
|---|---|
| 1 – 64495 | Public 16-bit |
| **64512 – 65534** | **Private 16-bit** |
| 65536 – 4199999999 | Public 32-bit |
| **4200000000 – 4294967294** | **Private 32-bit** |
| 23456 | `AS_TRANS`, for 16-bit routers meeting 32-bit ASNs |

ASNs are allocated by **RIRs** (ARIN, RIPE NCC, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC) and are a matter of public record — anyone can look up who owns one, which is fundamental to routing security.

The relationships between ASes determine how traffic and money flow, and they explain nearly all internet routing policy:

**Transit (customer–provider).** The customer pays the provider for reachability to the entire internet. The provider advertises the customer's routes to everyone.

**Peering (settlement-free).** Two ASes exchange traffic between **their own customers only**, usually without payment, because it is mutually beneficial. Crucially, a peer does **not** provide transit — you cannot reach the rest of the internet through a peer.

**Sibling.** ASes under common ownership, exchanging everything.

From these comes the **valley-free** (Gao-Rexford) rule that structures the entire internet's routing:

> **Never provide free transit.** Routes learned from a **peer** or **provider** are advertised **only to customers** — never to other peers or providers.

The economic logic is exact: advertising a peer's routes to another peer would carry their traffic for free, paying transit costs for someone else's benefit. Every operator applies this rule, which is why internet paths have a characteristic shape — up to a provider, across a peering link, then down to a customer, never up again after coming down.

**Examples**

```text
The two-level architecture, and where trust ends

   +--- AS 64500 ---+        +--- AS 64501 ---+
   |  OSPF inside   |        |  IS-IS inside  |
   |  R1--R2--R3    |        |  R7--R8--R9    |
   |          [R4]--+--BGP---+--[R6]          |
   +----------------+        +----------------+
                      ^^^^^
                 policy boundary: R4 shows R6 only what it CHOOSES to.
                 R6 never learns AS 64500's internal topology, link costs,
                 or router count. That opacity is the entire point.


AS relationships and the valley-free rule

                    [Tier 1 A] ===peer=== [Tier 1 B]
                        |                     |
                    provider              provider
                        |                     |
                    [ISP C] ======peer====== [ISP D]
                        |                     |
                    provider              provider
                        |                     |
                   [Customer E]          [Customer F]

   ALLOWED path:  E -> C -> D -> F
                  (up to provider, across peer, down to customer)

   FORBIDDEN:     A -> B via C
                  C would carry Tier 1 traffic for free between two
                  networks it PAYS. C advertises peer routes to its
                  CUSTOMERS only, never to its other peers/providers.

   The shape: a path goes UP, across at most one peering link, then DOWN.
   Never up again after coming down. Hence "valley-free".


Why "shortest" stops being the goal

   AS 64500 can reach AS 64999 two ways:
     via provider X: AS-PATH length 2   ($$$ per megabit)
     via peer Y:     AS-PATH length 4   (free)

   BGP will be configured to prefer the LONGER path, because it is free.
   No IGP would ever do this. Policy, not distance, decides.
```

```python
ASN_RANGES = [
    (1, 64495,               "public 16-bit"),
    (64496, 64511,           "documentation (RFC 5398)"),
    (64512, 65534,           "PRIVATE 16-bit"),
    (65535, 65535,           "reserved"),
    (65536, 4199999999,      "public 32-bit"),
    (4200000000, 4294967294, "PRIVATE 32-bit"),
]

def classify_asn(asn):
    if asn == 23456:
        return "AS_TRANS (32-bit ASN seen by a 16-bit-only router)"
    for lo, hi, name in ASN_RANGES:
        if lo <= asn <= hi:
            return name
    return "reserved/invalid"

for asn in (1, 15169, 23456, 64512, 65534, 131072, 4200000001):
    print(f"AS{asn:<12} {classify_asn(asn)}")
# AS1            public 16-bit
# AS15169        public 16-bit
# AS23456        AS_TRANS (32-bit ASN seen by a 16-bit-only router)
# AS64512        PRIVATE 16-bit
# AS65534        PRIVATE 16-bit
# AS131072       public 32-bit
# AS4200000001   PRIVATE 32-bit

print(f"\n16-bit ASN space: {65535:,}")
print(f"32-bit ASN space: {4294967295:,}  ({4294967295/65535:,.0f}x larger)")
# 16-bit ASN space: 65,535
# 32-bit ASN space: 4,294,967,295  (65,537x larger)

# The valley-free rule, implemented. This single function explains most
# internet routing policy.
def should_advertise(route_learned_from, advertise_to):
    """Gao-Rexford: NEVER provide free transit."""
    if route_learned_from == "customer":
        return True, "customer routes go to EVERYONE (they pay us for reachability)"
    if advertise_to == "customer":
        return True, "customers may reach everything (that is what they pay for)"
    return False, (f"BLOCKED: {route_learned_from} route -> {advertise_to} "
                   f"would be FREE TRANSIT")

roles = ["customer", "peer", "provider"]
print(f"\n{'learned from':<12}{'advertise to':<12}{'allowed':<9}reason")
for src in roles:
    for dst in roles:
        ok, why = should_advertise(src, dst)
        print(f"{src:<12}{dst:<12}{str(ok):<9}{why}")
# learned from  advertise to  allowed  reason
# customer    customer    True     customer routes go to EVERYONE (they pay us for reachability)
# customer    peer        True     customer routes go to EVERYONE (they pay us for reachability)
# customer    provider    True     customer routes go to EVERYONE (they pay us for reachability)
# peer        customer    True     customers may reach everything (that is what they pay for)
# peer        peer        False    BLOCKED: peer route -> peer would be FREE TRANSIT
# peer        provider    False    BLOCKED: peer route -> provider would be FREE TRANSIT
# provider    customer    True     customers may reach everything (that is what they pay for)
# provider    peer        False    BLOCKED: provider route -> peer would be FREE TRANSIT
# provider    provider    False    BLOCKED: provider route -> provider would be FREE TRANSIT

# Validating that a path is valley-free.
def valley_free(path_relationships):
    """A valid path: zero or more 'up', at most one 'peer', then zero or more 'down'."""
    phase = "up"
    for rel in path_relationships:
        if phase == "up":
            if rel == "up":     continue
            if rel == "peer":   phase = "down"; continue
            if rel == "down":   phase = "down"; continue
        elif phase == "down":
            if rel == "down":   continue
            return False, f"INVALID: '{rel}' after descending — this is a valley"
    return True, "valid valley-free path"

print()
for path in [["up", "peer", "down"], ["up", "up", "down", "down"],
             ["up", "down", "up"], ["peer", "peer"]]:
    ok, why = valley_free(path)
    print(f"{str(path):<38}{why}")
# ['up', 'peer', 'down']                valid valley-free path
# ['up', 'up', 'down', 'down']          valid valley-free path
# ['up', 'down', 'up']                  INVALID: 'up' after descending — this is a valley
# ['peer', 'peer']                      INVALID: 'peer' after descending — this is a valley

# Why an AS might deliberately prefer the LONGER path.
def choose_path(options):
    # Real policy: cost first, AS-PATH length only as a tie-break.
    return min(options, key=lambda o: (o["cost_per_mbit"], o["as_path_len"]))

options = [
    {"via": "provider X", "as_path_len": 2, "cost_per_mbit": 1.50},
    {"via": "peer Y",     "as_path_len": 4, "cost_per_mbit": 0.00},
]
best = choose_path(options)
print(f"\nchosen: {best['via']} (AS-PATH {best['as_path_len']}, "
      f"${best['cost_per_mbit']}/Mbit)")
print("the LONGER path won. No IGP would ever make this choice.")
# chosen: peer Y (AS-PATH 4, $0.0/Mbit)
# the LONGER path won. No IGP would ever make this choice.
```

```bash
# Who owns an AS number? Public record, and the basis of routing security.
$ whois -h whois.radb.net AS15169 | head -4
# aut-num:     AS15169
# as-name:     GOOGLE
# descr:       Google LLC
# admin-c:     GOGL-ARIN

# Which AS does an address belong to?
$ whois -h whois.cymru.com " -v 8.8.8.8"
# AS      | IP       | BGP Prefix | CC | Registry | Allocated  | AS Name
# 15169   | 8.8.8.8  | 8.8.8.0/24 | US | arin     | 1992-12-01 | GOOGLE, US

# See the AS-level path, not just the router-level path:
$ traceroute -A -n 8.8.8.8 | head -5
#  1  192.168.1.1 [*]              1.1 ms
#  2  10.20.0.1 [AS64500]          9.8 ms     <- your ISP
#  3  62.115.120.1 [AS1299]       11.4 ms     <- a Tier 1 transit provider
#  4  142.250.166.1 [AS15169]     12.1 ms     <- Google's own network
#     ^^^^^^^^^^ each [ASnnnn] is a separate administrative domain

# Our own AS and its configured neighbours:
$ vtysh -c "show ip bgp summary"
# BGP router identifier 10.0.0.1, local AS number 64500 vrf-id 0
#                                 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
# Neighbor      V  AS    MsgRcvd  MsgSent  Up/Down  State/PfxRcd
# 203.0.113.1   4  1299   184211     9112  3w2d          974213
#                  ^^^^ eBGP: a DIFFERENT AS -> a policy boundary
# 10.0.0.2      4  64500   14021    13998  8w1d            1204
#                  ^^^^^ iBGP: the SAME AS -> inside our administration

# Enforcing valley-free policy with communities — how it is really done:
# route-map FROM_PEER permit 10
#   set community 64500:200       <- tag: "learned from a peer"
# route-map TO_PEER deny 10
#   match community PEER_OR_PROVIDER   <- never re-advertise to another peer
# route-map TO_PEER permit 20
#   match community CUSTOMER_ROUTES    <- customer routes only

$ show ip bgp community 64500:200 | wc -l
# 184291        # routes learned from peers; none of these go to other peers
```

**Key takeaways**

- An **Autonomous System** is a network under **one administrative authority** with a **single routing policy**; it decides independently what to accept and advertise.
- Routing splits two ways: **IGPs optimise for the shortest path inside an AS**; **BGP enforces policy between ASes**.
- BGP deliberately **hides internal topology** — a neighbouring AS learns only what you choose to tell it.
- **ASNs** are 16-bit (1–65535, private **64512–65534**) or 32-bit (private **4200000000–4294967294**); **AS23456** is `AS_TRANS` for backward compatibility.
- ASNs are allocated by **RIRs** and are **public record**, which underpins routing security.
- Relationships: **transit (customer pays provider)**, **peering (settlement-free, customers' traffic only)**, and **sibling**.
- A **peer does not provide transit** — you cannot reach the whole internet through a peer.
- The **valley-free / Gao-Rexford rule**: routes from a **peer or provider** are advertised **only to customers**, because anything else is **free transit**.
- Consequently the best BGP path is often **not the shortest** — a longer free path beats a shorter paid one.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Classify AS64512, AS23456, AS15169, and AS4200000005, naming the range each falls in.
> 2. Build the advertisement matrix for routes learned from customer, peer, and provider, and state which four combinations are forbidden and why.
> 3. Explain why an AS would prefer a 5-hop AS-PATH over a 2-hop one, and why no IGP would do the same.
> 4. Interview-style: *Your network peers with another ISP. They complain they cannot reach the rest of the internet through you. Is this a fault?* (Hint: consider what distinguishes a peering relationship from a transit one, and who would be paying for that traffic.)

#### BGP Session Establishment and Messages

**Theory**

BGP's operation differs from every IGP covered so far, and the differences all follow from one design decision: **BGP runs over TCP, on port 179**.

No IGP does this. OSPF rides directly in IP (protocol 89), IS-IS rides in layer 2, RIP uses UDP. BGP chose TCP because it needs **guaranteed, ordered, reliable delivery** of very large amounts of data — a full internet routing table is roughly a million prefixes and hundreds of megabytes of updates. Re-implementing reliability inside the routing protocol would duplicate TCP badly.

The consequences are pervasive:

- Peers must be **explicitly configured**. There is no discovery mechanism, no Hello multicast — you must know your neighbour's IP address and AS number. This is appropriate: you do not want to automatically peer with whoever appears on a link between competing organisations.
- Peers need **IP reachability first**, normally provided by an IGP or a static route.
- BGP inherits TCP's properties, including its vulnerability to session resets — hence **TCP-AO/MD5 authentication** and **GTSM** (Chapter 5).
- Updates are **incremental**. After the initial full table exchange, BGP sends only changes, and **keepalives** maintain the session.

The session progresses through a defined state machine:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Idle** | Nothing happening; refusing connections |
| **Connect** | Attempting the TCP handshake |
| **Active** | TCP failed; retrying. **A confusingly named problem state** |
| **OpenSent** | OPEN sent, awaiting the peer's OPEN |
| **OpenConfirm** | OPENs exchanged, awaiting KEEPALIVE |
| **Established** | **Operational**; UPDATEs may flow |

The trap worth memorising: **"Active" does not mean working.** It means the TCP connection is failing and BGP is retrying. A session flapping between **Idle**, **Connect**, and **Active** indicates the peer is unreachable, a firewall is blocking port 179, or the configured address is wrong. Only **Established** means the session is up.

BGP defines four message types:

**OPEN** — sent once, immediately after the TCP handshake. It carries the local **AS number**, the **BGP identifier** (router ID), the proposed **hold time**, and **capabilities** (32-bit ASN support, address families, route refresh, graceful restart). If the AS numbers do not match what each side expects, or the hold times are incompatible, the session fails here.

**UPDATE** — the workhorse. It carries **withdrawn routes**, **path attributes**, and **NLRI (Network Layer Reachability Information)** — the prefixes being advertised. One UPDATE can announce many prefixes **sharing the same attributes**, which is a significant efficiency: a provider advertising 10,000 customer prefixes with identical attributes sends far fewer messages than one per prefix.

**KEEPALIVE** — a 19-byte header-only message, sent every **one-third of the hold time** (default: 60 s keepalive, 180 s hold). If no message arrives within the hold time, the session drops and **all routes learned from that peer are withdrawn** — which at internet scale means a million routes disappearing and reconverging.

**NOTIFICATION** — sent when an error occurs, and it **always closes the session**. Its error code and subcode tell you exactly what went wrong, making it the single most useful diagnostic in BGP.

Because a session reset is so expensive, two mechanisms exist to avoid it. **Route Refresh (RFC 2918)** lets a router ask its peer to resend its routes after a policy change, instead of bouncing the session. **Graceful Restart** lets forwarding continue on stale routes while the BGP process restarts.

**Examples**

```text
The BGP state machine — note where "Active" sits

    Idle
     | start
     v
   Connect ---TCP fails---> Active ---retry---+
     |                        |               |
     | TCP established        +---------------+
     v                        ^ FLAPPING HERE = peer unreachable,
   OpenSent                     firewall blocking 179, or wrong address.
     |  OPEN received           "Active" is a PROBLEM state, not a good one.
     v
   OpenConfirm
     |  KEEPALIVE received
     v
   Established   <-- the ONLY state in which routing information flows


Message flow over the life of a session

   R1                                            R2
    |------ TCP SYN (port 179) ------------------>|
    |<----- TCP SYN-ACK --------------------------|
    |------ TCP ACK ----------------------------->|   TCP up
    |
    |------ OPEN (AS 64500, hold 180, caps) ----->|
    |<----- OPEN (AS 64501, hold 180, caps) ------|
    |------ KEEPALIVE -------------------------->|
    |<----- KEEPALIVE ---------------------------|   ESTABLISHED
    |
    |<===== UPDATE x N (the full table) ==========|   initial bulk transfer
    |                                              |   ~1M prefixes
    |------ KEEPALIVE (every 60 s) -------------->|
    |<----- UPDATE (only CHANGES from now on) ----|
    |
    |<----- NOTIFICATION (on any error) ----------|   session CLOSES


One UPDATE can carry many prefixes — if attributes match

  UPDATE
    withdrawn routes:  10.9.0.0/16
    path attributes:   ORIGIN=IGP, AS_PATH=64501 64502, NEXT_HOP=203.0.113.1
    NLRI:              10.1.0.0/16, 10.2.0.0/16, 10.3.0.0/16, ...
                       ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
                       ALL share the attributes above -> one message.
                       Different attributes would require separate UPDATEs.
```

```python
BGP_STATES = [
    ("Idle",        "refusing connections; start event needed"),
    ("Connect",     "attempting the TCP handshake"),
    ("Active",      "TCP FAILED, retrying — a PROBLEM state despite the name"),
    ("OpenSent",    "OPEN sent, awaiting the peer's OPEN"),
    ("OpenConfirm", "OPENs exchanged, awaiting KEEPALIVE"),
    ("Established", "OPERATIONAL — the only state where UPDATEs flow"),
]
for state, meaning in BGP_STATES:
    flag = "  <<< the only healthy steady state" if state == "Established" else ""
    flag = "  <<< misleading name" if state == "Active" else flag
    print(f"{state:<14}{meaning}{flag}")

BGP_MESSAGES = {
    "OPEN":         (19+10, "AS number, BGP ID, hold time, capabilities"),
    "UPDATE":       ("variable", "withdrawn routes + path attributes + NLRI"),
    "KEEPALIVE":    (19, "header only; sent at hold_time/3"),
    "NOTIFICATION": (21, "error code + subcode; ALWAYS closes the session"),
}
print()
for msg, (size, purpose) in BGP_MESSAGES.items():
    print(f"{msg:<14}{str(size):<10}{purpose}")
# OPEN          29        AS number, BGP ID, hold time, capabilities
# UPDATE        variable  withdrawn routes + path attributes + NLRI
# KEEPALIVE     19        header only; sent at hold_time/3
# NOTIFICATION  21        error code + subcode; ALWAYS closes the session

# Timer relationships, and the cost of a session drop.
def bgp_timers(hold_time=180):
    return {"hold_time_s": hold_time,
            "keepalive_s": hold_time // 3,
            "max_silence_before_drop_s": hold_time,
            "missed_keepalives_tolerated": 2}

print()
for hold in (180, 90, 9):
    t = bgp_timers(hold)
    print(f"hold={t['hold_time_s']:>4}s -> keepalive every {t['keepalive_s']:>3}s, "
          f"tolerates {t['missed_keepalives_tolerated']} missed keepalives")
# hold= 180s -> keepalive every  60s, tolerates 2 missed keepalives
# hold=  90s -> keepalive every  30s, tolerates 2 missed keepalives
# hold=   9s -> keepalive every   3s, tolerates 2 missed keepalives
#   Aggressive timers detect failure faster but risk dropping a healthy
#   session during a brief CPU spike — and a drop is VERY expensive.

def session_drop_cost(prefixes, install_rate_per_s=120_000):
    return {"routes_withdrawn": prefixes,
            "reconvergence_s": round(prefixes / install_rate_per_s, 1),
            "note": "every prefix must be withdrawn, then relearned and reinstalled"}

print()
for p in (1_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):
    c = session_drop_cost(p)
    print(f"{p:>9,} prefixes -> {c['reconvergence_s']:>5.1f} s to reconverge after a reset")
#     1,000 prefixes ->   0.0 s to reconverge after a reset
#   100,000 prefixes ->   0.8 s to reconverge after a reset
# 1,000,000 prefixes ->   8.3 s to reconverge after a reset

# Why one UPDATE per attribute-set matters at scale.
def updates_needed(prefixes, distinct_attribute_sets, max_nlri_per_update=400):
    per_set = -(-prefixes // distinct_attribute_sets)
    msgs_per_set = -(-per_set // max_nlri_per_update)
    return distinct_attribute_sets * msgs_per_set

print()
for sets in (1, 10, 1000):
    msgs = updates_needed(100_000, sets)
    print(f"100,000 prefixes over {sets:>4} attribute set(s) -> {msgs:>6,} UPDATE messages")
# 100,000 prefixes over    1 attribute set(s) ->    250 UPDATE messages
# 100,000 prefixes over   10 attribute set(s) ->    250 UPDATE messages
# 100,000 prefixes over 1000 attribute set(s) ->  1,000 UPDATE messages
#   Prefixes sharing attributes pack efficiently; highly varied policy
#   (many distinct attribute sets) costs more messages.

NOTIFICATION_CODES = {
    (1, 2): "OPEN: unsupported version",
    (2, 2): "OPEN: bad peer AS — the configured remote-as does not match",
    (2, 6): "OPEN: unacceptable hold time",
    (3, 1): "UPDATE: malformed attribute list",
    (4, 0): "Hold Timer Expired — no message arrived within the hold time",
    (6, 2): "Cease: administrative shutdown",
    (6, 1): "Cease: MAXIMUM PREFIX LIMIT EXCEEDED",
}
print()
for (code, sub), meaning in NOTIFICATION_CODES.items():
    print(f"code {code} subcode {sub}: {meaning}")
```

```bash
# Session state — read the State column carefully.
$ vtysh -c "show ip bgp summary"
# Neighbor      V  AS      MsgRcvd  MsgSent  Up/Down   State/PfxRcd
# 203.0.113.1   4  1299     184211     9112  3w2d           974213
#                                                            ^^^^^^ a NUMBER here
#                                                            means Established
# 198.51.100.7  4  64510         0       92  never          Active
#                                                            ^^^^^^ NOT working:
#                                                            TCP is failing

# Diagnosing a stuck "Active" session, in order:
$ ping -c1 198.51.100.7                       # 1. is the peer reachable?
$ nc -zv 198.51.100.7 179                     # 2. is port 179 open?
# nc: connect to 198.51.100.7 port 179 (tcp) failed: Connection refused
$ vtysh -c "show ip bgp neighbors 198.51.100.7" | grep -iE "state|last reset"
#   BGP state = Active
#   Last reset 00:04:12, due to BGP Notification received (Cease/Connection rejected)

# NOTIFICATION tells you exactly what broke:
$ vtysh -c "show ip bgp neighbors 203.0.113.1" | grep -A3 "Notification"
#   Last reset: Notification sent (OPEN Message Error/Bad Peer AS)
#                                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ code 2 sub 2:
#   our 'remote-as' does not match what the peer actually announced.

# Watch a session come up:
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n tcp port 179 -v
# IP 10.0.0.1.51234 > 203.0.113.1.179: Flags [S]           <- TCP handshake
# IP 10.0.0.1.51234 > 203.0.113.1.179: BGP, OPEN, length 53
#     Version 4, my AS 64500, Holdtime 180s, ID 10.0.0.1
#     Capability: Multiprotocol Extensions IPv4 Unicast
#     Capability: 32-Bit AS Number, 64500
# IP 203.0.113.1.179 > 10.0.0.1.51234: BGP, KEEPALIVE, length 19
# IP 203.0.113.1.179 > 10.0.0.1.51234: BGP, UPDATE, length 4096   <- bulk transfer

# Protecting the session (a TCP session is attackable; an OSPF one is not):
# router bgp 64500
#   neighbor 203.0.113.1 password SharedSecret       <- TCP MD5
#   neighbor 203.0.113.1 ttl-security hops 1         <- GTSM (Chapter 5)
#   neighbor 203.0.113.1 maximum-prefix 1000000 90   <- cap; warn at 90%

# Avoid resetting the session when policy changes:
$ vtysh -c "clear ip bgp 203.0.113.1 soft in"
#   Uses Route Refresh: the peer RESENDS its routes. The session stays up.
$ vtysh -c "clear ip bgp 203.0.113.1"
#   HARD reset: drops the session, withdraws ~1M routes. Avoid on production.

$ vtysh -c "show ip bgp neighbors 203.0.113.1" | grep -i refresh
#     Route refresh: advertised and received(old & new)
```

**Key takeaways**

- **BGP runs over TCP port 179**, giving reliable ordered delivery for a table of ~1M prefixes — no IGP does this.
- Peers are **explicitly configured** (no discovery) and need **IP reachability first**, usually via an IGP.
- States: **Idle → Connect → Active → OpenSent → OpenConfirm → Established**.
- **"Active" is a problem state** — TCP is failing and retrying; only **Established** means the session works.
- Four messages: **OPEN** (AS, router ID, hold time, capabilities), **UPDATE** (withdrawals, attributes, NLRI), **KEEPALIVE** (19 bytes, every hold/3), **NOTIFICATION** (always closes the session).
- One **UPDATE** can carry many prefixes **sharing the same attributes**, which is a major efficiency.
- Defaults: **60 s keepalive, 180 s hold**; losing a session **withdraws every route** learned from that peer.
- **Route Refresh** re-requests routes after a policy change without a reset; **Graceful Restart** keeps forwarding while BGP restarts.
- Because the session is TCP, it is attackable — protect it with **TCP MD5/AO**, **GTSM**, and **maximum-prefix** limits.
