#### DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS

**Theory**

DNSSEC closed the authenticity gap and left the other one wide open. Classic DNS travels over **UDP port 53 in cleartext**, so every device on the path — your ISP, the café Wi-Fi, a transit provider — can read every name you look up, and can block or rewrite the answers.

That leak is more revealing than people assume. Even with HTTPS protecting page contents, the *sequence of names* you resolve reconstructs your browsing history: which sites, in what order, at what time. DNS was, for most of the web's history, the last plaintext record of user behaviour.

Two encrypted transports emerged, differing mainly in how much they try to blend in.

**DNS over TLS (DoT)**, RFC 7858, is the straightforward answer: ordinary DNS messages inside a TLS session on **port 853**. Clean, purpose-built, easy to implement in a resolver. Because it has a dedicated port, it is trivially identifiable on the network — which is good for network operators who want to audit or enforce policy, and bad for users in networks that would rather block it.

**DNS over HTTPS (DoH)**, RFC 8484, wraps DNS queries in HTTPS requests on **port 443**, indistinguishable from any other web traffic. A query is an HTTP GET with a base64url-encoded DNS message, or a POST with the message as the body, using content type `application/dns-message`. Because it is indistinguishable from web traffic, it cannot be selectively blocked without blocking HTTPS — a property its advocates consider the point and its critics consider the problem.

| | Classic DNS | DoT | DoH |
|---|---|---|---|
| Port | 53 | **853** | **443** |
| Encryption | None | TLS | TLS (inside HTTP/2 or HTTP/3) |
| Blockable selectively | Yes | Yes (port) | **No** (looks like web traffic) |
| Network visibility | Full | Metadata only | **None** |
| Implemented in | OS stub | OS stub | **Often the browser** |
| Overhead | ~1 RTT | +TLS handshake | +TLS +HTTP framing |

**DoQ (DNS over QUIC)**, RFC 9250, is the newer addition on port 853/UDP, giving DoT's encryption without TCP head-of-line blocking — a natural fit since DNS was always a datagram protocol.

The genuine controversy is not cryptographic; it is about **where trust moves**. Encrypting DNS does not remove the observer — it relocates it. Your ISP can no longer see your lookups; the DoH provider can see all of them, now conveniently centralised across millions of users. If a browser ships with a default DoH provider, that provider gains a view of user behaviour that no single ISP ever had.

The operational objections are concrete and worth taking seriously:

- **Split-horizon DNS breaks.** Corporate names that resolve only on the internal resolver stop resolving when the browser bypasses it.
- **Security filtering is bypassed.** Malware-blocking and parental controls implemented at the resolver stop applying.
- **Troubleshooting gets harder.** The OS no longer knows what the browser resolved.

The mitigations are policy-shaped rather than technical: **Canary domains** (`use-application-dns.net`, which a network answers NXDOMAIN to signal "do not use DoH here"), enterprise policy that disables application-level DoH, and the emerging **Discovery of Designated Resolvers (DDR)** for advertising a network's own encrypted resolver so clients can encrypt *to the right place* rather than bypassing it.

The realistic summary: encrypted DNS is strictly better than plaintext against on-path observers, and the remaining argument is entirely about **which single party** you would rather have the complete log.

**Examples**

```text
What each transport exposes to whom

  CLASSIC DNS (port 53, plaintext)
  [you] --"www.medical-site.com?"--> [ISP] --> [root/TLD/auth]
              ^ visible to: ISP, Wi-Fi operator, every transit hop,
                and anyone running tcpdump on the path

  DoT (port 853, TLS)
  [you] ===encrypted===> [resolver] --> [root/TLD/auth]
         ^ ISP sees: "TLS to 1.1.1.1:853, 240 bytes"
           It knows you are doing DNS, and with whom, not WHAT.
           Selectively blockable: just drop port 853.

  DoH (port 443, HTTPS)
  [you] ===encrypted===> [resolver] --> [root/TLD/auth]
         ^ ISP sees: "HTTPS to 1.1.1.1, 240 bytes"
           Indistinguishable from any web request.
           To block it, you must block HTTPS to that address.

  IN ALL THREE CASES the resolver still sees everything,
  and the authoritative servers still see the queries they answer.
  Encryption relocates the observer; it does not remove one.
```

```python
# Building a DoH query by hand -- it is genuinely just HTTP.
import base64, struct

def build_dns_query(name, qtype=1):
    """A wire-format DNS query: identical bytes for UDP/53, DoT, and DoH."""
    header = struct.pack('>HHHHHH',
                         0x0000,   # ID: MUST be 0 for DoH (HTTP handles matching)
                         0x0100,   # flags: RD=1
                         1, 0, 0, 0)
    qname = b''.join(bytes([len(l)]) + l.encode() for l in name.split('.')) + b'\x00'
    return header + qname + struct.pack('>HH', qtype, 1)   # QTYPE, QCLASS=IN

q = build_dns_query("www.example.com")
print(q)
# b'\x00\x00\x01\x00\x00\x01\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x03www\x07example\x03com\x00\x00\x01\x00\x01'

# GET form: base64url-encoded, unpadded, in the ?dns= parameter.
encoded = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(q).decode().rstrip('=')
print(f"\nGET https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?dns={encoded}")
# GET https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?dns=AAABAAABAAAAAAAAA3d3dwdleGFtcGxlA2NvbQAAAQAB
#   Note the stripped '=' padding: required by RFC 8484.
#   Note ID=0: DoH must zero it so identical queries share an HTTP cache entry.

# What each observer learns, side by side.
observers = {
    "classic/53": {"ISP": "full query names", "resolver": "full query names",
                   "cafe wifi": "full query names"},
    "DoT/853":    {"ISP": "you use DNS, and which resolver", "resolver": "full query names",
                   "cafe wifi": "you use DNS, and which resolver"},
    "DoH/443":    {"ISP": "you contacted an IP over HTTPS", "resolver": "full query names",
                   "cafe wifi": "you contacted an IP over HTTPS"},
}
for transport, who in observers.items():
    print(f"\n{transport}")
    for party, sees in who.items():
        print(f"   {party:<12} sees: {sees}")
# classic/53
#    ISP          sees: full query names
#    resolver     sees: full query names
#    cafe wifi    sees: full query names
# DoT/853
#    ISP          sees: you use DNS, and which resolver
#    resolver     sees: full query names
#    cafe wifi    sees: you use DNS, and which resolver
# DoH/443
#    ISP          sees: you contacted an IP over HTTPS
#    resolver     sees: full query names
#    cafe wifi    sees: you contacted an IP over HTTPS
#   The resolver column NEVER changes. That is the whole debate.

# Connection setup cost -- encrypted DNS is only expensive when cold.
costs = {"classic UDP": 1, "DoT (cold, TLS1.3)": 3, "DoT (warm, reused)": 1,
         "DoH/2 (cold)": 3, "DoH/2 (warm)": 1, "DoQ (cold, 0-RTT)": 1}
for name, rtts in costs.items():
    print(f"{name:<22} {rtts} RTT{'s' if rtts > 1 else ''}")
#   Warm connections are the common case: the cost is amortised to nearly zero.
```

```bash
# DoH via curl -- it is an ordinary HTTPS request with a special content type:
$ curl -s -H 'accept: application/dns-json' \
    'https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=example.com&type=A' | jq -c '.Answer'
# [{"name":"example.com","type":1,"TTL":85652,"data":"93.184.216.34"}]

# The RFC 8484 binary form (what browsers actually send):
$ curl -s -H 'accept: application/dns-message' \
    'https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?dns=AAABAAABAAAAAAAAA3d3dwdleGFtcGxlA2NvbQAAAQAB' \
    | xxd | head -2
# 00000000: 0000 8180 0001 0001 0000 0000 0377 7777  .............www

# DoT with a purpose-built client -- note the port and the certificate check:
$ kdig -d @1.1.1.1 +tls-ca +tls-host=cloudflare-dns.com example.com
# ;; DEBUG: TLS, peer certificate verified
# ;; DEBUG: TLS, handshake completed
# example.com.  85000  IN  A  93.184.216.34

# Configure the OS stub to use DoT system-wide (systemd-resolved):
$ resolvectl status | grep -E 'DNS Servers|DNSOverTLS'
# DNS Servers: 1.1.1.1 1.0.0.1
# +DNSOverTLS  +DNSSEC/supported          <- both on

# What an observer actually sees, per transport:
$ sudo tcpdump -i any -n port 53 -c 1 -A 2>/dev/null | grep -o 'example\.com'
# example.com          <- plaintext: the name is right there

$ sudo tcpdump -i any -n port 853 -c 1 -A 2>/dev/null | grep -o 'example\.com'
# (nothing: encrypted)

# The canary domain: how a network says "please do not use DoH here".
$ dig +short use-application-dns.net
# (an NXDOMAIN here signals Firefox to disable DoH on this network)
```

**Key takeaways**

- Classic DNS is **cleartext on UDP/53**, so the sequence of names you resolve is readable by every on-path party — a browsing history that HTTPS does not hide.
- **DoT (port 853)** puts DNS inside TLS: clean and purpose-built, but **identifiable and therefore blockable by port**.
- **DoH (port 443)** puts DNS inside HTTPS: **indistinguishable from web traffic**, which is simultaneously its main feature and the core objection to it.
- **DoQ (RFC 9250)** adds QUIC, removing TCP head-of-line blocking for a protocol that was always datagram-shaped.
- Encryption **relocates the observer rather than removing it**: the resolver still sees every query, now centralised across far more users.
- Real operational costs are **broken split-horizon DNS, bypassed security filtering, and harder troubleshooting**; mitigations include **canary domains, enterprise policy, and DDR**.

<a id="83-the-web-and-http"></a>
### 8.3 The Web and HTTP

HTTP carries more of the internet's traffic than any other application protocol: this subchapter builds it from the URL up through three major protocol versions and the push mechanisms layered on top.

#### URLs, URIs, and Resources

**Theory**

Before a protocol can fetch something, there must be a way to *name* it. The web's naming scheme is deliberately more general than "a file on a server", and understanding that generality explains a lot of otherwise puzzling design.

The vocabulary, from broadest to narrowest:

- A **URI (Uniform Resource Identifier)** identifies a resource. That is all it promises.
- A **URL (Uniform Resource Locator)** is a URI that also says **how to locate** it — it includes a scheme and enough information to access the thing.
- A **URN (Uniform Resource Name)** is a URI that names without locating: `urn:isbn:0140449132` identifies a book, but tells you nothing about where to get it.

In practice almost every URI you meet is a URL, and the modern WHATWG specification largely collapses the distinction. The concept worth keeping is **resource**: the abstract thing being identified, which is *not* the same as the bytes you get back. `/weather/london` is a resource; its **representation** changes every hour, and may be JSON or HTML depending on what you asked for. This separation is the foundation of content negotiation, caching, and REST.

The anatomy of a URL:

```text
  https://user@www.example.com:8443/path/to/page?q=networking&p=2#section-3
  \___/   \__/ \_____________/ \__/\___________/ \______________/ \_______/
  scheme  user     host        port    path          query        fragment
```

Each component has behaviour worth knowing:

- **Scheme** — the protocol, and it determines everything else's meaning. Case-insensitive.
- **Host** — a domain name or address literal; **case-insensitive**, and IPv6 literals must be bracketed: `http://[2001:db8::1]:80/`.
- **Port** — omitted means the scheme's default (80 for `http`, 443 for `https`).
- **Path** — **case-sensitive**, hierarchical, and entirely up to the server to interpret. It need not correspond to a file.
- **Query** — after `?`, conventionally `key=value` pairs joined by `&`. Sent to the server.
- **Fragment** — after `#`, **never sent to the server**. It is processed by the client alone, which is why single-page applications historically used it for routing and why analytics cannot see it server-side.

**Percent-encoding** is the part that causes real bugs. URLs may contain only a restricted ASCII set, so anything else — spaces, non-Latin characters, or a reserved character used literally — must be encoded as `%XX`. The trap is that **the reserved set differs by component**: `/` is legal and meaningful in a path but must be encoded inside a query value; `+` means a space in a form-encoded query but is a literal plus in a path. Encoding a whole URL with one function is a classic source of broken links, which is why JavaScript has both `encodeURI` (leaves structure alone) and `encodeURIComponent` (encodes everything).

**Relative references** resolve against a base URL by well-defined rules (RFC 3986): `//host/path` keeps the scheme, `/path` keeps scheme and host, `path` replaces the last path segment, and `?query` keeps everything but the query.

**Examples**

```text
URL anatomy and who sees what

  https://api.example.com:8443/v1/users/42?fields=name,email#bio
  \___/   \______________/\__/\___________/\_______________/\__/
    |            |          |        |             |          |
  scheme       host       port     path         query     fragment
    |            |          |        |             |          |
  chooses    resolved    default   opaque to    opaque to   NEVER
  transport  via DNS     if absent  the client  the client   SENT
  + default  case-       (80/443)  case-        (server      (client
    port     INSENSITIVE           SENSITIVE     parses)      only)

  What actually goes on the wire:

    GET /v1/users/42?fields=name,email HTTP/1.1
    Host: api.example.com
    ^ path + query only. The fragment "#bio" stayed in the browser.


  Same resource, different representations:

                    /weather/london          <- the RESOURCE (stable identity)
                     /        |      \
        Accept: json/    Accept: html   Accept-Language: fr
             |               |               |
      {"tempC":14}     <html>14C</html>  {"tempC":14,"desc":"nuageux"}
       ^-------------- three REPRESENTATIONS of one resource -----------^
```

```python
from urllib.parse import urlparse, urlencode, quote, quote_plus, urljoin, parse_qs

url = "https://user@www.example.com:8443/path/to/page?q=networking&p=2#section-3"
p = urlparse(url)
for field in ("scheme", "username", "hostname", "port", "path", "query", "fragment"):
    print(f"  {field:<9}: {getattr(p, field)}")
#   scheme   : https
#   username : user
#   hostname : www.example.com      <- note: lowercased, host is case-insensitive
#   port     : 8443
#   path     : /path/to/page        <- NOT lowercased: paths are case-sensitive
#   query    : q=networking&p=2
#   fragment : section-3            <- parsed here, but never transmitted

# The encoding trap: the safe set DEPENDS ON THE COMPONENT.
value = "a/b c&d=e"
print(f"\nraw value           : {value}")
print(f"as a PATH segment   : {quote(value, safe='/')}")      # '/' kept structural
print(f"as a QUERY value    : {quote(value, safe='')}")       # everything encoded
print(f"as FORM data        : {quote_plus(value)}")           # space -> '+'
# raw value           : a/b c&d=e
# as a PATH segment   : a/b%20c%26d%3De
# as a QUERY value    : a%2Fb%20c%26d%3De
# as FORM data        : a%2Fb+c%26d%3De
#   Using the wrong one silently splits your value into two parameters.

# What happens when you get it wrong:
bad  = f"https://api.example.com/search?q={value}"
good = f"https://api.example.com/search?q={quote(value, safe='')}"
print(f"\nbad  -> {parse_qs(urlparse(bad).query)}")
print(f"good -> {parse_qs(urlparse(good).query)}")
# bad  -> {'q': ['a/b c'], 'd': ['e']}      <- one parameter became two
# good -> {'q': ['a/b c&d=e']}              <- intact

# Relative resolution (RFC 3986) -- each form keeps a different prefix.
base = "https://example.com/docs/guide/intro.html"
for ref in ("style.css", "/assets/app.js", "../api/v2.html",
            "//cdn.example.net/lib.js", "?page=2", "#top"):
    print(f"  {ref:<26} -> {urljoin(base, ref)}")
#   style.css                  -> https://example.com/docs/guide/style.css
#   /assets/app.js             -> https://example.com/assets/app.js
#   ../api/v2.html             -> https://example.com/docs/api/v2.html
#   //cdn.example.net/lib.js   -> https://cdn.example.net/lib.js
#   ?page=2                    -> https://example.com/docs/guide/intro.html?page=2
#   #top                       -> https://example.com/docs/guide/intro.html#top

# IPv6 literals must be bracketed, or the colons are ambiguous with the port:
print(urlparse("http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/x").hostname,
      urlparse("http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/x").port)
# 2001:db8::1 8080
```

```bash
# Prove the fragment never leaves the browser:
$ curl -v 'https://example.com/page#secret-section' 2>&1 | grep '^> GET'
# > GET /page HTTP/2
#   The fragment is absent. Server-side logs and analytics cannot see it.

# Paths are case-sensitive; hosts are not:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://EXAMPLE.COM/
# 200
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com/INDEX.HTML
# 404      <- same server, different path

# Let curl handle encoding rather than building strings by hand:
$ curl -G --data-urlencode 'q=a/b c&d=e' -w '\n%{url_effective}\n' \
       -o /dev/null https://example.com/search
# https://example.com/search?q=a%2Fb%20c%26d%3De

# Content negotiation: one URL, several representations:
$ curl -s -H 'Accept: application/json' https://api.example.com/weather/london
# {"tempC":14}
$ curl -s -H 'Accept: text/html' https://api.example.com/weather/london
# <html><body>14C</body></html>
#   Same resource. Same URL. Different representation.
```

**Key takeaways**

- A **URI identifies**, a **URL also locates**, a **URN names without locating** — in practice nearly everything is a URL.
- A **resource** is the abstract thing identified; a **representation** is the bytes returned — one resource can have many representations.
- **Host is case-insensitive, path is case-sensitive**; the port defaults from the scheme; IPv6 literals require brackets.
- The **fragment is never sent to the server** — it is client-side only, invisible to server logs and analytics.
- **Percent-encoding rules differ per component**: encoding a whole URL with one function is a standard source of broken parameters.
- **Relative references** resolve by RFC 3986 rules, each form inheriting a different amount of the base URL.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Break `https://shop.example.co.uk/items/AB-12?sort=price&dir=asc#reviews` into its components and state exactly which bytes appear in the request line.
> 2. A search value is `100% & rising`. Show the correctly encoded query string and explain what breaks if it is not encoded.
> 3. Resolve `../images/logo.png` and `/images/logo.png` against the base `https://example.com/a/b/c/page.html`.
> 4. Interview-style: *Why can server-side analytics not tell you which tab of a single-page application a user opened, when the URL clearly shows it?* (Hint: look again at which component crosses the network.)

#### HTTP Request and Response Structure

**Theory**

HTTP/1.1 is a **text-based, stateless, request-response** protocol, and its wire format is simple enough to type by hand — which is exactly why it won. You can debug it with `telnet`, and every proxy, cache, and load balancer in the world could be written without a specialised parser.

Both messages share one shape:

```text
  <start line>
  <header>: <value>
  <header>: <value>
  <blank line>              <- CRLF CRLF: the critical delimiter
  [body]
```

A **request** start line is `METHOD SP request-target SP HTTP-version`:

```text
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
```

A **response** start line (the *status line*) is `HTTP-version SP status-code SP reason-phrase`:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

Details that matter in practice:

**Line endings are CRLF (`\r\n`)**, not bare LF. The blank line that separates headers from body is therefore `\r\n\r\n`, and this exact sequence is what every HTTP parser scans for. Ambiguity about it is the root of an entire class of **request smuggling** vulnerabilities, where a front-end proxy and a back-end server disagree about where one message ends and the next begins.

**`Host` is mandatory in HTTP/1.1.** This is the single change that made virtual hosting possible: one IP address can serve thousands of sites because the request names which one it wants. In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 the same information moves into the `:authority` pseudo-header.

**Body length must be unambiguous**, and there are exactly two ways to express it:

- **`Content-Length: N`** — the body is exactly N bytes. Simple, but requires knowing the size in advance.
- **`Transfer-Encoding: chunked`** — the body arrives as a sequence of size-prefixed chunks, terminated by a zero-length chunk. This allows streaming a response whose length is not yet known, which is how server-generated content is sent without buffering it entirely first.

Sending both is forbidden, and a mismatch between what a proxy believes and what a server believes is, again, request smuggling.

**Headers are case-insensitive** in name, may repeat (combining as a comma-separated list where the field allows it), and are conventionally either standard (registered with IANA) or application-defined. The old `X-` prefix convention for non-standard headers was deprecated by RFC 6648.

**Statelessness** is the design decision with the widest consequences. The server is not required to remember anything between requests. That makes any server able to answer any request — the property that makes load balancing and horizontal scaling trivial — and it is why state has to be smuggled back in through cookies, tokens, or the URL.

**Examples**

```text
An HTTP/1.1 exchange, byte for byte

REQUEST                                  bytes on the wire
+-----------------------------------+
| GET /api/users?limit=10 HTTP/1.1\r\n |  <- start line
| Host: api.example.com\r\n            |  <- MANDATORY in 1.1
| User-Agent: curl/8.4.0\r\n           |
| Accept: application/json\r\n         |
| \r\n                                 |  <- BLANK LINE ends the headers
+-----------------------------------+      (no body for a GET)

RESPONSE
+-----------------------------------+
| HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n                  |  <- status line
| Content-Type: application/json\r\n   |
| Content-Length: 27\r\n               |  <- body is EXACTLY 27 bytes
| \r\n                                 |
| {"users":[{"id":1}],"n":1}           |  <- body
+-----------------------------------+


CHUNKED: streaming a body of unknown length

  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  Transfer-Encoding: chunked
  <blank>
  1a\r\n                       <- chunk size in HEXADECIMAL (26 bytes)
  {"partial":"first piece"}\n\r\n
  12\r\n                       <- next chunk, 18 bytes
  {"more":"data"}\n\r\n
  0\r\n                        <- zero-length chunk = end of body
  \r\n

  Why it exists: the server can start sending before it knows the total size.
```

```python
# Speaking HTTP/1.1 by hand -- no library, just bytes on a socket.
import socket

def raw_http_get(host, path="/", port=80):
    request = (
        f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1\r\n"        # start line: METHOD TARGET VERSION
        f"Host: {host}\r\n"               # mandatory: selects the virtual host
        f"User-Agent: hand-written/1.0\r\n"
        f"Connection: close\r\n"          # ask the server to close when done
        f"\r\n"                           # BLANK LINE: headers are finished
    )
    s = socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=5)
    s.sendall(request.encode())
    data = b""
    while chunk := s.recv(4096):
        data += chunk
    s.close()
    return data

# Parsing is equally mechanical: split on the CRLF CRLF delimiter.
def parse_response(raw):
    head, _, body = raw.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")   # THE critical split
    lines = head.decode("iso-8859-1").split("\r\n")
    version, code, reason = lines[0].split(" ", 2)
    headers = {}
    for line in lines[1:]:
        name, _, value = line.partition(":")
        headers[name.lower().strip()] = value.strip()   # names are case-insensitive
    return {"version": version, "status": int(code), "reason": reason,
            "headers": headers, "body": body}

sample = (b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
          b"Content-Type: application/json\r\n"
          b"Content-Length: 26\r\n"
          b"\r\n"
          b'{"users":[{"id":1}],"n":1}')
r = parse_response(sample)
print(r["status"], r["reason"], r["headers"]["content-type"], len(r["body"]))
# 200 OK application/json 26

# Decoding a chunked body: size line, data, repeat until a 0-size chunk.
def decode_chunked(body):
    out, pos = b"", 0
    while True:
        end = body.index(b"\r\n", pos)
        size = int(body[pos:end].split(b";")[0], 16)   # HEX size, optional ext
        if size == 0:
            return out                                  # terminating chunk
        start = end + 2
        out += body[start:start + size]
        pos = start + size + 2                          # skip the trailing CRLF

chunked = (b"1a\r\n" + b"{'partial':'first piece'}\n" + b"\r\n"
           b"f\r\n"  + b"{'more':'data'}"              + b"\r\n"
           b"0\r\n\r\n")
print(decode_chunked(chunked))
# b"{'partial':'first piece'}\n{'more':'data'}"

# Why sending BOTH length headers is forbidden -- the smuggling primitive:
front_end_reads = "Content-Length"      # proxy trusts one header
back_end_reads  = "Transfer-Encoding"   # origin trusts the other
print(f"\nproxy uses {front_end_reads}, origin uses {back_end_reads}")
print("-> they disagree about where the request ends")
print("-> leftover bytes are parsed as the START of the next request")
#   This is HTTP request smuggling. RFC 9112 requires rejecting such messages.
```

```bash
# Watch the raw bytes, request and response, with nothing hidden:
$ curl -v --http1.1 https://example.com/ 2>&1 | grep -E '^[><]'
# > GET / HTTP/1.1
# > Host: example.com
# > User-Agent: curl/8.4.0
# > Accept: */*
# >
# < HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# < Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
# < Content-Length: 1256
# <

# Type HTTP by hand -- it really is this simple:
$ printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' \
  | openssl s_client -quiet -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | head -5
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8

# Omit the mandatory Host header and a 1.1 server must reject you:
$ printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n' | nc example.com 80 | head -1
# HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request

# Virtual hosting: same IP, different Host header, different site:
$ curl -s -H 'Host: site-a.example.com' http://93.184.216.34/ | grep -o '<title>.*'
# <title>Site A</title>
$ curl -s -H 'Host: site-b.example.com' http://93.184.216.34/ | grep -o '<title>.*'
# <title>Site B</title>

# Chunked in the wild -- note there is no Content-Length:
$ curl -sI https://api.example.com/stream | grep -iE 'transfer-encoding|content-length'
# transfer-encoding: chunked
```

**Key takeaways**

- Every HTTP/1.1 message is **start line, headers, blank line, optional body**, with **CRLF** line endings and `\r\n\r\n` as the header/body delimiter.
- The request start line is `METHOD target HTTP/version`; the response status line is `HTTP/version code reason`.
- **`Host` is mandatory in HTTP/1.1**, which is what enables **virtual hosting**; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry it as `:authority`.
- Body length is expressed by **`Content-Length`** or **`Transfer-Encoding: chunked`** — never both, because disagreement between proxy and origin enables **request smuggling**.
- **Chunked encoding** lets a server stream a response whose total size is not yet known.
- HTTP is **stateless by design**: any server can serve any request, which makes horizontal scaling easy and forces state into cookies, tokens, or URLs.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write, byte for byte including CRLFs, a valid HTTP/1.1 POST of a 12-byte JSON body to `/api/v1/notes` on `api.example.com`.
> 2. Decode this chunked body by hand: `5\r\nHello\r\n6\r\n World\r\n0\r\n\r\n`.
> 3. Explain what a server must do if a request contains both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding`, and why.
> 4. Interview-style: *HTTP is stateless, yet you stay logged in across requests. Where does the state actually live, and what does statelessness buy the operator?* (Hint: think about what must be true for a load balancer to send your next request to a different machine.)

#### Methods, Status Codes, and Headers

**Theory**

The message format is a container; methods, status codes, and headers are the vocabulary that gives it meaning. Each has a small set of properties that determine how every intermediary on the path is allowed to treat the message — which is why getting them right matters far beyond style.

**Methods** declare intent. The two properties that govern them are:

- **Safe** — the request does not change server state. A crawler, a prefetcher, or a browser preview may issue it without asking permission.
- **Idempotent** — issuing it N times has the same effect as issuing it once. This is what makes automatic retry possible after a timeout.

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Body | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **GET** | Yes | Yes | No | Retrieve a representation |
| **HEAD** | Yes | Yes | No | GET's headers only |
| **OPTIONS** | Yes | Yes | No | Query capabilities; CORS preflight |
| **POST** | **No** | **No** | Yes | Submit data; create subordinate |
| **PUT** | No | **Yes** | Yes | Replace the resource entirely |
| **PATCH** | No | **No** | Yes | Partial modification |
| **DELETE** | No | **Yes** | Optional | Remove the resource |

The distinction that matters operationally: **PUT is idempotent, POST is not.** `PUT /users/42` with the same body ten times leaves one user in one state. `POST /users` ten times creates ten users. This is precisely why a browser warns before re-submitting a form, and why a client library may safely retry a PUT after a network timeout but must not retry a POST without an idempotency key.

**Status codes** are grouped by first digit, and the class is meaningful even when the specific code is not recognised:

| Class | Meaning | Codes worth knowing |
|---|---|---|
| **1xx** | Informational | `100 Continue`, `101 Switching Protocols` |
| **2xx** | Success | `200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content`, `206 Partial Content` |
| **3xx** | Redirection | `301` permanent, `302`/`307` temporary, `304 Not Modified` |
| **4xx** | Client error | `400`, `401`, `403`, `404`, `409`, `418`, `429` |
| **5xx** | Server error | `500`, `502`, `503`, `504` |

Three pairs are routinely confused and worth stating precisely:

- **401 vs 403.** `401 Unauthorized` actually means *unauthenticated* — "I do not know who you are, try again with credentials", and it must carry `WWW-Authenticate`. `403 Forbidden` means *authenticated but not permitted* — "I know who you are and the answer is still no". Retrying with credentials helps only with 401.
- **301 vs 302 vs 307/308.** `301` is permanent and aggressively cached, sometimes forever, by browsers — deploy one by mistake and users may be stuck with it. `302` is temporary but historically caused clients to change POST into GET; `307` and `308` were defined to preserve the method explicitly.
- **502 vs 503 vs 504.** `502 Bad Gateway` means an upstream returned garbage; `503 Service Unavailable` means "I am up but cannot serve now" (and should carry `Retry-After`); `504 Gateway Timeout` means an upstream did not answer in time. In a load-balanced deployment, these three point at three different components.

**Headers** carry the metadata that makes HTTP extensible without changing the protocol. They fall into rough categories: **representation** (`Content-Type`, `Content-Encoding`, `Content-Language`), **negotiation** (`Accept`, `Accept-Encoding`, `Accept-Language`), **conditional** (`If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since`), **caching** (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Age`), **authentication** (`Authorization`, `WWW-Authenticate`), **connection** (`Connection`, `Upgrade`), and **security** (`Strict-Transport-Security`, `Content-Security-Policy`).

**Content negotiation** deserves highlighting because it is the mechanism behind the resource/representation split: the client states preferences with quality values (`Accept: text/html;q=0.9, application/json;q=1.0`), and the server picks, signalling what varies with the `Vary` header so caches do not serve the wrong representation to the next client.

**Examples**

```text
Choosing a method: the decision that determines retry safety

  Does it change server state?
     |                         \
     NO                         YES
     |                            |
   SAFE                    Is the result the same if repeated?
   GET / HEAD / OPTIONS       |                    \
   (crawlers may fetch       YES                    NO
    freely, caches may       |                       |
    store)               IDEMPOTENT            NOT IDEMPOTENT
                         PUT / DELETE           POST / PATCH
                         (safe to retry         (retry needs an
                          after a timeout)       idempotency key)


Status code classes at a glance

  1xx  |  hold on, more is coming
  2xx  |  it worked
  3xx  |  it is somewhere else / you already have it
  4xx  |  YOU made a mistake       <- do not retry unchanged
  5xx  |  I made a mistake         <- retry MAY help

  The confusable pairs:

  401 "who are you?"        -> send credentials, retry helps
  403 "I know. Still no."   -> retry is pointless

  301 permanent   -> browser may cache FOREVER. Very hard to undo.
  302 temporary   -> some clients rewrite POST -> GET (historical bug)
  307 temporary   -> method PRESERVED, explicitly
  308 permanent   -> method PRESERVED, explicitly

  502 upstream returned nonsense   -> look at the backend
  503 I am here but refusing        -> look at capacity/maintenance
  504 upstream never answered       -> look at timeouts and network
```

```python
# Retry logic driven entirely by method properties and status class.

SAFE       = {"GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS", "TRACE"}
IDEMPOTENT = SAFE | {"PUT", "DELETE"}

def may_retry(method, status=None, timed_out=False, has_idempotency_key=False):
    """The rules every well-behaved HTTP client implements."""
    if timed_out:
        # No response at all: only safe-to-repeat requests may be re-sent.
        return method in IDEMPOTENT or has_idempotency_key
    if status is None:
        return False
    if 500 <= status < 600 and status != 501:
        return method in IDEMPOTENT or has_idempotency_key
    if status == 429:
        return True                     # rate limited: honour Retry-After
    return False                        # 4xx: the request itself is wrong

cases = [
    ("GET",    None, True,  False), ("POST",   None, True,  False),
    ("POST",   None, True,  True),  ("PUT",    503,  False, False),
    ("POST",   503,  False, False), ("GET",    404,  False, False),
    ("GET",    429,  False, False),
]
print(f"{'method':<8}{'status':<8}{'timeout':<9}{'idem-key':<10}retry?")
for m, s, t, k in cases:
    print(f"{m:<8}{str(s):<8}{str(t):<9}{str(k):<10}{may_retry(m, s, t, k)}")
# method  status  timeout  idem-key  retry?
# GET     None    True     False     True
# POST    None    True     False     False    <- may have already created a user
# POST    None    True     True      True     <- key makes it safe
# PUT     503     False    False     True
# POST    503     False    False     False
# GET     404     False    False     False    <- 4xx: retrying changes nothing
# GET     429     False    False     True     <- back off and retry

# Idempotency in practice: the same PUT twice vs the same POST twice.
users = {}
next_id = [1]

def put_user(uid, data):
    users[uid] = data                        # REPLACE: repeating changes nothing
    return 200 if uid in users else 201

def post_user(data):
    uid = next_id[0]; next_id[0] += 1        # CREATE: repeating creates again
    users[uid] = data
    return 201, uid

for _ in range(3):
    put_user(42, {"name": "alice"})
print(f"\nafter 3 identical PUTs : {len(users)} user(s)")   # after 3 identical PUTs : 1 user(s)
users.clear(); next_id[0] = 1
for _ in range(3):
    post_user({"name": "alice"})
print(f"after 3 identical POSTs: {len(users)} user(s)")     # after 3 identical POSTs: 3 user(s)

# Content negotiation with quality values.
def negotiate(accept_header, available):
    prefs = []
    for part in accept_header.split(","):
        media, _, params = part.strip().partition(";")
        q = 1.0
        for p in params.split(";"):
            if p.strip().startswith("q="):
                q = float(p.strip()[2:])
        prefs.append((media.strip(), q))
    prefs.sort(key=lambda x: -x[1])               # highest q wins
    for media, q in prefs:
        if media in available:
            return media, q
        if media == "*/*":
            return available[0], q
    return None, 0

hdr = "text/html;q=0.8, application/json;q=1.0, */*;q=0.1"
print(f"\nnegotiated: {negotiate(hdr, ['application/json', 'text/html'])}")
# negotiated: ('application/json', 1.0)
#   The server MUST then send `Vary: Accept` so caches key on it.
```

```bash
# HEAD: all the metadata, none of the bytes -- ideal for checking a large file:
$ curl -sI https://example.com/large.iso | grep -iE 'content-length|content-type'
# content-length: 4294967296
# content-type: application/octet-stream
#   4 GB of information obtained without downloading 4 GB.

# 401 vs 403 -- note what the 401 carries:
$ curl -si https://api.example.com/private | head -3
# HTTP/2 401
# www-authenticate: Bearer realm="api"
#   ^ present on 401 by requirement: it tells you HOW to authenticate
$ curl -si -H 'Authorization: Bearer valid-but-unprivileged' \
       https://api.example.com/admin | head -1
# HTTP/2 403
#   No www-authenticate: more credentials will not help.

# Follow a redirect chain and see each hop's code:
$ curl -sIL http://example.com/old | grep -E '^HTTP|^location'
# HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
# location: https://example.com/old
# HTTP/2 308
# location: https://example.com/new
# HTTP/2 200
#   308, not 302: the method is preserved across the redirect.

# 503 should always tell you when to come back:
$ curl -sI https://api.example.com/ | grep -iE '^HTTP|retry-after'
# HTTP/2 503
# retry-after: 120

# Content negotiation and the Vary header that makes it cache-safe:
$ curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' https://example.com/ | grep -iE 'content-encoding|vary'
# content-encoding: gzip
# vary: Accept-Encoding
#   Without Vary, a cache would serve gzipped bytes to a client that cannot decode them.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Methods are characterised by **safe** (no state change) and **idempotent** (repeating equals doing once); these properties drive caching, prefetching, and retry.
- **PUT is idempotent, POST is not** — which is why POST needs an **idempotency key** to be safely retried after a timeout.
- Status **classes** carry meaning on their own: **4xx means do not retry unchanged; 5xx means a retry may help**.
- **401 means unauthenticated** (and must carry `WWW-Authenticate`); **403 means authenticated but forbidden** — only 401 is fixed by credentials.
- **301 is cached aggressively and hard to undo**; **307/308 preserve the request method** where 302 historically did not.
- **502/503/504 point at different components** — bad upstream response, deliberate unavailability, and upstream timeout respectively.
- Content negotiation uses **`Accept` with q-values**, and the server must send **`Vary`** so caches key on the right dimension.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Classify PUT, POST, PATCH, and DELETE as safe and/or idempotent, and state which may be retried automatically after a timeout.
> 2. An API returns 403 to a request with no credentials at all. Explain why 401 would be more correct and what header the 401 must carry.
> 3. A deployment accidentally served `301` to the wrong host for an hour. Explain why the impact outlasts the fix and what you would do about it.
> 4. Interview-style: *A client sees 504 from your load balancer while every application server reports healthy and idle.* (Hint: 504 names which component failed to answer — check what sits between the balancer and the servers it is timing out on.)

#### Persistent Connections and Pipelining

**Theory**

HTTP/1.0 opened a TCP connection, sent one request, read one response, and closed. On a page with eighty images, that is eighty connections. The cost is not the connections themselves but the **round trips** each one requires before a single byte of content moves.

Count them for one HTTPS request on a cold connection:

```text
  TCP SYN -> SYN/ACK -> ACK          1 RTT
  TLS ClientHello -> ... -> Finished 1 RTT (TLS 1.3) or 2 (TLS 1.2)
  HTTP request -> response           1 RTT
                                     ----
                                     3 RTTs before the first content byte
```

At 80 ms RTT that is 240 ms **per resource**, before transferring anything. There is also a slower, subtler cost: every new TCP connection restarts **congestion control** at the initial window (Chapter 7), so it begins slow even when the path is fast.

**Persistent connections** (**keep-alive**), default in HTTP/1.1, fix this by reusing one TCP connection for many request-response exchanges. The handshakes are paid once, and the congestion window stays warm and grows. `Connection: close` opts out; in HTTP/1.0 the opposite applied and you needed `Connection: keep-alive` to opt in.

**Pipelining** was the next step: send multiple requests without waiting for the responses in between. It works in principle and failed in practice, for one decisive reason — **HTTP/1.1 responses must return in request order**. A slow first response blocks every response behind it, even if they are ready. This is **head-of-line blocking at the application layer**, and combined with buggy proxies that mishandled pipelined requests, it led every major browser to disable pipelining.

What browsers did instead was **open several parallel connections** — conventionally six per origin. It is a workaround with real costs: six TCP handshakes, six TLS handshakes, six congestion windows competing with each other on the same bottleneck, and six times the server's per-connection memory. It also spawned the **domain sharding** hack, spreading assets across `img1.example.com`, `img2.example.com` and so on to get past the six-connection limit — an optimisation that becomes actively harmful under HTTP/2.

This is exactly the problem HTTP/2 was designed to solve, and the reason it is described in terms of *multiplexing*: many concurrent exchanges on **one** connection, without the ordering constraint that killed pipelining.

**Examples**

```text
Three strategies, same eight resources, 80 ms RTT

 HTTP/1.0: connection per request
  [SYN..TLS..GET..resp][SYN..TLS..GET..resp][SYN..TLS..GET..resp]...
  |<-- 240 ms -->|<-- 240 ms -->|<-- 240 ms -->|  x8 = 1920 ms

 HTTP/1.1 keep-alive: one connection, sequential requests
  [SYN..TLS][GET..resp][GET..resp][GET..resp]...
  |<-160ms->|<- 80ms ->|<- 80ms ->|          160 + 8x80 = 800 ms

 HTTP/1.1 keep-alive x6 parallel connections
  conn1 [SYN..TLS][GET..resp][GET..resp]
  conn2 [SYN..TLS][GET..resp]
  ...                                        ~160 + 2x80 = 320 ms
  cost: 6 handshakes, 6 congestion windows competing


 PIPELINING and why it died:

  requests:   GET /a  GET /b  GET /c     (sent back to back, no waiting)
  server:     /a is a slow database query; /b and /c are ready instantly

  responses:  [....... /a (900 ms) .......][/b][/c]
              ^ /b and /c were READY but MUST wait: responses are ordered
                                                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
              head-of-line blocking at the APPLICATION layer
```

```python
# Quantify the round trips. This is the whole argument for keep-alive.

def page_load_ms(resources, rtt=80, tls=True, mode="keepalive", parallel=1):
    handshake = rtt + (rtt if tls else 0)      # TCP 1 RTT + TLS 1.3 1 RTT
    if mode == "close":                         # HTTP/1.0: reconnect every time
        total = resources * (handshake + rtt)
    else:                                       # handshake once per connection
        per_conn = -(-resources // parallel)    # ceil division
        total = handshake + per_conn * rtt
    return total

print(f"{'strategy':<34}{'ms':>8}")
print(f"{'HTTP/1.0 (new conn each)':<34}{page_load_ms(8, mode='close'):>8}")
print(f"{'HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, 1 conn':<34}{page_load_ms(8):>8}")
print(f"{'HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, 6 conns':<34}{page_load_ms(8, parallel=6):>8}")
print(f"{'HTTP/2 multiplexed, 1 conn':<34}{page_load_ms(8, parallel=8):>8}")
# strategy                                ms
# HTTP/1.0 (new conn each)              1920
# HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, 1 conn            800
# HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, 6 conns           320
# HTTP/2 multiplexed, 1 conn             240
#   Note HTTP/2 is only slightly better than 6 connections HERE --
#   the real win appears with dozens of resources and on lossy links.

# Head-of-line blocking: why pipelining failed.
def pipelined_completion(service_times_ms):
    """Responses must be returned IN ORDER, regardless of readiness."""
    ready, done, elapsed = [], [], 0
    for i, t in enumerate(service_times_ms):
        ready.append(t)                          # each is ready after its own time
    for i, t in enumerate(service_times_ms):
        elapsed = max(elapsed, t)                # cannot finish before it is ready
        done.append((i, elapsed))                # ...and cannot jump the queue
    return done

slow_first = [900, 10, 10, 10]
print("\npipelined, slow request first:")
for i, finish in pipelined_completion(slow_first):
    print(f"  response {i}: ready at {slow_first[i]:>4} ms, delivered at {finish:>4} ms")
# pipelined, slow request first:
#   response 0: ready at  900 ms, delivered at  900 ms
#   response 1: ready at   10 ms, delivered at  900 ms   <- blocked 890 ms
#   response 2: ready at   10 ms, delivered at  900 ms
#   response 3: ready at   10 ms, delivered at  900 ms
#   Three fast responses held hostage by one slow one. HTTP/2 removes this
#   constraint at the application layer (TCP-level HOL blocking remains).

# The hidden cost of parallel connections: congestion windows do not share.
def effective_start_rate(conns, iw_segments=10, mss=1460, rtt_ms=80):
    """Each new connection starts at the initial window, then must grow."""
    first_rtt_bytes = conns * iw_segments * mss
    return first_rtt_bytes * 8 / (rtt_ms / 1000) / 1e6   # Mb/s in the first RTT

for c in (1, 6):
    print(f"\n{c} connection(s): {effective_start_rate(c):.1f} Mb/s in the first RTT")
# 1 connection(s): 1.5 Mb/s in the first RTT
# 6 connection(s): 8.8 Mb/s in the first RTT
#   Faster start -- but 6 windows now probe the same bottleneck independently,
#   which is unfair to other flows and causes more loss.
```

```bash
# Prove reuse: 3 requests, 1 connection.
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'connects=%{num_connects} time=%{time_total}\n' \
    https://example.com/a https://example.com/b https://example.com/c
# connects=1 time=0.412
#             ^ one TCP+TLS handshake served all three

# Force a new connection each time and watch the cost:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -H 'Connection: close' \
    -w 'connects=%{num_connects} time=%{time_total}\n' \
    https://example.com/a https://example.com/b https://example.com/c
# connects=3 time=0.907

# Where the time actually goes on a cold connection:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} tcp=%{time_connect} \
tls=%{time_appconnect} first_byte=%{time_starttransfer}\n' https://example.com/
# dns=0.021 tcp=0.103 tls=0.288 first_byte=0.371
#           ^1 RTT     ^+1 RTT     ^+1 RTT      = 3 RTTs before content

# Server-side keep-alive settings decide how long reuse is possible:
$ curl -sI https://example.com/ | grep -i keep-alive
# keep-alive: timeout=5, max=100
#   5 s idle before close; 100 requests per connection.

# Count a browser's parallel connections to one origin:
$ ss -tn dst 93.184.216.34 | wc -l
# 6        <- the conventional per-origin limit for HTTP/1.1
```

**Key takeaways**

- A cold HTTPS request costs about **three round trips** (TCP, TLS 1.3, HTTP) before the first content byte, plus a cold congestion window.
- **Persistent connections** (default in HTTP/1.1) amortise handshakes across many exchanges and keep the congestion window warm.
- **Pipelining** sends requests without waiting but requires **in-order responses**, causing **application-layer head-of-line blocking** — which, with buggy proxies, is why browsers disabled it.
- Browsers worked around this with **~6 parallel connections per origin**, paying six handshakes and running six competing congestion windows.
- **Domain sharding** extended that hack further and becomes counterproductive under HTTP/2.
- HTTP/2's multiplexing exists precisely to get pipelining's benefit **without the ordering constraint**.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Compute total load time for 20 resources at 60 ms RTT under HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1 single connection, and 6 parallel connections.
> 2. Explain why pipelining a slow request ahead of three fast ones is worse than not pipelining at all.
> 3. List three distinct costs of opening six parallel connections instead of one.
> 4. Interview-style: *Domain sharding made sites faster under HTTP/1.1 and slower under HTTP/2. Explain both halves.* (Hint: ask what sharding was buying, and whether HTTP/2 still has the limit it was buying around — then count handshakes and congestion windows.)

#### Cookies and Session State

**Theory**

HTTP is stateless: the server is not obliged to remember anything between requests. That is excellent for scaling and useless for anything involving a logged-in user. Cookies are the retrofit that reconciles the two.

The mechanism is deliberately minimal. The server sends `Set-Cookie: name=value` in a response; the browser stores it and returns `Cookie: name=value` on every subsequent matching request. The server remains stateless in the sense that any of its machines can handle any request — the state travels with the client.

There are two fundamentally different ways to use that channel, and confusing them causes both security and scaling problems:

- **Session identifier.** The cookie holds an opaque random ID; the real state lives server-side in a session store. The cookie is small and reveals nothing, but every request requires a lookup, and the store becomes shared infrastructure that must be replicated.
- **Self-contained token.** The cookie holds the state itself, signed or encrypted (a JWT, for example). No lookup is needed and servers stay genuinely stateless, but the token is larger, is sent on every request, and **cannot be revoked before it expires** without reintroducing server-side state.

The attributes are where the security lives, and each one closes a specific attack:

| Attribute | Effect | Attack it addresses |
|---|---|---|
| **`Secure`** | Sent only over HTTPS | Network interception |
| **`HttpOnly`** | Invisible to JavaScript | XSS stealing the session |
| **`SameSite=Strict`** | Never sent cross-site | CSRF |
| **`SameSite=Lax`** | Sent on top-level GET navigation only | CSRF, with usable links |
| **`SameSite=None`** | Always sent; **requires `Secure`** | Deliberate cross-site use |
| **`Domain`** | Widens scope to subdomains | (Widening is a risk, not a defence) |
| **`Path`** | Restricts to a path prefix | Weak scoping |
| **`Max-Age` / `Expires`** | Lifetime; absent means session-only | Limits the theft window |
| **`__Host-` prefix** | Forces Secure, no Domain, Path=/ | Subdomain cookie injection |

Two subtleties that matter:

**Cookies ignore ports and are only partly scoped by scheme.** A cookie set by `example.com:8080` is sent to `example.com:443`. The same-origin policy that governs JavaScript does **not** govern cookies, which is why `Secure` and `__Host-` prefixes exist as explicit corrections.

**`SameSite` changed defaults.** Modern browsers treat a cookie with no `SameSite` attribute as `Lax`, which broke a great deal of legitimate cross-site integration and is a common cause of "it works in one browser" reports.

The alternatives are worth knowing because they have different trade-offs rather than being strictly better. `localStorage` is not sent automatically, so it avoids CSRF entirely but is fully readable by JavaScript, so XSS defeats it — many teams switch to it for CSRF reasons and quietly worsen their XSS exposure. The `Authorization: Bearer` header must be attached explicitly, which is why it is the norm for APIs where there is no browser to manage cookie jars.

**Examples**

```text
The cookie round trip, and what each attribute closes off

  1. Client logs in
     POST /login  { user, pass }

  2. Server responds with state the client must carry back
     HTTP/1.1 200 OK
     Set-Cookie: sid=9f2a...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600; Path=/
                 \_______/   \____/  \______/  \___________/ \__________/
                 the value   HTTPS   no JS     no cross-site  expiry
                             only    access     sending

  3. Every later request carries it automatically
     GET /account
     Cookie: sid=9f2a...


  WHAT EACH ATTRIBUTE BLOCKS

  no Secure    -> [attacker on cafe wifi] reads sid from a plaintext request
  no HttpOnly  -> [XSS payload] document.cookie -> exfiltrates sid
  no SameSite  -> [evil.com] auto-submits a form to bank.com; browser
                  helpfully attaches YOUR cookie = CSRF


  SESSION ID vs SELF-CONTAINED TOKEN

  sid=9f2a...              (32 bytes)        JWT eyJhbGci... (800 bytes)
      |                                          |
      v                                          v
  [session store]                            [verify signature]
  lookup per request                         no lookup
  revoke instantly  <-- the key difference --> cannot revoke early
  shared infrastructure                      truly stateless servers
```

```python
# Building a session cookie correctly, and showing what each flag prevents.
import secrets, hmac, hashlib, base64, json, time

SECRET = secrets.token_bytes(32)

def set_cookie_header(name, value, *, secure=True, http_only=True,
                      same_site="Lax", max_age=3600, path="/", domain=None):
    parts = [f"{name}={value}", f"Path={path}", f"Max-Age={max_age}"]
    if domain:     parts.append(f"Domain={domain}")   # widens scope: use sparingly
    if secure:     parts.append("Secure")             # HTTPS only
    if http_only:  parts.append("HttpOnly")           # invisible to document.cookie
    if same_site:  parts.append(f"SameSite={same_site}")
    return "Set-Cookie: " + "; ".join(parts)

sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(24)                        # opaque, unguessable
print(set_cookie_header("__Host-sid", sid))
# Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=Xk3...; Path=/; Max-Age=3600; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
#   The __Host- prefix makes the browser REJECT the cookie unless it is
#   Secure, has no Domain, and has Path=/ -- it cannot be set by a subdomain.

# Self-contained token: state in the cookie, integrity by signature.
def make_token(payload, ttl=3600):
    body = {**payload, "exp": int(time.time()) + ttl}
    raw = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps(body).encode()).rstrip(b"=")
    sig = hmac.new(SECRET, raw, hashlib.sha256).digest()
    return raw.decode() + "." + base64.urlsafe_b64encode(sig).rstrip(b"=").decode()

def verify_token(token):
    raw, _, sig = token.partition(".")
    expected = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(
        hmac.new(SECRET, raw.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()).rstrip(b"=").decode()
    if not hmac.compare_digest(sig, expected):
        return None, "bad signature"                   # tampering detected
    body = json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw + "=="))
    if body["exp"] < time.time():
        return None, "expired"
    return body, "ok"

tok = make_token({"uid": 42, "role": "user"})
print(f"\ntoken length: {len(tok)} bytes (sent on EVERY request)")
print(verify_token(tok))
# token length: 131 bytes (sent on EVERY request)
# ({'uid': 42, 'role': 'user', 'exp': 1758...}, 'ok')

forged = tok[:-4] + "AAAA"                             # attacker edits the signature
print(verify_token(forged))
# (None, 'bad signature')

# The revocation problem, stated plainly:
print("\nUser clicks 'log out of all devices' at t=0, token expires at t=3600:")
print("  session ID : delete the row -> revoked INSTANTLY")
print("  JWT        : token stays valid for up to 3600 s unless you keep")
print("               a denylist -- which is server-side state again")

# Overhead comparison over a page load:
for name, size in (("session id", 32), ("JWT", 800)):
    print(f"\n{name:<12} {size:>4} B x 60 requests = {size*60/1024:>6.1f} KB uploaded")
# session id     32 B x 60 requests =    1.9 KB uploaded
# JWT           800 B x 60 requests =   46.9 KB uploaded
#   On a slow uplink, cookie size is a real page-load cost.
```

```bash
# Inspect the cookies a site sets and audit the flags:
$ curl -sI https://example.com/login | grep -i '^set-cookie'
# set-cookie: sid=9f2a8c...; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600

# A jar shows scope: domain, path, secure flag, and expiry:
$ curl -s -c jar.txt https://example.com/login > /dev/null && cat jar.txt
# #HttpOnly_example.com  FALSE  /  TRUE  1790000000  sid  9f2a8c...
#  ^HttpOnly            ^domain   ^path ^secure ^expiry  ^name ^value

# Reuse the jar on a later request -- this is what the browser does for you:
$ curl -s -b jar.txt https://example.com/account | grep -o 'Welcome [a-z]*'
# Welcome alice

# Demonstrate that cookies ignore the PORT:
$ curl -s -b 'sid=x' http://example.com:8080/ -v 2>&1 | grep -i '^> cookie'
# > Cookie: sid=x
#   The same cookie goes to :80, :443, and :8080 alike.
#   Same-origin policy governs JavaScript, NOT the cookie jar.

# Audit a whole site's cookies for missing protections:
$ curl -sI https://example.com/ | grep -i '^set-cookie' | \
    grep -vE 'HttpOnly' && echo 'WARNING: cookie readable by JavaScript'

# Bearer tokens: nothing is automatic, which is the point for APIs:
$ curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://api.example.com/me
# {"uid":42,"role":"user"}
#   No cookie jar, no automatic attachment, therefore no CSRF surface.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Cookies retrofit state onto a stateless protocol: `Set-Cookie` from the server, automatic `Cookie` on every matching request thereafter.
- **Session IDs** keep state server-side (small, instantly revocable, needs a shared store); **self-contained tokens** keep state in the cookie (no lookup, but **not revocable before expiry**).
- **`Secure`** blocks plaintext interception, **`HttpOnly`** blocks XSS theft, **`SameSite`** blocks CSRF — each attribute closes a specific, different attack.
- **Cookies ignore ports** and are not governed by the same-origin policy — the `__Host-` prefix exists to impose strict scoping.
- Modern browsers default absent `SameSite` to **`Lax`**, which silently breaks legitimate cross-site flows.
- `localStorage` avoids CSRF but is **fully exposed to XSS**; `Authorization: Bearer` requires explicit attachment, which is why APIs prefer it.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Write a `Set-Cookie` header for a one-hour session cookie that is HTTPS-only, invisible to JavaScript, and not sent cross-site.
> 2. Explain precisely which attack each of `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, and `SameSite` prevents, and which one none of them prevent.
> 3. Compare session IDs and JWTs on revocation, request size, and infrastructure requirements; pick one for a banking app and justify it.
> 4. Interview-style: *A team moves session tokens from cookies to `localStorage` "to avoid CSRF". Evaluate the change.* (Hint: they removed one attack surface and enlarged another — ask what a successful XSS can now read that it previously could not.)

#### Web Caching and Conditional Requests

**Theory**

The fastest request is the one never sent; the second fastest is the one answered with "nothing changed". HTTP caching provides both, and it is probably the single highest-leverage performance mechanism on the web.

Caches exist at several layers, and a response may be stored at any of them: the **browser cache** (private, one user), a **proxy or corporate cache** (shared), a **CDN edge** (shared, geographically distributed), and a **reverse proxy** in front of the origin. The distinction between **private** and **shared** matters enormously — marking a personalised response cacheable by a shared cache leaks one user's data to another, one of the more serious misconfigurations in web operations.

There are two complementary models.

**Freshness (no request at all).** The server declares how long a response may be reused. While it is fresh, the cache serves it without contacting the origin — zero latency, zero traffic. `Cache-Control` directives govern this:

| Directive | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **`max-age=N`** | Fresh for N seconds |
| **`s-maxage=N`** | Same, but for shared caches only (overrides max-age) |
| **`public`** | May be stored by shared caches |
| **`private`** | Browser only — never a CDN or proxy |
| **`no-cache`** | May store, but **must revalidate** before each reuse |
| **`no-store`** | Must not be written down at all |
| **`must-revalidate`** | Once stale, do not serve without checking |
| **`immutable`** | Will never change — do not even revalidate on reload |
| **`stale-while-revalidate=N`** | Serve stale for N s while refreshing in the background |

`no-cache` and `no-store` are the pair people get wrong: `no-cache` means "check first", `no-store` means "do not keep it". Sensitive data needs `no-store`.

**Validation (a cheap request).** When freshness expires, the cache does not need to re-download — it asks whether anything changed, sending a **validator**:

- **`ETag`** — an opaque version identifier, sent back in `If-None-Match`. Strong (`"abc"`) means byte-identical; weak (`W/"abc"`) means semantically equivalent.
- **`Last-Modified`** — a timestamp, sent back in `If-Modified-Since`. Only one-second resolution, and useless for content that changes more often.

If nothing changed, the server replies **`304 Not Modified`** with headers and **no body**. On a 2 MB image that turns a 2 MB transfer into roughly 200 bytes, at the cost of one round trip.

The strategy that falls out of this, and which every modern build tool implements, is the **cache-busting / immutable pattern**: give static assets content-hashed filenames (`app.4f9a2c.js`) and serve them with `max-age=31536000, immutable`. Because the *name* changes whenever the content does, the asset can be cached forever with no revalidation, and a deployment invalidates nothing — it simply references new names. The HTML that points at them stays short-lived or `no-cache`.

`Vary` is the final piece: it tells caches which request headers form part of the cache key. Serving gzipped content without `Vary: Accept-Encoding` means a client that cannot decode gzip may be handed the compressed bytes.

**Examples**

```text
The decision a cache makes on every request

              request arrives at the cache
                          |
                is there a stored response?
                   /                  \
                  NO                   YES
                  |                      |
             fetch from origin      is it still FRESH?
                                   (age < max-age)
                                     /          \
                                   YES           NO
                                    |             |
                              SERVE FROM       do we have a validator?
                              CACHE            (ETag / Last-Modified)
                              0 RTT, 0 bytes    /          \
                                              YES           NO
                                               |             |
                                     conditional GET    full fetch
                                     If-None-Match      200 + body
                                        /      \
                                 304 (no body)  200 (new body)
                                 ~200 bytes     full transfer
                                 1 RTT          1 RTT


 Cost of the three outcomes for a 2 MB image on a 50 ms RTT link:

   fresh hit        0 ms,        0 bytes
   304 revalidate  50 ms,    ~200 bytes      <- 99.99% saved
   200 full fetch  ~370 ms, 2,000,000 bytes
```

```python
# A cache implementing both freshness and validation.
import hashlib, time

class HTTPCache:
    def __init__(self):
        self.store = {}     # url -> dict(body, etag, stored_at, max_age, private)

    def _fresh(self, entry, now):
        return (now - entry["stored_at"]) < entry["max_age"]

    def fetch(self, url, origin, now=None, shared=False):
        now = now or time.time()
        entry = self.store.get(url)

        if entry:
            if shared and entry["private"]:
                pass                               # a shared cache MUST NOT use it
            elif self._fresh(entry, now):
                age = int(now - entry["stored_at"])
                return "HIT (fresh)", len(entry["body"]), 0, age
            else:
                # Stale: revalidate rather than re-download.
                status, body, etag = origin(url, if_none_match=entry["etag"])
                if status == 304:
                    entry["stored_at"] = now       # refreshed, body reused
                    return "HIT (304 revalidated)", 200, 1, 0
                entry.update(body=body, etag=etag, stored_at=now)
                return "MISS (changed)", len(body), 1, 0

        status, body, etag = origin(url)
        self.store[url] = {"body": body, "etag": etag, "stored_at": now,
                           "max_age": 300, "private": False}
        return "MISS (cold)", len(body), 1, 0

IMAGE = b"x" * 2_000_000
def origin(url, if_none_match=None):
    etag = '"' + hashlib.md5(IMAGE).hexdigest()[:12] + '"'
    if if_none_match == etag:
        return 304, b"", etag                      # unchanged: no body at all
    return 200, IMAGE, etag

c, t0 = HTTPCache(), 1_000_000
print(f"{'t':>6}  {'result':<24}{'bytes':>10}{'rtts':>6}")
for offset in (0, 60, 299, 400):
    result, nbytes, rtts, age = c.fetch("/img.png", origin, now=t0 + offset)
    print(f"{offset:>6}  {result:<24}{nbytes:>10,}{rtts:>6}")
#      t  result                       bytes  rtts
#      0  MISS (cold)              2,000,000     1
#     60  HIT (fresh)              2,000,000     0    <- no network at all
#    299  HIT (fresh)              2,000,000     0
#    400  HIT (304 revalidated)          200     1    <- 2 MB avoided

# The immutable pattern: the NAME encodes the content, so nothing expires.
def asset_url(path, content):
    digest = hashlib.sha256(content).hexdigest()[:8]
    stem, _, ext = path.rpartition(".")
    return f"/{stem}.{digest}.{ext}"

v1 = b"console.log('v1')"
v2 = b"console.log('v2')"
print(f"\nv1 -> {asset_url('app.js', v1)}   Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable")
print(f"v2 -> {asset_url('app.js', v2)}   (a DIFFERENT url: nothing to invalidate)")
# v1 -> /app.9d4b1e02.js   Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
# v2 -> /app.4f2a7c81.js   (a DIFFERENT url: nothing to invalidate)
#   Deployment changes the HTML reference; the old file simply stops being requested.

# Why Vary exists -- the bug it prevents:
print("\nWithout `Vary: Accept-Encoding`:")
print("  client A (gzip capable)     -> cache stores GZIPPED bytes")
print("  client B (no gzip support)  -> cache serves the SAME gzipped bytes")
print("  -> client B receives unreadable binary")
```

```bash
# Read the caching policy of a response:
$ curl -sI https://example.com/static/app.4f9a2c.js | grep -iE 'cache-control|etag|age'
# cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
# etag: "4f9a2c81b3"
# age: 84213
#   ^ this response has been sitting in a shared cache for ~23 hours

# Perform a conditional request by hand and observe the 304:
$ ETAG=$(curl -sI https://example.com/img.png | awk '/etag/{print $2}' | tr -d '\r')
$ curl -sI -H "If-None-Match: $ETAG" https://example.com/img.png | head -1
# HTTP/2 304
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'bytes=%{size_download}\n' \
       -H "If-None-Match: $ETAG" https://example.com/img.png
# bytes=0        <- a 304 carries NO body

# Measure what caching is actually worth:
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'cold  %{time_total}s %{size_download} bytes\n' \
       https://example.com/img.png
# cold  0.371s 2000000 bytes
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '304   %{time_total}s %{size_download} bytes\n' \
       -H "If-None-Match: $ETAG" https://example.com/img.png
# 304   0.052s 0 bytes

# no-cache vs no-store -- check that sensitive pages use the right one:
$ curl -sI https://bank.example.com/statement | grep -i cache-control
# cache-control: no-store, private
#   no-store: never written to disk. `no-cache` would still be STORED.

# Confirm a personalised response is not marked public:
$ curl -sI -b jar.txt https://example.com/account | grep -iE 'cache-control|vary'
# cache-control: private, no-store
# vary: Cookie
#   `public` here would let a CDN serve alice's account page to bob.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Caching offers two wins: **freshness** (no request at all) and **validation** (a ~200-byte `304` instead of the full body).
- **`max-age`/`s-maxage`** set freshness; **`private` vs `public`** decides whether shared caches and CDNs may store a response — mismarking this leaks user data.
- **`no-cache` means revalidate before reuse; `no-store` means never write it down** — sensitive data requires `no-store`.
- **`ETag`/`If-None-Match`** and **`Last-Modified`/`If-Modified-Since`** are the validators; `304 Not Modified` returns headers with **no body**.
- The **content-hashed immutable pattern** (`app.4f9a2c.js` with `max-age=31536000, immutable`) makes static assets permanently cacheable and deployments invalidation-free.
- **`Vary`** declares which request headers belong to the cache key — omitting `Vary: Accept-Encoding` can deliver unreadable compressed bytes.

#### HTTP/2 Multiplexing and Header Compression

**Theory**

HTTP/1.1's problems were all consequences of one design choice: **one connection carries one exchange at a time, in order**. Pipelining could not fix it, and parallel connections only worked around it at real cost. HTTP/2 (RFC 7540, 2015, derived from Google's SPDY) changes the framing layer underneath while keeping HTTP's semantics — the same methods, status codes, and headers — completely intact.

Four changes matter.

**1. Binary framing.** HTTP/2 messages are binary frames, not text lines. Each frame has a 9-byte header: 24-bit length, 8-bit type, 8-bit flags, 31-bit stream identifier. This is less human-readable and far less ambiguous — the entire class of parsing discrepancies behind request smuggling largely disappears, because a frame's length is explicit.

**2. Multiplexing over streams.** A connection carries many independent **streams**, each with an ID; frames from different streams interleave freely. Because every frame is tagged, responses may arrive **in any order** — which is exactly the constraint that made pipelining useless. One connection now does what six were doing, without ordering the responses.

**3. Header compression (HPACK).** HTTP headers are extraordinarily repetitive: the same `User-Agent`, `Accept`, and `Cookie` on every one of a hundred requests. HPACK compresses them using a **static table** of 61 common header entries, a **dynamic table** of values seen earlier on this connection, and Huffman coding for literals. A repeated header can shrink to a single index byte, turning kilobytes of per-request overhead into tens of bytes.

**4. Stream prioritisation and flow control.** Streams carry dependency and weight information so a client can express that the stylesheet matters more than a below-the-fold image, and there is per-stream and per-connection flow control independent of TCP's.

**Server push** was the fifth feature and is the instructive failure. The idea — send the CSS before the browser asks for it — foundered because the server cannot know what the client already has cached, so pushes were frequently wasted bandwidth. Chrome removed support in 2022; the replacement is **`103 Early Hints`**, which tells the client what to fetch and lets the cache decide.

The one problem HTTP/2 does **not** solve is the decisive one for HTTP/3: **TCP-level head-of-line blocking**. HTTP/2 removed the ordering constraint at the application layer, but all streams still ride a single TCP connection, and TCP delivers bytes strictly in order. Lose one segment and **every** stream stalls until it is retransmitted — even streams whose data already arrived. On a clean link HTTP/2 is a clear win; on a lossy mobile link it can be *worse* than HTTP/1.1 with six connections, because six connections at least fail independently.

A practical consequence: **stop sharding domains.** HTTP/2 wants one connection per origin so that HPACK's dynamic table, prioritisation, and a single congestion window all work. Sharding splits them back apart.

**Examples**

```text
HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 on one connection

 HTTP/1.1 (ordered, one at a time)
  conn: [--- req A ---][--- resp A ---][--- req B ---][--- resp B ---]
        responses MUST come back in request order

 HTTP/2 (multiplexed, interleaved, any order)
  conn: [A:HEADERS][B:HEADERS][C:HEADERS][B:DATA][C:DATA][A:DATA][B:DATA]
         \_______/  \_______/             \____/  \____/  \____/
         stream 1   stream 3              B finishes FIRST, even though
                                          it was requested second

 The 9-byte frame header that makes this possible:

   0                   1                   2                   3
   +-----------------------------------------------+
   |                 Length (24)                   |
   +---------------+---------------+---------------+
   |   Type (8)    |   Flags (8)   |
   +-+-------------+---------------+-------------------------------+
   |R|                 Stream Identifier (31)                      |
   +=+=============================================================+
   |                   Frame Payload                               |
   +---------------------------------------------------------------+
      ^ every frame is TAGGED with its stream -> interleaving is safe


 WHAT HTTP/2 DOES NOT FIX: TCP head-of-line blocking

  TCP byte stream:  [s1][s3][s5][XX][s1][s3][s5][s1]
                                  ^^ one lost segment
  TCP will not deliver ANY later bytes until XX is retransmitted.
  Streams 3 and 5 are stalled by a loss that belonged to stream 1.

  6 x HTTP/1.1 connections: a loss stalls ONE connection.
  1 x HTTP/2 connection:    a loss stalls ALL streams.
  This is why HTTP/2 can lose to HTTP/1.1 on a lossy mobile link.
```

```python
# HPACK: why header compression matters so much on a real page.

STATIC_TABLE = {                       # abbreviated RFC 7541 static table
    ":method GET": 2, ":path /": 4, ":scheme https": 7,
    ":status 200": 8, "accept-encoding gzip, deflate": 16,
}

class HPACKEncoder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.dynamic = {}              # values learned on THIS connection
        self.next_index = 62           # dynamic table starts after the static one

    def encode(self, headers):
        out = 0
        for name, value in headers:
            key = f"{name} {value}"
            if key in STATIC_TABLE:
                out += 1                                   # a single index byte
            elif key in self.dynamic:
                out += 1                                   # seen before: 1 byte
            else:
                self.dynamic[key] = self.next_index        # remember for next time
                self.next_index += 1
                out += len(name) + len(value) + 2          # literal, roughly
        return out

request = [
    (":method", "GET"), (":scheme", "https"), (":authority", "example.com"),
    ("user-agent", "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 "
                   "(KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0 Safari/537.36"),
    ("accept", "text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8"),
    ("accept-encoding", "gzip, deflate"),
    ("cookie", "sid=9f2a8c1d4b7e; prefs=dark; consent=all; ab_test=variant_b"),
]

enc = HPACKEncoder()
uncompressed = sum(len(n) + len(v) + 4 for n, v in request)
sizes = [enc.encode([(n, v if n != ":path" else f"/asset{i}.js")
                     for n, v in request]) for i in range(1, 6)]

print(f"uncompressed, per request : {uncompressed} bytes")
for i, s in enumerate(sizes, 1):
    print(f"  HPACK request {i}        : {s:>4} bytes")
print(f"\n100 requests uncompressed : {uncompressed*100:>7,} bytes")
print(f"100 requests with HPACK   : {sizes[0] + sizes[-1]*99:>7,} bytes")
# uncompressed, per request : 359 bytes
#   HPACK request 1        :  296 bytes
#   HPACK request 2        :    7 bytes
#   HPACK request 3        :    7 bytes
#   HPACK request 4        :    7 bytes
#   HPACK request 5        :    7 bytes
#
# 100 requests uncompressed :  35,900 bytes
# 100 requests with HPACK   :     989 bytes
#   ~97% saved. The first request pays; every later one is nearly free.

# TCP head-of-line blocking, measured.
def completion_times(n_streams, loss_at_ms=None, rtt=80, stream_ms=100):
    """All streams share one TCP connection: a loss stalls everything."""
    times = {}
    for s in range(n_streams):
        t = stream_ms
        if loss_at_ms is not None and loss_at_ms < stream_ms:
            t += rtt                                    # ALL streams wait for RTO
        times[s] = t
    return times

clean  = completion_times(5)
lossy  = completion_times(5, loss_at_ms=40)
print(f"\nclean link : all 5 streams finish at {max(clean.values())} ms")
print(f"1 loss     : all 5 streams finish at {max(lossy.values())} ms")
print("           ^ four streams were delayed by a loss that was not theirs")
# clean link : all 5 streams finish at 100 ms
# 1 loss     : all 5 streams finish at 180 ms
```

$ nghttp -nv https://example.com/ 2>&1 | grep -E 'recv|send' | head -8
# send HEADERS frame <length=42, flags=0x25, stream_id=1>
# send HEADERS frame <length=38, flags=0x25, stream_id=3>
# recv HEADERS frame <length=91, flags=0x04, stream_id=3>   <- 3 answers FIRST
# recv DATA frame <length=1024, flags=0x00, stream_id=3>
# recv HEADERS frame <length=88, flags=0x04, stream_id=1>
#   Stream ids are odd for client-initiated streams; interleaving is visible.

# Measure HPACK's effect:
$ nghttp -nv https://example.com/ 2>&1 | grep -E 'HEADERS.*length'
# send HEADERS frame <length=289, ...>   <- first request: literals
# send HEADERS frame <length=12, ...>    <- second: indexed from the dynamic table

# 103 Early Hints, the replacement for server push:
$ curl -sI --http2 https://example.com/ | head -4
# HTTP/2 103
# link: </style.css>; rel=preload; as=style
# HTTP/2 200

# Check whether an origin still shards domains (counterproductive now):
$ curl -s https://example.com/ | grep -oE 'https://[a-z0-9]+\.example\.com' | sort -u
