> 2. State what happens if a program calls `select()` on file descriptor 2000, and why this is worse than an error.
> 3. Explain why every socket in an event loop must be non-blocking, giving a concrete failure scenario.
> 4. Interview-style: *A `poll()`-based server serving 20,000 mostly idle connections burns 60% CPU while handling almost no traffic.* (Hint: count the work done per call versus the number of events returned, and ask what the kernel has to redo every time.)

#### epoll and kqueue

**Theory**

The defect in `select` and `poll` is structural: **the kernel is told the entire watch list on every call, and therefore must examine all of it every time**. Nothing is remembered. If you watch the same 10,000 sockets a thousand times per second, you describe those 10,000 sockets a thousand times per second.

**`epoll`** (Linux 2.5.44, 2002) and **`kqueue`** (FreeBSD 4.1, 2000) fix this by **moving the watch list into the kernel**. You register interest once; the kernel maintains the set and, crucially, maintains a **ready list** updated by the network stack as events occur. When you call `epoll_wait()`, the kernel returns the ready list directly — **O(number of ready events)**, entirely independent of how many descriptors are being watched.

This is the change that made 10,000+ connections routine, and it is why every modern server and async runtime is built on one of these interfaces.

`epoll` has three calls:

- **`epoll_create1()`** — create an epoll instance, itself a file descriptor.
- **`epoll_ctl()`** — `ADD`, `MOD`, or `DEL` a descriptor and the events you care about. Called once per change, not once per loop.
- **`epoll_wait()`** — block until events occur; returns **only the ready ones**.

The genuinely important concept is the **trigger mode**:

**Level-triggered (LT)**, the default and the same semantics as `poll`: report readiness **as long as the condition holds**. If 1,000 bytes are readable and you read 100, the next `epoll_wait()` reports it readable again. Forgiving, harder to misuse, and the right default.

**Edge-triggered (ET)**: report **only on a transition** — when new data arrives. If you do not drain the socket completely, you will **not be told again**, and the connection silently hangs. ET requires that you **loop reading until `EAGAIN`**, and it mandates non-blocking sockets. In exchange it produces fewer wakeups, which matters at very high event rates.

| | Level-triggered | Edge-triggered |
|---|---|---|
| Notifies | While the condition holds | **Only on a change** |
| Must drain fully | No | **Yes, until `EAGAIN`** |
| Risk | Extra wakeups | **Silent stalls if you under-read** |
| Non-blocking required | Recommended | **Mandatory** |
| Used by | nginx (default), most code | High-performance event loops |

`kqueue` is the BSD and macOS equivalent, and is arguably the better design: a single `kevent()` call both registers interest and retrieves events, and it handles more than sockets — file changes, process exits, signals, and timers all flow through the same mechanism. `epoll` needs `signalfd`, `timerfd`, and `inotify` to cover the same ground.

Because these interfaces are platform-specific, portable code uses a wrapper — **libevent**, **libev**, or **libuv** (which powers Node.js) — that selects `epoll`, `kqueue`, or `poll` at runtime. Almost nobody writes directly against `epoll` outside of the runtimes themselves.

**Examples**

```text
Where the watch list lives

  poll(): described in full, every call
     userspace                          kernel
     [10,000 pollfd entries] --copy--> scan all 10,000
                            <-returns- "3 are ready"
     ^ 10,000 entries crossing the boundary, every single call

  epoll: registered ONCE; kernel maintains a READY LIST
     userspace                          kernel
     epoll_ctl(ADD, fd) x 10,000 -----> +-------------------+
        (once, at registration)         | interest set      |
                                        |   (red-black tree)|
     epoll_wait() -------------------->  | ready list        |
                                        |   [fd 7][fd 12]   | <- updated by the
                 <-- returns 2 entries -+-------------------+    network stack
     ^ only the READY ones cross the boundary


 COST COMPARISON: 10,000 watched, 3 active

   select/poll : 10,000 units of work -> 3 events    (3,333 units per event)
   epoll       :      3 units of work -> 3 events    (    1 unit  per event)


 LEVEL-TRIGGERED vs EDGE-TRIGGERED

  1000 bytes arrive; your handler reads only 100.

  LEVEL-TRIGGERED                     EDGE-TRIGGERED
  epoll_wait -> fd readable           epoll_wait -> fd readable
  read 100 (900 remain)               read 100 (900 remain)
  epoll_wait -> fd readable AGAIN     epoll_wait -> ...BLOCKS...
  read 100 (800 remain)               ^ NO new data arrived, so no new EDGE.
  ...                                   The 900 bytes sit there forever.
  eventually drained                    THE CONNECTION HANGS SILENTLY.

  ET is correct only with:
     while ((n = read(fd, buf, size)) > 0) { process(buf, n); }
     if (n < 0 && errno == EAGAIN) { /* NOW it is genuinely drained */ }
```

```c
#include <sys/epoll.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <fcntl.h>
#include <errno.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>

#define MAX_EVENTS 512

static void set_nonblocking(int fd) {
    int flags = fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0);
    fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK);
}

int main(void) {
    int listen_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    int yes = 1;
    setsockopt(listen_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof yes);
    struct sockaddr_in addr = { .sin_family = AF_INET,
                                .sin_port = htons(8080),
                                .sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY) };
    bind(listen_fd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr);
    listen(listen_fd, 512);
    set_nonblocking(listen_fd);

    /* The epoll instance is itself a file descriptor. */
    int ep = epoll_create1(0);

    struct epoll_event ev = { .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = listen_fd };
    epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd, &ev);   /* registered ONCE */

    struct epoll_event events[MAX_EVENTS];

    for (;;) {
        /* Returns ONLY ready descriptors: O(ready), not O(watched). */
        int n = epoll_wait(ep, events, MAX_EVENTS, -1);

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int fd = events[i].data.fd;

            if (events[i].events & (EPOLLERR | EPOLLHUP)) {
                epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_DEL, fd, NULL);
                close(fd);
                continue;
            }

            if (fd == listen_fd) {
                /* EDGE-TRIGGERED listener: accept ALL pending connections,
                 * or the ones you skip will never be reported again. */
                for (;;) {
                    int conn = accept(listen_fd, NULL, NULL);
                    if (conn < 0) {
                        if (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK) break;
                        break;
                    }
                    set_nonblocking(conn);
                    /* EPOLLET = edge-triggered. Without it, level-triggered. */
                    struct epoll_event cev = { .events = EPOLLIN | EPOLLET,
                                               .data.fd = conn };
                    epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, conn, &cev);
                }
                continue;
            }

            if (events[i].events & EPOLLIN) {
                /* EDGE-TRIGGERED: drain until EAGAIN, or the remainder is lost
                 * and this connection stalls forever with no error. */
                for (;;) {
                    char buf[4096];
                    ssize_t r = read(fd, buf, sizeof buf);
                    if (r > 0) {
                        write(fd, buf, (size_t)r);
                    } else if (r == 0) {              /* peer closed */
                        epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_DEL, fd, NULL);
                        close(fd);
                        break;
                    } else {
                        if (errno == EAGAIN || errno == EWOULDBLOCK)
                            break;                     /* NOW genuinely drained */
                        if (errno == EINTR) continue;
                        epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_DEL, fd, NULL);
                        close(fd);
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

```python
import select, socket, errno

# Python exposes epoll directly on Linux.
def epoll_server(port=8080, edge_triggered=False):
    srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    srv.bind(("0.0.0.0", port)); srv.listen(512)
    srv.setblocking(False)

    ep = select.epoll()
    mask = select.EPOLLIN | (select.EPOLLET if edge_triggered else 0)
    ep.register(srv.fileno(), select.EPOLLIN)      # registered ONCE
    conns = {}

    try:
        while True:
            for fd, event in ep.poll(timeout=1):   # returns ONLY ready fds
                if event & (select.EPOLLHUP | select.EPOLLERR):
                    ep.unregister(fd); conns.pop(fd).close()

                elif fd == srv.fileno():
                    while True:                     # drain the accept queue
                        try:
                            conn, _ = srv.accept()
                        except BlockingIOError:
                            break                   # EAGAIN: no more pending
                        conn.setblocking(False)
                        conns[conn.fileno()] = conn
                        ep.register(conn.fileno(), mask)

                elif event & select.EPOLLIN:
                    conn = conns[fd]
                    if edge_triggered:
                        # MUST loop until EAGAIN, or the rest is never reported.
                        while True:
                            try:
                                data = conn.recv(4096)
                            except BlockingIOError:
                                break               # fully drained
                            if not data:
                                ep.unregister(fd); conns.pop(fd).close(); break
                            conn.sendall(data)
                    else:
                        data = conn.recv(4096)      # LT: one read is fine
                        if not data:
                            ep.unregister(fd); conns.pop(fd).close()
                        else:
                            conn.sendall(data)
    finally:
        ep.close(); srv.close()

# The scaling difference, in one table.
def syscall_cost(watched, active, mechanism, ns_per_fd=20, ns_base=500):
    if mechanism in ("select", "poll"):
        return (watched * ns_per_fd * 2 + ns_base) / 1000   # both directions
    return (active * ns_per_fd + ns_base) / 1000            # epoll: O(active)

print(f"{'watched':>9}{'active':>8}{'poll (us)':>12}{'epoll (us)':>13}{'speedup':>10}")
for watched in (100, 1_000, 10_000, 100_000):
    active = max(1, watched // 100)
    p = syscall_cost(watched, active, "poll")
    e = syscall_cost(watched, active, "epoll")
    print(f"{watched:>9,}{active:>8,}{p:>12.1f}{e:>13.1f}{p/e:>9.0f}x")
#   watched  active   poll (us)   epoll (us)   speedup
#       100       1         4.5          0.5        9x
#     1,000      10        40.5          0.7       58x
#    10,000     100       400.5          2.5      160x
#   100,000   1,000     4,000.5         20.5      195x
#   epoll's cost tracks ACTIVITY; poll's tracks the connection COUNT.

# The edge-triggered bug, made concrete.
def et_simulation(bytes_available, read_size, loop_until_eagain):
    remaining, reads = bytes_available, 0
    if loop_until_eagain:
        while remaining > 0:
            remaining -= min(read_size, remaining); reads += 1
        return reads, remaining, "fully drained -- correct"
    remaining -= min(read_size, remaining); reads = 1
    return reads, remaining, ("STALLED: no new edge will fire, "
                              f"{remaining} bytes stranded forever")

print()
for loop in (False, True):
    reads, left, note = et_simulation(10_000, 4096, loop)
    print(f"  ET, loop_until_eagain={str(loop):<5} reads={reads} left={left:>5}  {note}")
#   ET, loop_until_eagain=False reads=1 left= 5904  STALLED: no new edge will fire, ...
#   ET, loop_until_eagain=True  reads=3 left=    0  fully drained -- correct
#   The stall produces NO error. The connection simply stops responding.

# Portability: what real code actually uses.
wrappers = {
    "libevent": "epoll / kqueue / poll / select, chosen at runtime",
    "libev":    "smaller, faster libevent alternative",
    "libuv":    "powers Node.js; adds a thread pool for file I/O",
    "asyncio":  "Python; uses epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD",
    "netty":    "Java; epoll transport with a NIO fallback",
}
print()
for name, what in wrappers.items():
    print(f"  {name:<10} {what}")
```


**Key takeaways**

- `epoll` and `kqueue` **move the watch list into the kernel** and maintain a **ready list**, making `epoll_wait()` **O(ready events)** rather than O(watched descriptors).
- The three calls are **`epoll_create1`** (make an instance), **`epoll_ctl`** (register once, not per loop), and **`epoll_wait`** (retrieve only ready descriptors).
- **Level-triggered** reports readiness **while the condition holds** and is the safe default; **edge-triggered** reports **only on transitions**.
- Edge-triggered code **must loop until `EAGAIN`** — under-reading produces a **silent stall with no error**, and it requires non-blocking sockets.
- **`kqueue` is the more general design**, covering files, signals, processes, and timers in one interface, where `epoll` needs `signalfd`/`timerfd`/`inotify`.
- Both are **platform-specific**, so portable code uses **libevent, libev, or libuv**, which pick the best mechanism at runtime.

> 2. Describe exactly what goes wrong when edge-triggered code reads 4 KB from a socket holding 10 KB and then returns to the event loop.
> 3. State two reasons an accept loop under edge-triggered mode must call `accept()` repeatedly until it fails.
> 4. Interview-style: *When would you deliberately choose level-triggered over edge-triggered, despite ET's lower wakeup count?* (Hint: weigh the cost of a few extra wakeups against the cost of one connection hanging with no error, and consider who maintains the handler code.)

#### Event Loops and Async I/O

**Theory**

`epoll` solved the mechanism; it did not solve the **programming model**. Raw event-loop code inverts control — you no longer write "read the request, query the database, send the response" as a sequence. Instead you register a callback for the read, which registers a callback for the query, which registers a callback for the send. The logic of one request is scattered across a dozen functions, and error handling has to be threaded through all of them. This is **callback hell**, and it is a real maintainability problem rather than an aesthetic complaint.

An **event loop** is the runtime that wraps the mechanism: it owns the `epoll`/`kqueue` instance, dispatches ready events to handlers, and typically also manages timers and a task queue. Node.js, Python's `asyncio`, libuv, Netty, and Tokio are all event loops.

The **async/await** syntax is what made the model usable. A coroutine can **suspend** at an `await` point and resume later, so the code *reads* sequentially while *executing* as callbacks. The compiler or runtime performs the transformation into a state machine. The cost of a suspended coroutine is a few hundred bytes — versus a thread's kilobytes — which is why a single process can hold hundreds of thousands of in-flight operations.

Two rules govern correctness in this model, and violating either is the dominant source of bugs:

**1. Never block the event loop.** There is typically one loop thread. Any blocking call — a synchronous file read, a `time.sleep`, a CPU-heavy computation, a blocking database driver — stops **every** connection, not just the one being handled. A 200 ms synchronous call in a handler adds 200 ms of latency to all 10,000 connections. Blocking work belongs in a thread pool, reached through the runtime's `run_in_executor` or equivalent.

**2. File I/O is not truly asynchronous on most systems.** `epoll` works on sockets and pipes; regular files are always "ready", so the readiness model does not apply. Runtimes therefore fake it with a thread pool — libuv does exactly this. Linux's **`io_uring`** (5.1+) is the first interface to make file *and* socket I/O genuinely asynchronous through shared submission and completion ring buffers, reducing syscall overhead dramatically.

It is worth distinguishing **readiness** from **completion** models, because they are genuinely different:

| | Readiness (`epoll`, `kqueue`) | Completion (IOCP, `io_uring`) |
|---|---|---|
| Kernel says | "You can read now" | **"The read is done"** |
| Buffer supplied | At read time | **At submission time** |
| Syscalls per op | 2 (wait, then read) | **Can be 0 with polling mode** |
| Platform | Linux, BSD | Windows, Linux 5.1+ |

The honest assessment: event loops win decisively for **I/O-bound work with many concurrent connections**, which is most network servers. They win nothing for CPU-bound work — a single loop thread uses one core — so real deployments run **one event loop per core** (nginx workers, Node cluster mode, `SO_REUSEPORT`), combining both forms of concurrency.

**Examples**

```text
Callbacks vs async/await: the same logic, two shapes

  CALLBACK STYLE (control inverted)      ASYNC/AWAIT (reads sequentially)

  on_readable(conn, (req) => {           async def handle(conn):
    db.query(req, (rows) => {                req  = await conn.read()
      render(rows, (html) => {               rows = await db.query(req)
        conn.write(html, () => {             html = await render(rows)
          conn.close()                       await conn.write(html)
        })                                   conn.close()
      })
    })
  })
                                         Same execution: suspends at each
  error handling must be threaded        await, resumes on completion.
  through EVERY level                    try/except works normally.


 THE ONE RULE: NEVER BLOCK THE LOOP

  loop thread
     |
     +-- handler A: await db.query()      suspends -> loop continues
     +-- handler B: await conn.read()     suspends -> loop continues
     +-- handler C: time.sleep(0.2)       <-- BLOCKS THE WHOLE LOOP
     |                                        A, B, and 9,997 others
     |                                        are frozen for 200 ms
     v
  Latency added to EVERY connection, not just C's.


 ONE LOOP PER CORE (what production actually does)

   core 0   [event loop] -- 25,000 connections
   core 1   [event loop] -- 25,000 connections     all four bound to :443
   core 2   [event loop] -- 25,000 connections     via SO_REUSEPORT
   core 3   [event loop] -- 25,000 connections

   Event loops give CONCURRENCY. Multiple loops give PARALLELISM.


 READINESS vs COMPLETION

  epoll (readiness)                  io_uring (completion)
  1. epoll_wait -> "fd 7 readable"   1. submit read(fd 7, buf) to SQ ring
  2. read(fd 7, buf)                 2. kernel performs it
     -> 2 syscalls per operation     3. completion appears in CQ ring
                                        -> batched; can be ZERO syscalls
```

```python
import asyncio, time, concurrent.futures

# An async echo server: reads sequentially, executes as an event loop.
async def handle_client(reader, writer):
    peer = writer.get_extra_info("peername")
    try:
        while True:
            data = await reader.read(4096)      # SUSPENDS; loop serves others
            if not data:
                break                            # EOF: peer closed
            writer.write(data)
            await writer.drain()                 # SUSPENDS if the buffer is full
    finally:
        writer.close()
        await writer.wait_closed()

async def main():
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle_client, "0.0.0.0", 8080)
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()

# asyncio.run(main())

# The blocking mistake, measured.
async def blocking_handler():
    time.sleep(0.2)                    # WRONG: blocks the loop thread
    return "done"

async def correct_handler():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)           # RIGHT: suspends, loop stays free
    return "done"

async def compare(n=10):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*[blocking_handler() for _ in range(n)])
    blocking = time.perf_counter() - t0

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*[correct_handler() for _ in range(n)])
    concurrent_ = time.perf_counter() - t0
    return blocking, concurrent_

b, c = asyncio.run(compare())
print(f"10 handlers, 200 ms each:")
print(f"  time.sleep (blocking)   : {b:.2f} s   <- SERIALISED")
print(f"  asyncio.sleep (awaiting): {c:.2f} s   <- CONCURRENT")
# 10 handlers, 200 ms each:
#   time.sleep (blocking)   : 2.01 s   <- SERIALISED
#   asyncio.sleep (awaiting): 0.20 s   <- CONCURRENT
#   One blocking call converted a concurrent server into a serial one.

# CPU-bound work must go to a thread or process pool.
def cpu_heavy(n=8_000_000):
    return sum(i * i for i in range(n))

async def offloaded():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    with concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
        # Runs in a SEPARATE PROCESS; the loop thread stays responsive.
        return await loop.run_in_executor(pool, cpu_heavy)

# Memory per in-flight operation: the reason this model scales.
def memory_per_unit():
    return {
        "OS thread (8 MB stack, ~32 KB touched)": 32 * 1024,
        "goroutine / virtual thread":              4 * 1024,
        "async coroutine":                          400,
    }

print(f"\n{'unit':<42}{'bytes':>9}{'100k units':>14}")
for name, b in memory_per_unit().items():
    print(f"{name:<42}{b:>9,}{b*100_000/1e9:>11.2f} GB")
# unit                                          bytes    100k units
# OS thread (8 MB stack, ~32 KB touched)       32,768       3.28 GB
# goroutine / virtual thread                    4,096       0.41 GB
# async coroutine                                 400       0.04 GB
#   100,000 concurrent operations: 3.3 GB of threads, or 40 MB of coroutines.

# File I/O is NOT truly async under epoll -- runtimes use a thread pool.
async def file_reality():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    # There is no epoll-based async read for a regular file: a regular file
    # is ALWAYS "ready", so readiness notification is meaningless.
    return await loop.run_in_executor(None, lambda: open("/etc/hostname").read())

print("\nWhy regular files cannot use epoll:")
print("  a socket is 'ready' only when data has ARRIVED from the network")
print("  a regular file is ALWAYS ready -- the disk read still takes 10 ms")
print("  -> readiness tells you nothing; libuv/asyncio use a THREAD POOL")
print("  -> io_uring (Linux 5.1+) is the first genuine fix")

# One loop per core: concurrency plus parallelism.
def deployment_model(cores, conns_per_loop=25_000):
    return {"loops": cores, "total_connections": cores * conns_per_loop,
            "mechanism": "SO_REUSEPORT: kernel balances accepts across loops"}
print(f"\n{deployment_model(4)}")
# {'loops': 4, 'total_connections': 100000, 'mechanism': 'SO_REUSEPORT: ...'}

# Readiness vs completion: syscalls per operation.
def syscalls_per_op(model, batch=1):
    return {"epoll (readiness)": 2,
            "io_uring (completion)": 2 / batch,
            "io_uring (SQPOLL)": 0}[model]

print(f"\n{'model':<26}{'syscalls/op':>13}")
for m in ("epoll (readiness)", "io_uring (completion)", "io_uring (SQPOLL)"):
    print(f"{m:<26}{syscalls_per_op(m, batch=32):>13.2f}")
# model                       syscalls/op
# epoll (readiness)                  2.00
# io_uring (completion)              0.06
# io_uring (SQPOLL)                  0.00
#   At millions of operations per second, syscall overhead dominates.
```

```javascript
// Node.js: libuv underneath, the same rules apply.
const net = require('net');

const server = net.createServer((socket) => {
  socket.on('data', (data) => {
    socket.write(data);                    // echo; non-blocking
  });
  socket.on('end',   () => {});            // peer sent FIN
  socket.on('error', (err) => socket.destroy());
});

server.listen(8080);

// THE BLOCKING MISTAKE -- there is one thread, and this stops all of it.
function blockingHandler() {
  const start = Date.now();
  while (Date.now() - start < 200) { }     // busy-wait 200 ms
  // Every other connection is frozen for this entire duration.
}

// The correct form: yield to the loop.
async function correctHandler() {
  await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 200));
  // The loop serves other connections while this is suspended.
}

// CPU-bound work belongs in a worker thread, not on the loop.
const { Worker } = require('worker_threads');
function offloadCpuWork(payload) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const w = new Worker('./cpu-task.js', { workerData: payload });
    w.on('message', resolve);
    w.on('error', reject);
  });
}

// Parallelism requires multiple processes -- one loop uses ONE core.
const cluster = require('cluster');
const os = require('os');
if (cluster.isPrimary) {
  for (let i = 0; i < os.cpus().length; i++) cluster.fork();
  // Each worker gets its own event loop; the kernel balances accepts.
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Raw event-loop code **inverts control** into nested callbacks; **async/await** restores sequential-looking code while executing as a state machine.
- A suspended coroutine costs **hundreds of bytes** versus a thread's kilobytes, enabling hundreds of thousands of concurrent operations per process.
- **Never block the loop**: one synchronous call adds its full duration to the latency of **every** connection, not just the one being handled.
- **Regular file I/O cannot use `epoll`** (files are always "ready"), so runtimes fake it with a **thread pool**; **`io_uring`** is the first genuine fix.
- **Readiness models** (`epoll`, `kqueue`) say "you may read"; **completion models** (IOCP, `io_uring`) say "the read is done" and can amortise syscalls to near zero.
- An event loop provides **concurrency, not parallelism** — production runs **one loop per core** via `SO_REUSEPORT` or worker processes.
- CPU-bound work must be **offloaded to a thread or process pool**, or it defeats the entire model.

#### Thundering Herd and C10K Problem

**Theory**

This topic ties the subchapter together by naming the two problems that drove every transition in it.

**The C10K problem**, posed by Dan Kegel in 1999, asked a deliberately concrete question: why can a machine with sufficient bandwidth and memory not handle 10,000 simultaneous connections? The hardware could clearly do it. The answer was that the **software models were all O(n) in the wrong place**:

- **Process-per-connection**: ~1–10 MB each. 10,000 connections need tens of gigabytes.
- **Thread-per-connection**: cheaper, but the scheduler collapses at 10,000 runnable tasks.
- **`select`/`poll`**: O(n) scans on every call, so per-call cost grows with the connection count.

The resolution was **`epoll`/`kqueue` plus non-blocking I/O plus an event loop** — making cost proportional to **activity** rather than to **connection count**. The problem is now solved so thoroughly that the goalposts moved to **C10M** (ten million connections), where the remaining obstacles are kernel-bypass territory: per-packet syscall overhead, memory bandwidth, and lock contention inside the kernel, addressed by `io_uring`, DPDK, and XDP.

**The thundering herd** is the second problem, and it arises specifically from the pre-forking and multi-worker designs introduced earlier. When many workers block on `accept()` on the same listening socket, a single incoming connection wakes **all** of them. One succeeds; the rest find nothing, discover `EAGAIN`, and go back to sleep. With 64 workers, one connection causes 64 wakeups and 63 wasted context switches.

There are three fixes, in increasing order of quality:

- **A mutex around `accept()`** (nginx's `accept_mutex`): only one worker is eligible at a time. Effective, but serialises accepts and adds latency.
- **`EPOLLEXCLUSIVE`** (Linux 4.5+): the kernel wakes only one waiter per event. A direct fix requiring no application coordination.
- **`SO_REUSEPORT`** (Linux 3.9+): each worker has its **own listening socket** on the same port, and the kernel hashes incoming connections to one of them. No shared queue exists, so there is nothing to stampede on — and it distributes load better than the mutex approach.

A related and more subtle variant appears with `epoll` itself: if multiple threads share one epoll instance in **level-triggered** mode, an event wakes all of them. Edge-triggered mode reduces this, and `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` removes it.

The practical lesson generalises beyond both problems: **the winning models make cost proportional to work actually done**, not to resources merely held. That principle explains the whole progression from `fork()` to `epoll` to `io_uring`.

**Examples**

```text
The C10K wall: why each model stopped

   model                   limit           what breaks first
   ------------------------------------------------------------------
   process-per-conn        ~1,000          memory (1-10 MB each)
   thread-per-conn         ~5,000          scheduler + stacks
   select                  1,024 HARD      FD_SETSIZE
   poll                    ~10,000         O(n) scan per call
   epoll/kqueue            ~1,000,000      file descriptors, memory
   io_uring/XDP            ~10,000,000     syscalls, memory bandwidth

   The hardware was never the problem. The SOFTWARE MODEL was.


 THE THUNDERING HERD

  64 workers all blocked in accept() on the SAME listening socket

        [listening socket, one accept queue]
         /   /   /   |   \   \   \   ... 64 workers blocked
        w1  w2  w3  w4  w5  w6  w7

   ONE connection arrives
        |
        v
   ALL 64 workers wake up
        |
        +-- w17 wins accept()
        +-- the other 63 get EAGAIN and sleep again
            -> 63 wasted context switches PER CONNECTION


 THREE FIXES

  1. accept_mutex          only one worker eligible at a time
     [w1]* [w2] [w3]       * holds the mutex
     -> correct, but SERIALISES accepts (adds latency)

  2. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE        kernel wakes exactly ONE waiter
     [w1] [w2]* [w3]       kernel picks
     -> no application coordination needed

  3. SO_REUSEPORT          each worker has its OWN socket + queue
     [w1: queue1] [w2: queue2] [w3: queue3]
     kernel hashes the 4-tuple to one queue
     -> nothing shared, so nothing to stampede on. BEST option.
```

```c
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <sys/epoll.h>
#include <netinet/in.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>

/* FIX 1: SO_REUSEPORT -- each worker binds its own socket on the same port.
 * There is no shared accept queue, so there is no herd. */
int make_worker_listener(int port) {
    int fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    int yes = 1;

    setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &yes, sizeof yes);
    /* SO_REUSEPORT is the important one: it permits MULTIPLE sockets
     * to bind the same address:port, and the kernel load-balances. */
    setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEPORT, &yes, sizeof yes);

    struct sockaddr_in addr = { .sin_family = AF_INET,
                                .sin_port = htons(port),
                                .sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY) };
    bind(fd, (struct sockaddr *)&addr, sizeof addr);
    listen(fd, 512);
    return fd;
}

int main(void) {
    int workers = 4;
    for (int i = 0; i < workers; i++) {
        if (fork() == 0) {
            /* Each child creates its OWN listening socket AFTER forking. */
            int listen_fd = make_worker_listener(8080);
            printf("worker %d listening on its own socket fd=%d\n", i, listen_fd);

            int ep = epoll_create1(0);
            /* FIX 2: EPOLLEXCLUSIVE -- if workers DID share a socket, this
             * tells the kernel to wake only one of them per event. */
            struct epoll_event ev = { .events = EPOLLIN | EPOLLEXCLUSIVE,
                                      .data.fd = listen_fd };
            epoll_ctl(ep, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, listen_fd, &ev);

            struct epoll_event events[64];
            for (;;) {
                int n = epoll_wait(ep, events, 64, -1);
                for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                    int conn = accept(listen_fd, NULL, NULL);
                    if (conn >= 0) { write(conn, "ok\n", 3); close(conn); }
                }
            }
            _exit(0);
        }
    }
    for (;;) pause();
}
```

```python
import os, socket, time

# Quantify the herd: wasted wakeups per connection.
def herd_cost(workers, connections_per_sec, ctx_switch_us=3):
    wasted_per_conn = workers - 1
    wasted_per_sec = wasted_per_conn * connections_per_sec
    cpu_us = wasted_per_sec * ctx_switch_us
    return wasted_per_sec, cpu_us / 1_000_000

print(f"{'workers':>9}{'conns/s':>10}{'wasted wakeups/s':>20}{'CPU cores wasted':>19}")
for workers in (4, 16, 64):
    for rate in (1_000, 10_000):
        wasted, cores = herd_cost(workers, rate)
        print(f"{workers:>9}{rate:>10,}{wasted:>20,}{cores:>19.2f}")
#   workers   conns/s    wasted wakeups/s   CPU cores wasted
#         4     1,000               3,000               0.01
#         4    10,000              30,000               0.09
#        16     1,000              15,000               0.05
#        16    10,000             150,000               0.45
#        64     1,000              63,000               0.19
#        64    10,000             630,000               1.89
#   At 64 workers and 10k conn/s, nearly two cores do nothing but wake up
#   and go back to sleep.

# The three fixes, compared.
fixes = [
    ("accept_mutex",    "one eligible worker", "correct; serialises accepts, adds latency"),
    ("EPOLLEXCLUSIVE",  "kernel wakes one",    "Linux 4.5+; no app coordination needed"),
    ("SO_REUSEPORT",    "per-worker queue",    "Linux 3.9+; nothing shared; best balance"),
]
print()
for name, how, note in fixes:
    print(f"  {name:<18} {how:<22} {note}")

# SO_REUSEPORT: independent listeners, kernel-hashed distribution.
def reuseport_workers(n=4, port=8080):
    listeners = []
    for i in range(n):
        s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEPORT, 1)
        s.bind(("0.0.0.0", port))          # SAME port, DIFFERENT socket
        s.listen(512)
        listeners.append(s)
    return listeners

ls = reuseport_workers(4, 0)
print(f"\n{len(ls)} independent listening sockets, each with its own accept queue")
for s in ls: s.close()

# The C10K progression: where each model hits its wall.
models = [
    ("process-per-connection", 1_000,      "memory: 1-10 MB per process"),
    ("thread-per-connection",  5_000,      "scheduler run queue + stacks"),
    ("select",                 1_024,      "FD_SETSIZE, a HARD compile-time limit"),
    ("poll",                  10_000,      "O(n) scan on every call"),
    ("epoll/kqueue",       1_000_000,      "file descriptors and memory"),
    ("io_uring / XDP",    10_000_000,      "syscall and memory bandwidth"),
]
print(f"\n{'model':<26}{'practical limit':>18}  {'first bottleneck'}")
for name, limit, why in models:
    print(f"{name:<26}{limit:>18,}  {why}")

# Resource accounting at 10,000 connections, per model.
def resources(conns):
    return [
        ("process-per-conn", conns * 2.4,      conns, "GB"),
        ("thread-per-conn",  conns * 0.032,    conns, "GB"),
        ("epoll event loop", conns * 0.00001 + 0.05, 1, "GB"),
    ]
print(f"\nAt {10_000:,} connections:")
print(f"{'model':<20}{'memory':>10}{'OS tasks':>11}")
for name, mem, tasks, unit in resources(10_000):
    print(f"{name:<20}{mem:>7.2f} {unit}{tasks:>11,}")
# At 10,000 connections:
# model                   memory   OS tasks
# process-per-conn      24.00 GB     10,000
# thread-per-conn        0.32 GB     10,000
# epoll event loop       0.15 GB          1
#   The memory column killed processes; the task column killed threads.

# The principle that unifies the whole subchapter.
print("\nThe rule every winning model follows:")
print("  cost should be proportional to WORK DONE,")
print("  not to RESOURCES HELD.")
print("  fork -> threads -> poll -> epoll -> io_uring")
print("  is that principle applied four times.")
```

```bash
$ pidstat -w -C nginx 1 3
# UID  PID   cswch/s  nvcswch/s  Command
# 33  4821   8421.00     12.00   nginx: worker
# 33  4822   8398.00     14.00   nginx: worker
# 33  4823   8410.00     11.00   nginx: worker
#            ^^^^^^^ every worker switching at the same high rate while
#                    the connection rate is far lower = herd

# Compare with the connection rate to confirm:
$ ss -s | grep -i tcp
# TCP:   1204 (estab 1150, closed 12, orphaned 0, timewait 12)
$ nstat -az TcpActiveOpens TcpPassiveOpens
# TcpPassiveOpens  1021  0.0
#   ~1,000 connections/s but ~25,000 wakeups/s across workers.

# nginx's mutex-based fix:
$ grep -A2 'events {' /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
# events {
#     worker_connections 4096;
#     accept_mutex on;          # serialise accepts: fixes the herd
#     multi_accept on;          # take ALL pending connections per wakeup
# }

# The better fix: SO_REUSEPORT (one socket per worker):
$ grep 'listen' /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default
# listen 80 reuseport;
$ ss -tlnp | grep ':80 '
# LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=4821,fd=6))
# LISTEN 0 511 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:* users:(("nginx",pid=4822,fd=6))
#   Separate sockets: the kernel hashes connections, no herd exists.

# Verify the distribution is actually even:
$ for p in $(pgrep -f 'nginx: worker'); do
>   echo -n "pid $p: "; ss -tnp 2>/dev/null | grep -c "pid=$p"
> done
# pid 4821: 2504
# pid 4822: 2489
# pid 4823: 2511
# pid 4824: 2496
#   Within ~1%: the kernel's 4-tuple hash is distributing well.

# Raising the C10K-era limits before testing high connection counts:
$ ulimit -n 1048576
$ sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=65535
$ sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=65535
$ sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range='1024 65535'

# Confirm one process really is holding ~1M connections:
$ ss -s
# Total: 998412
# TCP:   998001 (estab 997890, closed 100, orphaned 0, timewait 11)
$ ps -o nlwp= -p $(pgrep -n epollserver)
# 1
```

**Key takeaways**

- **C10K** was never a hardware limit — every software model was **O(n) in the wrong place**: memory for processes, scheduler load for threads, per-call scans for `select`/`poll`.
- The resolution was **`epoll`/`kqueue` + non-blocking I/O + an event loop**, making cost proportional to **activity** rather than connection count.
- The frontier moved to **C10M**, where the obstacles are syscall overhead and kernel lock contention, addressed by **`io_uring`, DPDK, and XDP**.
- The **thundering herd** occurs when many workers block on one listening socket: **one connection wakes all of them**, wasting N−1 context switches.
- Fixes in increasing quality: **`accept_mutex`** (serialises), **`EPOLLEXCLUSIVE`** (kernel wakes one), and **`SO_REUSEPORT`** (per-worker queues, nothing shared).
- A level-triggered epoll instance shared across threads exhibits the same herd; edge-triggered and `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` mitigate it.
- The unifying principle: **make cost proportional to work done, not to resources held**.

> 🧪 Practice

> 2. Compute the wasted wakeups per second for 32 workers at 5,000 connections per second, and the approximate CPU cost at 3 µs per switch.
> 3. Explain why `SO_REUSEPORT` eliminates the thundering herd rather than merely mitigating it.
