> 1. Compute Q and the approximate SIR for reuse factors N = 4 and N = 12, and state which suits a dense urban area.
> 2. Explain how cell splitting increases capacity without acquiring additional spectrum.
> 3. Contrast Wi-Fi roaming with cellular handover in terms of who decides and what the consequence is.
> 4. Interview-style: *Why can a voice call survive a car journey at 120 km/h while a Wi-Fi video call often drops walking between rooms?* (Hint: compare who initiates the transition in each system, and what information that party has about the alternatives.)

#### Evolution from 2G to 5G

**Theory**

Each cellular generation solved the dominant problem of its era, and the sequence reads as a steady conversion of a telephone network into an IP network.

**1G** (1980s) was analogue voice — FDMA, no encryption, easily cloned. Its value here is as a baseline.

**2G (GSM)** digitised voice, which brought encryption, better spectral efficiency, and — almost as an afterthought — **SMS**. It used **TDMA**: each user gets a time slot on a shared frequency. Data arrived as **GPRS** (up to 114 kb/s) and **EDGE** (384 kb/s), both **packet-switched overlays on a circuit-switched network**. That hybrid nature is the defining awkwardness of 2G data.

**3G (UMTS/CDMA2000)** was designed for data from the start. **CDMA** replaced TDMA: all users transmit simultaneously on the same frequency, separated by orthogonal codes. **HSPA+** eventually reached ~42 Mb/s. Voice remained circuit-switched, so the network still maintained two parallel domains.

**4G (LTE)** made the decisive architectural break: **everything is IP, including voice**. The circuit-switched domain disappeared, and voice became an application (**VoLTE**) over the packet network. The radio moved to **OFDMA**, the same family of techniques as Wi-Fi, with MIMO and carrier aggregation. The **flat, all-IP architecture** removed several node types and cut latency substantially.

**5G (NR)** is best understood as **three different services** sharing one framework, rather than as "faster 4G":

- **eMBB (enhanced Mobile Broadband)** — multi-gigabit throughput; the consumer-facing headline.
- **URLLC (Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication)** — 1 ms air latency at 99.999% reliability, for industrial control, vehicles, and remote surgery.
- **mMTC (massive Machine-Type Communication)** — up to a million devices per square kilometre for sensors.

These have contradictory requirements, which is precisely why **network slicing** (a later topic) exists.

5G also introduced a spectrum split that explains most consumer confusion about it:

| Range | Frequencies | Speed | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Low-band** | < 1 GHz | ~100 Mb/s | Tens of km |
| **Mid-band** | 1–6 GHz | ~1 Gb/s | A few km |
| **mmWave** | 24–40 GHz | ~10 Gb/s | **100–300 m, blocked by walls and hands** |

The multi-gigabit demonstrations use mmWave, which barely penetrates a window; the 5G most people actually experience is low or mid-band. **Mid-band is where 5G's real value lies.**

One further distinction matters operationally: **NSA (Non-Standalone)** 5G uses a 5G radio anchored to an existing LTE core, which is how most networks launched. **SA (Standalone)** 5G uses a native 5G core and is required for slicing, URLLC, and the low latencies 5G promises. A phone showing "5G" on an NSA network gets the radio improvements but none of the architectural ones.

**Examples**

```text
The generations, and what each one actually changed

  1G  analogue voice          FDMA        no encryption, clonable
  2G  DIGITAL voice           TDMA        encryption, SMS, GPRS/EDGE data
  3G  data-capable            CDMA        HSPA+ ~42 Mb/s, voice still circuit
  4G  ALL-IP                  OFDMA       voice becomes an app (VoLTE)
  5G  three services          OFDMA+      eMBB / URLLC / mMTC, slicing

  The through-line: a telephone network gradually became an IP network,
  and in 4G the telephone part finally disappeared entirely.


 MULTIPLE ACCESS: how users are separated

  FDMA (1G)          TDMA (2G)              CDMA (3G)         OFDMA (4G/5G)
  freq                freq                   freq              freq
   ^ [A]               ^ [A|B|C|A|B|C]        ^ [ABC mixed]     ^ [A][B][C]
   | [B]               |                      |  all at once    | [B][C][A]
   | [C]               |                      |  separated by   | [C][A][B]
   +------> time       +------> time          +--> by CODE      +-----> time

  each user gets     each user gets        all users share    users get
  a FREQUENCY        a TIME SLOT           everything,        time-frequency
                                           separated by       BLOCKS
                                           orthogonal codes


 5G's THREE SERVICES have contradictory needs

                    throughput   latency    density    reliability
   eMBB               10 Gb/s     ~10 ms     normal      normal
   URLLC              low          1 ms      normal    99.999%
   mMTC               tiny        tolerant  1M/km2       normal

   One radio cannot optimise for all three simultaneously.
   -> hence NETWORK SLICING: virtual networks with different parameters.


 THE 5G SPECTRUM CONFUSION

   low-band  <1 GHz     ~100 Mb/s   tens of km    "5G" on your phone, often
                                                  barely faster than LTE
   mid-band  1-6 GHz    ~1 Gb/s     a few km      THE USEFUL ONE
   mmWave    24-40 GHz  ~10 Gb/s    100-300 m     the demo videos;
                                                  blocked by walls, leaves,
                                                  rain, and your own hand

   Marketing shows mmWave. Most users get low or mid-band.
```

```python
import math

# --- Generation comparison ---
GENERATIONS = [
    # name, year, access, peak_dl_mbps, latency_ms, voice, spectral_eff
    ("1G (AMPS)",   1983, "FDMA",  0.0024, 500, "analogue circuit", 0.06),
    ("2G (GSM)",    1991, "TDMA",  0.014,  300, "digital circuit",  0.17),
    ("2.5G (GPRS)", 2000, "TDMA",  0.114,  700, "circuit",          0.20),
    ("3G (UMTS)",   2001, "CDMA",  2.0,    200, "circuit",          0.51),

for name, yr, acc, dl, lat, voice, se in GENERATIONS:
    dl_s = f"{dl*1000:.1f} kb" if dl < 1 else f"{dl:,.0f} Mb"
    print(f"{name:<15}{yr:>6}{acc:>8}{dl_s:>12}{lat:>8} ms{se:>12.2f} b/Hz")
# generation       year  access     peak DL   latency  spectral eff
# 1G (AMPS)        1983    FDMA      2.4 kb    500 ms        0.06 b/Hz
# 2G (GSM)         1991    TDMA     14.0 kb    300 ms        0.17 b/Hz
# 2.5G (GPRS)      2000    TDMA    114.0 kb    700 ms        0.20 b/Hz
# 3G (UMTS)        2001    CDMA        2 Mb    200 ms        0.51 b/Hz
# 3.5G (HSPA+)     2008    CDMA       42 Mb    100 ms        1.50 b/Hz
# 4G (LTE)         2009   OFDMA      300 Mb     50 ms        3.00 b/Hz
# 4G (LTE-A)       2013   OFDMA    1,000 Mb     30 ms        6.00 b/Hz
# 5G (NR)          2019   OFDMA   10,000 Mb      1 ms       30.00 b/Hz
#   Spectral efficiency rose 500x from 1G to 5G -- that is the real story,
#   not peak rate, which also benefited from far more spectrum.

# How much of the gain is spectrum vs efficiency?
def decompose_gain(gen_a, gen_b, bw_a, bw_b):
    se_gain = gen_b[6] / gen_a[6]
    bw_gain = bw_b / bw_a
    return se_gain, bw_gain, se_gain * bw_gain

se, bw, total = decompose_gain(GENERATIONS[1], GENERATIONS[7], 0.2, 100)
print(f"\n2G -> 5G peak-rate gain decomposed:")
print(f"  spectral efficiency : {se:>8.0f}x")
print(f"  bandwidth           : {bw:>8.0f}x")
print(f"  combined            : {total:>8,.0f}x")
# 2G -> 5G peak-rate gain decomposed:
#   spectral efficiency :      176x
#   bandwidth           :      500x
#   combined            :   88,235x
#   MORE SPECTRUM did more of the work than cleverer radios did.

# --- 5G spectrum bands: the marketing vs reality gap ---
def coverage_area_km2(radius_km):
    return math.pi * radius_km ** 2

BANDS_5G = [("low-band (700 MHz)", 0.7, 100, 10.0),
            ("mid-band (3.5 GHz)", 3.5, 1000, 1.5),
            ("mmWave (28 GHz)", 28.0, 10000, 0.2)]
print(f"\n{'band':<22}{'peak':>10}{'radius':>9}{'area':>12}{'sites/100km2':>15}")
for name, ghz, mbps, radius in BANDS_5G:
    area = coverage_area_km2(radius)
    sites = math.ceil(100 / area)
    print(f"{name:<22}{mbps:>7,} Mb{radius:>8} km{area:>10.2f} km2{sites:>14,}")
# band                        peak   radius        area   sites/100km2
# low-band (700 MHz)       100 Mb     10 km    314.16 km2              1
# mid-band (3.5 GHz)     1,000 Mb    1.5 km      7.07 km2             15
# mmWave (28 GHz)       10,000 Mb    0.2 km      0.13 km2            796
#   mmWave needs ~800 sites where low-band needs 1. That economics is why
#   mmWave exists only in stadiums and a few city blocks.

# What actually blocks mmWave:
BLOCKERS = {"a brick wall": 40, "a window (low-e glass)": 25, "foliage": 15,
            "a human body": 20, "heavy rain (per km)": 10, "your hand": 15}
print(f"\nmmWave attenuation (link budget ~30 dB of margin):")
for what, db in BLOCKERS.items():
    verdict = "LINK LOST" if db >= 25 else "severe" if db >= 15 else "noticeable"
    print(f"  {what:<26}{db:>4} dB  {verdict}")
#   a brick wall                40 dB  LINK LOST
#   a window (low-e glass)      25 dB  LINK LOST
#   foliage                     15 dB  severe
#   a human body                20 dB  severe
#   heavy rain (per km)         10 dB  noticeable
#   your hand                   15 dB  severe
#   Holding the phone differently can drop a mmWave link. This is not a
#   defect; it is physics at 28 GHz.

# --- NSA vs SA: what a "5G" indicator actually means ---
def five_g_capabilities(mode):
    return {
        "NSA (non-standalone)": {
            "5G radio": True, "5G core": False, "network slicing": False,
            "URLLC (1 ms)": False, "VoNR": False,
            "note": "LTE anchor required; most launch networks",
        },
        "SA (standalone)": {
            "5G radio": True, "5G core": True, "network slicing": True,
            "URLLC (1 ms)": True, "VoNR": True,
            "note": "native 5G core; required for 5G's architectural promises",
        },
    }[mode]

print()
for mode in ("NSA (non-standalone)", "SA (standalone)"):
    caps = five_g_capabilities(mode)
    note = caps.pop("note")
    print(f"{mode}")
    for k, v in caps.items():
        print(f"   {k:<20}{'yes' if v else 'NO'}")
    print(f"   -> {note}\n")
#   A phone showing "5G" on an NSA network gets faster radio and nothing else.
#   Slicing, URLLC, and 1 ms latency all require SA.

# --- Latency: where 5G's 1 ms claim applies ---
def end_to_end_latency_ms(air_ms, ran_ms, core_ms, internet_ms):
    return air_ms + ran_ms + core_ms + internet_ms

print(f"{'scenario':<34}{'air':>6}{'RAN':>6}{'core':>6}{'net':>7}{'total':>8}")
SCENARIOS = [("4G to a distant server",     10, 5, 10, 40),
             ("5G to a distant server",      1, 2,  5, 40),
             ("5G to an edge node (MEC)",    1, 2,  1,  1),
             ("5G URLLC, on-premises core",  1, 1,  0,  0)]
for name, a, r, c, n in SCENARIOS:
    print(f"{name:<34}{a:>5}{r:>6}{c:>6}{n:>7}{end_to_end_latency_ms(a,r,c,n):>7}ms")
# scenario                             air   RAN  core    net   total
# 4G to a distant server                10     5    10     40     65ms
# 5G to a distant server                 1     2     5     40     48ms
# 5G to an edge node (MEC)               1     2     1      1      5ms
# 5G URLLC, on-premises core             1     1     0      0      2ms
#   The "1 ms" figure is AIR latency only. End to end, the internet path
#   dominates -- which is exactly why edge computing accompanies 5G.
```


**Key takeaways**

- The generations trace **a telephone network becoming an IP network**, completed in 4G when the circuit-switched domain disappeared and voice became **VoLTE**.
- Multiple access evolved **FDMA → TDMA → CDMA → OFDMA**, each separating users along a different axis: frequency, time, code, then time-frequency blocks.
- **2G digitised voice** and added SMS and packet data overlays; **3G was data-first** but kept circuit-switched voice; **4G went all-IP with a flat architecture**.
- **5G is three services in one framework** — **eMBB, URLLC, mMTC** — with contradictory requirements, which is why **network slicing** exists.
- The **5G band split explains consumer confusion**: mmWave delivers the demo speeds but is blocked by walls, foliage, and a hand; **mid-band is where the real value is**.
- **NSA 5G gives radio improvements only**; **SA 5G with a native core** is required for slicing, URLLC, and low latency.
- The **"1 ms" figure is air latency**; end-to-end latency is dominated by the path to the server, which is why **edge computing accompanies 5G**.

#### LTE EPC and 5G Core Components

**Theory**

A cellular core network does several things a home router never has to: authenticate a SIM against a national subscriber database, track a device that may be anywhere in the country, enforce per-subscriber policy and billing, and preserve a device's IP address as it moves between cells hundreds of kilometres apart.

**LTE's Evolved Packet Core (EPC)** divides this among four main elements, and the division is worth learning because 5G rearranges rather than replaces it:

| Element | Role |
|---|---|
| **MME** (Mobility Management Entity) | **Control plane**: attach, authentication, mobility, paging, bearer setup |
| **HSS** (Home Subscriber Server) | Subscriber database: identities, keys, service profiles |
| **S-GW** (Serving Gateway) | **User plane**: anchors traffic during handover between base stations |
| **P-GW** (PDN Gateway) | **User plane**: allocates the IP address, enforces policy, connects to the internet |
| **PCRF** | Policy and charging rules |

The structural principle is **control-plane / user-plane separation**, which is the same idea encountered in 8.1's hybrid architectures and Chapter 13's SDN. The MME signals but never touches user traffic; the gateways forward traffic but make no decisions. This lets the two scale independently — a network may need far more forwarding capacity than signalling capacity, or the reverse.

Two concepts do the heavy lifting:

A **bearer** is a virtual connection between the device and the P-GW with defined QoS characteristics. The **default bearer** is established at attach and is best-effort; **dedicated bearers** carry specific traffic with guaranteed bit rate — a VoLTE call gets its own dedicated bearer, which is why voice quality holds up while data is congested. Each bearer has a **QCI (QoS Class Identifier)** specifying priority, delay budget, and loss tolerance.

**Tunnelling with GTP** is how mobility is hidden from the IP layer. User traffic is encapsulated between the base station and the gateways, so the device keeps **one IP address allocated by the P-GW** no matter which base station it is attached to. The tunnel endpoints change during handover; the IP address does not. This is the cellular answer to the mobility problem that Mobile IP addresses in 10.5, and it works better because the whole path is under one operator's control.

**5G's Core (5GC)** re-architects this as a **Service-Based Architecture (SBA)**: network functions expose HTTP/2 REST APIs to one another rather than using purpose-built protocols over fixed interfaces. The mapping is roughly:

| LTE | 5G | Change |
|---|---|---|
| MME | **AMF** (Access and Mobility) + **SMF** (Session Management) | Split into two |
| S-GW + P-GW | **UPF** (User Plane Function) | Merged, and **deployable at the edge** |
| HSS | **UDM** + **AUSF** | Data and authentication separated |
| PCRF | **PCF** | Policy |
| — | **NRF, NEF, NSSF** | Service discovery, exposure, slice selection |

Three consequences matter. Splitting the MME into **AMF and SMF** lets mobility and session management scale separately. Merging the gateways into a **UPF that can be placed anywhere** — including at a cell site — is what makes edge computing and single-digit-millisecond latency achievable. And the **service-based interfaces** make the core a cloud-native software system rather than a set of specialised appliances, which is why 5G cores run on Kubernetes.

**Examples**

```text
LTE EPC: control plane and user plane separated

                        +--------+
                        |  HSS   |  subscriber database
                        +--------+
                            |  (S6a: authentication vectors)
                            |
   [UE] ---- radio ---- [eNodeB] ---- S1-MME ---- [MME]  CONTROL PLANE
     |                      |                       |    (signalling only)
     |                      |                       |
     |                      +----- S1-U ------- [S-GW] --- [P-GW] --- internet
     |                                              |          |
     +------------- GTP tunnel (user traffic) ------+----------+
                                                 USER PLANE
                                                 (forwarding only)

   The MME NEVER touches user traffic.
   The gateways NEVER make policy decisions.
   -> the two scale independently.


 5G CORE: service-based, and the UPF moves to the edge

                    +-----------------------------------+
                    |  service-based interfaces (HTTP/2)|
                    |  NRF  NEF  NSSF  PCF  UDM  AUSF   |
                    +-----------------------------------+
                         |            |
                      [AMF]        [SMF]      <- MME split in two
                         |            |
   [UE] --- radio --- [gNodeB] --- [UPF] --- data network
                                     ^
                                     |  the UPF can sit AT THE CELL SITE,
                                     |  which is what makes 1-5 ms possible

   LTE:  MME        -> 5G:  AMF (mobility) + SMF (sessions)
   LTE:  S-GW+P-GW  -> 5G:  UPF (merged, distributable)
   LTE:  HSS        -> 5G:  UDM (data) + AUSF (authentication)


 BEARERS: why your voice call survives a congested cell

   +---------------------- device ----------------------+
   |                                                    |
   | DEFAULT bearer  (QCI 9, best effort)               |
   |   -> web, email, app traffic: competes for capacity|
   |                                                    |
   | DEDICATED bearer (QCI 1, guaranteed bit rate)      |
   |   -> the VoLTE call: RESERVED capacity, 100 ms      |
   |      delay budget, 1e-2 loss tolerance             |
   +----------------------------------------------------+

   Congestion degrades the default bearer and leaves the dedicated one
   intact. This is why calls stay clear while browsing crawls.


 GTP TUNNELLING: how the IP address survives mobility

   device IP 10.4.2.9 (allocated by the P-GW, never changes)
        |
        |  encapsulated in GTP between eNodeB and S-GW
        v
   [eNodeB A] ==GTP==> [S-GW] ==GTP==> [P-GW] -> internet (sees 10.4.2.9)
        |
        |  handover: the TUNNEL endpoint changes
        v
   [eNodeB B] ==GTP==> [S-GW] ==GTP==> [P-GW] -> internet (STILL 10.4.2.9)

   The IP layer never learns the device moved. TCP connections survive.
```

```python
# --- EPC and 5GC element mapping ---
MAPPING = [
    ("MME",   "AMF + SMF", "control", "mobility and sessions split apart"),
    ("S-GW",  "UPF",       "user",    "merged with P-GW"),
    ("P-GW",  "UPF",       "user",    "merged; now DEPLOYABLE AT THE EDGE"),
    ("HSS",   "UDM + AUSF","control", "subscriber data vs authentication split"),
    ("PCRF",  "PCF",       "control", "policy, now service-based"),
    ("-",     "NRF",       "control", "NEW: service discovery between functions"),
    ("-",     "NSSF",      "control", "NEW: network slice selection"),
    ("-",     "NEF",       "control", "NEW: exposes capabilities to third parties"),
]
print(f"{'LTE (EPC)':<10}{'5G (5GC)':<14}{'plane':<10}{'what changed'}")
for lte, fiveg, plane, note in MAPPING:
    print(f"{lte:<10}{fiveg:<14}{plane:<10}{note}")

# --- Control/user plane separation: independent scaling ---
def dimension_core(subscribers, signalling_per_sub_per_hour=20,
                   mbps_per_active_sub=2, active_fraction=0.15):
    signalling_tps = subscribers * signalling_per_sub_per_hour / 3600
    user_gbps = subscribers * active_fraction * mbps_per_active_sub / 1000
    return signalling_tps, user_gbps

print(f"\n{'subscribers':>13}{'signalling (tps)':>19}{'user plane':>14}")
for subs in (100_000, 1_000_000, 10_000_000):
    tps, gbps = dimension_core(subs)
    print(f"{subs:>13,}{tps:>17,.0f}{gbps:>11,.0f} Gb/s")
#   subscribers   signalling (tps)     user plane
#       100,000                556         30 Gb/s
#     1,000,000              5,556        300 Gb/s
#    10,000,000             55,556      3,000 Gb/s
#   These scale at very different rates and have very different hardware
#   needs -- which is exactly why the planes are separated.

# --- QCI: the QoS classes that make VoLTE work ---
QCI_TABLE = [
    (1, "GBR",     2, 100, 1e-2, "conversational voice (VoLTE)"),
    (2, "GBR",     4, 150, 1e-3, "conversational video"),
    (3, "GBR",     3,  50, 1e-3, "real-time gaming"),
    (4, "GBR",     5, 300, 1e-6, "non-conversational video"),
    (5, "non-GBR", 1, 100, 1e-6, "IMS signalling"),
    (7, "non-GBR", 7, 100, 1e-3, "voice/video streaming"),
    (8, "non-GBR", 8, 300, 1e-6, "premium data"),
    (9, "non-GBR", 9, 300, 1e-6, "default bearer: best-effort data"),
]
print(f"\n{'QCI':>4}{'type':>10}{'priority':>10}{'delay':>9}{'loss':>9}  service")
for qci, typ, pri, delay, loss, svc in QCI_TABLE:
    print(f"{qci:>4}{typ:>10}{pri:>10}{delay:>7}ms{loss:>9.0e}  {svc}")
#  QCI      type  priority    delay     loss  service
#    1       GBR         2    100ms    1e-02  conversational voice (VoLTE)
#    2       GBR         4    150ms    1e-03  conversational video
#    ...
#    9   non-GBR         9    300ms    1e-06  default bearer: best-effort data
#   Note QCI 1 tolerates 1% LOSS but demands 100 ms delay -- exactly the
#   trade-off from 8.1: voice prefers a late-free stream over a perfect one.

# What happens to each bearer under congestion:
def bearer_under_congestion(qci_type, cell_load):
    if qci_type == "GBR":
        return "guaranteed rate maintained (admission control refuses new calls)"
    degraded = max(0.05, 1 - cell_load)
    return f"degraded to {degraded:.0%} of nominal throughput"

print(f"\ncell at 95% load:")
print(f"  QCI 1 (GBR)     : {bearer_under_congestion('GBR', 0.95)}")
print(f"  QCI 9 (non-GBR) : {bearer_under_congestion('non-GBR', 0.95)}")
#   QCI 1 (GBR)     : guaranteed rate maintained (admission control refuses new calls)
#   QCI 9 (non-GBR) : degraded to 5% of nominal throughput
#   Your call is clear; your browsing is unusable. By design.

# --- GTP tunnelling: how the IP address survives ---
class GTPTunnel:
    """User traffic is encapsulated; the endpoint changes, the IP does not."""
    def __init__(self, ue_ip, pgw):
        self.ue_ip = ue_ip            # allocated by the P-GW, PERMANENT for the session
        self.pgw = pgw
        self.enodeb = None
        self.teid = None              # tunnel endpoint identifier
        self.handovers = 0

    def attach(self, enodeb, teid):
        self.enodeb, self.teid = enodeb, teid

    def handover(self, new_enodeb, new_teid):
        old = self.enodeb
        self.enodeb, self.teid = new_enodeb, new_teid
        self.handovers += 1
        return f"{old} -> {new_enodeb}: TEID {self.teid}, UE IP UNCHANGED"

t = GTPTunnel("10.4.2.9", "pgw-lon-1")
t.attach("enb-0451", 0x1A2B3C4D)
print(f"\nUE IP: {t.ue_ip} (allocated by {t.pgw})")
for enb, teid in (("enb-0452", 0x1A2B3C4E), ("enb-0518", 0x1A2B3C4F),
                  ("enb-0603", 0x1A2B3C50)):
    print(f"  {t.handover(enb, teid)}")
print(f"after {t.handovers} handovers, UE IP is still {t.ue_ip}")
# UE IP: 10.4.2.9 (allocated by pgw-lon-1)
#   enb-0451 -> enb-0452: TEID 439041102, UE IP UNCHANGED
#   enb-0452 -> enb-0518: TEID 439041103, UE IP UNCHANGED
#   enb-0518 -> enb-0603: TEID 439041104, UE IP UNCHANGED
# after 3 handovers, UE IP is still 10.4.2.9
#   TCP connections survive every handover, because the IP layer never
#   learns the device moved. Contrast this with 10.5's Mobile IP.

# --- UPF at the edge: where 5G's latency actually comes from ---
def latency_by_upf_placement(placement):
    return {"central (national DC)": {"backhaul_ms": 12, "note": "one UPF per country"},
            "regional":              {"backhaul_ms": 4,  "note": "a few dozen sites"},
            "edge (cell site)":      {"backhaul_ms": 0.2,"note": "thousands of sites"}}[placement]

print(f"\n{'UPF placement':<26}{'air':>6}{'backhaul':>11}{'total':>9}  deployment")
for p in ("central (national DC)", "regional", "edge (cell site)"):
    d = latency_by_upf_placement(p)
    total = 1 + d["backhaul_ms"]
    print(f"{p:<26}{1:>5}ms{d['backhaul_ms']:>9}ms{total:>7.1f}ms  {d['note']}")
# UPF placement                air   backhaul    total  deployment
# central (national DC)        1ms       12ms    13.0ms  one UPF per country
# regional                     1ms        4ms     5.0ms  a few dozen sites
# edge (cell site)             1ms      0.2ms     1.2ms  thousands of sites
#   5G's URLLC latency target is unachievable with a central core, no matter
#   how good the radio is. The UPF MUST move closer -- hence edge computing.

# --- Service-based architecture: functions calling each other over HTTP/2 ---
SBI_EXAMPLE = {
    "AMF -> AUSF":  "POST /nausf-auth/v1/ue-authentications",
    "AMF -> UDM":   "GET  /nudm-sdm/v2/{supi}/am-data",
    "SMF -> PCF":   "POST /npcf-smpolicycontrol/v1/sm-policies",
    "SMF -> UPF":   "PFCP session establishment (not HTTP: user plane)",
    "any -> NRF":   "GET  /nnrf-disc/v1/nf-instances?target-nf-type=UDM",
}
print()
for call, api in SBI_EXAMPLE.items():
    print(f"  {call:<14}{api}")
#   AMF -> AUSF   POST /nausf-auth/v1/ue-authentications
#   AMF -> UDM    GET  /nudm-sdm/v2/{supi}/am-data
#   ...
#   any -> NRF    GET  /nnrf-disc/v1/nf-instances?target-nf-type=UDM
#   The core is now a set of REST microservices. This is why 5G cores
#   run on Kubernetes and why 9.3's API design principles apply directly.
```

```bash
# 09:14:22 cell= 0012A5F3 ip=10.4.2.9/30
# 09:14:32 cell= 0012A604 ip=10.4.2.9/30     <- cell changed, IP did NOT
# 09:14:47 cell= 0012A611 ip=10.4.2.9/30
#   This is GTP tunnelling doing its job.

# Confirm a TCP connection survives a handover:
$ ping -i 0.2 -c 300 8.8.8.8 | tail -3 &
# (walk or drive between cells during the test)
# 300 packets transmitted, 298 received, 0.7% packet loss
# rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 28.1/35.2/412.8/22.1 ms
#                                 ^^^^^ the handover shows as a LATENCY SPIKE,
#                                       not as a connection reset

# QoS class in use for a voice call (needs operator-level visibility):
$ mmcli -m 0 --command='AT+CGEQOS?'
# +CGEQOS: 1,9,,,,          <- QCI 9: default bearer, best effort
# +CGEQOS: 2,5,,,,          <- QCI 5: IMS signalling
# +CGEQOS: 3,1,128,128,,    <- QCI 1: GBR 128 kb/s -- the actual voice bearer
#   The third appears only during a call and disappears afterwards.

# Observe GTP on an operator's own network (lab/core-side only):
$ sudo tcpdump -i any -n 'udp port 2152' -c 3
# IP 10.100.1.5.2152 > 10.100.2.9.2152: UDP, length 1424
#                ^^^^ GTP-U: the user-plane tunnel port
#   Inside each of these is the subscriber's actual IP packet.

# 5G core functions as Kubernetes services (operator/lab environment):
$ kubectl get svc -n 5gc
# NAME   TYPE        CLUSTER-IP      PORT(S)
# amf    ClusterIP   10.96.12.4      38412/SCTP,8080/TCP
# smf    ClusterIP   10.96.12.5      8805/UDP,8080/TCP
# upf    NodePort    10.96.12.6      2152/UDP
# nrf    ClusterIP   10.96.12.7      8080/TCP
#                                    ^^^^ HTTP/2 service-based interfaces
$ kubectl exec -n 5gc deploy/amf -- curl -s http://nrf:8080/nnrf-disc/v1/nf-instances\?target-nf-type=UDM | jq -c '.nfInstances[0].nfType'
# "UDM"
#   Service discovery over REST -- exactly the patterns from 9.3.
```

**Key takeaways**

- The EPC divides work into **MME** (control: mobility, authentication, paging), **HSS** (subscriber database), and **S-GW/P-GW** (user plane forwarding and IP allocation).
- **Control-plane / user-plane separation** lets signalling and forwarding scale independently — the same principle as SDN and as 8.1's hybrid architectures.
- **Bearers carry QoS**: the **default bearer** is best-effort, while **dedicated GBR bearers** (QCI 1 for VoLTE) keep voice clear while data is congested.
- **GTP tunnelling preserves the device's IP address across handovers**, so TCP connections survive — the handover appears as a latency spike, not a reset.
- **5G splits the MME into AMF + SMF**, **merges the gateways into the UPF**, and **splits the HSS into UDM + AUSF**.
- The **UPF is deployable at the edge**, which is what makes single-digit-millisecond latency achievable — a central core cannot meet URLLC targets regardless of radio quality.
- The **5G core is service-based**: network functions call each other over **HTTP/2 REST APIs**, making it a cloud-native software system rather than specialised appliances.

#### Radio Access Network Concepts

**Theory**

The **RAN (Radio Access Network)** is everything between the device and the core: the antennas, the radios, and the baseband processing that turns radio waves into IP packets. It is where most of an operator's capital is spent, and where the interesting architectural changes of the last decade have happened.

The traditional design put everything at the tower: antenna, radio, and baseband unit in a cabinet at the base. This is simple and has two problems — each site is an isolated island that cannot coordinate with its neighbours, and every site needs power, cooling, and maintenance visits.

**C-RAN (Centralised RAN)** splits the base station in two. The **RRH/RU (Remote Radio Head/Unit)** stays at the antenna, doing only radio-frequency work. The **BBU (Baseband Unit)** moves to a central location serving many sites, connected by high-capacity **fronthaul** fibre. The benefits are real: **coordination between cells** becomes possible (joint scheduling, interference cancellation), baseband capacity can be **pooled** across sites that peak at different times, and there is less equipment to maintain in the field.

The cost is fronthaul bandwidth, and it is severe. The traditional **CPRI** interface carries **raw digitised radio samples**, requiring roughly 10 Gb/s per sector per 20 MHz carrier — far more than the user data it represents. A three-sector site with carrier aggregation can need 100 Gb/s of fronthaul to deliver a few gigabits of user traffic.

**Functional splits** address this. Rather than cutting between radio and baseband, the processing chain can be divided at one of eight defined points, trading fronthaul bandwidth against how much coordination remains possible. The widely adopted **Split 7.2x** keeps some physical-layer processing at the radio unit, cutting fronthaul requirements by roughly an order of magnitude while preserving most coordination benefits.

**O-RAN** is the industry effort to make these interfaces **open and multi-vendor**. Historically a base station was a single vendor's monolith; O-RAN defines standard interfaces so an operator can buy radio units from one supplier and baseband from another. It also introduces the **RIC (RAN Intelligent Controller)** — near-real-time and non-real-time — which allows programmable, policy-driven optimisation of the RAN, bringing SDN-style separation to the radio network.

Three further concepts appear constantly in practice:

**Carrier aggregation** bonds multiple frequency carriers, exactly as Wi-Fi bonds channels. A device can use an 800 MHz carrier for coverage and a 3.5 GHz carrier for capacity simultaneously.

**Coordinated Multi-Point (CoMP)** lets neighbouring cells cooperate — transmitting jointly to a cell-edge device or coordinating their scheduling to avoid interfering. This directly attacks the worst-served users.

**Massive MIMO** at the base station uses 64 or more antenna elements, applying the beamforming principles from 10.1 at a scale that allows dozens of simultaneous spatially-separated beams.

**Examples**

```text
Three RAN architectures

 TRADITIONAL (D-RAN)          C-RAN                    O-RAN
 everything at the tower      baseband centralised     open, multi-vendor

   [antenna]                    [antenna]                [antenna]
       |                            |                        |
   [radio]                      [RU: radio only]         [O-RU]  vendor A
       |                            |                        |
   [baseband]                    fronthaul (fibre)       open fronthaul
       |                            |                        |
   [backhaul] -> core          [BBU pool] serving        [O-DU] vendor B
                                many sites                   |
   isolated site                    |                    [O-CU] vendor C
   no coordination              [backhaul] -> core           |
   power+cooling per site                                [RIC] policy control
                                pooling + coordination        |
                                                         [backhaul] -> core


 THE FRONTHAUL PROBLEM

  CPRI carries RAW DIGITISED SAMPLES, not user data:

    20 MHz carrier, 2 antennas, 15-bit samples, I and Q
    = 30.72 Msps x 2 x 15 x 2 = ~2.5 Gb/s
    ...to deliver maybe 150 Mb/s of actual user traffic

    3 sectors x 4 carriers = ~30 Gb/s of fronthaul
    for ~1.8 Gb/s of user data       <- a 16x overhead

  This is why FUNCTIONAL SPLITS exist: move some processing back to
  the radio unit so the fronthaul carries something closer to data.


 FUNCTIONAL SPLITS: where to cut the processing chain

   RF -- [ADC] -- [FFT] -- [demap] -- [decode] -- [MAC] -- [RLC] -- [PDCP]
         |        |        |          |           |        |
      split 8  split 7.1  7.2x      split 6    split 5   split 2
         |        |        |          |           |        |
   fronthaul: 30 Gb/s   3 Gb/s     2 Gb/s      1.5 Gb/s   ~user rate
   coordination: BEST ---------------------------------> LEAST

   Split 7.2x is the industry's compromise: ~10x less fronthaul than CPRI,
   most coordination benefits retained.
```

```python
import math

# --- Fronthaul bandwidth: why CPRI does not scale ---
def cpri_rate_gbps(bandwidth_mhz, antennas, sample_bits=15, oversample=1.536):
    """CPRI carries raw I/Q samples: rate is independent of actual traffic."""
    sample_rate = bandwidth_mhz * oversample * 1e6
    return sample_rate * antennas * sample_bits * 2 / 1e9   # x2 for I and Q

def user_rate_gbps(bandwidth_mhz, spectral_efficiency=6):
    return bandwidth_mhz * spectral_efficiency / 1000

print(f"{'carrier':<12}{'antennas':>10}{'CPRI fronthaul':>17}{'user data':>12}{'overhead':>11}")
for bw, ant in ((20, 2), (20, 4), (100, 4), (100, 64)):
    fh = cpri_rate_gbps(bw, ant)
    ur = user_rate_gbps(bw)
    print(f"{f'{bw} MHz':<12}{ant:>10}{fh:>14.1f} Gb{ur:>9.2f} Gb{fh/ur:>10.0f}x")
#   carrier       antennas   CPRI fronthaul   user data    overhead
#   20 MHz               2           1.4 Gb      0.12 Gb         12x
#   20 MHz               4           2.8 Gb      0.12 Gb         23x
#   100 MHz              4          14.2 Gb      0.60 Gb         24x
#   100 MHz             64         226.9 Gb      0.60 Gb        378x
#   MASSIVE MIMO BREAKS CPRI ENTIRELY: 227 Gb/s of fronthaul for
#   600 Mb/s of user data. Functional splits are not optional at scale.

# --- Functional splits: the bandwidth/coordination trade-off ---
SPLITS = [
    ("Split 8 (CPRI)",  1.00, "best",     "raw I/Q; full centralisation"),
    ("Split 7.1",       0.35, "very good","post-FFT frequency domain"),
    ("Split 7.2x",      0.12, "good",     "INDUSTRY STANDARD (O-RAN)"),
    ("Split 6 (MAC-PHY)",0.06,"moderate", "PHY at the radio unit"),
    ("Split 2 (PDCP)",  0.02, "limited",  "close to user data rate"),
]
base = cpri_rate_gbps(100, 64)
print(f"\n100 MHz, 64 antennas (massive MIMO):")
print(f"{'split':<22}{'fronthaul':>13}{'coordination':>15}  notes")
for name, factor, coord, note in SPLITS:
    print(f"{name:<22}{base*factor:>10.1f} Gb{coord:>15}  {note}")
# split                     fronthaul     coordination  notes
# Split 8 (CPRI)              226.9 Gb             best  raw I/Q; full centralisation
# Split 7.1                    79.4 Gb        very good  post-FFT frequency domain
# Split 7.2x                   27.2 Gb             good  INDUSTRY STANDARD (O-RAN)
# Split 6 (MAC-PHY)            13.6 Gb         moderate  PHY at the radio unit
# Split 2 (PDCP)                4.5 Gb          limited  close to user data rate
#   7.2x cuts fronthaul by 8x while keeping most coordination benefits.

# --- Baseband pooling: the C-RAN economic argument ---
def pooling_savings(sites, peak_per_site, diversity_factor=0.55):
    """Sites peak at different times, so pooled capacity < sum of peaks."""
    dedicated = sites * peak_per_site
    pooled = sites * peak_per_site * diversity_factor
    return dedicated, pooled, 1 - pooled / dedicated

print(f"\n{'sites':>7}{'dedicated BBUs':>17}{'pooled':>11}{'saving':>9}")
for n in (10, 50, 200, 1000):
    ded, pool, saving = pooling_savings(n, 1)
    print(f"{n:>7}{ded:>15.0f} U{pool:>10.0f} U{saving:>8.0%}")
#     sites   dedicated BBUs      pooled    saving
#        10              10 U         6 U       45%
#        50              50 U        28 U       45%
#       200             200 U       110 U       45%
#      1000            1000 U       550 U       45%
#   A residential area peaks in the evening, a business district at midday.
#   Pooling exploits that: ~45% less baseband hardware for the same service.

# --- Carrier aggregation ---
def aggregate_throughput(carriers, spectral_efficiency=6):
    total_mhz = sum(c["mhz"] for c in carriers)
    return total_mhz * spectral_efficiency, total_mhz

CA_CONFIG = [
    {"band": "n28 (700 MHz)",  "mhz": 10,  "role": "coverage"},
    {"band": "n3 (1800 MHz)",  "mhz": 20,  "role": "capacity"},
    {"band": "n78 (3500 MHz)", "mhz": 100, "role": "capacity"},
]
print(f"\ncarrier aggregation:")
running = []
for c in CA_CONFIG:
    running.append(c)
    tput, mhz = aggregate_throughput(running)
    print(f"  + {c['band']:<18}{c['mhz']:>4} MHz  "
          f"total {mhz:>4} MHz -> {tput:>6,.0f} Mb/s ({c['role']})")
#   + n28 (700 MHz)       10 MHz  total   10 MHz ->     60 Mb/s (coverage)
#   + n3 (1800 MHz)       20 MHz  total   30 MHz ->    180 Mb/s (capacity)
#   + n78 (3500 MHz)     100 MHz  total  130 MHz ->    780 Mb/s (capacity)
#   Exactly analogous to Wi-Fi channel bonding, but ACROSS BANDS:
#   low-band for reach, mid-band for throughput, used simultaneously.

# --- CoMP: helping the worst-served users ---
def cell_edge_sinr(serving_dbm, interferers_dbm, noise_dbm=-104, comp=False):
    serving = 10 ** (serving_dbm / 10)
    noise = 10 ** (noise_dbm / 10)
    if comp:
        # Joint transmission: interferers become CONTRIBUTORS.
        signal = serving + sum(10 ** (i / 10) for i in interferers_dbm)
        interference = 0
    else:
        signal = serving
        interference = sum(10 ** (i / 10) for i in interferers_dbm)
    return 10 * math.log10(signal / (interference + noise))

edge = (-95, [-97, -99])
print(f"\ncell-edge device, serving {edge[0]} dBm, interferers {edge[1]}:")
for comp in (False, True):
    sinr = cell_edge_sinr(*edge, comp=comp)
    label = "with CoMP (joint transmission)" if comp else "without CoMP"
    print(f"  {label:<34}SINR {sinr:>6.1f} dB")
print("  -> the same towers that were INTERFERING now CONTRIBUTE")
# cell-edge device, serving -95 dBm, interferers [-97, -99]:
#   without CoMP                      SINR    0.3 dB
#   with CoMP (joint transmission)    SINR    11.6 dB
#   -> the same towers that were INTERFERING now CONTRIBUTE
#   11 dB at the cell edge is the difference between 6 Mb/s and 40 Mb/s.

# --- Massive MIMO beams ---
def massive_mimo_capacity(antennas, users_per_cell, per_beam_mbps=100):
    beams = min(antennas // 4, users_per_cell)     # rule of thumb
    return beams * per_beam_mbps, beams

print(f"\n{'antennas':>10}{'simultaneous beams':>21}{'cell capacity':>16}")
for a in (4, 16, 64, 128):
    cap, beams = massive_mimo_capacity(a, 32)
    print(f"{a:>10}{beams:>21}{cap:>13,} Mb")
#   antennas   simultaneous beams   cell capacity
#          4                    1         100 Mb
#         16                    4         400 Mb
#         64                   16       1,600 Mb
#        128                   32       3,200 Mb
#   Massive MIMO multiplies CELL capacity by serving many users at once --
#   the same MU-MIMO principle from 10.1, at a much larger scale.
```

```bash

$ mmcli -m 0 --command='AT+QCAINFO'
# +QCAINFO: "PCC",504990,100,"NR5G BAND 78",1,...     <- primary, 100 MHz
# +QCAINFO: "SCC",1850,20,"LTE BAND 3",1,...          <- secondary, 20 MHz
# +QCAINFO: "SCC",3050,20,"LTE BAND 7",1,...          <- secondary, 20 MHz
#   140 MHz aggregated across three carriers in two generations.

# Number of aggregated carriers correlates directly with throughput:
$ mmcli -m 0 --command='AT+QCAINFO' | grep -c QCAINFO
# 3
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{speed_download}\n' https://speed.example.com/100MB | \
    awk '{printf "%.0f Mb/s\n", $1*8/1e6}'
# 684 Mb/s

# Massive MIMO layers reported by the modem:
$ mmcli -m 0 --command='AT+QENG="servingcell"'
# +QENG: "servingcell","CONNECT","NR5G-SA","TDD",234,15,...,4,...

# Fronthaul link on an O-RAN deployment (operator side):
$ ethtool fh0 | grep -E 'Speed|Duplex'

#         Duplex: Full
$ ip -s link show fh0
#     RX: bytes  packets  errors  dropped
#     8.4e+14    6.1e+11  0       0

# O-RAN components running as containerised functions:
$ kubectl get pods -n oran
# NAME                    READY   STATUS    AGE
# o-du-5f8c7d9b4-x2k9p    1/1     Running   14d
# o-cu-cp-7d4b8f6c5-m1n2  1/1     Running   14d
# o-cu-up-6b9c4d8f7-p3q4  1/1     Running   14d
# near-rt-ric-84f7...     1/1     Running   14d
#   Distributed unit, central unit (control and user planes), and the RIC.

# RIC policies driving RAN optimisation:
$ curl -s http://near-rt-ric:8080/a1-p/policytypes/20008/policies | jq -c '.[]'
# {"policy_id":"qos-boost-1","scope":{"sliceId":"urllc"},"qosObjectives":{"priorityLevel":1}}
#   A1 policies let the operator steer RAN behaviour per slice, declaratively.

# CoMP / coordination features advertised by the cell:
$ mmcli -m 0 --command='AT+QENG="neighbourcell"' | head -3
# +QENG: "neighbourcell intra","NR5G",636666,142,-88,-11,-62,...
# +QENG: "neighbourcell intra","NR5G",636666,411,-91,-13,-64,...
#   Two intra-frequency neighbours at similar strength -- a cell-edge
#   situation where CoMP joint transmission would help substantially.

# Compare cell-centre and cell-edge performance to see the CoMP case:
$ for loc in centre edge; do
>   read -p "Move to cell $loc, press enter..."
>   mmcli -m 0 --signal-get | awk '/rsrp|snr/{printf "%s ", $3}'
>   curl -s -o /dev/null -w "-> %{speed_download}\n" https://speed.example.com/10MB | \
>     awk '{printf "%.0f Mb/s\n", $NF*8/1e6}'
> done
# -89.00 14.20 -> 412 Mb/s        <- cell centre
# -103.00 2.10 -> 28 Mb/s         <- cell edge: 15x worse
#   Cell-edge users are what CoMP and massive MIMO beamforming target.
```

**Key takeaways**

- The **RAN** spans antenna, radio, and baseband; traditional **D-RAN** puts all of it at the tower, leaving each site isolated and unable to coordinate.
- **C-RAN** centralises the **BBU** and leaves an **RRH/RU** at the antenna, enabling **inter-cell coordination** and **baseband pooling** (~45% hardware saving from traffic diversity).
- The cost is **fronthaul**: **CPRI carries raw I/Q samples**, needing 10–200× more bandwidth than the user data it delivers — massive MIMO breaks it entirely.
- **Functional splits** cut the processing chain at different points; **Split 7.2x** is the industry compromise, roughly 8× less fronthaul with most coordination retained.
- **O-RAN** opens the interfaces for multi-vendor deployment and adds the **RIC** for programmable, policy-driven RAN control.
- **Carrier aggregation** bonds carriers across bands (low-band reach plus mid-band capacity); **CoMP** turns interfering neighbours into contributors, worth ~11 dB at the cell edge.
- **Massive MIMO** applies beamforming at 64+ elements to serve many users simultaneously, multiplying **cell** capacity rather than link speed.

#### Network Slicing and Edge Computing

**Theory**

The 5G evolution topic ended on a tension: eMBB, URLLC, and mMTC have contradictory requirements, and one network cannot be optimised for all three at once. **Network slicing** is the resolution.

A **network slice** is a complete, logically isolated virtual network running on shared physical infrastructure — its own radio scheduling policy, its own core network functions, its own QoS guarantees, and its own security boundary. It is the same virtualisation idea as VLANs or VPNs, but applied **end to end** across radio, transport, and core.

The critical property is **isolation**: congestion or failure in one slice must not affect another. A stadium full of people streaming video should not degrade the slice carrying the venue's emergency communications.

Slices are identified by an **S-NSSAI**, containing a **slice/service type (SST)** — standardised values 1 for eMBB, 2 for URLLC, 3 for mMTC, 4 for V2X — plus an optional differentiator so an operator can run several slices of the same type for different customers.

The parameters that differ between slices are exactly the ones that conflict:

| Slice | Latency | Throughput | Reliability | Density |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **eMBB** | ~20 ms | **High** | Standard | Moderate |
| **URLLC** | **< 5 ms** | Low | **99.999%** | Low |
| **mMTC** | Tolerant | Very low | Standard | **1M/km²** |
| **V2X** | **< 10 ms** | Moderate | **High** | Moderate |

**Edge computing (MEC)** is the necessary companion. As computed in the core topic, a 1 ms air interface is irrelevant if the server is 40 ms away — the internet path dominates. **Multi-access Edge Computing** places compute and storage at or near the cell site, inside the operator's network, so the round trip never leaves the region.

The applications that require this are specific, and it is worth being precise about which genuinely do:

- **Cloud gaming and AR/VR** — motion-to-photon latency above ~20 ms causes discomfort.
- **Industrial automation** — control loops need deterministic single-digit milliseconds.
- **Autonomous vehicles** — reaction time is a safety property.
- **Video analytics** — processing at the edge avoids backhauling raw camera streams.

Edge computing also reduces **backhaul cost**, which is often the stronger commercial argument: analysing video where it is captured and sending only events is far cheaper than transporting every frame to a central data centre.

The honest caveats: slicing requires **5G Standalone**, so NSA networks cannot offer it; slice isolation is a *policy* guarantee enforced by scheduling and admission control, not a physical one; and edge deployment multiplies the number of sites an operator must secure, update, and operate — which is a substantial operational burden compared with a handful of central data centres.

**Examples**

```text
Network slicing: one infrastructure, several virtual networks

  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
  |               SHARED PHYSICAL INFRASTRUCTURE                 |
  |       radio | transport | compute | core network functions   |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------+
        |                    |                     |
  +-----------+      +--------------+      +---------------+
  | eMBB      |      | URLLC        |      | mMTC          |
  | SST=1     |      | SST=2        |      | SST=3         |
  |           |      |              |      |               |
  | 20 ms     |      | < 5 ms       |      | tolerant      |
  | 1 Gb/s    |      | 10 Mb/s      |      | 10 kb/s       |
  | 99.9%     |      | 99.999%      |      | 99%           |
  | consumers |      | factory robots|     | 1M sensors/km2|
  +-----------+      +--------------+      +---------------+

  ISOLATION: a stadium crowd saturating the eMBB slice must NOT
  affect the URLLC slice carrying the venue's safety systems.


 WHY EDGE COMPUTING IS NOT OPTIONAL FOR URLLC

   WITHOUT MEC                          WITH MEC
   [device] -1ms- [gNB] -12ms- [core]   [device] -1ms- [gNB] -0.2ms- [UPF+MEC]
                                 |                                      |
                          -40ms- [cloud]                          application
                                                                   runs HERE
   total: 53 ms                          total: ~2 ms

   The 1 ms air interface is irrelevant when the server is 40 ms away.
   URLLC is an END-TO-END property, not a radio property.


 THE SLICE SELECTION FLOW

   device requests S-NSSAI (SST=2, SD=0x000001)
        |
        v
   [AMF] -- asks --> [NSSF]  "which slice instance serves this?"
        |                |
        |                +-- checks subscription, location, load
        |                +-- returns the slice instance
        v
   [SMF for that slice] -- selects --> [UPF for that slice]
        |                                      |
        v                                      v
   session established with the slice's QoS    traffic steered to the
   parameters and admission control            slice's user plane
```

```python
import math

# --- Slice definitions and their conflicting requirements ---
SLICES = {
    "eMBB (SST=1)":  {"latency_ms": 20,  "throughput_mbps": 1000, "reliability": 0.999,
                      "density_km2": 1000,    "use": "consumer broadband, video"},
    "URLLC (SST=2)": {"latency_ms": 2,   "throughput_mbps": 10,   "reliability": 0.99999,
                      "density_km2": 100,     "use": "industrial control, robotics"},
    "mMTC (SST=3)":  {"latency_ms": 5000,"throughput_mbps": 0.01, "reliability": 0.99,
                      "density_km2": 1_000_000,"use": "sensors, meters"},
    "V2X (SST=4)":   {"latency_ms": 10,  "throughput_mbps": 50,   "reliability": 0.9999,
                      "density_km2": 500,     "use": "vehicle communication"},
}
print(f"{'slice':<16}{'latency':>10}{'throughput':>13}{'reliability':>14}{'density/km2':>14}")
for name, s in SLICES.items():
    print(f"{name:<16}{s['latency_ms']:>8}ms{s['throughput_mbps']:>10,.2f}Mb"
          f"{s['reliability']:>13.5f}{s['density_km2']:>14,}")
# slice              latency   throughput    reliability   density/km2
# eMBB (SST=1)          20ms  1,000.00Mb        0.99900         1,000
# URLLC (SST=2)          2ms     10.00Mb        0.99999           100
# mMTC (SST=3)        5000ms      0.01Mb        0.99000     1,000,000
# V2X (SST=4)           10ms     50.00Mb        0.99990           500
#   No single set of radio parameters satisfies all four. Slicing is the
#   architectural admission that they must be configured separately.

# --- Why one configuration cannot serve all three ---
def radio_config_for(slice_name):
    s = SLICES[slice_name]
    if s["latency_ms"] < 5:
        return {"TTI": "0.125 ms (mini-slot)", "HARQ": "aggressive retransmit",
                "scheduling": "pre-emptive, reserved resources",
                "cost": "low spectral efficiency: capacity sacrificed for latency"}
    if s["density_km2"] > 100_000:
        return {"TTI": "long", "HARQ": "minimal",
                "scheduling": "grant-free, contention-based",
                "cost": "high latency, but supports huge device counts"}
    return {"TTI": "1 ms", "HARQ": "standard", "scheduling": "proportional fair",
            "cost": "balanced: maximises aggregate throughput"}

print()
for name in ("eMBB (SST=1)", "URLLC (SST=2)", "mMTC (SST=3)"):
    cfg = radio_config_for(name)
    print(f"{name}")
    print(f"   TTI={cfg['TTI']}, scheduling={cfg['scheduling']}")
    print(f"   trade-off: {cfg['cost']}\n")
#   The URLLC configuration deliberately WASTES spectrum to guarantee latency.
#   Running the whole network that way would be commercially absurd --
#   which is exactly the argument for slicing.

# --- Slice isolation: admission control under load ---
class SlicedCell:
    def __init__(self, total_capacity_mbps=1000):
        self.total = total_capacity_mbps
        self.allocations = {}     # slice -> (guaranteed, max)

    def reserve(self, slice_name, guaranteed, maximum):
        committed = sum(g for g, _ in self.allocations.values())
        if committed + guaranteed > self.total:
            return False, "admission REFUSED: would break existing guarantees"
        self.allocations[slice_name] = (guaranteed, maximum)
        return True, f"reserved {guaranteed} Mb/s guaranteed"

    def allocate(self, demands):
        """Guarantees are honoured first; spare capacity is shared."""
        result, spare = {}, self.total
        for name, (guar, _) in self.allocations.items():
            give = min(demands.get(name, 0), guar)
            result[name] = give
            spare -= guar                       # the guarantee is RESERVED
        for name, (guar, mx) in self.allocations.items():
            extra = min(max(0, demands.get(name, 0) - result[name]),
                        mx - result[name], max(0, spare))
            result[name] += extra
            spare -= extra
        return result

cell = SlicedCell(1000)
for name, g, m in (("URLLC", 100, 150), ("V2X", 150, 250), ("eMBB", 400, 900)):
    ok, msg = cell.reserve(name, g, m)
    print(f"  reserve {name:<6}: {msg}")
print()

print(f"{'scenario':<34}{'URLLC':>9}{'V2X':>8}{'eMBB':>8}")
for label, demands in (("normal load", {"URLLC": 80, "V2X": 120, "eMBB": 300}),
                       ("eMBB surge (stadium)", {"URLLC": 80, "V2X": 120, "eMBB": 5000}),
                       ("everything saturated", {"URLLC": 500, "V2X": 500, "eMBB": 5000})):
    a = cell.allocate(demands)
    print(f"{label:<34}{a['URLLC']:>7.0f}Mb{a['V2X']:>6.0f}Mb{a['eMBB']:>6.0f}Mb")
# scenario                              URLLC     V2X    eMBB
# normal load                             80Mb   120Mb   300Mb
# eMBB surge (stadium)                    80Mb   120Mb   900Mb
# everything saturated                   150Mb   250Mb   900Mb
#   Note the middle row: eMBB demand went to 5 Gb/s and URLLC was UNAFFECTED.
#   That is isolation, enforced by admission control and scheduling.

# --- Edge computing: where latency actually goes ---
def end_to_end_ms(air, ran, transport, compute, placement):
    return {"central cloud":   air + ran + transport + 40 + compute,
            "regional DC":     air + ran + transport + 8 + compute,
            "edge (MEC)":      air + ran + 0.2 + compute}[placement]

print(f"\n{'placement':<18}{'total latency':>15}  supports")
for p in ("central cloud", "regional DC", "edge (MEC)"):
    lat = end_to_end_ms(1, 1, 2, 3, p)
    supports = ("URLLC, AR/VR, cloud gaming" if lat < 10 else
                "video streaming, web" if lat < 30 else "bulk data only")
    print(f"{p:<18}{lat:>12.1f} ms  {supports}")
# placement            total latency  supports
# central cloud                47.0 ms  bulk data only
# regional DC                  15.0 ms  video streaming, web
# edge (MEC)                    5.2 ms  URLLC, AR/VR, cloud gaming

# Latency budgets for applications that genuinely need the edge:
BUDGETS = [("cloud gaming", 20), ("AR/VR motion-to-photon", 20),
           ("industrial control loop", 5), ("autonomous vehicle reaction", 10),
           ("video streaming", 200), ("web browsing", 300)]
print(f"\n{'application':<32}{'budget':>9}{'central':>10}{'edge':>8}")
for app, budget in BUDGETS:
    central = end_to_end_ms(1, 1, 2, 3, "central cloud")
    edge = end_to_end_ms(1, 1, 2, 3, "edge (MEC)")
    print(f"{app:<32}{budget:>7}ms{'OK' if central<=budget else 'FAIL':>10}"
          f"{'OK' if edge<=budget else 'FAIL':>8}")
# application                       budget   central    edge
# cloud gaming                        20ms      FAIL      OK
# AR/VR motion-to-photon              20ms      FAIL      OK
# industrial control loop              5ms      FAIL      OK
# autonomous vehicle reaction         10ms      FAIL      OK
# video streaming                    200ms        OK      OK
# web browsing                       300ms        OK      OK
#   The edge matters for exactly four of these six. Video and web do not
#   need it -- and claiming otherwise is how edge projects lose credibility.

# --- The backhaul argument, often stronger than the latency one ---
def video_analytics_backhaul(cameras, mbps_each, hours=24, edge=False):
    if edge:
        # Only detected EVENTS are sent, not raw video.
        gb_per_day = cameras * 0.002 * hours * 3600 / 1000
    else:
        gb_per_day = cameras * mbps_each * hours * 3600 / 8 / 1000
    return gb_per_day

print(f"\n{'cameras':>9}{'raw backhaul/day':>20}{'edge backhaul/day':>21}{'reduction':>12}")
for n in (10, 100, 1000):
    raw = video_analytics_backhaul(n, 4)
    edge = video_analytics_backhaul(n, 4, edge=True)
    print(f"{n:>9}{raw:>17,.0f} GB{edge:>18,.1f} GB{1-edge/raw:>11.1%}")
#   cameras   raw backhaul/day   edge backhaul/day   reduction
#        10          4,320 GB               1.7 GB      100.0%
#       100         43,200 GB              17.3 GB      100.0%
#     1,000        432,000 GB             172.8 GB      100.0%
#   Processing where the video is captured and shipping only events
#   eliminates essentially all backhaul. This is usually the stronger
#   business case -- stronger than latency, in most deployments.
```

```bash
$ mmcli -m 0 --command='AT+CNSSAI?'
# +CNSSAI: 1,"01","000001"      <- SST=1 (eMBB), SD=000001
# +CNSSAI: 2,"02","000002"      <- SST=2 (URLLC)
#   The allowed NSSAI comes from the subscription and the serving network.

# Which slice is the current session on?
$ mmcli -m 0 --command='AT+CGDCONT?'
# +CGDCONT: 1,"IPV4V6","internet","10.4.2.9",0,0,0,0,0,0,1,,,,,,,,,,"01000001"
#                                                                    ^^^^^^^^ S-NSSAI
#   SST=01, SD=000001: the eMBB slice.

# Slice configuration on a 5G core (operator/lab):
$ kubectl get networkslices -n 5gc
# NAME          SST   SD       STATUS   UPF           LATENCY-TARGET
# embb-public   1     000001   Active   upf-regional  20ms
# urllc-factory 2     000002   Active   upf-edge-04   2ms
# mmtc-meters   3     000003   Active   upf-regional  5000ms
#   Note urllc-factory points at an EDGE UPF -- that is what makes 2 ms possible.

$ kubectl describe networkslice urllc-factory -n 5gc | grep -A6 'QoS'
# QoS:
#   5QI:                  82
#   Priority:             19
#   Packet Delay Budget:  10ms
#   Packet Error Rate:    1e-4
#   Guaranteed Bitrate:   10Mbps
#   Resource Type:        GBR

# Verify isolation: load one slice, measure another:
$ kubectl exec -n 5gc load-gen -- iperf3 -c embb-upf -t 60 -P 32 &
$ ping -I wwan0 -c 60 -i 0.1 -q urllc-endpoint | tail -2
# 60 packets transmitted, 60 received, 0% packet loss
# rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 1.8/2.1/3.4/0.3 ms
#   The eMBB slice is saturated; URLLC latency is untouched. Isolation works.

# Edge nodes and their distance from the cell site:
$ kubectl get nodes -l node-role=edge -o custom-columns=\
NAME:.metadata.name,ZONE:.metadata.labels.topology\\.kubernetes\\.io/zone
# NAME              ZONE
# edge-site-0451    cell-0451
# edge-site-0452    cell-0452
#   Compute co-located with the radio site.

# Measure the latency difference directly:
$ for target in edge-app.local regional-app.example central-app.example; do
>   echo -n "$target: "
>   ping -c 10 -q $target | awk -F'/' '/rtt/{printf "%.1f ms\n", $5}'
> done
# edge-app.local: 2.3 ms
# regional-app.example: 14.8 ms
# central-app.example: 46.2 ms

# MEC application deployed at the edge:
$ kubectl get pods -n mec --field-selector spec.nodeName=edge-site-0451
# NAME                        READY   STATUS    AGE
# video-analytics-7f8c...     1/1     Running   9d
# ar-render-5d9b...           1/1     Running   9d
#   Video is analysed here; only detected events traverse the backhaul.

# Confirm slicing requires Standalone:
$ mmcli -m 0 --command='AT+QENG="servingcell"' | grep -o 'NR5G-[SN]A'
# NR5G-SA
#   NSA would return NR5G-NSA, and slicing would be unavailable regardless
#   of what the marketing material promises.
```

**Key takeaways**

- A **network slice** is an end-to-end virtual network — radio, transport, and core — with its own QoS, isolation, and security boundary on shared infrastructure.
- Slicing exists because **eMBB, URLLC, and mMTC have contradictory radio requirements**: a URLLC configuration deliberately sacrifices spectral efficiency for latency.
- Slices are identified by **S-NSSAI (SST + optional differentiator)**, with standard SSTs of 1 (eMBB), 2 (URLLC), 3 (mMTC), 4 (V2X).
- **Isolation is enforced by admission control and scheduling**, so a saturated eMBB slice leaves URLLC latency untouched — it is a policy guarantee, not a physical one.
- **Edge computing is required for URLLC**: a 1 ms air interface is meaningless when the server is 40 ms away, since latency is an **end-to-end** property.
- Only some applications genuinely need the edge — **gaming, AR/VR, industrial control, autonomous vehicles** — while video streaming and web browsing do not.
- **Backhaul reduction is often the stronger business case**: analysing video at the edge and shipping only events removes essentially all transport cost.
- **Slicing requires 5G Standalone**; NSA networks cannot provide it.

> 4. Interview-style: *A retailer wants edge computing for its in-store video analytics. Argue the business case without mentioning latency.* (Hint: work out how many gigabytes per day 200 cameras generate, and what it costs to move all of it versus moving only the detections.)

<a id="104-short-range-and-iot-networking"></a>
### 10.4 Short-Range and IoT Networking

Battery-powered devices invert every assumption behind Wi-Fi and cellular: this subchapter covers the protocols designed for milliwatts, kilobytes, and years of unattended operation.

#### Bluetooth and BLE

**Theory**

Wi-Fi and cellular optimise for throughput. A sensor that must run for five years on a coin cell has an entirely different objective function, and Bluetooth Low Energy is the clearest illustration of what changes when **energy, not bandwidth, is the scarce resource**.

**Classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR)** was designed to replace cables: wireless headsets, keyboards, file transfer, car audio. It maintains a **continuous connection** with 1–3 Mb/s throughput, using **frequency-hopping spread spectrum** across 79 channels at 1,600 hops per second. Hopping is why Bluetooth coexists tolerably with Wi-Fi in the same band — an interfered hop is simply retried on the next frequency. Its power draw, though, is tens of milliwatts, which rules out battery-powered sensors.

**BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy)**, introduced in Bluetooth 4.0, is a **different protocol that shares a name and a band**. The distinction matters: BLE is not "Bluetooth with power saving", it is a separate radio and stack designed from scratch around a single principle — **stay asleep**.

The design choices all follow from that principle:

- **40 channels of 2 MHz** instead of 79 of 1 MHz, with **3 advertising channels** (37, 38, 39) placed deliberately in the gaps between Wi-Fi channels 1, 6, and 11.
- **Connectionless operation is the default.** A device broadcasts an advertising packet, listens briefly, and returns to sleep. No association, no maintained link.
- **Tiny packets** (up to 255 bytes) and short exchanges, so the radio is on for milliseconds rather than continuously.
- **Connection intervals** from 7.5 ms to 4 seconds, negotiated by the application, letting a device sleep between them.

The consequence is a duty cycle of well under 1%. A BLE sensor advertising once per second draws an *average* of a few microamps, which is how coin-cell devices last years.

BLE's data model is also distinctive. **GATT (Generic Attribute Profile)** organises data as **services** containing **characteristics** — named, typed attributes that can be read, written, or subscribed to for notifications. A heart-rate monitor exposes a Heart Rate Service containing a Heart Rate Measurement characteristic. This is a small, self-describing data model, closer to a REST resource than to a byte stream, and it is why BLE devices interoperate across vendors.

| | Classic Bluetooth | BLE |
|---|---|---|
| Throughput | **1–3 Mb/s** | 0.27 Mb/s (1 Mb/s PHY) |
| Range | 10–100 m | 10–100 m (LE Coded: ~1 km) |
| Power | ~30 mW active | **~0.01–10 mW average** |
| Connection | **Continuous** | Connectionless or brief |
| Latency to connect | ~100 ms | **~3 ms** |
| Battery life | Days | **Years** |
| Use | Audio, file transfer | Sensors, beacons, wearables |

Later versions added **LE Coded PHY** (forward error correction trading rate for ~4× range), **2 Mb/s PHY**, **LE Audio** with the LC3 codec, **direction finding** for sub-metre positioning, and **Bluetooth Mesh** for many-to-many networks of hundreds of nodes.

**Examples**

```text
Classic Bluetooth vs BLE: the duty cycle is the whole story

  CLASSIC BLUETOOTH (a headset)
  radio: [################################################] continuous
         ~30 mW sustained -> a 200 mAh battery lasts ~1 day

  BLE (a sensor advertising once per second)
  radio: [#]                          [#]                  [#]
         ^ 1.5 ms awake               ^ 1.5 ms             ^ 1.5 ms
         |<-------- 1000 ms asleep -------->|
         duty cycle 0.15%
         ~6 uA average -> a 220 mAh coin cell lasts ~4 YEARS

  Same band, same distance, 5000x difference in energy.


 BLE CHANNEL LAYOUT: advertising channels dodge Wi-Fi

   2402 ------------------------------------------------- 2480 MHz
     |                                                       |
   [37]      Wi-Fi ch 1        Wi-Fi ch 6       Wi-Fi ch 11  |
     ^      [==========]      [==========]     [==========]  |
     |            [38]                             [39]      |
     |             ^                                ^        |
     +-------------+--------------------------------+
        the three ADVERTISING channels sit in the GAPS
        between the three non-overlapping Wi-Fi channels

   37 data channels fill the rest and are used with adaptive
   frequency hopping, avoiding channels found to be busy.


 THE GATT DATA MODEL: services and characteristics

   Device: heart-rate monitor
   |
   +-- Service: Heart Rate (UUID 0x180D)
   |    +-- Characteristic: Heart Rate Measurement (0x2A37)  [NOTIFY]
   |    |      value: 0x06 0x48  -> 72 bpm
   |    +-- Characteristic: Body Sensor Location (0x2A38)    [READ]
   |           value: 0x02 -> wrist
   |
   +-- Service: Battery (0x180F)
        +-- Characteristic: Battery Level (0x2A19)           [READ, NOTIFY]
               value: 0x5B -> 91%

   Self-describing, typed, standardised UUIDs -> cross-vendor
   interoperability without per-device drivers.


 CONNECTION INTERVAL: the application's power/latency dial

   7.5 ms  -> responsive (a mouse), high power
   50 ms   -> balanced (a fitness band)
   1000 ms -> sluggish, very low power (a temperature sensor)
   4000 ms -> maximum sleep (a beacon)
```

```python
import math

# --- Energy model: why BLE lasts years ---
def average_current_ua(tx_current_ma, tx_duration_ms, interval_ms,
                       sleep_current_ua=1.0):
    duty = tx_duration_ms / interval_ms
    return tx_current_ma * 1000 * duty + sleep_current_ua * (1 - duty)

def battery_life_years(capacity_mah, avg_current_ua):
    hours = capacity_mah * 1000 / avg_current_ua
    return hours / 24 / 365

print(f"{'scenario':<34}{'duty':>8}{'avg current':>14}{'CR2032 life':>14}")
SCENARIOS = [
    ("classic BT headset (continuous)", 15.0, 1000, 1000),
    ("BLE mouse (7.5 ms interval)",      8.0,  1.2,  7.5),
    ("BLE fitness band (50 ms)",         8.0,  1.2,   50),
    ("BLE sensor (1 s advertising)",     8.0,  1.5, 1000),
    ("BLE beacon (4 s advertising)",     8.0,  1.5, 4000),
]
for name, ma, dur, interval in SCENARIOS:
    avg = average_current_ua(ma, dur, interval)
    life = battery_life_years(220, avg)          # CR2032 = 220 mAh
    life_s = f"{life:.1f} yr" if life >= 1 else f"{life*365:.0f} days"
    print(f"{name:<34}{dur/interval:>7.1%}{avg:>11.1f} uA{life_s:>14}")
# scenario                            duty   avg current   CR2032 life
# classic BT headset (continuous)   100.0%    15000.0 uA      1 days
# BLE mouse (7.5 ms interval)        16.0%     1280.8 uA     18 days
# BLE fitness band (50 ms)            2.4%      193.0 uA     130 days
# BLE sensor (1 s advertising)        0.2%       12.9 uA      1.9 yr
# BLE beacon (4 s advertising)        0.0%        4.0 uA      6.3 yr
#   The ONLY variable that changed is how often the radio wakes.
#   Everything else about BLE's design exists to make sleeping possible.

# The connection interval is a direct power/latency trade-off:
print(f"\n{'interval':>10}{'avg current':>14}{'battery life':>15}{'response latency':>19}")
for interval in (7.5, 20, 50, 200, 1000, 4000):
    avg = average_current_ua(8.0, 1.2, interval)
    life = battery_life_years(220, avg)
    life_s = f"{life:.1f} yr" if life >= 1 else f"{life*365:.0f} days"
    print(f"{interval:>8.1f}ms{avg:>11.1f} uA{life_s:>15}{interval:>16.0f} ms")
#   interval   avg current    battery life   response latency
#      7.5ms     1280.8 uA         18 days                 8 ms
#     20.0ms      481.0 uA         52 days                20 ms
#     50.0ms      193.0 uA        130 days                50 ms
#    200.0ms       49.0 uA          1.4 yr               200 ms
#   1000.0ms       10.6 uA          2.4 yr              1000 ms
#   4000.0ms        3.4 uA          7.4 yr              4000 ms
#   An application chooses a point on this curve. A mouse must be at the
#   top; a temperature sensor belongs at the bottom.

# --- Channel layout: why advertising channels are where they are ---
def ble_channel_freq(ch):
    """BLE data channels 0-36, advertising 37/38/39."""
    ADV = {37: 2402, 38: 2426, 39: 2480}
    if ch in ADV:
        return ADV[ch]
    return 2404 + ch * 2 if ch < 11 else 2428 + (ch - 11) * 2

WIFI = {1: (2401, 2423), 6: (2426, 2448), 11: (2451, 2473)}
print(f"\n{'BLE adv ch':>11}{'freq':>8}  overlaps Wi-Fi?")
for ch in (37, 38, 39):
    f = ble_channel_freq(ch)
    clash = [w for w, (lo, hi) in WIFI.items() if lo <= f <= hi]
    print(f"{ch:>11}{f:>6}MHz  {'ch ' + str(clash) if clash else 'NO -- sits in a gap'}")
#   BLE adv ch    freq  overlaps Wi-Fi?
#           37  2402MHz  ch [1]
#           38  2426MHz  ch [6]
#           39  2480MHz  NO -- sits in a gap
#   The placement is deliberate: advertising on three widely separated
#   channels means Wi-Fi interference on one does not block discovery.

# --- GATT: the data model ---
class GATTServer:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.services = name, {}

    def add_service(self, uuid, label):
        self.services[uuid] = {"label": label, "characteristics": {}}
        return self

    def add_characteristic(self, service_uuid, uuid, label, props, value):
        self.services[service_uuid]["characteristics"][uuid] = {
            "label": label, "properties": props, "value": value}
        return self

hrm = GATTServer("Heart Rate Monitor")
hrm.add_service(0x180D, "Heart Rate")
hrm.add_characteristic(0x180D, 0x2A37, "Heart Rate Measurement",
                       ["notify"], bytes([0x06, 0x48]))
hrm.add_characteristic(0x180D, 0x2A38, "Body Sensor Location",
                       ["read"], bytes([0x02]))
hrm.add_service(0x180F, "Battery")
hrm.add_characteristic(0x180F, 0x2A19, "Battery Level", ["read", "notify"],
                       bytes([0x5B]))

print(f"\n{hrm.name}")
for suuid, svc in hrm.services.items():
    print(f"  Service 0x{suuid:04X}  {svc['label']}")
    for cuuid, c in svc["characteristics"].items():
        props = ",".join(c["properties"])
        print(f"    Char 0x{cuuid:04X}  {c['label']:<26}[{props}]  "
              f"= {c['value'].hex()}")
# Heart Rate Monitor
#   Service 0x180D  Heart Rate
#     Char 0x2A37  Heart Rate Measurement    [notify]  = 0648
#     Char 0x2A38  Body Sensor Location      [read]  = 02
#   Service 0x180F  Battery
#     Char 0x2A19  Battery Level             [read,notify]  = 5b

# Decoding a standardised characteristic -- no vendor driver needed:
def decode_heart_rate(value: bytes):
    flags = value[0]
    if flags & 0x01:                      # bit 0: 16-bit value
        return int.from_bytes(value[1:3], "little")
    return value[1]                       # 8-bit value

print(f"\nHeart Rate Measurement 0x{hrm.services[0x180D]['characteristics'][0x2A37]['value'].hex()}"
      f" -> {decode_heart_rate(bytes([0x06, 0x48]))} bpm")
# Heart Rate Measurement 0x0648 -> 72 bpm
#   The UUID 0x2A37 means the same thing on EVERY vendor's device.

# --- PHY options: range vs rate ---
PHYS = [("LE 1M (default)",   1000, 1.0, "standard"),
        ("LE 2M",             2000, 0.8, "faster, ~20% less range"),
        ("LE Coded S=2",       500, 2.0, "2x range"),
        ("LE Coded S=8",       125, 4.0, "4x range, 1/8 rate")]
print(f"\n{'PHY':<20}{'rate':>10}{'relative range':>17}  use")
for name, kbps, rng, note in PHYS:
    print(f"{name:<20}{kbps:>7} kb{rng:>16.1f}x  {note}")
# PHY                       rate   relative range  use
# LE 1M (default)        1000 kb             1.0x  standard
# LE 2M                  2000 kb             0.8x  faster, ~20% less range
# LE Coded S=2            500 kb             2.0x  2x range
# LE Coded S=8            125 kb             4.0x  4x range, 1/8 rate
#   LE Coded trades data rate for forward error correction -- the same
#   coding-rate trade-off as 10.1's adaptive modulation.
```

```bash
$ sudo bluetoothctl scan on
# Discovery started
# [NEW] Device C4:7C:8D:6A:1B:2F Heart Rate Monitor
# [NEW] Device 3C:A3:08:91:04:7E Tile Tracker
$ sudo hcitool lescan --duplicates | head -5

# Raw advertising packets, showing how small they are:
$ sudo btmon | grep -A6 'Advertising Report'
# > HCI Event: LE Meta Event (0x3e) plen 42
#       LE Advertising Report (0x02)

#         Data length: 26
#         Flags: 0x06
#         16-bit Service UUIDs: Heart Rate (0x180d)
#         RSSI: -67 dBm
#   26 bytes of payload. The radio is on for ~1.5 ms to send this.

# Explore a device's GATT structure:
$ sudo gatttool -b C4:7C:8D:6A:1B:2F -I
# [C4:7C:8D:6A:1B:2F][LE]> connect
# [CON][C4:7C:8D:6A:1B:2F][LE]> primary
# attr handle: 0x0001, end grp handle: 0x0007 uuid: 00001800-...   (Generic Access)
# attr handle: 0x0008, end grp handle: 0x000b uuid: 0000180d-...   (Heart Rate)
# attr handle: 0x000c, end grp handle: 0x000f uuid: 0000180f-...   (Battery)

# Read a standardised characteristic:
$ sudo gatttool -b C4:7C:8D:6A:1B:2F --char-read --handle=0x000e
# Characteristic value/descriptor: 5b
$ python3 -c "print(f'battery: {0x5b}%')"
# battery: 91%

# Subscribe to notifications (the low-power way to receive data):
$ sudo gatttool -b C4:7C:8D:6A:1B:2F --char-write-req --handle=0x000a --value=0100
$ sudo gatttool -b C4:7C:8D:6A:1B:2F --listen --char-read --handle=0x0009
# Notification handle = 0x0009 value: 06 48
#   The device pushes when the value changes, instead of being polled --
#   the same push-vs-poll argument as 8.1, applied to battery life.

# Negotiated connection parameters -- the power/latency setting:
$ sudo btmon | grep -A4 'Connection Update'
#         Connection interval: 50.00 msec
#         Connection latency: 4
#         Supervision timeout: 5000 msec
#   Connection latency 4 = the peripheral may SKIP 4 intervals if it has
#   nothing to say, extending sleep further.

# Which PHY is in use?
$ sudo btmon | grep -i 'PHY'
#         TX PHY: LE 2M (0x02)
#         RX PHY: LE 2M (0x02)

# Classic vs LE on the same adapter:
$ hciconfig -a hci0 | grep -E 'Type|Features'
#         Type: Primary  Bus: USB
#         Features: 0xbf 0xfe 0xcf 0xfe 0xdb 0xff 0x7b 0x87
$ sudo btmgmt info | grep -i 'supported settings'
# supported settings: powered connectable discoverable bondable ssp br/edr le
#                                                                 ^^^^^ ^^ both
#   "br/edr" and "le" are two DIFFERENT radios sharing one chip.

# Measure a device's actual advertising interval:
$ sudo timeout 30 hcitool lescan --duplicates 2>/dev/null | \
    grep -c 'C4:7C:8D:6A:1B:2F'
# 29
$ python3 -c "print(f'~{30/29:.2f} s advertising interval')"
# ~1.03 s advertising interval
```

**Key takeaways**

- **BLE is a different protocol from Classic Bluetooth**, sharing only a name and a band — it was designed around one principle: **stay asleep**.
- **Duty cycle is the entire energy story**: a BLE sensor advertising once per second is awake ~0.15% of the time and lasts years on a coin cell.
- The **connection interval (7.5 ms – 4 s) is the application's power/latency dial**, and choosing it is the main design decision.
- **Three advertising channels (37, 38, 39)** are deliberately placed in the gaps between Wi-Fi channels 1, 6, and 11.
- **GATT organises data as services and characteristics** with standardised UUIDs, giving cross-vendor interoperability without per-device drivers.
- **Notifications replace polling**, which matters for battery life exactly as push-versus-poll mattered for server load in 8.1.
- **LE Coded PHY** trades data rate for forward error correction, reaching ~4× range at 1/8 the rate — the same coding trade-off as adaptive modulation.

> 3. Describe the GATT hierarchy for a device reporting temperature and battery level, including why standardised UUIDs matter.
