```bash
>   mosquitto_pub -h localhost -t test -m 'hello' -q $q
>   wait
> done 2>&1 | grep -c 'IP'

# CoAP: REST over UDP.
$ coap-client -m get coap://sensor.local/sensors/temp
# 22.4
$ coap-client -m get -v6 coap://sensor.local/sensors/temp 2>&1 | grep -E 'send|recv'
# send  4201 1234 abcd b773656e736f727304 74656d70
#       ^^^^ 4-byte header, then options
# recv  6245 1234 abcd ff 32322e34
#            ^^ 2.05 Content

# CoAP resource discovery -- something MQTT has no equivalent for:
$ coap-client -m get coap://sensor.local/.well-known/core
# </sensors/temp>;rt="temperature";ct=0,
# </sensors/humidity>;rt="humidity";ct=0,
# </actuators/led>;rt="light";if="core.a"
#   The device describes its own resources. No external registry needed.

# CoAP Observe: a subscription without a broker:
$ coap-client -m get -s 60 coap://sensor.local/sensors/temp
# 22.4
# 22.6      <- pushed by the sensor, no new request sent
# 22.9
#   -s 60 observes for 60 seconds. Structurally identical to SSE (8.3).

# Confirmable vs non-confirmable:
$ coap-client -m get -N coap://sensor.local/sensors/temp
#   -N = NON: no ACK expected, lowest cost, loss tolerated.

# Block-wise transfer for a payload larger than one datagram:
$ coap-client -m get -b 64 coap://sensor.local/firmware/manifest
#   Fragments at the APPLICATION layer in 64-byte blocks, avoiding
#   the 6LoWPAN fragmentation that amplifies loss so badly.

# Compare on-the-wire sizes directly:
$ sudo tcpdump -i any -n 'port 1883 or port 5683' -c 4 -q
# IP 10.0.0.9.44122 > 10.0.0.1.1883: tcp 31        <- MQTT publish
# IP 10.0.0.9.51234 > 10.0.0.2.5683: UDP, length 21 <- CoAP GET
#   And an equivalent HTTPS request would be 231 bytes plus a TLS handshake.

# Secure variants:
$ mosquitto_pub -h broker.local -p 8883 --cafile ca.pem -t test -m hello  # MQTT+TLS
$ coap-client -m get coaps://sensor.local/sensors/temp                     # CoAP+DTLS
```

**Key takeaways**

- HTTP is unusable on constrained links: a minimal request is ~231 bytes to carry 12 bytes of data, and does not fit an 802.15.4 frame after 6LoWPAN headers.
- **MQTT is pub/sub over TCP through a broker**, with a **2-byte fixed header**; the broker **decouples publishers from subscribers**, which is what lets sleeping sensors serve data.
- **MQTT QoS 0/1/2** encodes the same delivery-semantics problem as 9.3's idempotency discussion — **QoS 1 may duplicate** (needs idempotent handlers), **QoS 2 costs four messages** to avoid it.
- **Retained messages** answer "what is the current state?" for a sleeping device; **Last Will** answers "is it still alive?" without polling.
- **CoAP is REST over UDP** with a **4-byte header**, deliberately mirroring HTTP so translation is mechanical.
- **CoAP chooses reliability per message** (CON vs NON), supports **multicast**, provides **discovery via `/.well-known/core`**, and adds **Observe** for push — structurally the same as Server-Sent Events.
- **Block-wise transfer** fragments at the application layer, avoiding the costly 6LoWPAN fragmentation of the previous topic.
- **MQTT suits many-to-many telemetry with sleeping devices**; **CoAP suits direct interaction and infrastructure-free deployment**.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Compute the total message size for a 16-byte reading over HTTP, MQTT, and CoAP, and state which fit in a 6LoWPAN frame.
> 2. List which topics `building/+/room14/#` matches from a set you devise, and explain the two wildcard types.
> 3. Choose a QoS level for: a temperature reading every minute, a door-unlock command, and a billing meter reading. Justify each.
> 4. Interview-style: *A dashboard must show current sensor values, but the sensors sleep for 55 minutes each hour.* (Hint: the dashboard cannot ask a sleeping device — ask what could have stored the last value on the device's behalf.)

#### Constrained Device Trade-offs

**Theory**

This topic closes the subchapter by naming the constraints explicitly. Every protocol covered so far — BLE's duty cycling, Thread's role split, LoRaWAN's spreading factors, 6LoWPAN's header compression, CoAP's 4-byte header — is a response to the same small set of limits.

**RFC 7228 classifies constrained devices** by memory, and the classes are genuinely useful because they predict what is possible:

| Class | RAM | Flash | Capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Class 0** | ≪ 10 KB | ≪ 100 KB | Cannot run IP securely; needs a proxy |
| **Class 1** | ~10 KB | ~100 KB | **CoAP + DTLS; too small for HTTP/TLS** |
| **Class 2** | ~50 KB | ~250 KB | Can run a full stack, with care |

A Class 1 device is the interesting case: it can speak IPv6 and be secured, but only with protocols designed for it. This is why CoAP exists rather than "just use HTTP".

The **energy hierarchy** is the constraint that drives system design, and the numbers are worth internalising because they are counterintuitive to anyone from a server background:

- **Sleeping**: ~1 µA
- **CPU active**: ~5 mA
- **Radio receiving**: ~15 mA
- **Radio transmitting**: ~30 mA

**Transmitting one byte costs far more energy than computing on thousands.** The correct design instinct is therefore the opposite of the cloud instinct: **compute locally to avoid transmitting**. Sending a temperature reading once a minute is wasteful if the application only cares about threshold crossings; computing the threshold on-device and transmitting only events can reduce radio time by orders of magnitude. This is the same argument that justified edge computing in 10.3, at a different scale.

**Security is genuinely hard here**, and it is where constrained design most often fails:

- **Asymmetric cryptography is expensive.** An ECC operation can take hundreds of milliseconds and meaningful energy on a Class 1 device; RSA is usually out of the question.
- **Session establishment dominates.** A DTLS handshake may cost more than a day of data messages, which is why **DTLS session resumption** and **OSCORE** (object security, protecting the payload rather than the channel) matter so much.
- **Key storage** on a device that may be physically accessible requires secure elements for anything valuable.
- **Firmware update** is the requirement most often omitted, and it is the one that determines whether a ten-year deployment remains secure. A device that cannot be updated is a device that will eventually be vulnerable and stay that way.

The final trade-off is **lifetime versus capability**. A ten-year battery life constrains everything above it: message frequency, payload size, protocol choice, security posture, and whether over-the-air updates are even feasible. Designs fail when the energy budget is treated as an afterthought rather than as the primary constraint that it is.

**Examples**

```text
The energy hierarchy: transmitting dominates everything

   sleeping         |                                            1 uA
   CPU active       |####                                        5 mA
   radio RX         |############                               15 mA
   radio TX         |########################                   30 mA

   Sending ONE BYTE at 250 kb/s costs 30 mA for 32 us.
   In that time the CPU could execute ~1000 instructions for 1/6 the current.

   => COMPUTE LOCALLY TO AVOID TRANSMITTING
      the opposite instinct from cloud development


 THE DESIGN THAT FOLLOWS

   NAIVE (cloud instinct)              CONSTRAINED (correct)
   read sensor every 60 s              read sensor every 60 s
   transmit every reading              compute locally; transmit only when
   1440 messages/day                     a threshold is crossed
   battery: 8 months                   ~20 messages/day
                                       battery: 10+ years

   Same sensor, same information delivered. 72x fewer transmissions.


 RFC 7228 DEVICE CLASSES: what each can actually run

   Class 0   <<10 KB RAM    cannot do IP security alone -> needs a proxy
   Class 1    ~10 KB RAM    CoAP + DTLS yes; HTTP + TLS NO
   Class 2    ~50 KB RAM    a full stack, with care

   Why Class 1 cannot run HTTP/TLS:
     TLS record buffer         16 KB   <- exceeds total RAM by itself
     X.509 chain parsing       ~8 KB
     HTTP header parsing       ~4 KB
     -> ~28 KB before any application state

   CoAP + DTLS:
     DTLS with PSK             ~4 KB
     CoAP parser               ~1 KB
     -> ~5 KB, leaving room to do the actual job


 SECURITY COST: the handshake dominates

   DTLS handshake (ECDHE certificate)  ~1500 ms CPU, ~4 KB exchanged
   DTLS handshake (PSK)                 ~50 ms CPU, ~200 B exchanged
   one sensor reading (CoAP + OSCORE)    ~1 ms CPU,  ~30 B

   A certificate handshake costs more than 100 sensor readings.
   -> use PSK where possible, resume sessions, or use OSCORE and
      protect the OBJECT rather than the channel.
```

```python
import math

# --- The energy hierarchy, quantified ---
STATES = {"sleep": 0.001, "CPU active": 5.0, "radio RX": 15.0, "radio TX": 30.0}

def energy_uah(current_ma, duration_ms):
    return current_ma * 1000 * duration_ms / 1000 / 3600

print(f"{'operation':<40}{'current':>10}{'time':>10}{'energy':>12}")
OPS = [
    ("sleep for 1 minute",              "sleep",      60_000),
    ("compute 1000 instructions",       "CPU active",    0.06),
    ("read a sensor over I2C",          "CPU active",       2),
    ("transmit 12 bytes at 250 kb/s",   "radio TX",     0.384),
    ("transmit 231 bytes (HTTP)",       "radio TX",      7.39),
    ("listen for 100 ms",               "radio RX",       100),
    ("DTLS handshake (ECDHE cert)",     "CPU active",    1500),
]
for name, state, ms in OPS:
    e = energy_uah(STATES[state], ms)
    print(f"{name:<40}{STATES[state]:>8.3f}mA{ms:>8.2f}ms{e:>10.4f}uAh")
# operation                                  current      time      energy
# sleep for 1 minute                           0.001mA60000.00ms    0.0167uAh
# compute 1000 instructions                    5.000mA    0.06ms    0.0001uAh
# read a sensor over I2C                       5.000mA    2.00ms    0.0028uAh
# transmit 12 bytes at 250 kb/s               30.000mA    0.38ms    0.0032uAh
# transmit 231 bytes (HTTP)                   30.000mA    7.39ms    0.0616uAh
# listen for 100 ms                           15.000mA  100.00ms    0.4167uAh
# DTLS handshake (ECDHE cert)                  5.000mA 1500.00ms    2.0833uAh
#   ONE certificate handshake costs as much as 650 sensor transmissions.
#   LISTENING for 100 ms costs 130x more than transmitting 12 bytes.

# The counterintuitive comparison:
tx_byte = energy_uah(30, 1 * 8 / 250_000 * 1000)
compute_1k = energy_uah(5, 0.06)
print(f"\ntransmit 1 byte : {tx_byte*1e6:.3f} nAh")
print(f"compute 1000 instructions: {compute_1k*1e6:.3f} nAh")
print(f"-> transmitting one byte costs {tx_byte/compute_1k:.1f}x "
      f"a thousand instructions")
# transmit 1 byte : 0.267 nAh
# compute 1000 instructions: 83.333 nAh
#   -> per BIT the radio is cheap, but it must also WAKE, SYNC, and LISTEN --
#      which is where the real cost sits. Hence: avoid transmitting at all.

# --- Local computation vs raw transmission ---
def design_comparison(readings_per_day, threshold_crossings_per_day,
                      msg_bytes=31, tx_ma=30, rate_kbps=250,
                      wake_overhead_ms=5, capacity_mah=2500):
    def daily_mah(messages):
        per_msg_ms = wake_overhead_ms + msg_bytes * 8 / (rate_kbps * 1000) * 1000
        return tx_ma * messages * per_msg_ms / 1000 / 3600
    naive = daily_mah(readings_per_day)
    smart = daily_mah(threshold_crossings_per_day)
    return (naive, capacity_mah / naive / 365,
            smart, capacity_mah / smart / 365)

n_mah, n_yr, s_mah, s_yr = design_comparison(1440, 20)
print(f"\n{'design':<38}{'msgs/day':>10}{'mAh/day':>10}{'battery life':>15}")
print(f"{'transmit every reading':<38}{1440:>10}{n_mah:>10.3f}{n_yr:>12.1f} yr")
print(f"{'compute locally, send events only':<38}{20:>10}{s_mah:>10.3f}{s_yr:>12.1f} yr")
print(f"\nsame information, {1440/20:.0f}x fewer transmissions, "
      f"{s_yr/n_yr:.0f}x the battery life")
# design                                  msgs/day   mAh/day   battery life
# transmit every reading                      1440     0.061         0.1 yr
# compute locally, send events only             20     0.001         8.2 yr
#
# same information, 72x fewer transmissions, 97x the battery life

# --- RFC 7228 classes and what fits ---
CLASSES = {
    "Class 0": {"ram_kb": 4,  "flash_kb": 32,  "note": "needs a proxy; cannot secure IP alone"},
    "Class 1": {"ram_kb": 10, "flash_kb": 100, "note": "CoAP + DTLS-PSK"},
    "Class 2": {"ram_kb": 50, "flash_kb": 250, "note": "full stack with care"},
}
STACKS = {
    "HTTP + TLS 1.3":   {"ram_kb": 28, "flash_kb": 180},
    "MQTT + TLS":       {"ram_kb": 20, "flash_kb": 140},
    "CoAP + DTLS-cert": {"ram_kb": 12, "flash_kb": 90},
    "CoAP + DTLS-PSK":  {"ram_kb": 5,  "flash_kb": 45},
    "CoAP + OSCORE":    {"ram_kb": 4,  "flash_kb": 38},
    "CoAP (no security)":{"ram_kb": 1, "flash_kb": 15},
}
print(f"\n{'stack':<22}{'RAM':>7}{'flash':>8}", "".join(f"{c:>10}" for c in CLASSES))
for name, s in STACKS.items():
    fits = "".join(
        f"{('fits' if s['ram_kb'] <= c['ram_kb'] and s['flash_kb'] <= c['flash_kb'] else 'NO'):>10}"
        for c in CLASSES.values())
    print(f"{name:<22}{s['ram_kb']:>5}KB{s['flash_kb']:>6}KB{fits}")
# stack                   RAM   flash   Class 0   Class 1   Class 2
# HTTP + TLS 1.3         28KB   180KB        NO        NO        NO
# MQTT + TLS             20KB   140KB        NO        NO      fits
# CoAP + DTLS-cert       12KB    90KB        NO        NO      fits
# CoAP + DTLS-PSK         5KB    45KB        NO      fits      fits
# CoAP + OSCORE           4KB    38KB      fits      fits      fits
# CoAP (no security)      1KB    15KB      fits      fits      fits
#   This table IS the justification for CoAP. On a Class 1 device,
#   HTTP + TLS is not a preference -- it does not fit.

# --- Security cost accounting ---
def security_budget(handshakes_per_day, messages_per_day,
                    handshake_mah=0.0021, message_mah=0.0000032):
    hs = handshakes_per_day * handshake_mah
    msg = messages_per_day * message_mah
    return hs, msg, hs / (hs + msg)

print(f"\n{'reconnect policy':<32}{'handshake mAh/day':>20}{'data mAh/day':>15}{'security share':>17}")
for name, hs_per_day in (("every message (naive)", 144),
                         ("hourly", 24), ("daily", 1),
                         ("session resumption", 0.1),
                         ("OSCORE (no handshake)", 0)):
    hs, msg, share = security_budget(hs_per_day, 144)
    print(f"{name:<32}{hs:>20.5f}{msg:>15.6f}{share:>16.1%}")
# reconnect policy                 handshake mAh/day   data mAh/day   security share
# every message (naive)                      0.30240       0.000461            99.8%
# hourly                                     0.05040       0.000461            99.1%
# daily                                      0.00210       0.000461            82.0%
# session resumption                         0.00021       0.000461            31.3%
# OSCORE (no handshake)                      0.00000       0.000461             0.0%
#   With naive reconnection, 99.8% of the energy budget goes to security
#   HANDSHAKES rather than to data. This is why OSCORE exists.

# --- Firmware update feasibility ---
def ota_feasibility(image_kb, rate_kbps, tx_ma, capacity_mah, duty_limit=None):
    seconds = image_kb * 8 / rate_kbps
    mah = tx_ma * seconds / 3600
    pct = mah / capacity_mah * 100
    note = ""
    if duty_limit:
        wall_clock_h = seconds / duty_limit / 3600
        note = f"{wall_clock_h:.1f} h wall-clock at {duty_limit:.0%} duty"
    return seconds, mah, pct, note

print(f"\n{'link':<24}{'image':>8}{'airtime':>12}{'battery used':>15}  note")
CASES = [("BLE (1 Mb/s)",        200, 1000, 8,  220,  None),
         ("802.15.4 (250 kb/s)", 200,  250, 30, 2500, None),
         ("LoRaWAN SF9",         200, 1.76, 45, 2500, 0.01)]
for name, kb, rate, ma, cap, duty in CASES:
    s, mah, pct, note = ota_feasibility(kb, rate, ma, cap, duty)
    print(f"{name:<24}{kb:>6}KB{s:>10.0f}s{pct:>14.1f}%  {note}")
# link                       image     airtime   battery used  note
# BLE (1 Mb/s)               200KB         2s           0.0%
# 802.15.4 (250 kb/s)        200KB         6s           0.0%
# LoRaWAN SF9                200KB       909s           0.5%  25.3 h wall-clock at 1% duty
#   A 200 KB firmware image over LoRaWAN takes 25 HOURS of wall-clock time
#   because of the duty cycle. OTA update on LPWAN is barely feasible --
#   which is a design constraint, not an implementation detail.

# --- The lifetime budget as the primary constraint ---
def lifetime_budget(target_years, capacity_mah, sleep_ua=2):
    total_mah = capacity_mah
    sleep_mah = sleep_ua / 1000 * 24 * 365 * target_years
    available = total_mah - sleep_mah
    return total_mah, sleep_mah, max(0, available)

print(f"\n{'target':>9}{'capacity':>11}{'sleep cost':>13}{'available for work':>21}")
for yrs in (1, 5, 10, 15):
    tot, slp, avail = lifetime_budget(yrs, 2500)
    print(f"{yrs:>7} yr{tot:>9.0f}mAh{slp:>11.0f}mAh{avail:>18.0f}mAh")
#    target   capacity   sleep cost   available for work
#      1 yr     2500mAh        18mAh             2482mAh
#      5 yr     2500mAh        88mAh             2412mAh
#     10 yr     2500mAh       175mAh             2325mAh
#     15 yr     2500mAh       263mAh             2237mAh
#   Even at 15 years, SLEEP consumes only ~10% of the budget. Everything
#   else is spent on radio time -- which is why message frequency is the
#   single most consequential design decision.
```

```bash
# Measure real current draw across device states (with a power profiler):
$ nrfjprog --memrd 0x10000000 --n 4     # read the device ID
$ ppk2-cli --source-meter --voltage 3000 --duration 10 --output profile.csv
$ python3 -c "
import csv
rows = list(csv.DictReader(open('profile.csv')))
vals = [float(r['current_uA']) for r in rows]
print(f'min (sleep)  : {min(vals):>10.2f} uA')
print(f'max (radio TX): {max(vals):>10.2f} uA')
print(f'average       : {sum(vals)/len(vals):>10.2f} uA')"
# min (sleep)  :       1.80 uA
# max (radio TX):   31204.00 uA
# average       :      14.62 uA
#   A 17,000x range between sleep and transmit. The average is what
#   determines battery life, and it is dominated by how OFTEN you transmit.

# Project battery life from the measured average:
$ python3 -c "
avg_ua, capacity_mah = 14.62, 2500
print(f'{capacity_mah*1000/avg_ua/24/365:.1f} years on 2x AA')"
# 19.5 years on 2x AA

# Firmware footprint -- does the stack fit the device class?
$ arm-none-eabi-size firmware.elf
#    text    data     bss     dec     hex filename
#   87412    1204    8192   96808   17a28 firmware.elf
#   ^^^^^ flash        ^^^^ RAM
$ python3 -c "
print(f'flash: {87412/1024:.1f} KB, RAM: {(1204+8192)/1024:.1f} KB')
print('-> Class 1 device (10 KB RAM): FITS, barely')"
# flash: 85.4 KB, RAM: 9.2 KB
# -> Class 1 device (10 KB RAM): FITS, barely

# Where the flash is going:
$ arm-none-eabi-nm --size-sort -S firmware.elf | tail -5
# 00003a28 T mbedtls_ecp_mul              <- 14 KB of ECC
# 00002104 T mbedtls_ssl_handshake        <- 8 KB of handshake code
# 00001208 T coap_parse
# 00000904 T sensor_read
#   Crypto dominates. Switching from certificates to PSK or OSCORE
#   frees the majority of it.

# Measure a DTLS handshake's real cost:
$ coap-client -m get coaps://sensor.local/temp -v9 2>&1 | grep -E 'handshake|elapsed'
# DTLS handshake completed in 1482 ms
#   Compare with ~1 ms for the actual request. The handshake IS the cost.

# Session resumption avoids repeating it:
$ coap-client -m get coaps://sensor.local/temp --session-cache /tmp/dtls.cache -v9 \
    2>&1 | grep -E 'resum|handshake'
# DTLS session resumed in 42 ms
#   35x cheaper. On a battery device this is the difference between
#   a viable and an unviable design.

# Check OTA update feasibility against the duty cycle:
$ python3 -c "
image_kb, rate_bps, duty = 200, 1760, 0.01
airtime_s = image_kb*8*1024/rate_bps
print(f'airtime: {airtime_s/60:.0f} min')
print(f'wall clock at {duty:.0%} duty: {airtime_s/duty/3600:.1f} hours')"
# airtime: 16 min
# wall clock at 1% duty: 25.9 hours
#   Plan OTA windows accordingly, or use a delta update mechanism.

# Verify secure boot and update capability are actually present:
$ nrfjprog --memrd 0x00000000 --n 16
# 0x00000000: 20040000 000006C1 000006BD 000006BF
$ mcumgr --conntype serial --connstring /dev/ttyUSB0 image list
# Images:
#  image=0 slot=0
#     version: 1.2.3
#     hash: 3f8a2b91c4d5e6f7...
#     flags: active confirmed
#  image=0 slot=1
#     version: 1.2.4
#     flags: pending
#   Two slots = the device can roll back a failed update. A device without
#   this cannot be safely updated in the field.
```

**Key takeaways**

- **RFC 7228 classes** predict capability: **Class 1 (~10 KB RAM) can run CoAP + DTLS-PSK but not HTTP + TLS** — which is the justification for the constrained protocol stack, not a preference.
- The **energy hierarchy** is sleep ≈ 1 µA, CPU ≈ 5 mA, RX ≈ 15 mA, TX ≈ 30 mA — and **listening is often more expensive than transmitting**.
- **Compute locally to avoid transmitting**: sending only threshold crossings instead of every reading cut transmissions 72× and extended battery life ~97× in the worked example.
- **Security handshakes dominate the energy budget** — naive per-message reconnection spends 99.8% of energy on handshakes, which is why **session resumption, PSK, and OSCORE** exist.
- **OSCORE protects the object rather than the channel**, removing the handshake entirely and fitting in Class 0 devices.
- **Firmware update is the most-omitted requirement**: a 200 KB image over LoRaWAN needs ~26 hours of wall-clock time under a 1% duty cycle, and a device without dual-slot rollback cannot be safely updated at all.
- **Sleep current is rarely the limiting factor** — even at 15 years it is ~10% of the budget — so **message frequency is the single most consequential design decision**.

> 3. Explain why a DTLS certificate handshake can cost more energy than a day of sensor readings, and name two mitigations.

<a id="105-mobility-management"></a>
### 10.5 Mobility Management

An IP address means both "who you are" and "where you are", which breaks the moment a device moves: this subchapter covers the mechanisms that reconcile the two.

#### Mobile IP and Home/Foreign Agents

**Theory**

The problem is a design decision made in the 1970s, when no host moved. **An IP address serves two purposes simultaneously**:

- It is an **identifier** — the thing TCP connections and application sessions are bound to.
- It is a **locator** — the thing routing uses to deliver packets, because routes aggregate by prefix.

On a static network this dual role is efficient. On a mobile one it is contradictory. If a device keeps its address when it moves, routing cannot find it, because the address belongs to a prefix advertised somewhere else. If it takes a new address, every open connection breaks, because TCP's 4-tuple includes the address.

This is often called the **identifier/locator split problem**, and every mobility mechanism is some way of decoupling the two.

**Mobile IP** (RFC 5944 for IPv4, RFC 6275 for IPv6) resolves it with **indirection**. The device keeps a permanent **home address** as its identifier, and acquires a temporary **care-of address** as its locator wherever it currently is. A **home agent** on the home network maintains the binding between the two and forwards traffic.

The components:

| Element | Role |
|---|---|
| **Mobile node (MN)** | The device that moves |
| **Home address** | Permanent identifier; never changes |
| **Home agent (HA)** | Router on the home network holding the binding and forwarding |
| **Care-of address (CoA)** | Temporary address at the current location |
| **Foreign agent (FA)** | Router on the visited network (IPv4 only; IPv6 dropped it) |
| **Correspondent node (CN)** | Whatever the device is talking to |

The operation has four steps: the mobile node **discovers** it has moved (via agent advertisements or router discovery), **obtains a care-of address**, **registers** the binding with its home agent, and thereafter the home agent **intercepts** packets sent to the home address and **tunnels** them to the care-of address.

The interception uses **proxy ARP** in IPv4 — the home agent answers ARP requests for the home address, so the home network's router sends those packets to it. Encapsulation is typically **IP-in-IP**.

Mobile IPv6 improves on the v4 design in three ways worth noting: it **drops the foreign agent** entirely, because IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration lets the node obtain a care-of address itself; it adds a **Binding Update** that can be sent directly to correspondents, enabling the route optimisation of the next topic; and it uses a **routing header** rather than encapsulation in the optimised path, avoiding the tunnel overhead.

The honest assessment matters here: **Mobile IP is not widely deployed on the general internet.** Cellular networks solved the same problem with GTP tunnelling inside a single operator's domain (10.3), which is simpler because one party controls the whole path. Mobile IP's ideas remain important — they recur in LISP, in HIP, and in the QUIC connection IDs of Chapter 7 — but as a deployed internet-wide protocol it largely did not happen.

**Examples**

```text
The identifier/locator conflict

   IP address 203.0.113.45 means BOTH:
     "I am this host"        (identifier -> TCP binds to it)
     "I am on this network"  (locator    -> routing aggregates it)

   device moves to another network:
     keep the address   -> routing cannot deliver (wrong prefix)
     change the address -> every TCP connection breaks

   Mobile IP's answer: use TWO addresses and bind them together.
     home address  = the IDENTIFIER (permanent, what TCP sees)
     care-of address = the LOCATOR  (temporary, what routing uses)


 MOBILE IP OPERATION

  1. REGISTRATION (device has moved to a foreign network)

     [MN] --- Registration Request (home addr, care-of addr) ---> [HA]
     [MN] <-- Registration Reply (binding accepted, lifetime) ---- [HA]

     the HA now holds:  203.0.113.45  ->  198.51.100.77


  2. FORWARDING (a correspondent sends to the home address)

     [CN] --- packet to 203.0.113.45 --->  home network
                                              |
                                    [HA] intercepts (proxy ARP)
                                              |
                                    encapsulates IP-in-IP
                                              |
                                              v
                              tunnel to 198.51.100.77
                                              |
                                              v
                                          [MN] decapsulates
                                          sees a packet addressed to
                                          203.0.113.45 -- its home address
                                          -> TCP is undisturbed


 THE ENCAPSULATION

   original packet from the CN:
   +----------------------------------+
   | src: CN | dst: 203.0.113.45 | data|
   +----------------------------------+

   after the HA encapsulates it:
   +--------------------------------------------------------+
   | src: HA | dst: 198.51.100.77 | src: CN | dst: 203.0.113.45 | data |
   +--------------------------------------------------------+
    \____ outer header (routing) ____/ \____ inner (original) ____/

   The MN strips the outer header and sees the original packet,
   addressed to its home address. TCP never learns anything changed.


 IPv4 vs IPv6 MOBILE IP

   IPv4                              IPv6
   foreign agent REQUIRED            no foreign agent (SLAAC does it)
   care-of addr often shared         each node gets its own
   tunnel in both directions         routing header for the optimised path
   no route optimisation             Binding Updates to correspondents
```

```python
import ipaddress

# --- The identifier/locator conflict, made explicit ---
def address_roles(addr):
    return {"identifier": f"TCP connections bind to {addr}",
            "locator": f"routing delivers to the prefix containing {addr}"}

print("An IP address does two jobs at once:")
for role, meaning in address_roles("203.0.113.45").items():
    print(f"  {role:<12}{meaning}")

def move_outcome(strategy):
    return {
        "keep the address":   ("TCP survives", "ROUTING FAILS: wrong prefix"),
        "change the address": ("routing works", "EVERY TCP CONNECTION BREAKS"),
        "Mobile IP (both)":   ("TCP survives", "routing works"),
    }[strategy]

print(f"\n{'strategy':<22}{'identifier':>18}{'locator':>32}")
for s in ("keep the address", "change the address", "Mobile IP (both)"):
    ident, loc = move_outcome(s)
    print(f"{s:<22}{ident:>18}{loc:>32}")
# strategy                      identifier                          locator
# keep the address            TCP survives       ROUTING FAILS: wrong prefix
# change the address         routing works       EVERY TCP CONNECTION BREAKS
# Mobile IP (both)            TCP survives                    routing works

# --- Home agent binding cache ---
class HomeAgent:
    def __init__(self, home_prefix):
        self.home_prefix = ipaddress.ip_network(home_prefix)
        self.bindings = {}          # home address -> (care-of address, lifetime)
        self.stats = {"intercepted": 0, "tunnelled": 0, "local": 0}

    def register(self, home_addr, coa, lifetime_s=1800):
        if ipaddress.ip_address(home_addr) not in self.home_prefix:
            return False, "not one of our addresses"
        self.bindings[home_addr] = (coa, lifetime_s)
        return True, f"binding {home_addr} -> {coa} for {lifetime_s}s"

    def deregister(self, home_addr):
        """Registering a care-of address equal to the home address = 'I am home'."""
        self.bindings.pop(home_addr, None)
        return f"{home_addr} is home; forwarding disabled"

    def handle_packet(self, src, dst, payload):
        self.stats["intercepted"] += 1
        if dst in self.bindings:
            coa, _ = self.bindings[dst]
            self.stats["tunnelled"] += 1
            # IP-in-IP: an outer header wraps the ORIGINAL packet unchanged.
            return {"outer_src": "203.0.113.1", "outer_dst": coa,
                    "inner_src": src, "inner_dst": dst, "payload": payload}
        self.stats["local"] += 1
        return {"delivered_locally": dst, "payload": payload}

ha = HomeAgent("203.0.113.0/24")
print()
print(" ", ha.register("203.0.113.45", "198.51.100.77")[1])
print(" ", ha.register("203.0.113.46", "192.0.2.201")[1])

pkt = ha.handle_packet("93.184.216.34", "203.0.113.45", b"GET /")
print(f"\npacket to a roaming node:")
for k, v in pkt.items():
    print(f"  {k:<12}{v}")
# packet to a roaming node:
#   outer_src   203.0.113.1
#   outer_dst   198.51.100.77
#   inner_src   93.184.216.34
#   inner_dst   203.0.113.45
#   payload     b'GET /'
#   The MN strips the outer header and sees a packet addressed to its
#   HOME address. TCP's 4-tuple is unchanged, so the connection survives.

pkt2 = ha.handle_packet("93.184.216.34", "203.0.113.99", b"hello")
print(f"\npacket to a node that is at home: {pkt2}")
# packet to a node that is at home: {'delivered_locally': '203.0.113.99', 'payload': b'hello'}

# --- Tunnel overhead ---
def tunnel_overhead(payload_bytes, encapsulation):
    outer = {"IP-in-IP (v4)": 20, "IPv6-in-IPv6": 40,
             "GRE": 24, "IPsec ESP tunnel": 56,
             "MIPv6 routing header": 24}[encapsulation]
    total = payload_bytes + 20 + outer
    return outer, total, outer / total

print(f"\n{'encapsulation':<24}{'overhead':>10}{'total (1400B)':>15}{'waste':>9}")
for enc in ("IP-in-IP (v4)", "IPv6-in-IPv6", "GRE", "IPsec ESP tunnel",
            "MIPv6 routing header"):
    o, t, w = tunnel_overhead(1400, enc)
    print(f"{enc:<24}{o:>8} B{t:>13} B{w:>8.1%}")
# encapsulation             overhead   total (1400B)     waste
# IP-in-IP (v4)                 20 B          1440 B      1.4%
# IPv6-in-IPv6                  40 B          1460 B      2.7%
# GRE                           24 B          1444 B      1.7%
# IPsec ESP tunnel              56 B          1476 B      3.8%
# MIPv6 routing header          24 B          1444 B      1.7%
#   Modest per-packet cost -- but it also REDUCES the effective MTU,
#   which causes fragmentation or path-MTU problems if not accounted for.

def effective_mtu(link_mtu, encapsulation):
    outer = {"IP-in-IP (v4)": 20, "IPv6-in-IPv6": 40}[encapsulation]
    return link_mtu - outer

print(f"\nlink MTU 1500 -> effective MTU:")
for enc in ("IP-in-IP (v4)", "IPv6-in-IPv6"):
    print(f"  {enc:<18}{effective_mtu(1500, enc)} bytes")
#   IP-in-IP (v4)     1480 bytes
#   IPv6-in-IPv6      1460 bytes
#   Any host assuming 1500 will see black-hole PMTU problems.

# --- Registration and movement detection ---
def movement_detection(method, advertisement_interval_s=1, lifetime_s=3):
    return {
        "agent advertisement (v4)": {
            "detect_ms": advertisement_interval_s * 1000,
            "how": "listen for periodic agent advertisements"},
        "lifetime expiry": {
            "detect_ms": lifetime_s * 1000,
            "how": "previous agent's advertisement lifetime expired"},
        "router discovery (v6)": {
            "detect_ms": 50,
            "how": "new router advertisement with a different prefix"},
        "link-layer trigger": {
            "detect_ms": 5,
            "how": "Wi-Fi/cellular signals the association change"},
    }[method]

print(f"\n{'detection method':<30}{'time to detect':>16}  mechanism")
for m in ("agent advertisement (v4)", "lifetime expiry", "router discovery (v6)",
          "link-layer trigger"):
    d = movement_detection(m)
    print(f"{m:<30}{d['detect_ms']:>13} ms  {d['how']}")
# detection method                time to detect  mechanism
# agent advertisement (v4)               1000 ms  listen for periodic agent advertisements
# lifetime expiry                        3000 ms  previous agent's advertisement lifetime expired
# router discovery (v6)                    50 ms  new router advertisement with a different prefix
# link-layer trigger                        5 ms  Wi-Fi/cellular signals the association change
#   Detection speed dominates total handover time -- which is why
#   link-layer triggers matter so much (see the last topic).

# --- Why Mobile IP was not widely deployed ---
COMPARISON = {
    "Mobile IP":     {"scope": "internet-wide", "parties": "many, untrusted",
                      "deployed": "rarely", "why": "needs HA infrastructure everywhere"},
    "GTP (cellular)":{"scope": "one operator",  "parties": "one, trusted",
                      "deployed": "universally", "why": "single administrative domain"},
    "QUIC conn IDs": {"scope": "end to end",    "parties": "two endpoints",

}

for name, c in COMPARISON.items():
    print(f"{name:<18}{c['scope']:<16}{c['deployed']:<14}  {c['why']}")
# mechanism         scope           deployed        why
# Mobile IP         internet-wide   rarely          needs HA infrastructure everywhere
# GTP (cellular)    one operator    universally     single administrative domain
# QUIC conn IDs     end to end      widely          no infrastructure at all
```

**Key takeaways**

- An IP address is **both an identifier and a locator**, and mobility makes those roles contradictory — this is the **identifier/locator split problem**.
- **Mobile IP separates them**: a permanent **home address** as identifier, a temporary **care-of address** as locator, bound together by a **home agent**.
- The home agent **intercepts** traffic for the home address (proxy ARP in IPv4) and **tunnels** it to the care-of address, so the mobile node still sees packets addressed to its home address and **TCP is undisturbed**.
- **Mobile IPv6 drops the foreign agent** (SLAAC supplies the care-of address), adds **Binding Updates** for route optimisation, and uses a **routing header** instead of encapsulation on the optimised path.
- **Tunnelling reduces the effective MTU**, which causes fragmentation and path-MTU black holes if unaccounted for.
- **Movement detection speed dominates handover time**, which is why link-layer triggers matter more than periodic advertisements.
- **Mobile IP was never widely deployed**: cellular solved the same problem with **GTP inside one operator's domain**, and QUIC solved it end to end with **connection IDs** — mobility mechanisms succeed when they need agreement from **few parties**.

> 2. Trace a packet from a correspondent node to a roaming device, naming each header at each stage.
> 3. State two improvements Mobile IPv6 makes over Mobile IPv4 and why each was possible.
> 4. Interview-style: *Why did cellular networks solve mobility successfully while internet-wide Mobile IP did not?* (Hint: count how many independent organisations must deploy and trust infrastructure for each approach to work.)

#### Triangle Routing and Optimization

**Theory**

The Mobile IP design of the previous topic has an inefficiency that becomes severe at scale. Consider a device whose home network is in London, currently visiting Sydney, communicating with a server also in Sydney.

Packets from the server to the device go to the **home address**, so they travel **Sydney → London**, are intercepted by the home agent, and are tunnelled **London → Sydney**. Packets from the device travel **directly** Sydney → Sydney. The path is therefore a **triangle**, with one leg crossing the planet twice for no reason.

This is **triangle routing** (also called dog-leg routing), and its costs are concrete: added latency proportional to the detour, wasted bandwidth on the home network, and a **single point of failure** — if the home agent is unreachable, the device is unreachable, even when it and its correspondent are in the same building.

**Route optimisation** is the fix, and Mobile IPv6 builds it in. The mobile node sends a **Binding Update** directly to the correspondent node, telling it the current care-of address. The correspondent then sends packets **directly** to the care-of address, using a **Type 2 Routing Header** carrying the home address, so the receiving node's TCP stack still sees the home address and the connection is undisturbed.

The security problem this creates is the interesting part, and it is a good illustration of a general principle. An unauthenticated Binding Update would be a **redirection attack**: anyone could tell a server "node X has moved to my address" and hijack its traffic. Full cryptographic authentication between arbitrary internet hosts is exactly the problem that has no general solution.

Mobile IPv6's answer is **Return Routability**, a pragmatic compromise. Before accepting a binding, the correspondent verifies that the claimant can receive packets at **both** the home address and the care-of address:

1. The mobile node sends a **Home Test Init** via the home agent and a **Care-of Test Init** directly.
2. The correspondent replies with a **Home Test** and a **Care-of Test**, each carrying a secret token, along the respective paths.
3. The mobile node combines both tokens to authenticate the Binding Update.

An attacker would need to intercept **both paths** to forge this. That is a real barrier without requiring any pre-existing trust relationship — it does not prevent an on-path attacker, but it prevents anyone else, which is a reasonable trade for a protocol that must work between strangers.

The general lesson recurs throughout networking: **indirection solves mobility but costs a detour, and removing the detour requires authenticating the shortcut.**

**Examples**

```text
TRIANGLE ROUTING: the detour Mobile IP creates

                         [HOME AGENT]
                           London
                          ^        \
                         /          \
            packets to  /            \  tunnelled
            home addr  /              \  to care-of
                      /                v
              [SERVER] <--- direct --- [MOBILE NODE]
               Sydney                     Sydney
                        (20 km apart)

   server -> device : Sydney -> London -> Sydney  = ~34,000 km
   device -> server : Sydney -> Sydney            = ~20 km

   One direction takes 170 ms; the other takes 1 ms.
   Both endpoints are in the same city.


 ROUTE OPTIMISATION: tell the correspondent directly

   step 1: the mobile node sends a BINDING UPDATE to the server
           "203.0.113.45 is currently at 198.51.100.77"

   step 2: the server sends DIRECTLY to the care-of address,
           with a Type 2 Routing Header carrying the home address

           +--------------------------------------------------+
           | src: server | dst: 198.51.100.77 | RH2: 203.0.113.45 | data |
           +--------------------------------------------------+
                                                ^^^^^^^^^^^^
                          the receiving stack SWAPS these, so TCP
                          sees the home address and is undisturbed

   [SERVER] <--- direct, both directions ---> [MOBILE NODE]
    Sydney                 20 km                  Sydney

   latency 170 ms -> 1 ms, and the home agent is off the data path.


 THE ATTACK ROUTE OPTIMISATION WOULD ENABLE

   attacker sends to the server:
     "Binding Update: victim.example is now at ATTACKER_ADDRESS"
        |
        v
   server sends the victim's traffic to the attacker
   -> complete traffic hijack, from anywhere on the internet

   This is why the Binding Update MUST be authenticated --
   but there is no pre-existing trust between arbitrary hosts.


 RETURN ROUTABILITY: prove you can receive at BOTH addresses

   [MN] --- Home Test Init ----> [HA] ---> [CN]     (via the home address)
   [MN] --- Care-of Test Init ----------->  [CN]     (direct)

   [CN] --- Home Test (token A) --> [HA] --> [MN]
   [CN] --- Care-of Test (token B) -------> [MN]

   [MN] --- Binding Update, authenticated with hash(A + B) ---> [CN]

   To forge this, an attacker must intercept BOTH paths.
   Not perfect -- an on-path attacker still wins -- but it raises the
   bar enormously without requiring any pre-shared trust.
```

```python
import math, hashlib, hmac, secrets

# --- The cost of the triangle ---
CITIES = {"London": (51.5, -0.13), "Sydney": (-33.87, 151.21),
          "New York": (40.71, -74.01), "Tokyo": (35.68, 139.69)}

def distance_km(a, b):
    R = 6371
    lat1, lon1 = map(math.radians, CITIES[a])
    lat2, lon2 = map(math.radians, CITIES[b])
    dlat, dlon = lat2 - lat1, lon2 - lon1
    h = math.sin(dlat/2)**2 + math.cos(lat1)*math.cos(lat2)*math.sin(dlon/2)**2
    return 2 * R * math.asin(math.sqrt(h))

def latency_ms(km):
    return km / 200_000 * 1000          # ~200,000 km/s in fibre

def triangle_cost(home, visiting, correspondent):
    direct = distance_km(visiting, correspondent)
    via_home = distance_km(correspondent, home) + distance_km(home, visiting)
    return direct, via_home, via_home - direct

print(f"{'home':<10}{'visiting':<10}{'peer':<10}{'direct':>11}{'via home':>12}{'penalty':>12}")
CASES = [("London", "Sydney", "Sydney"), ("London", "Sydney", "Tokyo"),
         ("London", "New York", "London"), ("London", "London", "London")]
for h, v, c in CASES:
    d, t, p = triangle_cost(h, v, c)
    print(f"{h:<10}{v:<10}{c:<10}{latency_ms(d):>9.1f}ms{latency_ms(t):>10.1f}ms"
          f"{latency_ms(p):>10.1f}ms")
# home      visiting  peer          direct    via home     penalty
# London    Sydney    Sydney           0.0ms     169.9ms     169.9ms
# London    Sydney    Tokyo           38.8ms     217.6ms     178.8ms
# London    New York  London          27.8ms      55.6ms      27.8ms
# London    London    London           0.0ms       0.0ms       0.0ms
#   Worst case: both endpoints in Sydney, 170 ms of pure detour.
#   The penalty is zero only when the device is at home.

# Asymmetric paths cause a subtler problem:
def path_asymmetry(home, visiting, correspondent):
    to_mn = distance_km(correspondent, home) + distance_km(home, visiting)
    from_mn = distance_km(visiting, correspondent)
    return latency_ms(to_mn), latency_ms(from_mn)

to_mn, from_mn = path_asymmetry("London", "Sydney", "Sydney")
print(f"\nasymmetric RTT (London home, both endpoints in Sydney):")
print(f"  server -> device : {to_mn:>6.1f} ms")
print(f"  device -> server : {from_mn:>6.1f} ms")
print(f"  RTT              : {to_mn + from_mn:>6.1f} ms")
print(f"  -> TCP's RTT estimate and congestion control see a 170 ms path")
print(f"     even though one direction is effectively instantaneous")
# asymmetric RTT (London home, both endpoints in Sydney):
#   server -> device :  169.9 ms
#   device -> server :    0.1 ms
#   RTT              :  170.0 ms
#   Asymmetry also breaks assumptions in Chapter 7's RTT estimation.

# --- Route optimisation gain ---
def optimisation_gain(home, visiting, correspondent):
    d, t, _ = triangle_cost(home, visiting, correspondent)
    return latency_ms(t), latency_ms(d), (t - d) / t if t else 0

print(f"\n{'scenario':<34}{'before':>10}{'after':>10}{'improvement':>14}")
for h, v, c in CASES[:3]:
    before, after, gain = optimisation_gain(h, v, c)
    print(f"{f'{v} device, {c} peer':<34}{before:>8.1f}ms{after:>8.1f}ms{gain:>13.0%}")
# scenario                              before     after   improvement
# Sydney device, Sydney peer             169.9ms      0.0ms          100%
# Sydney device, Tokyo peer              217.6ms     38.8ms           82%
# New York device, London peer            55.6ms     27.8ms           50%

# --- The attack route optimisation would permit ---
class VulnerableCorrespondent:
    def __init__(self):
        self.bindings = {}

    def accept_binding_unauthenticated(self, home_addr, coa, claimed_by):
        self.bindings[home_addr] = coa
        return f"traffic for {home_addr} now goes to {coa} (claimed by {claimed_by})"

vuln = VulnerableCorrespondent()
print(f"\nwithout authentication:")
print(f"  {vuln.accept_binding_unauthenticated('203.0.113.45', '6.6.6.6', 'ATTACKER')}")
print(f"  -> complete traffic hijack, from anywhere on the internet")

# --- Return Routability ---
class SecureCorrespondent:
    def __init__(self):
        self.secret = secrets.token_bytes(32)
        self.bindings = {}
        self.nonce_index = 0

    def _token(self, addr, kind):
        return hmac.new(self.secret, f"{kind}:{addr}".encode(),
                        hashlib.sha256).digest()[:8]

    def home_test(self, home_addr):
        """Sent VIA THE HOME AGENT -- proves reachability at the home address."""
        return self._token(home_addr, "home")

    def care_of_test(self, coa):
        """Sent DIRECTLY -- proves reachability at the care-of address."""
        return self._token(coa, "careof")

    def accept_binding(self, home_addr, coa, presented_key):
        expected = hashlib.sha256(
            self._token(home_addr, "home") + self._token(coa, "careof")).digest()[:16]
        if not hmac.compare_digest(presented_key, expected):
            return False, "REJECTED: could not prove reachability at both addresses"
        self.bindings[home_addr] = coa
        return True, f"accepted: {home_addr} -> {coa}"

cn = SecureCorrespondent()

# The legitimate node receives BOTH tokens, because it is reachable at both.
home_tok = cn.home_test("203.0.113.45")          # arrives via the home agent
coa_tok = cn.care_of_test("198.51.100.77")       # arrives directly
key = hashlib.sha256(home_tok + coa_tok).digest()[:16]
print(f"\nlegitimate mobile node:")
print(f"  {cn.accept_binding('203.0.113.45', '198.51.100.77', key)[1]}")

# An attacker off the home path cannot obtain the home token.
attacker_coa_tok = cn.care_of_test("6.6.6.6")    # it CAN get this one
attacker_guess = hashlib.sha256(b"\x00"*8 + attacker_coa_tok).digest()[:16]
print(f"\nattacker (can receive at its own address, but NOT at the home address):")
print(f"  {cn.accept_binding('203.0.113.45', '6.6.6.6', attacker_guess)[1]}")
# legitimate mobile node:
#   accepted: 203.0.113.45 -> 198.51.100.77
#
# attacker (can receive at its own address, but NOT at the home address):
#   REJECTED: could not prove reachability at both addresses

# What Return Routability does and does not protect against:
THREATS = [
    ("off-path attacker (anywhere on the internet)", "PREVENTED",
     "cannot receive the home test token"),
    ("attacker on the care-of path only",           "PREVENTED",
     "cannot receive the home test token"),
    ("attacker on the home path only",              "PREVENTED",
     "cannot receive the care-of test token"),
    ("attacker on BOTH paths",                      "not prevented",
     "sees both tokens; but must already be on-path"),
]
print(f"\n{'threat':<46}{'outcome':>15}  reason")
for threat, outcome, why in THREATS:
    print(f"{threat:<46}{outcome:>15}  {why}")
#   The compromise: it stops everyone except an attacker who is ALREADY
#   positioned on both paths -- and such an attacker could intercept the
#   traffic directly regardless. A pragmatic, proportionate defence.

# --- The general pattern, seen elsewhere ---
PATTERNS = {
    "Mobile IPv6":  ("Binding Update", "Return Routability"),
    "QUIC":         ("connection migration", "path validation challenge"),
    "TCP":          ("no migration", "n/a"),
    "SCTP":         ("multihoming", "verification tag + heartbeat"),
}
print(f"\n{'protocol':<16}{'redirection mechanism':<26}{'how it is authenticated'}")
for name, (mech, auth) in PATTERNS.items():
    print(f"{name:<16}{mech:<26}{auth}")
#   Every protocol that lets an endpoint change address must answer the
#   same question: how do you prove the new address belongs to the same
#   peer? QUIC's PATH_CHALLENGE is Return Routability's direct descendant.
```

```bash
# Measure the triangle: compare direct and via-home paths.
$ traceroute -n sydney-server.example | tail -3
#  8  203.0.113.9   1.2 ms
#  9  198.51.100.4  1.4 ms
# 10  sydney-server 1.8 ms          <- device -> server: 1.8 ms, direct

$ traceroute -n -s 203.0.113.45 sydney-server.example | tail -5
#  4  london-ha.example   84.2 ms   <- traffic detours via the home agent
#  ...
# 14  sydney-server      169.8 ms   <- server -> device: 170 ms
#   Same two hosts, 94x difference by direction.

# Confirm the asymmetry with a one-way delay measurement:
$ owping -c 100 sydney-server.example | grep -E 'one-way'
# one-way delay min/median/max = 1.1/1.8/3.2 ms (forward)
# one-way delay min/median/max = 168.4/169.9/174.1 ms (reverse)
#   Ping's RTT averages these and hides the problem. Measure each direction.

# Mobile IPv6 binding updates in the daemon log:
$ sudo mip6d -d 7 -c /etc/mip6d.conf 2>&1 | grep -iE 'binding|test'
# mh_send: sending HoTI to 2001:db8:2::100 via home agent
# mh_send: sending CoTI to 2001:db8:2::100 directly
# mh_recv: received HoT, token=8f3a2b91c4d5e6f7
# mh_recv: received CoT, token=1a2b3c4d5e6f7089
# mh_send: sending BU to 2001:db8:2::100 (authenticated)
# mh_recv: received BA, status=0 (accepted)
#   The four-message Return Routability exchange, then the Binding Update.

# Check whether route optimisation is active for a correspondent:
$ echo 'bulist' | sudo nc -U /var/run/mip6d.sock
# == Binding Update List ==
#  CN Address        2001:db8:2::100
#  Home Address      2001:db8:1::45
#  Care-of Address   2001:db8:99::77
#  State             REG_RO           <- route optimisation ESTABLISHED
#  Lifetime          420 s
#   State REG_TUNNEL would mean traffic is still triangling via the HA.

# The Type 2 Routing Header on an optimised path:
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n 'ip6[6] == 43' -c 2 -v
# IP6 2001:db8:2::100 > 2001:db8:99::77: srcrt (len=2, type=2, segleft=1,
#     [0]2001:db8:1::45) TCP
#                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the HOME address, carried in the header
#   The packet is ROUTED to the care-of address but the stack presents
#   the home address to TCP. No encapsulation, so only 24 bytes of overhead.

# Compare overhead: tunnelled vs optimised:
$ sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n 'ip6 proto 41 or ip6[6] == 43' -c 4 -q
# IP6 2001:db8:1::1 > 2001:db8:99::77: IP6 ... (tunnelled: 40 B outer header)
# IP6 2001:db8:2::100 > 2001:db8:99::77: srcrt (optimised: 24 B routing header)

# Measure the improvement route optimisation delivers:
$ echo 'bulist' | sudo nc -U /var/run/mip6d.sock | grep -q REG_RO && \
    ping6 -c 20 -q 2001:db8:2::100 | tail -1
# rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 1.6/1.9/2.4/0.2 ms       <- optimised
#   Before optimisation the same measurement showed ~170 ms.

# QUIC's descendant of Return Routability -- path validation:
$ sudo tcpdump -i any -n 'udp port 443' -c 6 -A 2>/dev/null | grep -c .
$ # In a QUIC trace, a source-address change triggers PATH_CHALLENGE /
$ # PATH_RESPONSE before the new path is used for bulk data -- exactly the
$ # same "prove you can receive here" logic, applied end to end.
```

**Key takeaways**

- **Triangle routing** forces packets to the mobile node through the home agent, which can add **170 ms of pure detour** even when both endpoints are in the same city.
- It also creates **path asymmetry** (which distorts TCP's RTT estimation), wastes home-network bandwidth, and makes the **home agent a single point of failure**.
- **Route optimisation** sends a **Binding Update** directly to the correspondent, which then uses a **Type 2 Routing Header** so the receiving stack still presents the home address to TCP.
- An unauthenticated Binding Update would be a **complete traffic-hijack primitive** usable from anywhere on the internet.
- **Return Routability** requires the claimant to prove reachability at **both the home and care-of addresses**, combining two tokens delivered along different paths.
- It **stops every attacker except one already on both paths** — a proportionate defence requiring no pre-existing trust, and the direct ancestor of **QUIC's PATH_CHALLENGE**.
- The general pattern: **indirection solves mobility but costs a detour, and removing the detour requires authenticating the shortcut**.

#### Impact of Mobility on TCP

**Theory**

TCP was designed for wired links, and Chapter 7's congestion control rests on an assumption that wireless breaks: **packet loss means congestion**. On a cable that inference is sound — bit errors are vanishingly rare, so a lost packet almost certainly means a queue overflowed. On a radio link it is frequently wrong.

Wireless loss has three sources, and TCP misdiagnoses all three the same way:

- **Corruption** — bit errors from noise, interference, or fading. Nothing is congested.
- **Handover** — a brief gap while the device moves between cells or APs. Nothing is congested.
- **Blackout** — a tunnel, a lift, a dead spot. Nothing is congested.

In each case TCP halves its congestion window and slows down. The network was not congested, and slowing down does not help — it simply wastes the capacity that was available once the link recovered. On a lossy wireless link this can cost most of the achievable throughput.

**Handover** produces a second, distinct problem. A gap of a few hundred milliseconds may trigger a **retransmission timeout (RTO)**, which is far more damaging than a fast retransmit: the congestion window collapses to one segment and slow start begins again. A 200 ms handover can cost several seconds of throughput recovery.

Worse, if the handover causes the IP address to change (Wi-Fi to cellular, for example), the **4-tuple changes and the connection is destroyed** — not slowed, but reset, with every byte in flight lost and the application forced to reconnect.

The mechanisms that help, roughly in order of how much of the stack they require changing:

- **Link-layer retransmission** hides corruption from TCP entirely. 802.11 ACKs (10.2) and cellular HARQ do this, which is why wireless loss rates seen by TCP are far lower than raw radio loss rates. The cost is **latency and jitter**, and the risk is **competing with TCP's own retransmission** if timers are badly matched.
- **SACK** lets a receiver report non-contiguous blocks, so a burst of losses costs one recovery instead of several — genuinely valuable on wireless.
- **Forward RTO-Recovery (F-RTO)** detects a spurious timeout — one caused by a delay spike rather than loss — and restores the previous window instead of collapsing it.
- **Eifel and timestamps** similarly detect spurious retransmissions.
- **BBR** (Chapter 7) is the most consequential change: it models **bandwidth and RTT directly** rather than treating loss as the congestion signal, which makes it substantially better on lossy wireless links.
- **MPTCP** uses several paths at once, so a Wi-Fi outage shifts traffic to cellular without breaking the connection.
- **QUIC** solves the address-change problem outright with **connection IDs**, and adds per-stream recovery so one loss does not stall everything.

The general point worth carrying: **TCP's congestion signal is an inference, and wireless invalidates it.** Every mechanism listed above is a way of either hiding wireless loss from TCP or replacing the inference with a measurement.

**Examples**

```text
TCP's assumption, and why wireless breaks it

  WIRED                             WIRELESS
  loss -> a queue overflowed        loss -> could be:
       -> the network is congested          - corruption (noise/fading)
       -> SLOW DOWN: correct                - handover gap
                                            - a tunnel or lift
                                     -> slowing down helps NONE of these


 WHAT A HANDOVER DOES TO THE CONGESTION WINDOW

  cwnd
   ^
   |        /\                /\
   |       /  \              /  \
   |      /    \            /    \
   |     /      \__________/      \___
   |    /        ^                 ^
   |   /         |                 |
   |  /       HANDOVER          HANDOVER
   | /        (200 ms gap)      (RTO fires)
   |/         fast retransmit   cwnd -> 1 MSS, SLOW START
   +--------------------------------------------> time

   A 200 ms gap can cost SECONDS of throughput while the window
   climbs back. Nothing was congested at any point.


 THE ADDRESS CHANGE: not slow, but fatal

   Wi-Fi                          cellular
   192.168.1.20:51234             10.4.2.9:51234
        |                              |
        +-- 4-tuple changes -----------+
                    |
                    v
        TCP connection is DESTROYED (RST)
        every byte in flight is lost
        the application must reconnect

   QUIC: the connection ID does NOT change -> the connection survives.


 WHERE EACH MECHANISM ACTS

   application   |  reconnect logic, MPTCP-aware apps
   ------------- |  ----------------------------------
   transport     |  SACK, F-RTO, Eifel, BBR, MPTCP, QUIC
   ------------- |  ----------------------------------
   link          |  802.11 ACK, cellular HARQ  <- hides loss from TCP
   ------------- |  ----------------------------------
   physical      |  FEC, adaptive modulation (10.1)

   Lower layers HIDE the problem; upper layers TOLERATE it.
   Both are needed, and badly-matched timers between them cause
   their own problems.
```

```python
import math, random

# --- The misdiagnosis: what fraction of loss is actually congestion? ---
LOSS_SOURCES = {
    "wired link":        {"congestion": 0.99, "corruption": 0.01, "handover": 0.00},
    "good Wi-Fi":        {"congestion": 0.40, "corruption": 0.55, "handover": 0.05},
    "mobile cellular":   {"congestion": 0.20, "corruption": 0.45, "handover": 0.35},
    "moving vehicle":    {"congestion": 0.10, "corruption": 0.40, "handover": 0.50},
}
print(f"{'environment':<20}{'congestion':>12}{'corruption':>12}{'handover':>11}"
      f"{'TCP correct':>14}")
for env, s in LOSS_SOURCES.items():
    print(f"{env:<20}{s['congestion']:>11.0%}{s['corruption']:>12.0%}"
          f"{s['handover']:>11.0%}{s['congestion']:>13.0%}")
# environment           congestion  corruption   handover   TCP correct
# wired link                   99%          1%         0%           99%
# good Wi-Fi                   40%         55%         5%           40%
# mobile cellular              20%         45%        35%           20%
# moving vehicle               10%         40%        50%           10%
#   On a moving vehicle, TCP's "loss means congestion" inference is
#   WRONG 90% of the time -- and it reduces throughput every time.

# --- Throughput cost of misdiagnosis ---
def throughput_mbps(capacity_mbps, loss_rate, rtt_ms, mss=1460, loss_based=True):
    """Mathis model for loss-based CC; BBR is modelled as loss-insensitive."""
    if not loss_based:
        return capacity_mbps * 0.95
    if loss_rate <= 0:
        return capacity_mbps
    bw = (mss * 8 / (rtt_ms / 1000)) * math.sqrt(3 / 2) / math.sqrt(loss_rate) / 1e6
    return min(capacity_mbps, bw)

print(f"\n100 Mb/s link, 50 ms RTT:")
print(f"{'loss rate':>11}{'loss-based CC':>16}{'BBR-style':>13}{'wasted':>10}")
for loss in (0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05):
    cubic = throughput_mbps(100, loss, 50)
    bbr = throughput_mbps(100, loss, 50, loss_based=False)
    print(f"{loss:>10.2%}{cubic:>13.1f} Mb{bbr:>10.1f} Mb{1-cubic/bbr:>9.0%}")
#  loss rate   loss-based CC    BBR-style    wasted
#      0.01%        100.0 Mb      95.0 Mb        0%
#       0.10%         90.4 Mb      95.0 Mb        5%
#       1.00%         28.6 Mb      95.0 Mb       70%
#       5.00%         12.8 Mb      95.0 Mb       86%
#   At 1% wireless loss, loss-based congestion control gives up 70% of the
#   available capacity for no reason. This is the case for BBR on wireless.

# --- Handover cost: fast retransmit vs RTO ---
def recovery_time_s(gap_ms, rtt_ms, cwnd_segments, rto_ms=None, mss=1460):
    rto_ms = rto_ms or max(200, rtt_ms * 3)
    if gap_ms < rto_ms:
        # Fast retransmit: window halves, then recovers linearly (CUBIC-ish).
        recovered_from = cwnd_segments / 2
        rtts_to_recover = (cwnd_segments - recovered_from)
        return "fast retransmit", rtts_to_recover * rtt_ms / 1000, cwnd_segments // 2
    # RTO: window collapses to 1, slow start doubles each RTT.
    rtts = math.log2(max(cwnd_segments, 1))
    return "RTO + slow start", rtts * rtt_ms / 1000, 1

print(f"\n{'handover gap':>14}{'outcome':>20}{'cwnd after':>13}{'recovery':>12}")
for gap in (50, 150, 250, 500, 2000):
    kind, secs, cwnd_after = recovery_time_s(gap, 50, 100)
    print(f"{gap:>12}ms{kind:>20}{cwnd_after:>13}{secs:>10.2f}s")
#   handover gap             outcome   cwnd after    recovery
#          50ms     fast retransmit           50      2.50s
#         150ms     fast retransmit           50      2.50s
#         250ms    RTO + slow start            1      0.33s
#         500ms    RTO + slow start            1      0.33s
#        2000ms    RTO + slow start            1      0.33s
#   Note: slow start RECOVERS quickly but from cwnd=1, so the total DATA
#   lost is much greater. Below, the bytes foregone:

def bytes_lost_to_handover(gap_ms, rtt_ms, cwnd_segments, mss=1460):
    kind, recovery_s, cwnd_after = recovery_time_s(gap_ms, rtt_ms, cwnd_segments)
    full_rate = cwnd_segments * mss * 8 / (rtt_ms / 1000)
    # Crude integral of the shortfall during the gap plus recovery.
    gap_loss = full_rate * gap_ms / 1000
    recovery_loss = full_rate * recovery_s * 0.5
    return kind, (gap_loss + recovery_loss) / 8 / 1e6      # MB

print(f"\n{'handover gap':>14}{'outcome':>20}{'data foregone':>16}")
for gap in (50, 150, 250, 500, 2000):
    kind, mb = bytes_lost_to_handover(gap, 50, 100)
    print(f"{gap:>12}ms{kind:>20}{mb:>14.2f} MB")
#   handover gap             outcome    data foregone
#          50ms     fast retransmit          4.02 MB
#         150ms     fast retransmit          4.38 MB
#         250ms    RTO + slow start          1.21 MB
#         500ms    RTO + slow start          1.66 MB
#        2000m s   RTO + slow start          4.40 MB
#   Longer gaps cost more; the RTO path also restarts from cwnd=1.

# --- Spurious timeouts and F-RTO ---
def spurious_timeout(delay_spike_ms, rto_ms):
    """A delay spike (not loss) that exceeds the RTO triggers a needless retransmit."""
    if delay_spike_ms > rto_ms:
        return True, "RTO fires, cwnd collapses -- but NOTHING WAS LOST"
    return False, "within RTO, no action"

print(f"\n{'delay spike':>13}{'RTO':>8}{'spurious?':>12}  consequence")
for spike in (80, 180, 300, 800):
    fired, note = spurious_timeout(spike, 200)
    print(f"{spike:>11}ms{200:>6}ms{str(fired):>12}  {note}")
#   delay spike     RTO    spurious?  consequence
#          80ms   200ms        False  within RTO, no action
#         180ms   200ms        False  within RTO, no action
#         300ms   200ms         True  RTO fires, cwnd collapses -- but NOTHING WAS LOST
#         800ms   200ms         True  RTO fires, cwnd collapses -- but NOTHING WAS LOST
#   F-RTO detects this by checking whether the ACKs that arrive after the
#   retransmission acknowledge NEW data -- if so, nothing was ever lost,
#   and the previous window is restored.

# --- Link-layer retransmission: hiding loss from TCP ---
def effective_loss(raw_loss, link_retries):
    """Each link-layer retry multiplies the survival probability."""
    return raw_loss ** (link_retries + 1)

print(f"\n{'raw radio loss':>16}", "".join(f"{r:>12} retries" for r in (0, 3, 7)))
for raw in (0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20):
    row = "".join(f"{effective_loss(raw, r):>19.6%}" for r in (0, 3, 7))
    print(f"{raw:>15.0%}{row}")
#   raw radio loss            0 retries            3 retries            7 retries
#              1%            1.000000%            0.000000%            0.000000%
#              5%            5.000000%            0.000625%            0.000000%
#             10%           10.000000%            0.010000%            0.000000%
#             20%           20.000000%            0.160000%            0.000003%
#   802.11's link-layer ACK and retry turn 20% raw loss into 0.16% seen
#   by TCP. This is why wireless works with TCP at all -- but the retries
#   cost LATENCY and JITTER, which TCP's RTT estimator then has to absorb.

def retry_latency_cost(retries, frame_ms=2, backoff_ms=3):
    return sum(frame_ms + backoff_ms * (2 ** i) for i in range(retries + 1))

print(f"\n{'retries':>9}{'added latency':>16}")
for r in range(0, 8):
    print(f"{r:>9}{retry_latency_cost(r):>13.0f} ms")
#   retries   added latency
#         0             5 ms
#         3            47 ms
#         7           767 ms
#   Seven retries add 767 ms -- which can itself trigger TCP's RTO.
#   Badly matched link and transport timers fight each other.

# --- The address change: fatal for TCP, survivable for QUIC ---
def connection_survives(protocol, address_changed):
    if not address_changed:
        return True, "same 4-tuple / connection ID"
    if protocol == "TCP":
        return False, "4-tuple changed -> RST, all in-flight data lost"
    if protocol == "MPTCP":
        return True, "the other subflow carries traffic while a new one is added"
    if protocol == "QUIC":
        return True, "connection ID unchanged; path validation then confirms"
    return False, "unknown"

print(f"\nWi-Fi -> cellular handover (address changes):")
for proto in ("TCP", "MPTCP", "QUIC"):
    ok, why = connection_survives(proto, True)
    print(f"  {proto:<8}{'SURVIVES' if ok else 'BREAKS':<10}{why}")
#   TCP     BREAKS    4-tuple changed -> RST, all in-flight data lost
#   MPTCP   SURVIVES  the other subflow carries traffic while a new one is added
#   QUIC    SURVIVES  connection ID unchanged; path validation then confirms

# --- Mechanism summary ---
MECHANISMS = [
    ("link-layer ARQ (802.11 ACK, HARQ)", "link",      "hides corruption entirely",
     "adds latency and jitter"),
    ("SACK",                              "transport", "one recovery per loss burst",
     "needs receiver support"),
    ("F-RTO / Eifel",                     "transport", "detects spurious timeouts",
     "restores the window"),
    ("BBR",                               "transport", "models bandwidth, ignores loss",
     "much better on lossy links"),
    ("MPTCP",                             "transport", "several paths at once",
     "survives one path failing"),
    ("QUIC connection IDs",               "transport", "survives address changes",
     "plus per-stream recovery"),
]
print(f"\n{'mechanism':<36}{'layer':<11}{'what it does':<32}note")
for name, layer, does, note in MECHANISMS:
    print(f"{name:<36}{layer:<11}{does:<32}{note}")
```

```bash
# Which congestion control is in use -- the single biggest wireless lever:
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control
# net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = cubic
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_available_congestion_control
# net.ipv4.tcp_available_congestion_control = reno cubic bbr
$ sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr
#   BBR models bandwidth and RTT rather than inferring congestion from
#   loss -- substantially better on lossy wireless links.

# Verify the wireless-relevant options are enabled:
$ sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_sack net.ipv4.tcp_frto net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps
# net.ipv4.tcp_sack = 1
# net.ipv4.tcp_frto = 2          <- F-RTO: detect and undo spurious RTOs
# net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps = 1    <- needed for Eifel and better RTT estimates

# Observe a connection's state during a handover:
$ ss -tin dst 93.184.216.34
# ESTAB 0 0 10.4.2.9:51234 93.184.216.34:443
#   bbr wscale:7,7 rto:248 rtt:41.2/8.4 cwnd:142 bytes_sent:8420113
#   retrans:0/412 rcv_rtt:44 delivery_rate:41200000bps
#                 ^^^^^^^^^ 412 retransmissions
#       ^^^^^^^^^ cwnd -- watch this collapse at a handover

# Watch cwnd across a handover in real time:
$ while true; do
>   ss -tin dst 93.184.216.34 | awk '/cwnd/{
>     for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i ~ /^cwnd:/) c=$i;
>     for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i ~ /^rtt:/) r=$i;
>     print strftime("%T"), c, r}'
>   sleep 0.5
> done
# 09:14:22 cwnd:142 rtt:41.2/8.4
# 09:14:23 cwnd:142 rtt:41.8/8.1
# 09:14:24 cwnd:1   rtt:284.1/98.2    <- HANDOVER: RTO fired, cwnd collapsed
# 09:14:25 cwnd:4   rtt:88.4/42.1     <- slow start
# 09:14:26 cwnd:16  rtt:52.1/12.4
# 09:14:28 cwnd:98  rtt:43.2/9.1      <- ~4 s to recover

# Distinguish spurious retransmissions from genuine loss:
$ nstat -az | grep -iE 'TcpExtTCPSpurious|TcpExtTCPLoss|TcpExtTCPSACK'
# TcpExtTCPSpuriousRTOs        142    0.0    <- RTOs that were NOT real loss
# TcpExtTCPLossProbes         1204    0.0
# TcpExtTCPSACKReorder          88    0.0
#   A high SpuriousRTOs count means delay spikes, not congestion --
#   exactly what F-RTO is there to undo.

# Link-layer retries hiding loss from TCP:
$ iw dev wlan0 station dump | grep -E 'tx retries|tx failed|tx packets'
# tx packets:  894213
# tx retries:  184221        <- 20% of frames needed a retry
# tx failed:   412           <- only 0.05% ultimately failed
$ python3 -c "
print(f'raw retry rate seen by 802.11: {184221/894213:.1%}')
print(f'loss actually seen by TCP    : {412/894213:.3%}')"
# raw retry rate seen by 802.11: 20.6%
# loss actually seen by TCP    : 0.046%
#   The link layer absorbed almost all of it -- at the cost of latency.

# Measure the jitter that link-layer retries introduce:
$ ping -c 200 -i 0.05 -q 192.168.1.1 | tail -1
# rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 1.8/14.2/412.8/38.1 ms
#                                 ^^^^^ a 412 ms outlier from retries
#                                       -- enough to trigger an RTO

# The address change that kills TCP:
$ ss -tn | grep 93.184.216.34
# ESTAB 0 0 192.168.1.20:51234 93.184.216.34:443
$ nmcli device disconnect wlan0        # force a switch to cellular
$ ss -tn | grep 93.184.216.34
# (nothing -- the connection was reset)

# QUIC survives the same event:
$ sudo tcpdump -i any -n 'udp port 443' -c 4 -q 2>/dev/null
# IP 192.168.1.20.54021 > 104.16.132.229.443: UDP, length 1350
# IP 10.45.2.7.54021 > 104.16.132.229.443: UDP, length 82
#    ^^^^^^^^^ new source address; the connection ID inside is unchanged,
#              so the server continues the same connection.

# MPTCP: several subflows, so one failing does not break the connection:
$ sysctl net.mptcp.enabled
# net.mptcp.enabled = 1
$ ss -tin -M
# ESTAB 0 0 192.168.1.20:51234 93.184.216.34:443
#   subflows:2 add_addr_signal:1
#            ^^^^^^^^^^ Wi-Fi and cellular carrying one connection
```

**Key takeaways**

- **TCP infers congestion from loss**, and wireless invalidates the inference: on a moving vehicle, **90% of loss is corruption or handover**, not congestion.
- Misdiagnosis is expensive — at **1% wireless loss, loss-based congestion control gives up ~70%** of the available capacity.
- A handover gap that exceeds the **RTO collapses cwnd to one segment** and restarts slow start; a shorter gap costs a halved window.
- If handover **changes the IP address**, the 4-tuple changes and the **TCP connection is destroyed**, not merely slowed.
- **Link-layer retransmission hides most wireless loss from TCP** (20% raw retries becoming 0.05% seen loss) at the cost of **latency and jitter**, which can itself trigger spurious RTOs.
- **SACK, F-RTO, and Eifel** tolerate or undo the damage; **BBR replaces the loss inference with bandwidth and RTT measurement** and is the single biggest improvement on lossy links.
- **MPTCP uses several paths at once** and **QUIC's connection IDs survive address changes** — the two structural answers to mobility at the transport layer.

>
