#### Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems

**Theory**

Firewalls decide whether a connection is **allowed**. They do not ask whether allowed traffic is **malicious**. An HTTP request to your public web server passes any sensible rule set — and may still be an exploit attempt. That gap is what **intrusion detection** fills: it analyses traffic and events looking for evidence of attack.

Two deployment models, differing in one decisive respect:

| | IDS (detection) | IPS (prevention) |
|---|---|---|
| Placement | Out of band, on a SPAN port or tap | **In line**, in the traffic path |
| Action | Alerts, logs | **Drops, resets, rewrites** |
| Failure mode | Misses nothing operationally: traffic flows regardless | A false positive **blocks real users**; a crash can break the network |
| Latency impact | None | Adds processing delay |
| Typical use | Broad visibility, investigation, tuning ground | Enforcement for well-understood, high-confidence signatures |

A common pattern is to deploy the same engine in IDS mode first, tune it against real traffic, then promote only high-confidence rules to blocking. The organisational lesson from practice: an IPS that blocks legitimate traffic gets disabled by the business, so precision matters more than coverage.

Detection uses three complementary methods:

- **Signature-based** (rule matching): look for known-bad patterns — a specific exploit string, a known malware TLS fingerprint, a request path used by one scanner. Precise, explainable, and cheap, but blind to anything not yet written down. Snort and Suricata rules are the standard form.
- **Anomaly-based**: build a baseline of normal behaviour and alert on deviation — a workstation suddenly serving SMB, a 20x spike in outbound volume at 03:00, a user authenticating from two continents. Can catch novel attacks, but produces false positives and needs a genuinely representative baseline.
- **Protocol / behavioural analysis**: parse protocols properly and alert on violations and semantics rather than byte patterns — a non-HTTP payload on port 80, a TLS session with no handshake, DNS responses that do not match any query. Zeek is the canonical tool, producing rich structured logs rather than alerts alone.

Two practical constraints shape every deployment. First, **encryption**: most traffic is TLS, so payload signatures apply only where you terminate TLS (your own reverse proxy) or to metadata — SNI, certificate details, JA3/JA4 fingerprints, packet sizes and timing. Modern network detection leans heavily on metadata and flow behaviour for that reason. Second, the **base-rate problem**: even a very accurate detector generates overwhelming false positives when attacks are rare relative to traffic volume, which is why tuning, suppression, and correlation (feeding into SIEM, 11.5's last topic) matter more than raw detection rates.

Placement follows the same logic as defence in depth: at the perimeter to see inbound attacks, on internal segments to see **east-west** lateral movement, and on hosts (**HIDS**, and endpoint detection) to see what never crosses a monitored link at all.

**Examples**

```text
IDS out of band vs IPS in line

  IDS                                        IPS
  Internet --> [switch] --> [servers]        Internet --> [IPS] --> [servers]
                  | SPAN (copy)                            |
              [IDS sensor] -> alerts                  drops / resets inline
  cannot block; never breaks traffic        can block; a false positive is an outage

Detection methods on the same event: 10,000 logins from one source in a minute

  signature : matches a rule for a known credential-stuffing tool's user-agent
              -> precise, but a renamed tool evades it
  anomaly   : login rate is 400x this endpoint's 30-day baseline
              -> catches the unknown tool, may also flag a legitimate migration
  protocol  : requests lack the session cookie a real browser flow always carries
              -> semantic evidence, robust to renaming

Where sensors go
  [Internet] =IPS= [DMZ] --- [core] --- [user VLANs]
                      |         |            |
                   sensor    sensor(east-west)  host agents
                 inbound     lateral movement    what never crosses a link
```

```python
# A small detection engine showing all three methods and the base-rate problem.
import re, statistics
from collections import defaultdict

# --- 1. Signature-based ---
SIGNATURES = [
    ("SCAN-UA",    re.compile(rb"(?i)user-agent:\s*(nikto|sqlmap|masscan)")),
    ("TRAVERSAL",  re.compile(rb"(\.\./){3,}")),
    ("SHELL-IN-UA",re.compile(rb"(?i)user-agent:.*\(\)\s*\{")),          # Shellshock shape
]

def signature_check(payload):
    return [name for name, rx in SIGNATURES if rx.search(payload)]

print(signature_check(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nUser-Agent: sqlmap/1.7\r\n"))      # ['SCAN-UA']
print(signature_check(b"GET /../../../../etc/passwd HTTP/1.1\r\n"))          # ['TRAVERSAL']
print(signature_check(b"GET /index.html HTTP/1.1\r\nUser-Agent: Mozilla\r\n"))  # []

# --- 2. Anomaly-based: compare against a learned baseline ---
class Baseline:
    def __init__(self, samples):
        self.mean = statistics.fmean(samples)
        self.sd = statistics.pstdev(samples) or 1.0

    def zscore(self, value):
        return (value - self.mean) / self.sd

hourly_logins = [12, 15, 9, 14, 11, 13, 10, 16, 12, 14]      # 10 hours of normal history
bl = Baseline(hourly_logins)
for observed in (13, 40, 4000):
    z = bl.zscore(observed)
    print(f"logins={observed:>5} z={z:6.1f} {'ALERT' if z > 4 else 'normal'}")
# logins=   13 z=   0.2 normal
# logins=   40 z=  13.0 ALERT
# logins= 4000 z=1892.3 ALERT

# --- 3. Protocol/behavioural: semantics, not bytes ---
def protocol_check(event):
    issues = []
    if event["dport"] == 80 and not event["payload"].startswith((b"GET", b"POST", b"HEAD", b"PUT")):
        issues.append("non-HTTP payload on port 80 (tunnelling or wrong service)")
    if event["dport"] == 443 and event["payload"][:1] != b"\x16":
        issues.append("port 443 without a TLS handshake record")           # 0x16 = Handshake
    if event.get("dns_response_without_query"):
        issues.append("DNS response with no matching outstanding query")
    return issues

print(protocol_check({"dport": 443, "payload": b"SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6"}))
# ['port 443 without a TLS handshake record']

# --- The base-rate problem: why precision dominates operations ---
def alert_math(events_per_day, attack_rate, detection_rate, false_positive_rate):
    attacks = events_per_day * attack_rate
    benign = events_per_day - attacks
    tp = attacks * detection_rate
    fp = benign * false_positive_rate
    return {"true alerts/day": round(tp, 1), "false alerts/day": round(fp, 1),
            "precision": f"{tp / (tp + fp):.2%}" if tp + fp else "n/a"}

print(alert_math(10_000_000, attack_rate=1e-6, detection_rate=0.99, false_positive_rate=0.0001))
# {'true alerts/day': 9.9, 'false alerts/day': 1000.0, 'precision': '0.98%'}
#   99% detection with a 0.01% false-positive rate still buries 10 real alerts under 1,000 false
#   ones. This is why tuning, suppression and correlation matter more than raw detection rate.
```

```bash
# Suricata rule anatomy (Snort-compatible syntax):
#   alert http $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET any ( \
#     msg:"Directory traversal attempt"; flow:established,to_server; \
#     http.uri; content:"../../"; fast_pattern; \
#     classtype:web-application-attack; sid:1000101; rev:2; )
#         ^ action  ^ protocol/direction        ^ what to match        ^ metadata

# Run in IDS mode against a capture first: tune before ever blocking.
$ suricata -r traffic.pcap -S local.rules -l ./out
$ jq -r 'select(.event_type=="alert") | "\(.alert.signature) \(.src_ip) -> \(.dest_ip)"' out/eve.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
#   842 SURICATA HTTP unable to match response to request 10.0.0.9 -> 10.0.20.11
#     3 Directory traversal attempt 203.0.113.9 -> 198.51.100.20
#   ^ 842 of these is a tuning problem, not 842 intrusions: suppress or fix the rule first

# Zeek: protocol analysis producing structured logs rather than alerts
$ zeek -r traffic.pcap && ls *.log
# conn.log  dns.log  http.log  ssl.log  notice.log  weird.log
$ zeek-cut id.orig_h server_name validation_status < ssl.log | grep -v ok | head -3
# 10.0.0.31  cdn-update-svc.example  self signed certificate in certificate chain
#   ^ TLS metadata is still informative even though the payload is encrypted

# Promote a tuned rule to blocking only when precision is proven (IPS mode):
#   drop http $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"..."; sid:1000101; rev:3;)
$ sudo suricata -i eth0 --af-packet -S local.rules   # inline requires careful capacity planning
```

**Key takeaways**

- A firewall decides **allowed**; an IDS/IPS asks whether allowed traffic is **malicious**.
- **IDS** is out of band and safe; **IPS** is in line and can block — so a false positive becomes an outage. Tune in IDS mode, then promote high-confidence rules.
- **Signatures** are precise but blind to the unknown; **anomaly detection** catches novelty with more noise; **protocol analysis** gives robust semantic evidence.
- Encryption pushes detection toward **metadata**: SNI, certificates, JA3/JA4, sizes, timing, flow behaviour.
- The **base-rate problem** means precision and correlation matter more than headline detection rates; place sensors at the perimeter, **east-west**, and on hosts.

#### DMZ and Network Segmentation

**Theory**

A flat network is a single blast radius: one compromised host can reach every other host, and the only real control is at the Internet edge. **Segmentation** divides the network into zones with controlled paths between them, so that compromise in one zone does not become compromise everywhere. It is the structural control that limits **lateral movement** (11.4), and in practice it is what determines whether an incident is one workstation or the whole company.

The classic form is the **DMZ (demilitarised zone)**: a separate segment for services that must be reachable from the Internet — web servers, mail relays, reverse proxies, VPN concentrators. The rules that make it a DMZ are directional:

- Internet → DMZ: permitted, only on required ports.
- DMZ → internal: **denied**, except narrowly defined flows to specific hosts and ports (for example one application server to one database port).
- Internal → DMZ: permitted as needed for management and publishing.
- DMZ → Internet: restricted to what the service genuinely needs (this is egress control again).

The point is the third rule. A public web server *will* eventually be exploited; the DMZ ensures that what the attacker inherits is a segment with almost no onward reach, rather than a foothold inside the trusted network.

Segmentation operates at several granularities:

| Approach | Boundary | Granularity | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **VLANs + routed ACLs** | Layer 2 domains, filtered at the router/firewall | Per subnet | Traditional; VLANs alone are not a security control without filtering between them |
| **Zone-based firewalls** | Named zones with inter-zone policy | Per zone | Clearer intent than per-interface rules |
| **Private VLANs / port isolation** | Within one subnet | Per port | Stops peer-to-peer traffic in, for example, a guest or server VLAN |
| **Microsegmentation** | Per workload, enforced by hypervisor, host firewall, or sidecar | **Per host or per service** | Cloud/SDN native; identity- or label-based rather than address-based |
| **Air gap / one-way** | Physical or data-diode | Absolute | Industrial control, high-assurance environments |

Typical zones in an enterprise: Internet, DMZ, user VLANs, server zones split by application tier, a dedicated **management network** (switch and hypervisor interfaces, out-of-band access), **PCI/regulated** scopes, guest Wi-Fi (Internet only), and **OT/IoT** networks — building controls, cameras, industrial equipment — which must be isolated because they are rarely patchable.

Two principles govern the rules themselves. **Default deny between zones**, with each permitted flow justified by a documented application requirement. And segment by **trust and function**, not by convenience: the reason a printer VLAN and a finance database must not share a zone has nothing to do with topology.

Segmentation's practical difficulty is not technology but **knowing your flows**. Projects fail when policy is written from assumptions; the reliable method is to log in permissive mode, derive the real dependency map from flow records, then tighten. Microsegmentation makes the enforcement fine-grained, which raises the cost of getting that map wrong.

**Examples**

```text
Zones and the direction of trust

                         Internet
                            |  only 443 inbound
                    +-------v--------+
                    |      DMZ       |  reverse proxy, VPN concentrator, mail relay
                    | 198.51.100.0/24|
                    +---+--------+---+
      DMZ -> internal: DENY except one flow |
                        |                   | app -> db: 10.0.30.11:5432 ONLY
        +---------------v---+       +--------v---------+     +------------------+
        |  user VLANs       |       |  app tier        |     |  management      |
        |  10.0.10.0/24     |       |  10.0.20.0/24    |     |  10.0.99.0/24    |
        +---------+---------+       +--------+---------+     +--------+---------+
                  | users -> app: 443 only            |               ^
                  +-----------------------------------+               | jump host only
        +-------------------+      +------------------+      +--------+---------+
        |  guest Wi-Fi      |      |  OT / IoT        |      |  db tier         |
        |  Internet only    |      |  no Internet,    |      |  10.0.30.0/24    |
        |  no internal      |      |  poll to 1 server|      |  no egress       |
        +-------------------+      +------------------+      +------------------+

 The decisive rule: DMZ -> internal is DENY by default.
 A compromised public web server then owns a segment, not the company.
```

```python
# Zone policy as code: default deny, explicit justified flows, and a lateral-movement test.
from dataclasses import dataclass
import ipaddress

ZONES = {
    "dmz":      ipaddress.ip_network("198.51.100.0/24"),
    "users":    ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.10.0/24"),
    "app":      ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.20.0/24"),
    "db":       ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.30.0/24"),
    "mgmt":     ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.99.0/24"),
    "guest":    ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.200.0/24"),
    "ot":       ipaddress.ip_network("10.0.240.0/24"),
}

# (src_zone, dst_zone, port) -> why it exists. Anything absent is denied.
POLICY = {
    ("internet", "dmz",  443):  "public web entry",
    ("users",    "app",  443):  "staff use the application",
    ("app",      "db",   5432): "application reads its database",
    ("dmz",      "app",  8080): "reverse proxy to app tier (only permitted DMZ->internal flow)",
    ("mgmt",     "app",  22):   "administration from the jump host",
    ("mgmt",     "db",   22):   "administration from the jump host",
    ("ot",       "app",  1883): "sensors publish telemetry (MQTT)",
    ("guest",    "internet", 443): "guest browsing only",
}

def zone_of(ip):
    addr = ipaddress.ip_address(ip)
    for name, net in ZONES.items():
        if addr in net:
            return name
    return "internet"

def permitted(src_ip, dst_ip, port):
    s, d = zone_of(src_ip), zone_of(dst_ip)
    if s == d:
        return True, f"intra-zone ({s}) -- consider microsegmentation if this should be filtered"
    why = POLICY.get((s, d, port))
    return (True, f"allowed: {why}") if why else (False, f"DENY {s}->{d}:{port} (no policy)")

tests = [
    ("198.51.100.20", "10.0.20.11", 8080, "proxy to app: expected to work"),
    ("198.51.100.20", "10.0.30.11", 5432, "compromised DMZ host reaching the database"),
    ("10.0.10.55",    "10.0.30.11", 5432, "workstation reaching the database directly"),
    ("10.0.200.7",    "10.0.10.55", 445,  "guest device scanning staff laptops"),
    ("10.0.240.9",    "10.0.20.11", 1883, "sensor telemetry"),
    ("10.0.20.11",    "10.0.99.10", 22,   "app tier into management network"),
]
for src, dst, port, label in tests:
    ok, reason = permitted(src, dst, port)
    print(f"{'ALLOW' if ok else 'BLOCK'}  {label:48} {reason}")
# ALLOW  proxy to app: expected to work                   allowed: reverse proxy to app tier (only permitted DMZ->internal flow)
# BLOCK  compromised DMZ host reaching the database       DENY dmz->db:5432 (no policy)
# BLOCK  workstation reaching the database directly       DENY users->db:5432 (no policy)
# BLOCK  guest device scanning staff laptops              DENY guest->users:445 (no policy)
# ALLOW  sensor telemetry                                 allowed: sensors publish telemetry (MQTT)
# BLOCK  app tier into management network                 DENY app->mgmt:22 (no policy)
#   ^ management is reachable FROM mgmt only: a compromised app server cannot pivot into it.
```

```bash
# Derive the real flow map BEFORE tightening policy (log-first method):
$ sudo nft add rule inet fw forward counter log prefix "flowmap: " accept   # permissive + logged
$ sudo journalctl -k | grep flowmap | grep -oE 'SRC=\S+ DST=\S+ DPT=[0-9]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
#  18422 SRC=10.0.20.11 DST=10.0.30.11 DPT=5432     <- real dependency: app -> db
#   3011 SRC=10.0.10.55 DST=10.0.20.11 DPT=443      <- real dependency: users -> app
#      6 SRC=10.0.20.11 DST=10.0.99.10 DPT=22       <- unexpected: investigate before allowing

# Enforce zone policy with nftables (default deny between zones, explicit flows only):
$ sudo nft -f - <<'EOF'
table inet zones {
  chain forward {
    type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;
    ct state established,related accept
    ip saddr 198.51.100.0/24 ip daddr 10.0.20.0/24 tcp dport 8080 accept   # dmz -> app
    ip saddr 10.0.20.0/24   ip daddr 10.0.30.0/24 tcp dport 5432 accept    # app -> db
    ip saddr 10.0.10.0/24   ip daddr 10.0.20.0/24 tcp dport 443  accept    # users -> app
    ip saddr 10.0.200.0/24  ip daddr 10.0.0.0/8 counter log prefix "guest-to-internal: " drop
    counter log prefix "zone-deny: " drop
  }
}
EOF

# Stop peer-to-peer traffic inside one subnet (private VLAN / port isolation, Cisco):
# switch(config)# vlan 200
# switch(config-vlan)# private-vlan isolated        ! guest devices cannot see each other

# Verify segmentation by testing from the wrong side (authorised validation):
$ nc -zv -w3 10.0.30.11 5432        # run from a user VLAN host: must FAIL
# nc: connect to 10.0.30.11 port 5432 (tcp) failed: Connection timed out   <- policy proven
```

**Key takeaways**

- Segmentation limits **blast radius** and is the structural defence against **lateral movement**.
- A **DMZ** hosts Internet-facing services with **DMZ → internal denied** except narrow, justified flows — so compromising a public server yields little.
- Granularity ranges from **VLANs with ACLs** to **microsegmentation** per workload; VLANs alone, without filtering between them, are not a security control.
- Isolate **management**, **guest**, and **OT/IoT** networks; unpatchable devices belong behind their own boundary.
· - Segment by **trust and function** with **default deny**, and derive the policy from **observed flows**, not assumptions.

Which control would have limited it most, and how would you validate that control afterwards?* (Hint: the malware had to *reach* those servers — think about which flows a workstation genuinely needs, and how you would prove the rest are blocked.)

#### Honeypots and Deception

**Theory**

Every control so far tries to keep attackers out or spot them in real traffic. **Deception** inverts the problem: deploy resources that have **no legitimate purpose**, so that *any* interaction with them is, by definition, suspicious. That property is what makes deception valuable — it sidesteps the base-rate problem that drowns conventional detection in false positives. Nobody has a reason to log into a decoy server, so an alert from one is high-signal almost by construction.

A **honeypot** is a system deliberately exposed to be attacked, instrumented to record what happens. Two axes describe them:

| Interaction level | What it emulates | Value | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Low-interaction** | Just enough of a service to capture the first moves (a fake banner, a fake login) | Credentials tried, sources, scanning trends | Low — nothing real to exploit |
| **High-interaction** | A real operating system and services | Deep insight into tools and post-exploitation behaviour | **Real risk**: it can be fully compromised and used to attack others |

| Purpose | Placement | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| **Research** | Internet-facing | Study attacker behaviour and trends at large |
| **Production** | Inside the network, among real assets | Detect intruders already inside — the highest-value use |

Related deception primitives are cheaper and often more useful than a full honeypot:

- **Honeytokens**: fake credentials, API keys, or AWS keys placed in configuration files, repositories, or password managers. Use of one proves both an intrusion and, usually, *where* the attacker looked.
- **Honey records** in a database (a fake customer row) reveal data theft when they appear elsewhere.
- **Honey files and shares**: a `salaries.xlsx` on a share nobody should browse, alerting on access.
- **Canary hosts** on internal VLANs that listen on common ports (SMB, RDP, SSH) and alert on any connection — extremely effective against the internal scanning that precedes lateral movement.
- **Tarpits** that answer very slowly to waste automated tooling's time.

Deployment discipline matters, because a honeypot is a deliberately weak machine:

1. **Isolate it.** Its own segment, with tight egress so it cannot be used to attack third parties. This is the ethical and legal obligation that comes with running one.
2. **Log off-box.** An attacker who controls the host controls its local logs; send telemetry to a system they cannot reach.
3. **Make it plausible but sterile.** Realistic enough to engage, holding no real data and no credentials that work anywhere else.
4. **Route alerts to a process.** A honeypot nobody monitors is just an extra vulnerable host.
5. **Do not counter-attack.** Deception is for detection and intelligence; retaliating against an attacking host is illegal in most jurisdictions and frequently hits an innocent compromised third party.

Deception does not replace prevention or monitoring; it adds a layer with unusually good precision, especially for detecting an intruder who is already past the perimeter.

**Examples**

```text
Why deception has near-perfect precision

  REAL SERVICE      thousands of legitimate requests/hour + rare attacks
                    -> detection must separate them: false positives inevitable

  DECOY SERVICE     zero legitimate requests, ever
                    -> ANY interaction = investigate. Precision approaches 100%.

Production placement: catch the intruder already inside

  [compromised workstation 10.0.10.55]
        | scans the /24 for SMB, RDP, SSH (lateral movement)
        v
  10.0.10.9  CANARY HOST: no users, no purpose, listens on 445/3389/22
        |
        +--> alert to SIEM: "10.0.10.55 connected to canary 10.0.10.9:445"
             first solid evidence of an intrusion, minutes after it starts

Honeytoken flow
  fake AWS key placed in an internal wiki page and a repo config
        -> attacker finds it during discovery and tries to use it
        -> cloud provider logs the attempt -> alert names the key's location
        -> you learn there is an intruder AND where they have already looked
```

```python
# A production canary service: listens on commonly-probed ports, alerts on any connection.
import socket, threading, json, datetime

CANARY_PORTS = [22, 445, 3389, 8080]          # what internal scanners look for first
BANNERS = {                                    # plausible, but the service does nothing
    22:   b"SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_8.9p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu0.4\r\n",
    445:  b"",
    3389: b"",
    8080: b"HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized\r\nWWW-Authenticate: Basic realm=\"Router Admin\"\r\n\r\n",
}

def alert(event):
    # Ship OFF-BOX: an attacker on this host must not be able to erase the evidence.
    line = json.dumps({"ts": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat(),
                       "severity": "high", "rule": "canary_touched", **event})
    print(line)                                # in production: syslog/HTTPS to the SIEM
    # syslog_socket.sendto(line.encode(), ("10.0.99.20", 514))

def serve(port):
    with socket.create_server(("0.0.0.0", port), reuse_port=True) as srv:
        while True:
            conn, addr = srv.accept()
            first = b""
            try:
                conn.settimeout(2)
                if BANNERS[port]:
                    conn.sendall(BANNERS[port])
                first = conn.recv(256)          # record what the client sent: tool fingerprint
            except OSError:
                pass
            finally:
                conn.close()
            alert({"src_ip": addr[0], "src_port": addr[1], "dst_port": port,
                   "first_bytes": first[:80].decode("latin-1", "replace")})

for p in CANARY_PORTS:
    threading.Thread(target=serve, args=(p,), daemon=True).start()

# Any connection produces an alert like:
# {"ts": "2026-09-24T12:41:09+00:00", "severity": "high", "rule": "canary_touched",
#  "src_ip": "10.0.10.55", "src_port": 51334, "dst_port": 445, "first_bytes": "\\x00\\x00\\x00\\xc0\\xfeSMB@..."}
#   -> 10.0.10.55 has no business here: treat as a compromised host and investigate it.
```

```python
# Honeytokens: generate decoy credentials, record where each was planted, alert on use.
import secrets, hashlib

class Honeytokens:
    def __init__(self):
        self.tokens = {}          # token -> placement description

    def mint(self, placement, kind="api_key"):
        token = f"AKIA{secrets.token_hex(8).upper()}" if kind == "aws" else secrets.token_urlsafe(24)
        self.tokens[token] = placement
        return token

    def check_use(self, presented_token, src_ip):
        placement = self.tokens.get(presented_token)
        if placement is None:
            return None                            # a real (or simply invalid) credential
        return {"severity": "critical",
                "rule": "honeytoken_used",
                "src_ip": src_ip,
                "planted_in": placement,
                "meaning": "intrusion confirmed; attacker reached this location"}

ht = Honeytokens()
wiki_key = ht.mint("internal wiki page 'Legacy S3 access'", kind="aws")
repo_key = ht.mint("config/settings.example.yml in the payments repo")
backup_key = ht.mint("credential manager entry 'old backup service'")
print(wiki_key)                                     # e.g. AKIA3F9C21B70E4D8A15

print(ht.check_use("ordinary-user-token", "10.0.10.55"))     # None
print(ht.check_use(repo_key, "203.0.113.9"))
# {'severity': 'critical', 'rule': 'honeytoken_used', 'src_ip': '203.0.113.9',
#  'planted_in': 'config/settings.example.yml in the payments repo',
#  'meaning': 'intrusion confirmed; attacker reached this location'}
#   The placement tells you the attacker read that repository -- scope the incident from there.
```

```bash
# Isolate a honeypot so it can never attack third parties (the ethical requirement):
$ sudo nft -f - <<'EOF'
table inet honeypot {
  chain input  { type filter hook input priority 0; policy accept; }   # let attackers in
  chain output {
    type filter hook output priority 0; policy drop;                   # but nothing out
    ct state established,related accept                                # replies only
    ip daddr 10.0.99.20 udp dport 514 accept                           # off-box logging only
  }
}
EOF

# Low-interaction SSH honeypot session recorded by Cowrie (research deployment):
$ jq -r 'select(.eventid=="cowrie.login.failed") | "\(.src_ip) \(.username):\(.password)"' \
     cowrie.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
#   412 203.0.113.44 root:123456
#   388 203.0.113.44 root:admin
#   201 198.51.100.9 admin:admin
#   ^ credential lists in active use -- feed these into your own password blocklist

# Canary alerts should be routed as high severity with no tuning needed:
$ logger -p auth.crit -t canary "canary_touched src=10.0.10.55 dst_port=445"
```

**Key takeaways**

- Deception works because decoys have **no legitimate use**, so any interaction is high-signal — sidestepping the base-rate problem.
- **Low-interaction** honeypots are safe and capture first moves; **high-interaction** ones yield deeper insight and carry **real compromise risk**.
- **Production** placement (canary hosts, honeytokens, honey files) detects intruders **already inside**, which is their highest-value use.
- **Honeytokens** reveal both the intrusion and **where the attacker looked**.
- Run them responsibly: **isolate with strict egress**, **log off-box**, keep them sterile, monitor the alerts, and never counter-attack.

#### SIEM and Traffic Analytics

**Theory**

By this point the network produces evidence from many places: firewall drops, proxy logs, DNS queries, IDS alerts, flow records, authentication events, endpoint telemetry, honeytoken hits. Each is a narrow view, and attacks rarely announce themselves in a single source. A **SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)** system centralises these events, normalises them, correlates across sources, and turns them into alerts and investigations.

The core value is **correlation**. Individually, a failed VPN login, a DNS query for an unknown domain, and a large upload are unremarkable. In sequence, from one user, within ten minutes, they are an incident. Only a system holding all three sources can see that.

A SIEM pipeline has recognisable stages:

1. **Collection**: agents and collectors gather syslog, Windows events, cloud audit logs (CloudTrail), flow records, proxy and DNS logs.
2. **Normalisation**: map wildly different formats onto common fields (`src_ip`, `user`, `action`, `outcome`) so a single query spans sources. Schemas like OCSF or ECS exist for this.
3. **Enrichment**: add context — geolocation, asset criticality, owner, threat-intelligence matches, whether the account is privileged. Enrichment is what turns "an IP" into "the finance database".
4. **Correlation and detection**: rules and statistics across sources and time windows.
5. **Alerting and triage**: route to analysts with enough context to act; suppress and tune relentlessly.
6. **Retention and search**: keep data long enough for investigations — attacks are often discovered months later — which makes **storage cost** the central design constraint.

Two adjacent capabilities complete the picture. **Traffic analytics** (NetFlow/IPFIX, Zeek logs, cloud VPC flow logs) provides cheap, complete *metadata* coverage of who talked to whom, when, and how much. Because it survives encryption and is far smaller than full packet capture, it is the practical substrate for the behavioural detections in 11.4 — beaconing, volume asymmetry, rare destinations, internal scanning. **UEBA** (user and entity behaviour analytics) baselines per-user and per-host behaviour and scores deviations, catching credential misuse that no signature describes.

Practical realities to plan for:

- **Volume and cost** dominate. Decide deliberately what to collect at full fidelity, what to sample, and what to summarise. Collecting everything and searching nothing is the common failure.
- **Time synchronisation** (NTP) and consistent time zones are prerequisites; correlation across sources is impossible without them.
- **Log integrity**: ship logs off-host immediately and make them append-only, because erasing local logs is standard practice for intruders.
- **Alert fatigue** is the main operational risk. Fewer, higher-precision, well-documented detections beat a large noisy rule set; every alert needs a documented response.
- **Coverage mapping**: frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK let you ask *which techniques would we actually see?* — usually more informative than counting rules.

**Examples**

```text
Correlation: three harmless events, one incident

  09:02  VPN     user=alice  result=success  src=203.0.113.9  geo=RO   (normally NL)
  09:04  DNS     src=10.99.0.23  query=cdn-update-svc.example  (first time seen in the org)
  09:06  proxy   src=10.99.0.23  user=alice  bytes_out=1.8 GB  dst=storage.example
  09:07  canary  src=10.99.0.23  dst_port=445

  individually : a trip abroad; an unknown domain; a big upload; one odd connection
  correlated   : impossible travel -> new C2 domain -> bulk egress -> internal scan
                 => account compromise with data exfiltration in progress

Data sources and what each answers

  firewall logs  : was it allowed or blocked, and between which addresses
  flow records   : who talked to whom, how much, how often   <- survives encryption, cheap
  proxy logs     : which URL, which user, which category
  DNS logs       : what names were resolved            <- earliest signal in most intrusions
  IDS alerts     : which known-bad pattern matched
  auth logs      : who logged in, from where, success or failure
  endpoint       : which process did it                <- links a connection to a binary
  honeytokens    : confirmed intrusion + where the attacker looked
```

```python
# A small correlation engine: normalise, enrich, then score sequences across sources.
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from collections import defaultdict
import datetime as dt

@dataclass
class Event:                    # the NORMALISED schema every source is mapped onto
    ts: dt.datetime
    source: str                 # vpn | dns | proxy | canary | auth
    user: str | None
    src_ip: str
    action: str
    outcome: str = "success"
    detail: dict = field(default_factory=dict)

ASSETS = {"10.0.30.11": {"name": "finance-db", "criticality": "high"},
          "10.99.0.23": {"name": "vpn-pool",   "criticality": "low"}}
HOME_GEOS = {"alice": {"NL"}}

def enrich(e: Event):
    e.detail["asset"] = ASSETS.get(e.src_ip, {}).get("name", "unknown")
    if e.source == "vpn" and e.user in HOME_GEOS:
        e.detail["unusual_geo"] = e.detail.get("geo") not in HOME_GEOS[e.user]
    return e

RULES = [
    ("impossible_travel", lambda e: e.source == "vpn" and e.detail.get("unusual_geo"), 3),
    ("rare_domain",       lambda e: e.source == "dns" and e.detail.get("first_seen"), 2),
    ("bulk_egress",       lambda e: e.source == "proxy" and e.detail.get("bytes_out", 0) > 1e9, 3),
    ("canary_touched",    lambda e: e.source == "canary", 5),
    ("brute_force",       lambda e: e.source == "auth" and e.outcome == "failure", 1),
]

def correlate(events, window_minutes=15, threshold=6):
    by_actor = defaultdict(list)
    for e in events:
        enrich(e)
        for name, test, weight in RULES:
            if test(e):
                by_actor[e.user or e.src_ip].append((e.ts, name, weight))
    incidents = []
    for actor, hits in by_actor.items():
        hits.sort()
        for i, (ts0, _, _) in enumerate(hits):
            window = [h for h in hits[i:] if (h[0] - ts0).total_seconds() <= window_minutes * 60]
            score = sum(w for _, _, w in window)
            if score >= threshold and len({n for _, n, _ in window}) >= 3:
                incidents.append({"actor": actor, "score": score, "started": ts0.strftime("%H:%M"),
                                  "signals": [n for _, n, _ in window]})
                break
    return incidents

t = lambda hhmm: dt.datetime.strptime(hhmm, "%H:%M")
events = [
    Event(t("09:02"), "vpn",    "alice", "203.0.113.9", "login", detail={"geo": "RO"}),
    Event(t("09:04"), "dns",    "alice", "10.99.0.23", "query",
          detail={"qname": "cdn-update-svc.example", "first_seen": True}),
    Event(t("09:06"), "proxy",  "alice", "10.99.0.23", "upload", detail={"bytes_out": 1.8e9}),
    Event(t("09:07"), "canary", "alice", "10.99.0.23", "connect", detail={"dst_port": 445}),
    Event(t("11:30"), "auth",   "bob",   "10.0.10.77", "login", outcome="failure"),
]
for inc in correlate(events):
    print(inc)
# {'actor': 'alice', 'score': 13, 'started': '09:02',
#  'signals': ['impossible_travel', 'rare_domain', 'bulk_egress', 'canary_touched']}
#   bob's single failed login scores 1 and never becomes an incident -- which is the point.
```

```bash
# Flow records: the cheap, encryption-proof backbone of traffic analytics.
# Top talkers by volume (nfdump against NetFlow/IPFIX collected from routers):
$ nfdump -R /var/flows -s record/bytes -n 5
# Date first seen     Duration Proto  Src IP:Port      Dst IP:Port      Packets  Bytes
# 2026-09-24 09:06:11  412.088 TCP    10.99.0.23:52344 198.51.100.40:443  1.2 M  1.8 G
#                                     ^ 1.8 GB outbound from a VPN client: investigate

# Cloud equivalent: VPC flow logs queried for internal scanning
$ aws logs start-query --log-group-name /vpc/flowlogs \
    --query-string 'fields srcAddr, dstPort | filter action="REJECT" | stats count_distinct(dstAddr) as hosts by srcAddr | filter hosts > 20'

# Centralise logs immediately so an intruder cannot erase them (rsyslog forwarding):
#   *.*  action(type="omfwd" target="10.0.99.20" port="6514"
#              protocol="tcp" StreamDriver="gtls" StreamDriverMode="1")
#                                    ^ TLS: the log channel itself needs integrity

# Time sync is a prerequisite for correlation -- verify it everywhere:
$ chronyc tracking | grep -E "System time|Last offset"
# System time     : 0.000004821 seconds fast of NTP time

# Sizing reality check before turning on full collection:
$ echo "scale=1; 40000 * 500 * 86400 / 1024/1024/1024" | bc
# 1608.0        <- 40k events/s at 500 bytes = ~1.6 TB/day raw: decide fidelity deliberately
```

**Key takeaways**

- A **SIEM** centralises, normalises, enriches, and **correlates** events; its value is seeing sequences no single source reveals.
- **Enrichment** (asset criticality, identity, geo, threat intel) is what makes an alert actionable.
- **Flow records** give complete, cheap metadata coverage that survives encryption — the substrate for behavioural detection; **UEBA** baselines per-user behaviour.
- Plan for **volume and cost**, insist on **NTP-synchronised clocks**, and **ship logs off-host** so they cannot be erased.
- **Alert fatigue** is the main failure mode: prefer fewer high-precision detections with documented responses, and map coverage with **MITRE ATT&CK**.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. List which log source would answer each question: which process opened a connection; whether a packet was blocked; which URL a user fetched; how much data left the network.
> 2. Write a correlation rule for "password spraying followed by one success from the same source", naming the sources and time window.
> 3. Estimate daily storage for 8,000 events per second at 400 bytes each, and propose what to sample if the budget allows 1 TB per day.
> 4. Interview-style: *Your SIEM produces 4,000 alerts a day and the team investigates 30. How do you fix this?* (Hint: the problem is precision, not volume of data — think about which alerts have ever led to a real finding, and what each remaining one should tell an analyst to do.)

<a id="12-quality-of-service-and-traffic-engineering"></a>
## 12. Quality of Service and Traffic Engineering

Every mechanism so far has assumed the network's default contract: it will try to deliver your packet, and it owes you nothing about when or whether it arrives. That contract is adequate for a file transfer and useless for a surgeon's video feed, because the moment a link is congested the network's arbitrary choices about who waits become the application's user experience. This chapter covers how to state service requirements numerically, the per-hop mechanisms that enforce them (classification, policing, shaping, scheduling, active queue management, admission control), and the two architectures — IntServ and DiffServ — that assemble those mechanisms into an end-to-end service, ending with MPLS and segment routing traffic engineering, which choose *paths* rather than queue positions.

<a id="121-qos-fundamentals"></a>
### 12.1 QoS Fundamentals

Quality of service begins as an exercise in specification rather than configuration: this subchapter covers how to describe what an application needs, how to divide an end-to-end requirement into a per-hop budget, what kinds of promises a network can actually make, and how those promises become contracts.

#### Traffic Classes and Service Requirements

**Theory**

A router with an empty queue gives every packet identical, excellent service, so QoS is invisible until the instant demand exceeds capacity. At that instant the router must decide which packet goes first and which packet is discarded, and the only question that matters is whether that decision is *deliberate* or *accidental*. Best-effort forwarding makes it accidental: with a single FIFO queue, a 2 GB backup pushes 40 ms of extra delay in front of every voice packet behind it, purely because the backup's packets arrived first. Traffic classes exist so that the decision can instead be made according to what each application can survive.

The fundamental split is between **elastic** and **inelastic** traffic. Elastic applications adapt: a file transfer finishes in 10 seconds or 30 seconds, and the only cost is impatience. Their throughput is what matters, and loss is not a catastrophe — it is TCP's congestion signal (Section 7.5), the mechanism by which the application discovers its fair share. Inelastic applications have a threshold: a voice call needs its packet within roughly 150 ms or the packet may as well not exist, because the conversation has already moved on. Sending it *faster* does not help, and sending it late is equivalent to losing it.

A useful analogy is a city street shared by ambulances, commuter cars, and gravel trucks. The ambulance is inelastic: arriving 20 minutes late is a total failure, and arriving 20 seconds early is worth nothing. The gravel truck is elastic: it cares only about tonnes delivered per day, and a detour costs nothing as long as the total holds. A single first-come-first-served rule serves the trucks well and kills the patient, which is exactly what one FIFO queue does to a mixed network.

Four requirement dimensions are enough to describe almost any class:

| Dimension | Question | Who is sensitive |
|---|---|---|
| **Bandwidth** | How many bits per second, and how bursty? | Video, bulk transfer |
| **Delay** | How long from sender to receiver, one way? | Voice, gaming, trading, control loops |
| **Jitter** | How much does delay *vary* packet to packet? | Voice, live video, industrial control |
| **Loss** | What fraction can be discarded without harm? | Voice tolerates some; bulk data tolerates none *visibly* |

The loss dimension is the most misunderstood. Voice appears *loss-sensitive* and is actually **loss-tolerant but retransmission-intolerant**: a G.711 codec with packet loss concealment interpolates a lost 20 ms sample well enough that 1% random loss is barely audible, but a retransmission arriving 90 ms later is worthless. Bulk TCP is the reverse — it never loses data visibly, because it retransmits everything, so loss shows up purely as reduced throughput. "Can this class lose packets?" therefore has two answers depending on whether the application or the transport is asked.

**RFC 4594** gives the standard industry class model, which is a good default because it is what vendor templates and service-provider offerings assume. The essential rows:

| Class | Example application | Bandwidth | One-way delay | Jitter | Loss tolerance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Network control** | routing protocols (BGP, OSPF), BFD | very low | low | low | very low |
| **Telephony** | VoIP bearer (RTP) | low, constant (~87 kb/s) | < 150 ms | < 30 ms | < 1% |
| **Signalling** | SIP, H.323 | very low, bursty | < 200 ms | loose | < 1% |
| **Interactive video** | video conferencing | 1-6 Mb/s, bursty | < 150 ms | < 30 ms | < 0.1% |
| **Streaming video** | on-demand video, IPTV | 3-25 Mb/s | < 4-5 s (buffered) | absorbed by buffer | < 0.1% |
| **Low-latency data** | transactional apps, RPC, SSH | low-medium, bursty | < 100-400 ms | loose | 0 (TCP) |
| **OAM** | SNMP, syslog, telemetry | low | loose | loose | low |
| **High-throughput data** | backups, replication, CI artefacts | high, sustained | irrelevant | irrelevant | 0 (TCP) |
| **Scavenger** | peer-to-peer, OS updates, opportunistic sync | whatever is left | irrelevant | irrelevant | high |

Two design rules follow. First, **the number of classes should be small** — typically four to eight. Each class needs a scheduler entry, a marking policy, thresholds, counters, and a documented meaning on every device in the path; twelve classes are twelve things to misconfigure, and operators cannot keep more than a handful straight. Second, **the scavenger class is as valuable as the priority class**. Giving backups a class that is explicitly allowed to starve is often the single most effective change in an enterprise network, because it removes the largest source of queue occupancy without needing to guarantee anything at all.

**Examples**

```text
Requirement space: where classes sit on the two axes that matter

  loss
  tolerance
     ^
 1%  |  [ telephony ]                          <- drop it, do not delay it
     |
     |
0.1% |        [ interactive video ]
     |                    [ streaming video ]
     |
  0  |  [ network control ]   [ low-latency data ]   [ bulk data ] [ scavenger ]
     +--------------------------------------------------------------------> delay
        10 ms         150 ms          1 s            10 s        unbounded
                      tolerance

 Reading the diagram:
   top-left    = inelastic real time  -> needs a scheduler guarantee, small queue
   bottom-left = control plane        -> needs protection, tiny volume
   bottom-right= elastic bulk         -> needs a big queue, nothing else
   Two classes in the same region of this plane should be merged.
```

```python
# One FIFO queue vs one deliberate decision, on the same arrival pattern.
# A 12 ms burst of bulk packets arrives, then a voice packet.

LINK_MBPS = 10
MTU_BITS = 1500 * 8
serialize_ms = MTU_BITS / (LINK_MBPS * 1000)      # 1.2 ms per full-size packet

backlog_packets = 10                               # bulk burst already queued
voice_bits = 200 * 8                               # G.711, 20 ms of audio + headers

# FIFO: the voice packet waits behind every byte that arrived before it.
fifo_wait = backlog_packets * serialize_ms
# Priority: it waits only for the packet currently on the wire (non-preemptive).
pq_wait = serialize_ms

print(f"FIFO     voice queueing delay: {fifo_wait:5.2f} ms")
print(f"Priority voice queueing delay: {pq_wait:5.2f} ms")
# FIFO     voice queueing delay: 12.00 ms
# Priority voice queueing delay:  1.20 ms
# The bulk transfer lost 10.8 ms of completion time out of several seconds;
# the voice call gained 10.8 ms out of a 150 ms end-to-end budget.

# Why the trade is asymmetric: express each cost as a fraction of its own budget.
bulk_transfer_ms = 8_000
print(f"cost to bulk:  {100*(fifo_wait-pq_wait)/bulk_transfer_ms:.3f}% of its budget")
print(f"gain to voice: {100*(fifo_wait-pq_wait)/150:.2f}% of its budget")
# cost to bulk:  0.135% of its budget
# gain to voice: 7.20% of its budget
```

```python
# Sizing a class plan against a real link: does the mix fit, and what starves?
link_mbps = 100

classes = [
    # name,               offered Mb/s, class, may_starve
    ("network control",     0.5,  "control",  False),
    ("telephony",           8.7,  "realtime", False),   # 100 G.711 calls
    ("interactive video",  20.0,  "realtime", False),
    ("low-latency data",   25.0,  "elastic",  False),
    ("high-throughput",    60.0,  "elastic",  False),
    ("scavenger",          30.0,  "elastic",  True),
]

offered = sum(c[1] for c in classes)
realtime = sum(c[1] for c in classes if c[2] == "realtime")
protected = sum(c[1] for c in classes if not c[3])       # everything but scavenger

print(f"offered   {offered:6.1f} Mb/s on a {link_mbps} Mb/s link "
      f"-> {offered/link_mbps:.0%} of capacity")
print(f"realtime  {realtime:6.1f} Mb/s -> {realtime/link_mbps:.0%} "
      f"(keep under 33%: see Section 12.2 on priority policing)")
print(f"protected {protected:6.1f} Mb/s -> fits: {protected <= link_mbps}")
# offered    144.2 Mb/s on a 100 Mb/s link -> 144% of capacity
# realtime    28.7 Mb/s -> 29% (keep under 33%: see Section 12.2 ...)
# protected  114.2 Mb/s -> fits: False
#
# Conclusion: scavenger absorbs 30 Mb/s of the overload, but 14.2 Mb/s of real
# demand still has nowhere to go. QoS cannot fix this link; only capacity can.
```

**Key takeaways**

- QoS has no effect on an uncongested link; it only makes the **choice at the moment of congestion** deliberate instead of accidental.
- **Elastic** traffic cares about throughput and treats loss as a signal; **inelastic** traffic has a delay threshold past which a packet is worthless.
- Voice is loss-tolerant but retransmission-intolerant — the right response to congestion for real-time traffic is to **drop, not delay**.
- Describe every class with four numbers: bandwidth, one-way delay, jitter, loss tolerance. Merge classes that land in the same region.
- Keep the class count between four and eight, and always define a **scavenger** class that is allowed to starve.
- If the sum of all non-starvable demand exceeds the link rate, no scheduler can help — that is a capacity problem.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Place these on the delay/loss-tolerance plane and name the class each belongs to: an SSH session, a 4K on-demand stream, a BGP keepalive, an hourly database replication job, a cloud-gaming stream.
> 2. A 10 Mb/s link carries 40 G.711 calls at 87 kb/s each plus one TCP backup. Compute the worst-case FIFO queueing delay if the backup keeps 50 full-size packets buffered, and say whether the calls meet a 150 ms end-to-end budget when propagation alone is 60 ms.
> 3. Write a four-class plan for a branch office running VoIP, a video-conferencing room, business web apps, and nightly backups. For each class give the four requirement numbers and say whether it may starve.
> 4. Interview-style: *An engineer proposes marking all of a company's traffic as high priority so nothing is ever delayed.* (Hint: ask what the scheduler is actually being told to do when every queue has the same priority, and compare the result with the original FIFO.)

#### Delay, Jitter, and Loss Budgets

**Theory**

A requirement like "one-way delay under 150 ms" is a statement about the whole path, but no single device controls the whole path. A **budget** turns the end-to-end requirement into a set of per-component allowances that can be designed and measured independently, exactly as a mechanical engineer divides a tolerance across a stack of parts. If the parts sum to less than the budget, the system works; if not, the budget says which part to attack.

The canonical figure comes from **ITU-T G.114** for interactive voice, measured mouth to ear in one direction:

| One-way delay | Experience |
|---|---|
| **< 150 ms** | Users notice nothing; normal conversation |
| **150-400 ms** | Usable but people begin talking over each other |
| **> 400 ms** | Unacceptable; speakers fall into walkie-talkie turn-taking |

That budget is consumed by five categories, only some of which a network engineer can change:

```text
end-to-end one-way delay =
      codec + packetization      (fixed by codec choice)
    + serialization per hop      (packet size / link rate)
    + propagation                (distance / speed in medium, ~5 us/km in fiber)
    + queueing per hop           (the only term QoS controls)
    + dejitter buffer            (chosen to absorb the queueing variation)
```

**Propagation** is the hard floor and the most commonly forgotten term. Light in fiber travels at roughly 200,000 km/s, which is 5 µs per kilometre, or **1 ms per 200 km** of fiber — and real fiber routes are typically 1.3 to 1.5 times the great-circle distance. London to New York is about 5,600 km straight, so roughly 8,000 km of fiber, so about 40 ms one way. No amount of bandwidth, queueing policy, or hardware upgrade changes that number; only moving the endpoints closer does, which is the entire justification for content delivery networks (Section 8.6).

**Serialization** is the time to clock a packet onto a link, `bits / rate`. It is negligible on modern core links (1500 bytes on 10 Gb/s is 1.2 µs) and dominant on slow access links (the same packet on a 1 Mb/s uplink is 12 ms). This is why fragmentation and interleaving mattered so much on narrowband WAN circuits and why they are irrelevant in a data centre.

**Queueing** is the variable term, and it is variable in two senses: it depends on load, and it differs packet to packet. That variation *is* jitter. **Jitter** matters because a real-time receiver must play out samples at a constant rate; if packets arrive unevenly, the playout buffer either runs dry (a gap in the audio) or overflows (a discarded sample). The fix is a **dejitter buffer** that deliberately delays playout by some amount D, converting variable arrival into constant playout. The cost is exact and unavoidable: **a dejitter buffer that absorbs D milliseconds of jitter adds D milliseconds of delay**. Jitter is therefore not a separate problem from delay; it is a tax paid in delay.

The loss budget works differently because loss is not additive in a useful way for real time. What matters for voice is the **loss pattern**: 1% of packets lost uniformly at random is concealed almost perfectly by a modern codec, while the same 1% arriving as a single 200 ms burst is an audible dropout. Consecutive losses defeat concealment because the interpolator has nothing recent to interpolate from. This is why tail-drop during a burst (Section 12.2) is worse for voice than the same average loss spread thinly, and why real-time classes want small queues with early, probabilistic discard rather than large queues that overflow all at once.

For elastic traffic, the loss budget is expressed differently again: as throughput. A classic approximation for a loss-based TCP flow gives throughput proportional to `MSS / (RTT * sqrt(p))`, so loss and RTT together cap a single flow's rate regardless of link capacity. On a 100 ms path, 0.1% loss caps one standard TCP flow at a few tens of Mb/s — which is why a fast link across an ocean often underperforms without either many parallel flows or a loss-insensitive congestion control such as BBR (Section 7.6).

**Examples**

```text
A voice budget, drawn as a ladder that must fit under 150 ms
(branch office in Milan to a data centre in Frankfurt, ~650 km, ~950 km of fiber)

  component                              ms     cumulative
  --------------------------------     -----    ----------
  codec look-ahead + packetization      20.0        20.0     <- G.711, 20 ms frames
  serialization, 2 Mb/s access link      0.8        20.8     <- 200 B at 2 Mb/s
  queueing, access link (priority)       1.5        22.3     <- one MTU ahead of us
  propagation, Milan -> Frankfurt        4.8        27.1     <- 950 km x 5 us/km
  queueing, 5 provider core hops         2.5        29.6     <- 0.5 ms each
  serialization, core hops               0.1        29.7
  queueing, DC access                    0.5        30.2
  dejitter buffer                       40.0        70.2     <- the largest term!
  --------------------------------     -----    ----------
  TOTAL one way                                    70.2 ms   budget 150 ms: PASS
                                                             headroom 79.8 ms

 Where the budget actually goes wrong in practice:
   - propagation underestimated (fiber route, not map distance)
   - dejitter buffer grown to hide jitter that QoS should have removed
   - one uncontrolled hop with a deep FIFO contributing 80+ ms by itself
```

```python
# Budget arithmetic: propagation floors, serialization, and the jitter tax.
FIBER_US_PER_KM = 5.0          # ~200,000 km/s in glass
ROUTE_FACTOR = 1.45            # real fiber path vs great-circle distance

def propagation_ms(great_circle_km, route_factor=ROUTE_FACTOR):
    return great_circle_km * route_factor * FIBER_US_PER_KM / 1000

for name, km in [("Milan-Frankfurt", 640), ("London-New York", 5_570),
                 ("London-Sydney", 16_990)]:
    ow = propagation_ms(km)
    print(f"{name:16s} one-way {ow:6.1f} ms   RTT {2*ow:6.1f} ms   "
          f"fits 150 ms one-way: {ow < 150}")
# Milan-Frankfurt  one-way    4.6 ms   RTT    9.3 ms   fits 150 ms one-way: True
# London-New York  one-way   40.4 ms   RTT   80.8 ms   fits 150 ms one-way: True
# London-Sydney    one-way  123.2 ms   RTT  246.4 ms   fits 150 ms one-way: True
# London-Sydney leaves only 26.8 ms for EVERYTHING else -> interactive voice
# on that path is inherently marginal, whatever the QoS policy says.

def serialization_ms(packet_bytes, link_mbps):
    return packet_bytes * 8 / (link_mbps * 1_000)

for rate in (1, 2, 10, 100, 10_000):
    print(f"1500 B at {rate:>6} Mb/s -> {serialization_ms(1500, rate):8.4f} ms")
# 1500 B at      1 Mb/s ->  12.0000 ms   <- dominant: one packet blocks a frame
# 1500 B at      2 Mb/s ->   6.0000 ms
# 1500 B at     10 Mb/s ->   1.2000 ms
# 1500 B at    100 Mb/s ->   0.1200 ms
# 1500 B at  10000 Mb/s ->   0.0012 ms   <- irrelevant
```

```python
# Sizing a dejitter buffer from measured arrival times, and paying its cost.
import statistics

# Sender emits every 20 ms; these are measured one-way delays in ms.
one_way = [31, 34, 30, 52, 33, 31, 47, 32, 30, 61, 33, 35, 30, 44, 32]

def buffer_sizing(delays, percentile=0.99):
    lo = min(delays)
    ordered = sorted(delays)
    idx = min(len(ordered) - 1, int(percentile * len(ordered)))
    hi = ordered[idx]                       # ignore the extreme tail on purpose
    return lo, hi, hi - lo

lo, hi, jitter = buffer_sizing(one_way)
print(f"min delay {lo} ms, p99 delay {hi} ms, jitter to absorb {jitter} ms")

# The buffer must hold at least `jitter`; playout delay = min delay + buffer.
buffer_ms = jitter
playout = lo + buffer_ms
late = [d for d in one_way if d > playout]  # these arrive after their slot
print(f"buffer {buffer_ms} ms -> playout delay {playout} ms, "
      f"packets discarded as late: {len(late)}/{len(one_way)} "
      f"({100*len(late)/len(one_way):.1f}%)")
# min delay 30 ms, p99 delay 61 ms, jitter to absorb 31 ms
# buffer 31 ms -> playout delay 61 ms, packets discarded as late: 0/15 (0.0%)

# The trade-off, made explicit: a smaller buffer saves delay and costs loss.
for b in (5, 10, 20, 31):
    p = lo + b
    late_n = sum(1 for d in one_way if d > p)
    print(f"buffer {b:2d} ms -> playout {p:2d} ms, late loss {100*late_n/len(one_way):5.1f}%")
# buffer  5 ms -> playout 35 ms, late loss  26.7%
# buffer 10 ms -> playout 40 ms, late loss  26.7%
# buffer 20 ms -> playout 50 ms, late loss  13.3%
# buffer 31 ms -> playout 61 ms, late loss   0.0%
# Reducing jitter in the network is what lets the buffer shrink; that is the
# real reason a real-time class wants a short, well-scheduled queue.
```

```python
# Why loss PATTERN matters more than loss RATE for concealed audio.
def audible_gaps(pattern, conceal_run=1):
    """A codec conceals runs up to conceal_run packets; longer runs are audible."""
    gaps, run = [], 0
    for lost in pattern:
        if lost:
            run += 1
        else:
            if run > conceal_run:
                gaps.append(run)
            run = 0
    if run > conceal_run:
        gaps.append(run)
    return gaps

n = 1000
uniform = [i % 100 == 0 for i in range(n)]              # 1% spread evenly
bursty  = [400 <= i < 410 for i in range(n)]            # 1% as one 200 ms burst
print(f"uniform 1%: loss={sum(uniform)/n:.1%} audible gaps={audible_gaps(uniform)}")
print(f"bursty  1%: loss={sum(bursty)/n:.1%} audible gaps={audible_gaps(bursty)}")
# uniform 1%: loss=1.0% audible gaps=[]         <- concealed, sounds fine
# bursty  1%: loss=1.0% audible gaps=[10]       <- a 200 ms hole: clearly heard
# Identical loss rate on a monitoring dashboard, opposite user experience.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Turn every end-to-end requirement into a **per-component budget**; the budget tells you which component to fix.
- **G.114**: under 150 ms one way is transparent for voice, 150-400 ms degrades, over 400 ms is unusable.
- **Propagation is a floor** at roughly 1 ms per 200 km of fiber, and real routes are about 1.4x map distance. Only moving endpoints changes it.
- **Serialization** dominates on slow access links and is negligible above ~1 Gb/s.
- Queueing is the only term QoS controls, and its *variation* is jitter.
- A dejitter buffer converts jitter into delay one-for-one: absorbing 40 ms of jitter costs 40 ms of delay.
- For real-time traffic the **loss pattern** matters more than the loss rate; bursty loss defeats concealment that handles the same rate spread thinly.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. Build a one-way delay budget for a voice call from a home DSL user (5 Mb/s up) to a cloud PBX 900 km away, using G.711 with 20 ms frames, three provider hops at 0.5 ms queueing each, and a 30 ms dejitter buffer. State the total and the headroom against 150 ms.
> 2. A monitoring system reports 0.8% loss on a voice class and users complain of "chopping". Explain what measurement you would add to distinguish a design problem from a reporting artefact.
> 3. On a 250 ms RTT satellite path with 0.5% loss, estimate whether a single classic TCP flow can fill a 100 Mb/s link, then name two changes that would help.
> 4. Interview-style: *A team reduces average latency on a voice path from 90 ms to 70 ms, but user-reported quality gets worse.* (Hint: the average is not what a playout buffer reacts to — ask what happened to the spread, and what the receiver does with a packet that misses its slot.)

#### Best-Effort vs Guaranteed Service

**Theory**

"Quality of service" covers a spectrum of promises, and the useful way to organise it is by what the network must *know* and *remember* in order to keep each promise. The stronger the guarantee, the more state and the more refusals it requires.

| Service model | Promise | State needed | Refuses traffic? | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Best effort** | none | none | never | the default Internet |
| **Overprovisioned best effort** | statistical, from headroom | none | never | most enterprise LANs, backbones |
| **Relative / differentiated** | class A beats class B | per-class (a handful) | no (but re-marks) | DiffServ, enterprise WAN |
| **Statistically guaranteed** | bound holds for ~99.x% of packets | per-class + admission | yes, at the edge | carrier voice, DS-TE |
| **Deterministically guaranteed** | bound holds for *every* packet | per-flow reservation | yes, per flow | IntServ, TSN, AVB |

The crucial insight is that **QoS never creates bandwidth**. A scheduler is a zero-sum allocator: every millisecond of delay it saves for one class is a millisecond it adds somewhere else. This sounds like a limitation and is actually the source of its value, because application sensitivities are wildly asymmetric — as the earlier arithmetic showed, moving 11 ms from a voice call to a backup costs the backup 0.1% of its budget and buys the call 7% of its own. QoS is profitable precisely because it trades a resource that one class values highly for a resource another class barely notices.

The second insight is that **guarantees require the right to say no**. If any number of flows may enter, then no per-flow guarantee can survive, because the guarantee's arithmetic depends on the total. This is why deterministic service always comes bundled with admission control, and why the Internet, which by design accepts traffic from anyone, cannot offer end-to-end deterministic service. A restaurant can promise you a table at 8 pm only if it can turn other people away at 8 pm.

The third insight is the **statistical multiplexing** trade-off, first met in Section 1.4. Reserving peak rate for every flow gives a hard guarantee and wastes most of the link, because flows peak at different times. Reserving less than peak and relying on aggregation gives far higher utilisation and a guarantee that holds "almost always". As the number of independent flows grows, the aggregate becomes smoother relative to its mean, so a fixed safety margin protects a larger and larger multiplex — which is why statistical guarantees work well in a carrier core with thousands of flows and badly on a branch link with three.

This leads to the most important practical judgement in the chapter: **overprovisioning versus mechanism**. If a link runs at 30% average utilisation with brief bursts, adding a sophisticated QoS policy buys almost nothing, because the queue is nearly always empty; adding a modest amount of capacity, or simply fixing an oversized buffer with an AQM (Section 12.2), buys much more. Conversely, on a link that is genuinely saturated for hours a day, no reasonable amount of extra capacity will protect real-time traffic as cheaply as a priority queue. The honest rule: **use capacity where it is cheap, use mechanism where capacity is expensive or where the requirement is absolute**. WAN circuits, mobile backhaul, satellite links, and industrial control networks are where mechanism earns its complexity.

**Examples**

```text
The same 100 Mb/s link under three models, during a 40 Mb/s voice + 200 Mb/s bulk offer

 BEST EFFORT (one FIFO)
   queue: [B B B V B B B B V B B]      voice interleaved with bulk
   voice delay = full queue depth      -> 30-80 ms, highly variable
   bulk throughput = ~60 Mb/s          -> both classes degraded, neither protected

 DIFFERENTIATED (priority queue for voice, policed at 33 Mb/s)
   voice queue: [V V]     served first, almost always short
   bulk queue:  [B B B B B B B B ...]  served with what remains
   voice delay = 1-2 ms                -> protected
   bulk throughput = ~67 Mb/s          -> unchanged in practice
   BUT: offered voice above 33 Mb/s is dropped by the policer, not queued

 GUARANTEED (per-flow reservation, admission control)
   admitted: 380 calls x 87 kb/s = 33 Mb/s reserved
   call 381 -> REJECTED with "network busy" before it starts
   voice delay = bounded for every admitted call
   the cost of the guarantee is a refusal the user can hear
```

```python
# QoS reallocates; it does not create. One link, three policies, same demand.
LINK = 100.0                         # Mb/s
voice_offer, bulk_offer = 40.0, 200.0

def best_effort(link, v, b):
    total = v + b
    share = link / total
    return v * share, b * share      # proportional degradation

def strict_priority(link, v, b, cap=None):
    served_v = min(v, cap if cap else link)
    return served_v, max(0.0, link - served_v)

def guaranteed(link, v, b, reserved):
    admitted_v = min(v, reserved)     # excess calls are REJECTED, not degraded
    return admitted_v, link - reserved  # reservation is held even when idle

for name, (v, b) in {
    "best effort": best_effort(LINK, voice_offer, bulk_offer),
    "priority (policed 33)": strict_priority(LINK, voice_offer, bulk_offer, 33.0),
    "guaranteed (reserve 33)": guaranteed(LINK, voice_offer, bulk_offer, 33.0),
}.items():
    print(f"{name:24s} voice {v:6.1f} Mb/s   bulk {b:6.1f} Mb/s   total {v+b:6.1f}")
# best effort              voice   16.7 Mb/s   bulk   83.3 Mb/s   total  100.0
# priority (policed 33)    voice   33.0 Mb/s   bulk   67.0 Mb/s   total  100.0
# guaranteed (reserve 33)  voice   33.0 Mb/s   bulk   67.0 Mb/s   total  100.0
# Every row sums to 100. The difference is WHO gets the shortfall and HOW they
# learn about it: silent degradation, a policer drop, or an explicit rejection.
```

```python
# Statistical multiplexing: why guarantees get cheaper as the multiplex grows.
import math

def required_capacity(n_flows, mean_mbps, peak_mbps, sigmas=3.0):
    """Gaussian approximation: mean + safety margin covering n independent flows."""
    p = mean_mbps / peak_mbps                      # activity probability
    var = n_flows * peak_mbps**2 * p * (1 - p)
    return n_flows * mean_mbps + sigmas * math.sqrt(var)

MEAN, PEAK = 0.2, 2.0                              # a bursty 2 Mb/s video source
for n in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    peak_alloc = n * PEAK
    stat_alloc = required_capacity(n, MEAN, PEAK)
    print(f"{n:5d} flows: peak-reserve {peak_alloc:8.1f} Mb/s   "
          f"statistical {stat_alloc:8.1f} Mb/s   gain {peak_alloc/stat_alloc:5.2f}x")
#     1 flows: peak-reserve      2.0 Mb/s   statistical      2.0 Mb/s   gain  1.00x
#    10 flows: peak-reserve     20.0 Mb/s   statistical      7.7 Mb/s   gain  2.60x
#   100 flows: peak-reserve    200.0 Mb/s   statistical     38.0 Mb/s   gain  5.26x
#  1000 flows: peak-reserve   2000.0 Mb/s   statistical    256.9 Mb/s   gain  7.78x
# A branch link with 1 flow gains nothing from statistical sharing, so it needs
# either peak reservation or real mechanism. A core with 1000 gains ~8x for free.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Service models form a ladder from best effort to deterministic guarantees, ordered by **how much state** the network keeps and **whether it may refuse** traffic.
- A scheduler is **zero-sum**: it moves delay and loss between classes. It is worth doing because application sensitivities are asymmetric, not because it adds capacity.
- **No guarantee without admission control.** Unbounded admission invalidates any per-flow bound.
- **Statistical multiplexing gain grows with the size of the multiplex**, so statistical guarantees are cheap in a core and expensive on a small link.
- Prefer **capacity where it is cheap** and **mechanism where it is not**; a link at 30% utilisation rarely benefits from an elaborate policy.
- The guarantee's visible cost is a refusal — a busy signal is a feature of a network that keeps its promises.

>
