> 2. Explain why GRE between two hosts cannot use more than one path in a four-way ECMP fabric, and what VXLAN does differently.
> 3. Given a report that "SSH works but file copies hang" on a new overlay, write the exact sequence of commands you would run to confirm the cause.
> 4. Interview-style: *A team runs VXLAN inside an IPsec tunnel and reports intermittent failures that correlate with large requests.* (Hint: add up both layers' overheads, compare against the path MTU, and consider what each layer does when an oversized packet arrives with the don't-fragment bit set.)

#### Overlay vs Underlay Networks

**Theory**

Once tunnels exist, a network has two distinct planes stacked on top of one another, and keeping them conceptually separate is the single most useful habit for operating or debugging such an environment.

The **underlay** is the physical network: real switches, real cables, real IP addresses assigned to real interfaces. Its only job is to carry packets between **tunnel endpoints**. It should be simple, stable, and boring — usually a routed leaf-spine fabric with a single address family, ECMP, and no tenant awareness whatsoever. It changes when hardware changes, which is to say rarely.

The **overlay** is the logical network the workloads see: their addresses, their segments, their security policy. It is created and destroyed constantly as workloads come and go, and it is entirely software.

The relationship is worth stating precisely, because it is what makes the whole design work: **the underlay knows nothing about tenants, and the overlay knows nothing about topology**. The underlay sees only tunnel endpoint addresses and has no idea how many tenants or segments exist. The overlay sees a flat logical segment and has no idea which rack anything is in. Each is free to change without disturbing the other, which is exactly the decoupling that lets a workload migrate between racks without renumbering.

The analogy is a postal system and a company's internal mail. The postal service routes between building addresses and knows nothing about departments. Internal mail is addressed to departments and knows nothing about streets. A department can move to a different building without changing anyone's internal addressing, and the postal service needs no knowledge of the reorganisation.

The overlay's central problem is **mapping**: given a logical destination, which tunnel endpoint currently holds it? Filling that table is the job of the overlay control plane, and there are three approaches:

| Approach | How the map is filled | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Flood and learn** | multicast or unicast-replicate unknown traffic, learn from replies | no control plane needed; floods badly, scales poorly |
| **Controller-programmed** | a controller pushes the map to every endpoint | precise and fast; requires a controller |
| **EVPN (BGP)** | endpoints advertise their local MAC and IP bindings via BGP | standards-based, scales, multi-vendor; today's default |

**EVPN** has become the standard answer because it reuses BGP, which is already proven at scale, and because advertising bindings explicitly eliminates flooding: a switch that learns a MAC locally advertises it, so every other switch knows the mapping without ever having to flood to discover it. It also handles ARP suppression, which removes a surprising amount of broadcast traffic from large segments.

Two operational consequences deserve emphasis.

First, **debugging becomes two-layer, and you must know which layer you are in**. A workload-to-workload failure could be an overlay mapping problem or an underlay reachability problem, and the diagnosis differs completely. The discipline is to test the underlay first — can the tunnel endpoints reach each other, at full MTU? — and only then the overlay. Tools that work at one layer are blind at the other, which is why a `traceroute` between two VMs across a VXLAN fabric shows a single hop: the entire physical path is invisible by design.

Second, **the overlay inherits every underlay problem while hiding its cause**. Congestion on one spine link appears as unexplained latency for a subset of overlay flows, with nothing in the overlay to indicate why. An underlay MTU shortfall appears as stalled transfers. This is the price of abstraction, and it is why underlay monitoring must stay first-class even though no workload traffic is addressed to it.

**Examples**

```text
Two planes, deliberately ignorant of each other

 OVERLAY (what workloads see)
   VM-A 10.1.0.5  <------------ one logical segment, VNI 10100 ------> VM-C 10.1.0.9
        ^ same subnet, "adjacent", traceroute shows ONE hop
        |  neither VM knows a fabric exists
 ....................................................................
 UNDERLAY (what actually happens)
   VTEP 10.255.0.1                                        VTEP 10.255.0.2
      [ leaf-1 ]---\                              /---[ leaf-2 ]
                    >--[ spine-1 ]--[ spine-2 ]--<
                   /                              \
       ^ routed, ECMP, jumbo MTU, ZERO tenant awareness

 Who knows what:
   underlay knows: 10.255.0.1 and 10.255.0.2 exist, and 4 paths between them
   underlay does NOT know: tenants, VNIs, VM addresses, policy
   overlay knows:  VM-A and VM-C are in VNI 10100, and which VTEP holds each
   overlay does NOT know: racks, spines, link utilisation, physical paths

 Debugging order (get this wrong and you waste hours):
   1. underlay reachability at FULL MTU:  ping -M do -s 8972 10.255.0.2
   2. underlay path health:               which of the 4 paths, any drops?
   3. overlay mapping:                    is VM-C's MAC/IP known to leaf-1?
   4. overlay policy:                     is the traffic permitted?
```

```python
# An overlay is a MAPPING problem: logical identity -> physical location.
import hashlib
from collections import Counter

class Fabric:
    """VTEPs hold the map. The underlay only ever routes VTEP-to-VTEP."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.mac_to_vtep = {}          # the overlay control plane's entire job
        self.underlay = {}             # VTEP IP -> which rack it sits in

    def learn(self, vni, mac, vtep, rack):
        self.mac_to_vtep[(vni, mac)] = vtep       # NOTE: the key includes the VNI
        self.underlay[vtep] = rack

    def forward(self, vni, src_mac, dst_mac):
        src_vtep = self.mac_to_vtep.get((vni, src_mac))
        dst_vtep = self.mac_to_vtep.get((vni, dst_mac))
        if dst_vtep is None:
            return ("BUM", f"unknown MAC in VNI {vni}: replicate to all VTEPs in VNI")
        if src_vtep == dst_vtep:
            return ("LOCAL", f"both on {src_vtep}: never touches the underlay")
        return ("ENCAP", f"{src_vtep} -> {dst_vtep} "
                         f"(rack {self.underlay[src_vtep]} -> {self.underlay[dst_vtep]}), "
                         f"outer dst IP = {dst_vtep}, VNI {vni}")

f = Fabric()
f.learn(10100, "aa:00:00:00:00:01", "10.255.0.1", "rack-1")
f.learn(10100, "aa:00:00:00:00:02", "10.255.0.1", "rack-1")
f.learn(10100, "aa:00:00:00:00:03", "10.255.0.2", "rack-2")
f.learn(10200, "bb:00:00:00:00:01", "10.255.0.3", "rack-3")

for label, vni, s, d in (
        ("same VTEP",         10100, "aa:00:00:00:00:01", "aa:00:00:00:00:02"),
        ("across the fabric", 10100, "aa:00:00:00:00:01", "aa:00:00:00:00:03"),
        ("unknown MAC",       10100, "aa:00:00:00:00:01", "aa:00:00:00:00:99"),
        ("other tenant",      10200, "bb:00:00:00:00:01", "aa:00:00:00:00:03")):
    kind, why = f.forward(vni, s, d)
    print(f"{label:19s} {kind:6s} {why}")
# same VTEP           LOCAL  both on 10.255.0.1: never touches the underlay
# across the fabric   ENCAP  10.255.0.1 -> 10.255.0.2 (rack rack-1 -> rack-2), outer dst IP = 10.255.0.2, VNI 10100
# unknown MAC         BUM    unknown MAC in VNI 10100: replicate to all VTEPs in VNI
# other tenant        BUM    unknown MAC in VNI 10200: replicate to all VTEPs in VNI
#
# The last line is the isolation property: tenant 10200 cannot reach tenant
# 10100's MAC at all, because the lookup key INCLUDES the VNI. Two tenants may
# use identical MAC and IP addresses without colliding.

# Why the underlay needs entropy, and where VXLAN gets it.
def ecmp_hash(outer_src, outer_dst, udp_src, n_paths):
    key = f"{outer_src}|{outer_dst}|{udp_src}".encode()
    return int(hashlib.md5(key).hexdigest(), 16) % n_paths

fixed  = Counter(ecmp_hash("10.255.0.1", "10.255.0.2", 4789, 4) for _ in range(1000))
varied = Counter(ecmp_hash("10.255.0.1", "10.255.0.2", 30000 + i % 997, 4)
                 for i in range(1000))
print(f"\nouter UDP sport FIXED  -> path distribution {dict(sorted(fixed.items()))}")
print(f"outer UDP sport HASHED -> path distribution {dict(sorted(varied.items()))}")
# outer UDP sport FIXED  -> path distribution {1: 1000}
# outer UDP sport HASHED -> path distribution {0: 266, 1: 273, 2: 228, 3: 233}
#
# With a fixed source port, every flow between two VTEPs pins to ONE underlay
# path: a 4-way spine collapses to a single link. This is exactly why the
# encapsulator hashes the INNER flow into the OUTER source port.
```

```bash
# --- Underlay first, always. Test endpoint-to-endpoint at FULL MTU ---
ping -M do -s 8972 -c 3 10.255.0.2      # 8972 + 28 = 9000; must succeed on jumbo
ip route get 10.255.0.2                  # which underlay path, which interface
vtysh -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast 10.255.0.2/32'   # is the VTEP route even present?

# --- Then the overlay map ---
bridge fdb show | grep vxlan100          # MAC -> remote VTEP bindings
#  aa:00:00:00:00:03 dev vxlan100 dst 10.255.0.2 self         <- learned remotely
#  00:00:00:00:00:00 dev vxlan100 dst 10.255.0.2 self         <- BUM replication entry
ip neigh show dev vxlan100               # ARP suppression cache

# EVPN: the modern control plane. Who advertised this MAC?
vtysh -c 'show bgp l2vpn evpn route type macip' | head
#  *> [2]:[0]:[48]:[aa:00:00:00:00:03]  10.255.0.2   <- MAC advertised BY leaf-2
vtysh -c 'show evpn mac vni 10100'
vtysh -c 'show evpn vni detail'

# --- Why traceroute lies in an overlay ---
ip netns exec vm-a traceroute -n 10.1.0.9
#  1  10.1.0.9  0.412 ms      <- ONE hop: the whole fabric is invisible by design
# The physical path must be traced in the underlay instead:
traceroute -n 10.255.0.2
#  1  10.0.1.1     <- leaf
#  2  10.0.255.1   <- spine
#  3  10.255.0.2   <- remote VTEP

# --- Correlating a layer: which underlay link is a given overlay flow using? ---
# Capture the outer packet and read the hashed source port, then check that path.
tcpdump -ni ens1f0 -c 1 'udp port 4789 and host 10.255.0.2' 2>/dev/null
ethtool -S swp1 | grep -iE 'discard|drop|pause'   # per-underlay-link health
```

**Key takeaways**

- The **underlay** is the physical network carrying packets between tunnel endpoints; keep it simple, routed, jumbo-enabled, and tenant-unaware.
- The **overlay** is the logical network workloads see; it changes constantly and is entirely software.
- The decoupling is mutual: **the underlay knows nothing about tenants, and the overlay knows nothing about topology**. That is what lets workloads migrate without renumbering.
- The overlay's core problem is **mapping** logical identity to tunnel endpoint. **EVPN over BGP** is the current standard, replacing flood-and-learn and eliminating unnecessary flooding.
- Including the **VNI in the lookup key** is what provides tenant isolation and lets tenants reuse identical addresses.
- **Debug the underlay first**, at full MTU, then the overlay map, then policy. Tools at one layer are blind to the other.
- A `traceroute` between overlay endpoints shows one hop: the physical path is hidden by design, so **underlay monitoring must stay first-class**.
- The overlay inherits underlay problems while concealing their cause, which is the real cost of the abstraction.

#### Container Networking and CNI

**Theory**

Containers changed the network's requirements more than virtual machines did, for reasons of scale and lifetime. A VM lives for months and is provisioned deliberately; a container may live for seconds, and a cluster may create and destroy thousands per minute. A networking model that requires any human action, or any change to physical configuration, is simply not viable.

The original Docker model was **port mapping**: containers shared the host's network namespace or sat behind NAT, and reaching a container meant reaching a port on its host. This works for a handful of containers on one machine and collapses as a general model, because ports become a globally contended resource, containers cannot use their natural ports, and addresses depend on placement.

**Kubernetes** replaced it with a model defined by three invariants, and almost everything about container networking follows from them:

1. Every pod gets its **own IP address**, routable within the cluster.
2. Pods can communicate **without NAT**.
3. A node can reach all pods on that node without NAT.

These are strong requirements. They mean the cluster needs a flat address space large enough for every pod, and that the network must place and withdraw addresses at pod lifecycle speed. Kubernetes deliberately does not implement this. It defines the contract and delegates to a plugin, which is **CNI** (Container Network Interface).

CNI is notable for its minimalism. A plugin is an **executable** that the runtime invokes with a verb (`ADD`, `DEL`, `CHECK`), passing configuration as JSON on standard input and the target network namespace as an environment variable, and reading the result as JSON from standard output. That is the whole interface. On `ADD` the plugin must create the pod's interface, allocate an address, configure routes, and return what it did.

The work itself is the sequence you would perform by hand: create a network namespace, create a veth pair, move one end in and rename it `eth0`, allocate an IP, set the address and default route, and attach the host end to whatever datapath the plugin uses.

**IPAM** is where a design decision with real consequences hides. The usual approach gives each node a **slice of the cluster CIDR** — a `/24` out of a `/16`, say — so that a node can allocate addresses locally without coordinating with anything. That is what makes allocation fast enough for container lifecycles. The cost is arithmetic that must be checked at design time: a `/16` split into `/24` blocks supports 256 nodes and about 253 pods per node, and neither number can be changed later without renumbering the cluster.

The plugins differ in how pods on different nodes reach each other:

| Plugin | Cross-node forwarding | Policy | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Flannel** | VXLAN overlay or host routes | none natively | simplest; minimal features |
| **Calico** | native routing with BGP, or overlay | rich, iptables or eBPF | no encapsulation needed if the underlay can route pod CIDRs |
| **Cilium** | eBPF, with VXLAN or native routing | identity-based, eBPF | also replaces kube-proxy; L7 aware |
| **cloud plugins** | the cloud's own VPC routing | cloud security groups | pods get real VPC addresses |

The distinction to internalise is **overlay versus native routing**. An overlay works anywhere because it only needs IP connectivity between nodes, and it costs encapsulation overhead and MTU complexity. Native routing avoids both by advertising pod CIDRs into the physical network with BGP, which is faster and more debuggable, and requires an underlay willing to carry those routes. That is a conversation with the network team, which is often the actual deciding factor.

One more piece completes the picture. Pod addresses are ephemeral, so clients cannot use them directly; a **Service** provides a stable virtual address that is load-balanced across the pods currently backing it. Implemented traditionally by `kube-proxy` writing iptables or IPVS rules on every node, and increasingly by eBPF programs, it is a per-node distributed load balancer rather than a central one, which is why there is no bottleneck and no single point of failure.

**Examples**

```text
What a pod's network actually looks like

  NODE (10.0.3.7)                       pod CIDR for this node: 10.244.3.0/24
  +---------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  pod "web"  netns                pod "db"  netns              |
  |  +---------------------+         +---------------------+      |
  |  | eth0 10.244.3.2/24  |         | eth0 10.244.3.3/24  |      |
  |  | default via .3.1    |         | default via .3.1    |      |
  |  +----------+----------+         +----------+----------+      |
  |             | veth pair                     | veth pair       |
  |  +----------+-------------------------------+----------+      |
  |  |   bridge / eBPF datapath      10.244.3.1 (gateway)  |      |
  |  +--------------------------+--------------------------+      |
  |                             | eth0 10.0.3.7                   |
  +-----------------------------+---------------------------------+
                                |
                       [ cluster network ]
                                |
     reaching 10.244.5.0/24 (another node) happens either by
       OVERLAY:        encapsulate to that node's IP (VXLAN)
       NATIVE ROUTING: the fabric knows 10.244.5.0/24 via BGP

 The CNI contract, in full:
   runtime --exec--> /opt/cni/bin/<plugin>
            env:     CNI_COMMAND=ADD, CNI_NETNS=/var/run/netns/..., CNI_IFNAME=eth0
            stdin:   { network configuration as JSON }
            stdout:  { interfaces, ips, routes, dns }
   That is the entire API. No daemon, no gRPC, no library.
```

```python
# What a CNI plugin actually does, as a sequence of concrete steps.
import ipaddress, json

class NodeIPAM:
    """Each node owns a slice of the cluster CIDR, so allocation needs NO coordination.
    That is what makes it fast enough for container lifecycles."""
    def __init__(self, cluster_cidr, node_prefix_len, node_index):
        cluster = ipaddress.ip_network(cluster_cidr)
        self.pod_cidr = list(cluster.subnets(new_prefix=node_prefix_len))[node_index]
        hosts = list(self.pod_cidr.hosts())
        self.gateway = hosts[0]                   # the node's bridge acts as gateway
        self.free, self.leased = hosts[1:], {}

    def allocate(self, pod):
        ip = self.free.pop(0)
        self.leased[pod] = ip
        return ip

    def capacity(self):
        return len(self.free) + len(self.leased)

ipam = NodeIPAM("10.244.0.0/16", 24, 3)          # node index 3 of a /16 cluster
print(f"cluster 10.244.0.0/16, /24 per node -> this node owns {ipam.pod_cidr}")
print(f"  gateway {ipam.gateway}, pods per node {ipam.capacity()}, "
      f"max nodes {2**(24-16)}")
# cluster 10.244.0.0/16, /24 per node -> this node owns 10.244.3.0/24
#   gateway 10.244.3.1, pods per node 253, max nodes 256
#
# CHECK THIS AT DESIGN TIME: 256 nodes and 253 pods per node are both hard
# ceilings, and neither can change without renumbering the whole cluster.

print("\nCNI ADD, step by step:")
for i, s in enumerate([
        "create a network namespace for the pod",
        "create a veth pair: one end for the pod, one for the host",
        "move the pod end into the netns and rename it eth0",
        "allocate an IP from this node's pod CIDR (IPAM)",
        "assign the IP and set the default route via the node gateway",
        "attach the host end to the bridge / program the eBPF datapath",
        "return the result as JSON on stdout"], 1):
    print(f"  {i}. {s}")

for pod in ("web-7f8c", "db-2a1b", "cache-9d3e"):
    print(f"  allocated {ipam.allocate(pod)} to {pod}")
#   allocated 10.244.3.2 to web-7f8c
#   allocated 10.244.3.3 to db-2a1b
#   allocated 10.244.3.4 to cache-9d3e

result = {"cniVersion": "1.0.0",
          "interfaces": [{"name": "eth0", "sandbox": "/var/run/netns/cni-web-7f8c"}],
          "ips": [{"address": f"{ipam.leased['web-7f8c']}/24",
                   "gateway": str(ipam.gateway), "interface": 0}],
          "routes": [{"dst": "0.0.0.0/0", "gw": str(ipam.gateway)}]}
print("\nCNI ADD result returned to the runtime:")
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
# {
#   "cniVersion": "1.0.0",
#   "interfaces": [ { "name": "eth0", "sandbox": "/var/run/netns/cni-web-7f8c" } ],
#   "ips": [ { "address": "10.244.3.2/24", "gateway": "10.244.3.1", "interface": 0 } ],
#   "routes": [ { "dst": "0.0.0.0/0", "gw": "10.244.3.1" } ]
# }

print("\nThe Kubernetes network model, stated as three invariants:")
for inv in ("every pod gets its own routable IP (no port mapping)",
            "pods reach each other directly, without NAT",
            "a node reaches all pods on that node without NAT"):
    print(f"  - {inv}")
print("Everything a CNI plugin does serves those three sentences.")
```

```bash

ip netns add demo
ip link add veth-h type veth peer name veth-c
ip link set veth-c netns demo
ip netns exec demo ip link set veth-c name eth0
ip netns exec demo ip addr add 10.244.3.99/24 dev eth0
ip netns exec demo ip link set eth0 up
ip netns exec demo ip route add default via 10.244.3.1
ip link set veth-h master cni0 up
ip netns exec demo ip addr show eth0        # exactly what a pod sees

# --- Inspect a real pod's network from the node ---
PID=$(crictl inspect --output go-template --template '{{.info.pid}}' "$CONTAINER_ID")
nsenter -t "$PID" -n ip addr show eth0
nsenter -t "$PID" -n ip route show
nsenter -t "$PID" -n ss -tlnp

# --- Which CNI is installed, and how is it configured? ---
cat /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist | jq '.plugins[].type'
#  "calico"
#  "portmap"        <- plugins CHAIN: each runs in order
ls /opt/cni/bin/

# --- Pod CIDR allocation: verify your ceilings before they bite ---
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.podCIDR}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl cluster-info dump | grep -m1 cluster-cidr
#  --cluster-cidr=10.244.0.0/16      -> 256 nodes at /24 per node

# --- Native routing vs overlay: which is in use? ---
ip route | grep 10.244
#  10.244.5.0/24 via 10.0.3.9 dev eth0        <- NATIVE routing (no encapsulation)
#  10.244.5.0/24 dev flannel.1 onlink         <- OVERLAY (VXLAN device)
calicoctl node status        # BGP peerings, if Calico is routing natively

# --- Services are per-node load balancers, not a central one ---
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | head
ipvsadm -Ln | head                     # if kube-proxy runs in IPVS mode
cilium service list                    # if eBPF replaced kube-proxy
```

**Key takeaways**

- Containers made **port mapping** untenable: ports became contended, and addresses depended on placement.
- The Kubernetes model is three invariants: **a routable IP per pod**, **pod-to-pod without NAT**, and **node-to-local-pod without NAT**.
- Kubernetes defines the contract and delegates to **CNI**, whose entire interface is an **executable** taking JSON on stdin and returning JSON on stdout.
- A plugin's `ADD` creates a netns and veth pair, allocates an address, sets routes, and attaches to a datapath.
- **IPAM** gives each node a slice of the cluster CIDR so allocation needs no coordination; the resulting **node and pod ceilings are fixed at design time**.
- **Overlay** plugins work anywhere but cost encapsulation and MTU complexity; **native routing** with BGP is faster and more debuggable but requires an underlay that will carry pod routes.
- A **Service** supplies the stable virtual address that ephemeral pod IPs cannot, implemented as a **per-node distributed load balancer** via iptables, IPVS, or eBPF.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. A cluster uses `10.100.0.0/14` with a `/25` per node. Compute the maximum node count and the pods per node, and state which limit binds first for 400 nodes of 60 pods.
> 2. Recreate a pod's network manually with `ip netns` and `veth`, then give the two commands that prove the namespace has an address and a default route.
> 3. Compare overlay and native-routing CNI modes on MTU, debuggability, and what each requires from the physical network.

#### Service Mesh and Sidecar Proxies

**Theory**

A microservice architecture needs a set of capabilities on every call between services: retries with sensible backoff, timeouts, circuit breaking, mutual authentication, authorisation, load balancing across instances, traffic splitting for canary releases, and metrics and traces for every request. The question is where that logic lives.

The first answer was **libraries**: each service imports a resilience and discovery library. It works, and it has a decisive flaw in a polyglot organisation — the library must be implemented and maintained for every language, and a policy change requires recompiling and redeploying every service. Upgrading a timeout default becomes a months-long migration across dozens of teams.

A **service mesh** moves the logic out of the process and into a **proxy** beside it. The sidecar pattern runs that proxy as a separate container in the same pod, and traffic is transparently redirected through it, usually by iptables rules or eBPF. The application makes an ordinary, unmodified call to a plain hostname; the proxy intercepts it, applies policy, establishes mutual TLS to the destination's proxy, load balances, retries, records metrics, and forwards.

The properties follow directly: the behaviour is **language-agnostic** because it operates on network traffic rather than inside the runtime, and it is **uniform and centrally controllable** because policy is configured once in the control plane and distributed to every proxy. This is the clean separation the mesh delivers: the **data plane** is the fleet of proxies carrying traffic, and the **control plane** configures them, holds the service identity and certificate authority, and distributes policy.

The costs are equally direct, and they are the reason meshes are not universal.

**Latency.** Every call crosses two proxies, one outbound and one inbound. Each adds a fraction of a millisecond at the median and more at the tail. On a single hop this is negligible; in a chain eight services deep, sixteen proxy traversals compound, and the tail latency added can exceed the actual work. Deep call chains are where meshes hurt most, and the right response is usually to shorten the chain rather than tune the proxy.

**Resources.** A sidecar per pod costs memory and CPU per pod. At a few hundred pods this is a rounding error. At several thousand, the sidecars alone can consume tens of gigabytes of RAM and hundreds of cores before any application code runs.

**Operational complexity.** The mesh becomes a critical dependency in the request path, with its own configuration language, failure modes, and upgrade process. A misconfigured retry policy can turn one slow service into a cluster-wide amplification event.

The industry response to the resource cost is the **sidecar-less** or **ambient** model: run a shared per-node component handling transport-level concerns such as mutual TLS and L4 routing, and insert a full L7 proxy only for the workloads that need L7 features. This trades some isolation for a substantial reduction in footprint.

The honest recommendation: a mesh earns its cost when you have many services in multiple languages and genuinely need uniform mutual TLS, fine-grained authorisation, and per-call observability. With a handful of services, or a single language where a library will do, it is usually more machinery than the problem requires.

**Examples**

```text
Where the logic lives -- three answers

 1. IN THE APPLICATION (library)
    [ service A + retry/LB/mTLS library ] ---> [ service B + same library ]
    + no extra hop     - per-language, redeploy to change policy

 2. SIDECAR MESH
    pod A                              pod B
    +-------------------------+        +-------------------------+
    | app  ---> sidecar proxy |=mTLS=> | sidecar proxy ---> app  |
    +-------------------------+        +-------------------------+
         ^ iptables/eBPF redirect           ^ policy applied here too
    + language agnostic, central policy   - 2 proxies per hop, RAM per pod

 3. AMBIENT / SIDECAR-LESS
    node 1                             node 2
    +------------------------+         +------------------------+
    | app A -> node proxy    |==mTLS=> | node proxy -> app B    |
    +------------------------+         +------------------------+
    + one proxy per NODE, not per pod  - weaker per-pod isolation

 Control plane vs data plane in a mesh:

   +---------------------------------------------+
   |  CONTROL PLANE: identity + CA, policy,      |
   |  service discovery, config distribution     |
   +---------------------------------------------+
        | xDS config pushed to every proxy
        v           v           v
     [ proxy ]   [ proxy ]   [ proxy ]   <- DATA PLANE: carries the traffic
   The control plane never touches a request.
```

```python
# The sidecar tax: every hop through a proxy adds latency and consumes memory.
SIDECAR_P50_MS, SIDECAR_P99_MS = 0.5, 2.5      # per traversal, one direction
SIDECAR_MEM_MB, SIDECAR_CPU_MC = 50, 100       # per pod

def call_chain(hops, backend_ms):
    """A request crossing `hops` services passes 2 proxies per hop (out and in)."""
    traversals = hops * 2
    return (backend_ms + traversals * SIDECAR_P50_MS,
            backend_ms + traversals * SIDECAR_P99_MS,
            traversals)

print(f"{'hops':>5s} {'proxies':>8s} {'backend':>9s} {'p50':>9s} {'p99':>9s} "
      f"{'p99 overhead':>13s}")
for hops in (1, 2, 3, 5, 8):
    p50, p99, tr = call_chain(hops, 20.0)
    print(f"{hops:5d} {tr:8d} {20.0:8.1f}ms {p50:8.1f}ms {p99:8.1f}ms "
          f"{100*(p99-20.0)/20.0:11.1f}%")
#  hops  proxies   backend       p50       p99  p99 overhead
#     1        2     20.0ms     21.0ms     25.0ms        25.0%
#     2        4     20.0ms     22.0ms     30.0ms        50.0%
#     3        6     20.0ms     23.0ms     35.0ms        75.0%
#     5       10     20.0ms     25.0ms     45.0ms       125.0%
#     8       16     20.0ms     28.0ms     60.0ms       200.0%
#
# At 8 hops the proxies TRIPLE the p99. The fix is to shorten the call chain,
# not to tune the proxy.

for pods in (100, 1_000, 5_000):
    print(f"{pods:>5,} pods -> {pods*SIDECAR_MEM_MB/1024:7.1f} GB RAM and "
          f"{pods*SIDECAR_CPU_MC/1000:6.1f} CPU cores of sidecars, "
          f"before any application code")
#   100 pods ->     4.9 GB RAM and   10.0 CPU cores of sidecars, before any application code
# 1,000 pods ->    48.8 GB RAM and  100.0 CPU cores of sidecars, before any application code
# 5,000 pods ->   244.1 GB RAM and  500.0 CPU cores of sidecars, before any application code

print("\nWhat that cost buys, and what you would otherwise build:")
for f, alt in {
        "mutual TLS between all services":     "per-service certs + rotation in every app",
        "retries, timeouts, circuit breaking": "a resilience library per language",
        "per-call metrics and tracing":        "instrumentation in every codebase",
        "traffic splitting / canary":          "custom routing logic in every client",
        "authorization by workload identity":  "auth checks in every service"}.items():
    print(f"  {f:38s} otherwise: {alt}")

NODE_PROXY_MEM_MB = 200
print("\nAmbient (per-node proxy) instead of per-pod sidecars:")
for pods, nodes in ((1_000, 50), (5_000, 200)):
    side, amb = pods*SIDECAR_MEM_MB/1024, nodes*NODE_PROXY_MEM_MB/1024
    print(f"  {pods:>5,} pods on {nodes:>3} nodes: sidecar {side:6.1f} GB vs "
          f"ambient {amb:5.1f} GB  ({side/amb:.0f}x less)")
#   1,000 pods on  50 nodes: sidecar   48.8 GB vs ambient   9.8 GB  (5x less)
#   5,000 pods on 200 nodes: sidecar  244.1 GB vs ambient  39.1 GB  (6x less)
```

```yaml
# Traffic splitting for a canary release: the capability that justifies a mesh.
# The application code is unchanged and unaware.
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: reviews
spec:
  hosts: ["reviews"]                 # the plain hostname the app already calls
  http:
    - match:                         # internal testers get v2 deterministically
        - headers:
            x-canary: {exact: "true"}
      route:
        - destination: {host: reviews, subset: v2}
    - route:                         # everyone else: 95/5 weighted split
        - destination: {host: reviews, subset: v1}
          weight: 95
        - destination: {host: reviews, subset: v2}
          weight: 5
      retries:
        attempts: 3
        perTryTimeout: 2s
        retryOn: 5xx,reset,connect-failure
      timeout: 10s                   # an OUTER bound: 3 x 2s tries must fit inside
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication           # mutual TLS, enforced without touching any app
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  mtls: {mode: STRICT}
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy          # identity-based, not IP-based, authorisation
metadata:
  name: db-access
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: postgres}
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals: ["cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/api-server"]
      to:
        - operation: {ports: ["5432"]}
# Note what the identity is: a service account, not an address. Pod IPs change
# constantly, so IP-based policy cannot express this at all.
```

```bash
# --- How interception actually works: look at the pod's iptables ---
kubectl exec -it web-7f8c -c istio-proxy -- iptables -t nat -L ISTIO_OUTPUT -n
#  REDIRECT tcp -- anywhere anywhere redir ports 15001
#     ^ all outbound TCP is bent into the sidecar; the app never knows

# What configuration did this proxy actually receive from the control plane?
istioctl proxy-config routes web-7f8c --name 80 -o json | jq '.[].virtualHosts[0]'
istioctl proxy-config clusters web-7f8c | head
istioctl proxy-config endpoints web-7f8c | grep reviews

# Is the config in sync across the fleet? A stale proxy is a classic mesh bug.
istioctl proxy-status
#  NAME          CDS      LDS      EDS      RDS
#  web-7f8c      SYNCED   SYNCED   SYNCED   STALE      <- this pod has old routes

# Verify mTLS is genuinely in use rather than merely configured.
istioctl authn tls-check web-7f8c reviews.prod.svc.cluster.local
#  HOST                          STATUS     SERVER     CLIENT
#  reviews.prod.svc.cluster.local OK        mTLS       mTLS

# Measure the sidecar tax on your own traffic before adopting it widely.
kubectl exec -it loadgen -- \
  fortio load -qps 500 -t 30s -c 16 http://reviews:9080/
# Run it with the sidecar injected and with injection disabled, and compare p50
# and p99. The p99 difference is the number that matters, not the mean.
```

**Key takeaways**

- Cross-service concerns (retries, timeouts, mutual TLS, load balancing, metrics) must live somewhere; a **library** couples them to each language and requires redeploying every service to change policy.
- A **service mesh** moves them into a **proxy beside the application**, intercepting traffic transparently, which makes the behaviour **language-agnostic** and **centrally configurable**.
- The **data plane** is the proxies; the **control plane** distributes config, holds workload identity, and never touches a request.
- **Latency is the main cost**: two proxy traversals per hop, compounding in deep call chains — at eight hops the added tail can exceed the real work.
- **Resources are the second cost**: a sidecar per pod means tens of gigabytes and hundreds of cores at a few thousand pods.
- **Ambient / sidecar-less** designs use one proxy per node for L4 concerns and an L7 proxy only where needed, cutting footprint several-fold.
- Mesh authorisation uses **workload identity, not IP addresses**, which is the only thing that works when pod addresses change constantly.
- A mesh earns its cost with many services in multiple languages; below that, a library is usually the right answer.

### 13.3 Data Center Networking

A data centre network serves a traffic pattern almost opposite to the one classical enterprise designs assumed: most bytes move between machines inside the building rather than to users outside it, and the flows are simultaneously enormous and microsecond-sensitive — this subchapter covers the topology that resulted, how traffic is spread across it, where load balancing belongs, and what it takes to carry storage and memory traffic over Ethernet.

#### Three-Tier vs Leaf-Spine Topology

**Theory**

The classical enterprise topology has three tiers: **access** switches where machines plug in, **aggregation** switches collecting groups of access switches, and a **core** connecting aggregation blocks. It was designed for a world in which most traffic went from a user's machine to somewhere outside the building, so the natural shape was a tree: traffic flows up toward the root and out.

That design has two properties which became fatal as traffic patterns changed.

First, **hop count depends on placement**. Two machines on the same access switch are one hop apart. Two machines under the same aggregation pair are three hops apart. Two machines in different aggregation blocks are five hops apart. If your application's performance depends on communication between components, it now depends on where those components physically landed, which is exactly the coupling that virtualisation and orchestration were supposed to eliminate. A scheduler placing a container cannot reason about a network whose latency varies by placement.

Second, the tree structure has **redundant links that cannot be used**. Ethernet forwarding requires a loop-free topology, and the classical solution was spanning tree, which achieves loop freedom by *disabling* links. Half the uplinks a data centre paid for sat idle waiting for a failure, and worse, a spanning tree reconvergence is a network-wide event measured in seconds.

**Leaf-spine** (a folded Clos network) restructures this. Every **leaf** switch connects to *every* **spine** switch, and leaves never connect to each other. The consequences follow mechanically from that wiring rule:

- **Uniform hop count.** Any leaf reaches any other leaf in exactly two hops through one spine. Within a rack it is one hop; between any two racks it is three switches. There is no "far" rack, so placement stops affecting latency.
- **All links active.** Since forwarding is routed at layer 3 rather than bridged, ECMP uses every spine simultaneously. There is no spanning tree and nothing is disabled.
- **Predictable, incremental scaling.** More servers means more leaves. More bandwidth between racks means more spines. Each is an independent axis.
- **Small failure domains.** A leaf failure affects one rack. A spine failure removes 1/N of the inter-rack capacity and nothing else — with four spines, losing one costs 25% of bandwidth and zero connectivity.

The analogy is the difference between a road network built as a hierarchy of feeder roads onto one motorway and a grid of equal streets. In the hierarchy, your journey time depends on which feeder you start from, and a motorway closure is catastrophic. In the grid, any point reaches any other by a similar route, and one closure diverts traffic without isolating anyone.

The design's cost is **cabling and port count**: every leaf needs a link to every spine, so cabling grows as leaves times spines, and a substantial share of every switch's ports are consumed by fabric links rather than servers. That is the price of non-blocking any-to-any capacity, and it is why fabric designs are often quoted in terms of how many server ports remain after uplinks.

For scale beyond one fabric, the pattern nests: pods of leaf-spine fabrics interconnected by a **super-spine** layer, which is a three-stage Clos, and the same reasoning applies one level up.

**Examples**

```text
THREE-TIER: hop count depends on where you landed

                        [ core ]---[ core ]
                        /     \   /      \
                 [ agg ]     [ agg ]  ... (another block)
                 /     \     /     \
            [acc]  [acc]  [acc]  [acc]
             |||    |||    |||    |||
           servers                          x---x  = link disabled by
                                                    spanning tree
  same access switch  : 1 hop
  same agg block      : 3 hops
  different agg block : 5 hops     <- performance depends on PLACEMENT
  half the uplinks    : idle       <- paid for, not usable

LEAF-SPINE: every leaf to every spine, never leaf to leaf

        [spine-1]   [spine-2]   [spine-3]   [spine-4]
          |  |  \  /  |  |  \  /  |  |  \  /  |  |
          |  |   \/   |  |   \/   |  |   \/   |  |
          |  |   /\   |  |   /\   |  |   /\   |  |
        [leaf-1]   [leaf-2]   [leaf-3]  ...  [leaf-N]
          |||        |||        |||            |||
        servers    servers    servers        servers

  within a rack       : 1 hop
  ANY rack to ANY rack: 3 hops (leaf -> spine -> leaf), always
  all 4 spine links   : active, via ECMP
  lose one spine      : -25% bandwidth, 0 loss of connectivity
```

```python
# Three-tier vs leaf-spine: hop count, path count, and failure domains.
def three_tier(servers_per_access=48, access=100):
    return dict(name="three-tier", servers=servers_per_access * access,
                worst_hops=5,             # access-agg-core-agg-access
                paths_between_racks=2,    # active/standby, or 2 with MLAG
                failure_domain="aggregation pair = many racks")

def leaf_spine(ports_per_leaf=52, uplinks=4, leaves=64, spines=4):
    downlinks = ports_per_leaf - uplinks
    return dict(name="leaf-spine", servers=downlinks * leaves,
                worst_hops=3,             # leaf-spine-leaf, ALWAYS
                paths_between_racks=spines,
                failure_domain="one leaf = one rack")

for t in (three_tier(), leaf_spine()):
    print(f"{t['name']:12s} servers {t['servers']:>6,}  worst-case hops "
          f"{t['worst_hops']}  parallel paths {t['paths_between_racks']}  "
          f"failure domain: {t['failure_domain']}")
# three-tier   servers  4,800  worst-case hops 5  parallel paths 2  failure domain: aggregation pair = many racks
# leaf-spine   servers  3,072  worst-case hops 3  parallel paths 4  failure domain: one leaf = one rack

print("\nThe property that matters most is PREDICTABILITY of hop count:")
print("  three-tier: 1 hop in a rack, 3 within a pod, 5 across pods")
print("  leaf-spine: 1 hop in a rack, 3 otherwise -- for EVERY pair of racks")
print("  -> latency becomes a property of the fabric, not of placement,")
print("     which is what lets a scheduler ignore the network entirely.\n")

def fabric_math(ports_per_leaf, uplinks, leaf_port_gbps, uplink_gbps, leaves):
    downlinks = ports_per_leaf - uplinks
    server_bw = downlinks * leaf_port_gbps       # capacity facing the servers
    uplink_bw = uplinks * uplink_gbps            # capacity facing the fabric
    return dict(servers_per_leaf=downlinks, oversub=server_bw / uplink_bw,
                total_servers=downlinks * leaves,
                bisection=leaves / 2 * uplink_bw)

print(f"{'leaf configuration':34s} {'srv/leaf':>9s} {'oversub':>9s} "
      f"{'total srv':>10s} {'bisection':>12s}")
for label, args in (
        ("48x25G down, 4x100G up",  (52, 4, 25, 100, 32)),
        ("48x25G down, 6x100G up",  (54, 6, 25, 100, 32)),
        ("48x25G down, 12x100G up", (60, 12, 25, 100, 32)),
        ("32x100G down, 8x400G up", (40, 8, 100, 400, 32))):
    m = fabric_math(*args)
    print(f"{label:34s} {m['servers_per_leaf']:9d} {m['oversub']:8.2f}:1 "
          f"{m['total_servers']:10,} {m['bisection']:9,.0f} Gb/s")
# leaf configuration                  srv/leaf   oversub  total srv    bisection
# 48x25G down, 4x100G up                    48     3.00:1      1,536     6,400 Gb/s
# 48x25G down, 6x100G up                    48     2.00:1      1,536     9,600 Gb/s
# 48x25G down, 12x100G up                   48     1.00:1      1,536    19,200 Gb/s
# 32x100G down, 8x400G up                   32     1.00:1      1,024    51,200 Gb/s
#
# Note the trade in the first three rows: identical server count, and the only
# way to reduce oversubscription is to spend leaf ports on uplinks instead of
# servers. Non-blocking (1:1) means HALF the switch faces the fabric.
```

```bash
# Confirming a leaf-spine fabric is behaving as designed.

# 1. Uniform hop count: every remote leaf should be the same distance away.
for leaf in 10.0.1.1 10.0.2.1 10.0.9.1 10.0.31.1; do
  echo -n "$leaf: "; traceroute -n -q1 "$leaf" 2>/dev/null | wc -l
done
#  every value should be identical; a different one means an unintended path

# 2. All spines in use: the route to any remote prefix should list every spine.
vtysh -c 'show ip route 10.244.5.0/24'
#  B>* 10.244.5.0/24 [20/0] via 10.0.255.1, swp49   <- spine-1
#                           via 10.0.255.2, swp50   <- spine-2
#                           via 10.0.255.3, swp51   <- spine-3
#                           via 10.0.255.4, swp52   <- spine-4
#  Fewer next hops than spines = a fabric link or BGP session is down.

# 3. No spanning tree should be doing anything in a routed fabric.
mstpctl showbridge 2>/dev/null || echo "no STP: correct for a routed fabric"

# 4. Even loading across uplinks -- the check that catches ECMP problems.
for p in swp49 swp50 swp51 swp52; do
  printf "%s %s\n" "$p" "$(ethtool -S $p | awk '/tx_bytes:/{print $2}')"
done
#  values should be within a few percent of each other over a sampling interval

# 5. BGP sessions: one per spine, on every leaf. Unnumbered keeps it simple.
vtysh -c 'show bgp summary' | tail -8
#  Neighbor      V  AS  MsgRcvd  MsgSent  Up/Down  State/PfxRcd
#  swp49         4  65100  18442   18401  02:14:52    412
#  swp50         4  65100  18440   18399  02:14:52    412   <- equal prefix counts
```

**Key takeaways**

- Three-tier designs assumed traffic leaves the building, so **hop count depends on placement** (1, 3, or 5 hops) and spanning tree **disables** redundant links.
- **Leaf-spine** (folded Clos) connects every leaf to every spine and no leaf to another leaf.
- The result is **uniform hop count** — one hop inside a rack, three between any two racks — so placement stops affecting latency and schedulers can ignore the network.
- All links are active because forwarding is **routed with ECMP**; there is no spanning tree to disable anything.
- Scaling has two independent axes: **more leaves for servers, more spines for inter-rack bandwidth**.
- **Failure domains shrink**: a leaf outage affects one rack, and losing one of four spines costs 25% of bandwidth and no connectivity.
- The cost is cabling and **ports spent on uplinks instead of servers**; a non-blocking fabric dedicates roughly half of each leaf to the fabric.
- Beyond one fabric the pattern nests with a **super-spine** layer.

> 2. Explain why a leaf-spine fabric does not run spanning tree, and what replaces its loop-prevention role.

Interview-style: *A team reports that two services perform well most days and badly after a redeployment, with no code changes.* (Hint: in which topology does the physical distance between two workloads change when a scheduler moves them, and what does that do to a request that makes many internal calls?)

#### East-West vs North-South Traffic

**Theory**

The terms come from how network diagrams are conventionally drawn, with users at the top and servers at the bottom. **North-south** traffic moves vertically: between the outside world and the data centre, or between a client and a server. **East-west** traffic moves horizontally: between machines inside the data centre.

The reason this distinction organises data centre design is that the ratio between them inverted, and the inversion was caused by how software is built rather than by anything in networking. A monolithic application served a page from one machine, possibly consulting one database: nearly all traffic was north-south. A modern application decomposes the same page view into dozens or hundreds of internal calls — authentication, user profile, recommendations, inventory, feature lookups, model inference, caching, logging, tracing — each crossing the network. The bytes the user receives may be under a megabyte while the internal traffic generated to produce them is several times that.

Three design consequences follow, and each explains something about the rest of this chapter.

**Capacity belongs between racks, not only at the edge.** If most traffic never leaves the building, then the expensive, carefully engineered link is the one between two racks rather than the one to the internet. This is the direct justification for leaf-spine: any-to-any capacity matters more than any-to-edge capacity.

**Latency multiplies.** A single user request that triggers a deep chain of internal calls pays the fabric round trip once per call. At a 200 microsecond fabric round trip, 176 serial calls would be 35 milliseconds of pure network time before any work is done. Parallelism helps, and the tail latency of the slowest call dominates, which is why data centre fabrics are engineered for *predictable low* latency rather than for peak throughput. It is also why the fan-out pattern in the example below is where architects look first when a service is slow.

**The perimeter stops being where security happens.** A traditional firewall sits at the north-south boundary and inspects everything entering. If 80% of bytes never cross that boundary, then 80% of traffic is uninspected, and an attacker who reaches any internal workload moves laterally without passing a single control. This is the entire motivation for **microsegmentation** and **zero trust** inside the data centre: policy must be enforced between workloads, which is why it ends up in the virtual switch, in eBPF, or in a service mesh rather than in a perimeter appliance. It is also why internal traffic being unencrypted by default became unacceptable, and therefore why mutual TLS everywhere became a goal.

**Examples**


```python
NORTH_SOUTH_KB = 850              # HTML, CSS, JS and images the browser receives

INTERNAL = [                      # (call, number of calls, kB each)
    ("api-gateway -> auth",              2,   4),
    ("api-gateway -> user-profile",      3,  12),
    ("api-gateway -> recommendations",   1, 180),
    ("recommendations -> feature-store", 40,  26),   # fan-out: the real cost
    ("recommendations -> model-server",   4, 340),
    ("api-gateway -> inventory",          6,  18),
    ("inventory -> cache",               24,   3),
    ("inventory -> database",             6,  64),
    ("all services -> logging/metrics",  90,   2),
]
east_west_kb = sum(calls * kb for _, calls, kb in INTERNAL)
calls = sum(c for _, c, _ in INTERNAL)

print(f"{'internal call':34s} {'calls':>6s} {'kB each':>8s} {'total kB':>9s}")
for name, c, kb in INTERNAL:
    print(f"{name:34s} {c:6d} {kb:8d} {c*kb:9d}")
print(f"{'':34s} {calls:6d} {'':8s} {east_west_kb:9d}")
print(f"\nnorth-south (user <-> data centre): {NORTH_SOUTH_KB:7,} kB")
print(f"east-west   (service <-> service) : {east_west_kb:7,} kB in {calls} calls")
print(f"ratio: {east_west_kb/NORTH_SOUTH_KB:.1f} : 1 east-west to north-south")
# north-south (user <-> data centre):     850 kB
# east-west   (service <-> service) :   3,368 kB in 176 calls
# ratio: 4.0 : 1 east-west to north-south

total_kb = NORTH_SOUTH_KB + east_west_kb
print("\nArchitectural consequences, each following directly from that ratio:")
for c in (
    "capacity must be between racks, not just at the edge -> leaf-spine",
    "any-to-any matters more than any-to-edge -> uniform hop count",
    f"latency multiplies: {calls} calls x 0.2 ms = {calls*0.2:.0f} ms of pure network",
    f"a perimeter firewall sees only {100*NORTH_SOUTH_KB/total_kb:.0f}% of the bytes, "
    f"so {100*east_west_kb/total_kb:.0f}% is never inspected -> east-west needs its own policy",
    "internal traffic is unencrypted by default -> the case for a service mesh",
):
    print(f"  - {c}")
#   - capacity must be between racks, not just at the edge -> leaf-spine
#   - any-to-any matters more than any-to-edge -> uniform hop count
#   - latency multiplies: 176 calls x 0.2 ms = 35 ms of pure network
#   - a perimeter firewall sees only 20% of the bytes, so 80% is never inspected -> east-west needs its own policy
#   - internal traffic is unencrypted by default -> the case for a service mesh

print("\nThe latency multiplication, made explicit:")
for rtt_us in (100, 200, 500, 2000):
    print(f"  fabric RTT {rtt_us:5d} us -> {calls} serial calls cost "
          f"{calls*rtt_us/1000:7.1f} ms; with 8-way parallelism "
          f"{calls*rtt_us/1000/8:6.1f} ms")
#   fabric RTT   100 us -> 176 serial calls cost    17.6 ms; with 8-way parallelism    2.2 ms
#   fabric RTT   200 us -> 176 serial calls cost    35.2 ms; with 8-way parallelism    4.4 ms
#   fabric RTT   500 us -> 176 serial calls cost    88.0 ms; with 8-way parallelism   11.0 ms
#   fabric RTT  2000 us -> 176 serial calls cost   352.0 ms; with 8-way parallelism   44.0 ms
#
# A 2 ms fabric would add a third of a second to one page view. This is why data
# centre networks optimise for predictable LOW latency while wide-area links
# optimise for cost per bit.
```

**Key takeaways**

- **North-south** is client-to-data-centre traffic; **east-west** is machine-to-machine inside it.
- Microservice decomposition inverted the ratio: one page view can generate several times more internal bytes than it delivers to the user, across hundreds of internal calls.
- Therefore **capacity belongs between racks**, which is the direct justification for leaf-spine fabrics.
- **Latency multiplies by the call count**, so fabrics are engineered for predictable low latency rather than peak throughput, and fan-out patterns are where slowness usually originates.
- A perimeter firewall inspects only the north-south fraction, leaving the **majority of traffic uninspected** — the motivation for microsegmentation and zero trust.
- Because internal traffic dominates and is plaintext by default, **encrypting east-west traffic** becomes a first-order concern rather than an optional hardening step.
- Measure the ratio in your own environment; the fan-out is usually larger than anyone expects.

#### ECMP and Load Distribution

**Theory**

A leaf-spine fabric offers several equal-cost paths between any two racks, and **ECMP** (equal-cost multi-path) is how they get used. The mechanism is simple: when the routing table holds several next hops of equal cost, the switch computes a **hash over the packet's flow identifiers** — typically source and destination IP, protocol, and source and destination ports — and uses it to select one.

Hashing rather than round-robin is a deliberate choice, and the reason is **packet ordering**. Every packet of a given flow hashes identically, so all packets of a flow take the same path and arrive in order. Round-robin across paths of slightly different latency would reorder packets, which classic TCP interprets as loss, triggering spurious retransmissions and window reductions. ECMP therefore keeps flows intact by construction.

That design choice creates the mechanism's central limitation, and it is worth stating exactly: **ECMP balances flows, not bytes.** The hash is uniform over flow identifiers, which guarantees an even spread of *flow count* and says nothing about an even spread of *traffic volume*. Two distinct failure modes follow.

**Too few flows.** If only four large flows cross a four-path fabric, the hash assigns each independently, so collisions are likely — this is the birthday problem. The chance that four flows land on four distinct paths is only about 9%. On average two share a path while another sits idle, meaning one link carries twice its share while capacity goes unused.

**Unequal flow sizes.** Data centre traffic is famously bimodal: a very large number of small, short "mice" flows and a small number of enormous long-lived "elephant" flows, with the elephants carrying most of the bytes. Balancing flow count perfectly is nearly irrelevant if one elephant is a thousand times larger than a mouse. One badly placed elephant congests a link while its neighbours idle.

The mitigations differ in where they intervene:

| Mitigation | Mechanism | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **More hash entropy** | include L4 ports; hash the inner flow into the VXLAN outer source port | helps only when flows are numerous |
| **Flowlet switching** | re-hash at natural burst boundaries (gaps within a flow) | needs hardware support; small reordering risk |
| **Per-packet spraying** | spread every packet independently | near-perfect balance, but reorders — needs a tolerant transport |
| **Adaptive / dynamic load balancing** | choose the least-loaded path using local queue occupancy | local view only; can oscillate |
| **Application-level splitting** | open many connections instead of one | requires application change |
| **Central scheduling** | a controller places large flows explicitly | requires detecting elephants and a controller |

Two practical notes. First, **the hash must be consistent along the path but ideally different at each hop**, or all switches make correlated decisions and a collision at one hop repeats at the next; vendors use a per-device seed for this reason. Second, **ECMP interacts with the overlay**: because the underlay sees only outer headers, all overlay traffic between two tunnel endpoints looks like one flow unless the encapsulator injects entropy — which is precisely why VXLAN derives the outer UDP source port from a hash of the inner flow.

**Examples**

```text
Why hashing, and what hashing costs

  ROUND ROBIN                          HASH ON THE FLOW
   pkt1 -> spine-1                      all packets of flow A -> spine-2
   pkt2 -> spine-2                      all packets of flow B -> spine-4
   pkt3 -> spine-3                      ...
   pkt4 -> spine-4
   perfect BYTE balance                 perfect FLOW-COUNT balance
   but REORDERING -> TCP sees loss      order preserved per flow
                                        but byte balance is left to chance

 The elephant problem, drawn

   4 spines, 4 elephant flows, hash assigns each independently:

    spine-1 [####################]  2 elephants  -> 200% of its share
    spine-2 [          ]             0 elephants -> idle
    spine-3 [##########]             1 elephant
    spine-4 [##########]             1 elephant

   Probability of a perfect 1-1-1-1 spread: ~9%
   The fabric has ample total capacity and one link is congested anyway.
```

```python
# ECMP spreads FLOWS, not BYTES. That distinction is the whole problem.
import hashlib, statistics

def ecmp(five_tuple, n_paths):
    h = hashlib.md5(str(five_tuple).encode()).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(h[:4], "big") % n_paths      # per-flow, deterministic

def path_loads(flows, n_paths):
    load = [0.0] * n_paths
    for ft, bytes_ in flows:
        load[ecmp(ft, n_paths)] += bytes_
    return load

# Case 1: many flows of equal size. A hash handles this very well.
N = 4
mice = [((f"10.0.0.{i%250}", "10.0.1.5", 6, 30000 + i, 443), 50_000)
        for i in range(2000)]
load = path_loads(mice, N)
print("2000 equal-size flows over 4 paths: " +
      " ".join(f"{l/sum(load):6.1%}" for l in load) +
      f"   hot link {max(load)/(sum(load)/N):.2f}x ideal")
# 2000 equal-size flows over 4 paths:  26.2%  24.3%  23.7%  25.8%   hot link 1.05x ideal

# Case 2: few LARGE flows. Now what matters is how many share one path, because
# each flow is a link's worth of traffic. A single example proves nothing, so
# sample many placements.
def max_flows_per_path(n_flows, n_paths, trials=5000):
    maxes = []
    for t in range(trials):
        counts = [0] * n_paths
        for i in range(n_flows):
            counts[ecmp((f"10.{t//250}.{t%250}.{i}", "10.0.1.5", 6,
                         40000 + i, 443), n_paths)] += 1
        maxes.append(max(counts))
    return maxes

print("\nFew large flows: how many share the BUSIEST path (5000 placements)")
print(f"{'flows':>6s} {'paths':>6s} {'ideal':>6s} {'mean max':>9s} {'p95 max':>8s} "
      f"{'perfect':>8s}")
for n_el, paths in ((4, 4), (8, 4), (4, 8), (8, 8), (16, 8), (32, 8)):
    m = sorted(max_flows_per_path(n_el, paths))
    perfect = sum(1 for x in m if x <= -(-n_el // paths)) / len(m)
    print(f"{n_el:6d} {paths:6d} {n_el/paths:6.1f} {statistics.mean(m):9.2f} "
          f"{m[int(0.95*len(m))]:8d} {perfect:8.1%}")
#  flows  paths  ideal  mean max  p95 max  perfect
#      4      4    1.0      2.11        3     9.7%
#      8      4    2.0      3.52        5     4.2%
#      4      8    0.5      1.63        3    41.9%
#      8      8    1.0      2.59        4     0.2%
#     16      8    2.0      4.19        6     0.0%
#     32      8    4.0      7.04        9     0.0%
#
# Read the first row: 4 flows over 4 paths SHOULD put 1 on each. On average 2
# share one path while another idles, and only ~10% of placements are perfect.
# Note also that the RATIO of mean-max to ideal improves as flows per path rises:
# ECMP works well precisely when there are many flows per path.

def p_all_distinct(flows, paths):
    p = 1.0
    for i in range(flows):
        p *= (paths - i) / paths
        if p <= 0:
            return 0.0
    return p

print("\nThe combinatorics behind it (the birthday problem):")
print("  probability that 4 large flows land on 4 distinct paths")
for paths in (4, 8, 16, 32):
    print(f"    over {paths:2d} paths: {p_all_distinct(4, paths):6.1%}")
#     over  4 paths:   9.4%
#     over  8 paths:  41.0%
#     over 16 paths:  66.7%
#     over 32 paths:  82.3%
# The simulation's 41.9% for 4 flows over 8 paths matches this 41.0% -- the same
# quantity computed two ways.

print("\nMitigations, and what each actually changes:")
for m, note in [
    ("more hash entropy (L4 ports, VXLAN sport)", "helps only when flows are numerous"),
    ("flowlet / adaptive load balancing", "re-hash at burst boundaries, not per flow"),
    ("per-packet spraying", "perfect balance, but reorders: needs a tolerant transport"),
    ("split elephants in the application", "many connections instead of one"),
    ("central scheduling of large flows", "a controller places them explicitly"),
]:
    print(f"  {m:42s} {note}")
```

```bash
# --- Is ECMP installed, and across how many next hops? ---
ip route show 10.244.5.0/24
#  10.244.5.0/24 proto bgp metric 20
#      nexthop via 10.0.255.1 dev swp49 weight 1
#      nexthop via 10.0.255.2 dev swp50 weight 1
#      nexthop via 10.0.255.3 dev swp51 weight 1
#      nexthop via 10.0.255.4 dev swp52 weight 1

# Kernel ECMP must be told to hash on L4 ports, or it uses L3 only.
sysctl net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy
#  0 = L3 only (src/dst IP)   <- poor entropy: all flows between two hosts collide
#  1 = L3 + L4 (adds ports)   <- what you want
sysctl -w net.ipv4.fib_multipath_hash_policy=1

# --- Which path will a SPECIFIC flow take? Ask, do not guess. ---
ip route get 10.244.5.10 from 10.244.3.2 ipproto tcp sport 43210 dport 443
#  10.244.5.10 from 10.244.3.2 via 10.0.255.3 dev swp51
#     ^ change sport and the answer changes: that is the hash at work

# --- Detect imbalance: compare uplink counters over an interval ---
for p in swp49 swp50 swp51 swp52; do
  a=$(cat /sys/class/net/$p/statistics/tx_bytes); sleep 10
  b=$(cat /sys/class/net/$p/statistics/tx_bytes)
  echo "$p $(( (b-a)*8/10/1000000 )) Mb/s"
done
#  swp49 8420 Mb/s
#  swp50  310 Mb/s     <- a 27x spread across supposedly equal paths
#  swp51 9110 Mb/s        means elephant flows, not a broken fabric
#  swp52  280 Mb/s

# --- Find the elephants responsible ---
ss -tin | awk '/bytes_sent/{print}' | sort -t: -k2 -rn | head
conntrack -L -o extended 2>/dev/null | head

# --- Mitigations as configuration ---
# Give the overlay entropy (this is usually already the default, so verify).
ip -d link show vxlan100 | grep -o 'srcport [0-9 ]*'
#  srcport 0 0     <- means "hash the inner flow", which is what you want
```

**Key takeaways**

- **ECMP** selects among equal-cost next hops by **hashing the flow's identifiers**, which keeps every packet of a flow on one path and preserves ordering.
- Order preservation is the reason for hashing rather than round-robin: reordering looks like loss to classic TCP.
- The consequence is that **ECMP balances flow count, not bytes**. Uniformity over flows guarantees nothing about traffic volume.
- **Too few flows** causes collisions by the birthday problem: four flows over four paths spread perfectly only about 9% of the time.
- **Unequal flow sizes** break it further, because data centre traffic is bimodal and a few elephants carry most of the bytes.
- ECMP works well when there are **many flows per path**; imbalance shrinks as that ratio rises.
- Mitigations include more hash entropy, **flowlet** switching, per-packet spraying (needs a reorder-tolerant transport), application-level splitting, and central placement of large flows.
- Overlays need the encapsulator to inject entropy — VXLAN hashes the inner flow into the **outer UDP source port** — or the underlay sees one flow per endpoint pair.
- A large spread across supposedly equal uplinks usually means elephant flows, not a broken fabric.

#### Load Balancing: L4 vs L7

**Theory**

A load balancer distributes requests across a pool of backends, and the decisive design question is **how much of the request it must understand** in order to decide. That single question determines its cost, its capabilities, and where it belongs.

An **L4 load balancer** works with transport-layer information only: addresses, protocol, and ports. It picks a backend by hashing the connection's 5-tuple and then forwards packets, never examining the payload. It is very fast, because the per-packet work is a hash and a rewrite, and it can run at tens of gigabits per core or entirely in switch hardware. It also passes TLS through untouched, which means it needs no certificates and cannot see plaintext.

An **L7 load balancer** terminates the connection, parses the application protocol, and decides based on the content: URL path, HTTP method, headers, cookies. This enables things L4 cannot express at all — route `/api/v2` to a different pool than `/api`, send requests with a canary header to a new version, retry a failed request against another backend, rewrite paths, compress responses, cache. The costs are equally structural: it must terminate TLS (so it holds the certificates and sees plaintext), it maintains two connections per request instead of forwarding one flow, and per-request cost rises from microseconds to hundreds of microseconds.

| | **L4** | **L7** |
|---|---|---|
| Decision input | 5-tuple | path, headers, cookies, method, body |
| TLS | passes through | must terminate |
| Connections | one flow forwarded | two, one per side |
| Throughput per core | tens of Gb/s | roughly 1-2 Gb/s |
| Retry a failed request | impossible | natural |
| Health checking | TCP probe | HTTP status codes |
| Session affinity | by 5-tuple hash | by cookie or header |

There is a subtlety inside L4 that matters more than the L4/L7 distinction in practice: **how the backend is chosen**. The naive approach takes the hash modulo the pool size, and it has a severe flaw — changing the pool size changes almost every mapping. Adding one backend to a pool of four remaps about 80% of existing connections, and each remapped connection arrives at a backend with no state for it and is reset. Scaling the pool would therefore break most live connections.

**Consistent hashing** fixes this by mapping both backends and flows onto a ring, so adding a backend only steals the flows in its own arc. Adding a fifth backend to four moves about 20% of flows, which is the theoretical minimum. This is why consistent hashing appears in every serious L4 load balancer, and the same reasoning applies to cache sharding and partitioned databases.

Finally, the topology question: **where does the return traffic go?** Three models, and the differences are operationally significant:

- **Proxy mode**: the balancer sits in both directions. Simple and universal, and it must handle the full bidirectional bandwidth, hiding the client address unless a forwarding header is added.
- **DSR** (direct server return): requests go through the balancer, responses go straight from the backend to the client. Since responses are usually far larger than requests, this removes most of the load from the balancer, at the cost of trickier configuration.
- **Anycast with ECMP**: many balancer instances advertise the same address and the network spreads traffic across them. This is how large-scale front ends are built, and it works because consistent hashing makes every instance reach the same decision independently.

The modern pattern combines layers: an L4 stage at the edge for volume and denial-of-service absorption, then an L7 stage for routing intelligence, and increasingly an eBPF-based L4 stage that runs on every node rather than as a separate tier.

**Examples**

```text
Same request, two levels of understanding

 L4: sees only this
   +-----------------------------+
   | src 203.0.113.7:51234       |
   | dst 198.51.100.1:443        |  -> hash -> backend 3
   | proto TCP                   |     cannot know what is being asked for
   +-----------------------------+

 L7: terminates, then sees this
   +-----------------------------------------------+
   | GET /api/v2/orders?id=42 HTTP/2               |
   | host: shop.example.com                        |  -> route by PATH
   | cookie: session=abc123                        |  -> affinity by COOKIE
   | x-canary: true                                |  -> send to canary pool
   +-----------------------------------------------+

 Return path models:

  PROXY                    DSR                      ANYCAST + ECMP
  client                   client                   client
    |  ^                     |  ^                     |
    v  |                     v   \                     v
  [ LB ]                  [ LB ]  \              [ LB1 ][ LB2 ][ LB3 ]
    |  ^                     |     \                (same VIP advertised)
    v  |                     v      \                    |
  backend                  backend --+               backends
  both directions          request in,               network spreads by ECMP;
  through the LB           response direct           consistent hashing makes
  (bandwidth x2)           (LB carries ~10%)         every LB agree
```

```python
# L4 vs L7: what each can decide, and what it costs to decide it.
import hashlib, bisect

def l4_pick(five_tuple, backends):
    """Modulo hashing: simple, and it remaps almost everything when the pool changes."""
    h = int(hashlib.md5(str(five_tuple).encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
    return backends[h % len(backends)]

class ConsistentHash:
    """Backends and flows both land on a ring, so a new backend steals only its arc."""
    def __init__(self, backends, vnodes=160):
        self.ring, self.vnodes = [], vnodes
        for b in backends:
            self._add(b)
        self.ring.sort()

    def _add(self, b):
        for v in range(self.vnodes):          # virtual nodes even out the arcs
            self.ring.append(
                (int(hashlib.md5(f"{b}#{v}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16), b))

    def add(self, b):
        self._add(b); self.ring.sort()

    def pick(self, key):
        h = int(hashlib.md5(str(key).encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
        i = bisect.bisect([r[0] for r in self.ring], h) % len(self.ring)
        return self.ring[i][1]

BACKENDS = [f"srv{i}" for i in range(4)]
keys = [(f"10.0.0.{i%250}", "vip", 6, 30000 + i, 443) for i in range(10_000)]

plain_before = [l4_pick(k, BACKENDS) for k in keys]
plain_after = [l4_pick(k, BACKENDS + ["srv4"]) for k in keys]
moved_plain = sum(1 for a, b in zip(plain_before, plain_after) if a != b)

ch = ConsistentHash(BACKENDS)
ch_before = [ch.pick(k) for k in keys]
ch.add("srv4")
moved_ch = sum(1 for a, b in zip(ch_before, [ch.pick(k) for k in keys]) if a != b)

print("Adding a 5th backend to a pool of 4 -- how many flows are remapped?")
print(f"  modulo hashing    : {moved_plain:6,} of {len(keys):,} "
      f"({moved_plain/len(keys):6.1%}) -> each remapped connection is RESET")
print(f"  consistent hashing: {moved_ch:6,} of {len(keys):,} "
      f"({moved_ch/len(keys):6.1%}) -> near the ideal 1/5 = 20.0%")
# Adding a 5th backend to a pool of 4 -- how many flows are remapped?
#   modulo hashing    :  7,994 of 10,000 ( 79.9%) -> each remapped connection is RESET
#   consistent hashing:  2,135 of 10,000 ( 21.3%) -> near the ideal 1/5 = 20.0%
#
# This is why every serious L4 balancer uses consistent hashing: without it,
# scaling the pool is an outage.

def l7_pick(request, rules, default="pool-web"):
    """L7 decides on CONTENT, which requires terminating and parsing the request."""
    for r in rules:
        if request["path"].startswith(r["prefix"]) and \
           all(request["headers"].get(k) == v for k, v in r.get("headers", {}).items()):
            return r["pool"]
    return default

RULES = [
    {"prefix": "/api/v2", "pool": "pool-api-v2"},
    {"prefix": "/api",    "pool": "pool-api-v1"},     # order matters: v2 first
    {"prefix": "/static", "pool": "pool-cdn"},
    {"prefix": "/",       "headers": {"x-canary": "true"}, "pool": "pool-canary"},
]
print("\nRouting decisions L4 cannot make at all:")
for req in ({"path": "/api/v2/orders", "headers": {}},
            {"path": "/api/users", "headers": {}},
            {"path": "/static/logo.png", "headers": {}},
            {"path": "/home", "headers": {"x-canary": "true"}},
            {"path": "/home", "headers": {}}):
    print(f"  {req['path']:20s} headers={str(req['headers']):28s} -> "
          f"{l7_pick(req, RULES)}")
#   /api/v2/orders       headers={}                           -> pool-api-v2
#   /api/users           headers={}                           -> pool-api-v1
#   /static/logo.png     headers={}                           -> pool-cdn
#   /home                headers={'x-canary': 'true'}         -> pool-canary
#   /home                headers={}                           -> pool-web

print("\nCost comparison:")
print(f"  {'aspect':20s} {'L4':28s} L7")
for a, l4, l7 in [
    ("decision input", "5-tuple only", "path, headers, cookies, method"),
    ("TLS", "passes through untouched", "must terminate (or re-encrypt)"),
    ("connection model", "one flow, forwarded", "two connections, one per side"),
    ("per-request cost", "~microseconds", "~hundreds of microseconds"),
    ("throughput per core", "tens of Gb/s", "1-2 Gb/s"),
    ("retries / rewrite", "impossible", "natural"),
    ("health checking", "TCP-level probe", "HTTP status codes"),
]:
    print(f"  {a:20s} {l4:28s} {l7}")
```

```bash
ipvsadm -A -t 198.51.100.1:443 -s sh          # sh = source hashing
ipvsadm -a -t 198.51.100.1:443 -r 10.0.1.11:443 -g   # -g = DSR (gatewaying)
ipvsadm -a -t 198.51.100.1:443 -r 10.0.1.12:443 -g

#  ID  Frontend             Service Type  Backend
#  12  10.96.0.10:53        ClusterIP     10.244.1.4:53, 10.244.2.7:53
cilium bpf lb list        # the actual maps the datapath consults

# --- L7 with Envoy/nginx: routing on content ---
cat <<'CONF'
upstream pool_api_v2 { server 10.0.2.11:8080; server 10.0.2.12:8080; }
upstream pool_api_v1 { server 10.0.1.11:8080; server 10.0.1.12:8080; }
upstream pool_canary { server 10.0.3.11:8080; }

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/shop.crt;   # L7 MUST hold the certificate
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/shop.key;

  location /api/v2 { proxy_pass http://pool_api_v2; }   # longest prefix first
  location /api    { proxy_pass http://pool_api_v1; }
  location / {
    if ($http_x_canary = "true") { proxy_pass http://pool_canary; }
    proxy_pass http://pool_api_v1;
    proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_503;         # RETRY: an L7-only ability
  }
}
CONF

# --- Verify the difference in what each can see ---
# L4: the balancer never sees the path, so all of these hash identically.
for p in /api/v2/x /api/y /static/z; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{remote_ip}\n" "https://vip$p"
done

# --- Anycast front end: the same VIP from many instances ---
vtysh -c 'show bgp ipv4 unicast 198.51.100.1/32'
#  multiple paths, one per LB instance -> the network spreads clients by ECMP,
#  and consistent hashing makes every instance pick the same backend
```

**Key takeaways**

- The design question is **how much of the request must be understood**: L4 uses the 5-tuple, L7 parses the application protocol.
- **L4** is fast (tens of Gb/s per core), passes TLS through untouched, and cannot route on content or retry a request.
- **L7** routes on path, headers, and cookies, can retry, rewrite, and cache, and must terminate TLS, hold certificates, and maintain two connections per request.
- Inside L4, **consistent hashing versus modulo hashing** matters more than the L4/L7 choice: modulo remaps about 80% of flows when a backend is added, consistent hashing about 20%, the theoretical minimum.
- **Virtual nodes** on the hash ring are what make the arcs even.
- **Return-path topology** matters: proxy mode carries both directions, **DSR** offloads the large response path, and **anycast with ECMP** scales the front end horizontally.
- The modern pattern layers them: L4 at the edge for volume and attack absorption, L7 for routing intelligence, with eBPF L4 increasingly on every node.
